generated_text: Honestly, she’s been a little angel this afternoon, hasn't she? A proper cuddle bug. Though the wind outside is  fierce  – glad we decided against that walk to the park.      Absolutely. And she slept for a good two hours after her feed, which is a miracle. You've got the magic touch, honestly. It’s amazing how quickly things settle into…well, not  routine  exactly, but a sort of rhythm. Remember how stressed we both were about the first few weeks with our own kids?      Stressed is an understatement! I was convinced I was doing everything wrong. Honestly, I spent half my time googling 'is baby turning blue?' every time Leo’s face changed colour. It's funny looking back now, isn’t it?      Terribly funny. I was the same with Chloe. Paranoia central! Speaking of kids, how is Leo doing with his GCSEs? He must be right in the thick of it now.      He’s… coping. He's not thrilled, naturally. History is his nemesis. He says it’s all just dates and dead people. I keep trying to explain the importance of understanding the past but…teenage boys. You know? He’s got mocks next week, and he's already predicting disaster.      Oh, that age. It's exhausting. Chloe’s applying for universities now, which is a whole new level of anxiety. She’s set her heart on Bristol, but the competition is insane. Have you and Mark started thinking about what you’re doing for his birthday?      Not properly. I thought maybe a weekend away? Somewhere quiet? He's been working so hard lately, he deserves a break. Though getting childcare for Leo is proving tricky. He’s got that football tournament, and everything seems to be scheduled simultaneously these days.      I know the feeling. Everything feels like a logistical nightmare. I was thinking about Mum and Dad. They’ve been asking when we’re going to visit. It feels like ages.      It has. I feel terrible, to be honest. We said we’d try and get down to Birmingham next month, but with work… It's just relentless at the moment. I’ve picked up a few new proofreading clients, which is good, but it means evenings and weekends are completely gone.      Honestly, you always were a workaholic. You need to learn to say no! I'm not working at the moment, which is bliss, but I already feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit.

...Honestly, the sheer  volume  of paperwork just to get a temporary residency permit for Berlin was ridiculous. I mean, I’m British, I used to just…  be  in Europe, yeah? Now it's like applying for a visa to another planet.      Tell me about it. My supervisor practically had to write a letter guaranteeing my return to Cambridge, stamped with blood oaths and everything, just for a conference in Amsterdam. A  conference . It felt… performative, you know? Like we were deliberately being made to jump through hoops.      Performative is the perfect word. It’s not about actual security checks, it's about… well, I don't know, making a point? It utterly killed the spontaneity, didn’t it? Remember when we’d just decide on a Friday night, “Right, road trip to Paris!”? Now, a ‘right, road trip to Paris’ is a six-month planning project.      God, those were the days. I still feel a pang of guilt whenever I suggest a little weekend jaunt. I’m convinced Customs will just look at me and say, “Oh, back for another extended stay are we, sneaking in research data?” It’s just… different. Did you manage to get any decent time exploring Berlin beyond the permit office, then?      Eventually! Once I’d navigated the Kafkaesque bureaucracy. It was brilliant, though, properly brilliant. I spent a week cycling around, just getting lost in different  kiez . Prenzlauer Berg was exactly how everyone describes it – all independent bookshops and overpriced avocado toast. But Kreuzberg was… raw. Much more my vibe.      Kreuzberg, yeah. That’s the one Sarah was rabbiting on about. She was doing some art installation over there last summer. Said it was completely anarchic. Did you try to use your German?      Tried. Failed spectacularly, mostly. I bluffed my way through ordering beers, which is a vital skill, obviously. But any genuine conversation quickly revealed the extent of my GCSE German. Everyone was too polite to truly call me out on it, though. They just switched to English pretty quickly. I felt awful. It’s a bit embarrassing, isn’t it? Being British and assuming everyone speaks English perfectly.      It is. We’re terrible for that. It's just ingrained, I think. My attempt at Dutch in Amsterdam was equally pathetic. I tried to ask for the bill, and I think I accidentally asked the waiter if he was married to a potato.      No!

Miss, Miss! Look! I found fiver under the sofa! Can we get… can we get a whole chocolate cake with this? A  really  big one? With sprinkles?      Oh, wow, Lily! That  is  a good find. Under the sofa, eh? Monopoly money tends to end up there too, doesn’t it? A whole chocolate cake... that might be a little ambitious, even for a fiver, sweetie. Remember how much the little ones cost at the village fair?      It’s not fair! I  always  land on Mayfair! Dad always charges me, like, a million pounds! And then I have to sell everything!      It's part of the game, Leo. That's how Monopoly works. You have to manage your money. And sometimes, unfortunately, you  do  have to sell your hotels. It teaches you… economic strategy! Though I agree, Dad  does  enjoy bankrupting you.      But what about the cake? Please? Even a small one? Maybe a really good brownie? They do those at Mrs. Higgins’ bakery, with the caramel swirl.      A brownie  is  a good idea. A caramel swirl brownie sounds excellent. We could definitely get a couple of those with a fiver. Although, we did have sticky toffee pudding last night, didn't we? It wouldn't be very balanced, would it? All this sugar…      Balanced? What's balanced? Is that like having equal hotels and houses? Because that never happens to me!      No, darling. Balanced means having a bit of everything. You need fruit and vegetables, and not  just  sweets. It’s like in Monopoly – you need more than just Park Lane and Mayfair to win. You need a variety of properties, and you need to save some money for emergencies.      So… like, having some Old Kent Road  and  some Mayfair? Even though Old Kent Road is rubbish?      Well, Old Kent Road isn’t  rubbish . It’s a starting point! Everyone starts somewhere. And if you get enough of the cheaper properties, you can still build houses and collect rent. It's all about playing the game strategically. This fiver… it’s a bit like starting with that Old Kent Road. It's not a lot, but we can use it wisely.      Can we at least  try  to get more money in Monopoly? Dad always makes me pay rent even when I don't have  any  money!      We can definitely discuss house rules. Perhaps we can agree on a maximum rent charge, or maybe a "get out of jail free" card for anyone who lands there three times in a row?

Honestly, this signal is shocking. You'd think being this close to a main road we'd get  something  decent. Just static, mostly.      Yeah, it's always been patchy round here. Remember Dad complaining about it every time he drove us up to visit Auntie Brenda? He’d always threaten to install a bigger aerial. Never did, though.      He threatened a lot of things he never did. Like learning to use the video recorder. Still had tapes piled up from the 90s when we cleared out the loft. Anyway… this whole weekend is just… a bit much, isn't it?      A bit much? You mean the Great Northern Family Gathering of Doom? It's annual, Liv. We knew it was coming.      I  know  it’s annual. It doesn't make it any less overwhelming. Twenty-odd relatives crammed into a farmhouse that hasn’t been updated since… well, since Auntie Brenda moved in. And then the interrogation. “So, Liv, still just… playing with computers?”      Oh, here we go. You and the ‘playing with computers’ comment. She just doesn’t get what corpus linguistics  is , does she?      No, she doesn't. She thinks it's something to do with corpses. Honestly. And when I try to explain, her eyes glaze over and she starts talking about young Master Thomas and his amazing football skills. It's exhausting. You, at least, understand I have an actual job.      Well, I did a postgraduate degree in engineering. I’m used to things that sound complicated. Plus, you’ve explained it a few times. It's… analyzing language patterns, right? Like, finding out how language is actually  used ?      Pretty much. It's fascinating, actually. But try explaining that to someone who thinks a computer is just for sending emails and looking at Facebook. And Gran! She'll corner me about finding a 'nice young man' again. As if my career isn't enough to talk about.      Gran’s a lost cause. She’s been trying to marry me off to her neighbour’s granddaughter for the past five years. Though, to be fair, Bethany  is  a very good baker.      Don’t encourage her! Seriously though, I'm dreading the inevitable questions about why I'm not settled down. Everyone else seems to be getting married and having babies.      Don’t compare yourself to them. You're doing brilliantly. You've got a good job, you’re happy, you’re living your life.

You know, Harold, it’s funny. I was down at the allotment this morning, trying to get the runner beans sorted - a right tangle they were – and old Mr. Davies was on about the council. Said they’re thinking of building another estate out towards Weston Longville.      Weston Longville, you say? Good Lord. That’ll be a disaster. More traffic, more noise… it’s bad enough as it is getting to the shops. They never think these things through, do they? Just concrete, concrete, concrete.      Honestly, it’s greedy. They’ve already swallowed up so much farmland. Remember when that field behind the church was all wheat? Lovely sight it was in the summer. Now it's just rows of identical houses.      I do. Used to take young Emily there, picking wildflowers. She’d be furious if she knew what they were planning now. She's proper passionate about the environment, our Emily is. More so than me, I reckon.      She gets that from her mother, I expect. Always one for the birds and the bees, wasn’t she? Still is, I imagine. Though I haven’t seen much of her lately, have you, Arthur? Seems everyone’s so busy these days.      A bit. She rings, of course, but it's never a long chat. Work, mainly. And little Thomas, bless him, keeps her on her toes. She’s doing well, though. Promotion, she mentioned last time. Something to do with project management.      A good girl, Emily. Works hard. It’s a shame she lives so far away now, though. We don't get to spoil Thomas as much as we'd like. Remember when we had the grandchildren every Saturday? The house was full of chaos, but happy chaos.      Chaos is putting it mildly! Little Thomas, he’s a chip off the old block, isn’t he? Always getting into mischief. Reminds me of myself at that age. My mother used to say I was a terror.      You always were a bit of a scamp, Harold. Though a good-hearted one. It's just... everything feels like it’s changing so quickly. Weston Longville, Emily living so far away… even the allotment, it's not what it used to be. Young folks aren't interested in growing their own anymore.      That's true. It’s all convenience food and screens, isn’t it? I worry a bit about what the world’s coming to.

...Honestly, the packaging is the thing stressing me out most now. I’ve got the labels designed, they look  really  good – minimalist, very ‘clean beauty’ - but figuring out what size box to order… it’s a nightmare. Everything feels either too big and wasteful, or too small and I’m terrified things will get damaged in the post.      Oh, I massively sympathise. It's a deceptively difficult part, isn't it? Especially when you’re doing everything yourself. What are you sending out, roughly? Just the one product at a time, or bundles? And what are the approximate dimensions of the jars themselves?      It’s mostly single jars of face cream at the moment, though I'm starting to offer a little ‘discovery’ set with smaller sizes of three different things. The jars are… hmm. Let me grab one. Okay, they’re about 6cm across, and maybe 5cm high. Not huge, but they’re glass, obviously. I don’t want them arriving in smithereens.      Six by five… Right. And the discovery sets, how much bigger are those? And what kind of packaging are  they  in?      The discovery set comes in little plastic pots, about 3cm across each. And there’s a leaflet and a little sample sachet of cleanser in there too. It all goes in a small cardboard box, but it feels… flimsy. I’ve had a few complaints about things shifting around during transit.      Okay. So, for the individual jars, I’d say you need something that allows for at least 2cm of padding all round. Bubble wrap, shredded paper, something like that. So that’s adding 4cm to each dimension at least. You’re looking at a box around 10cm cubed, minimum, just for the one jar.      Ten by ten! Blimey. That  does  sound big. I was hoping to stay a bit smaller, keep postage costs down. People are already moaning about the prices, even though I’m trying to keep everything really competitive.      I know, it’s a tricky balance. But think about the cost of a  broken  jar versus a slightly more expensive box. Also, presentation matters. A perfectly fitted box feels more premium, doesn’t it? Makes the whole experience feel more considered. That’s where Honest Skincare really shines, you’re not just selling cream, you’re selling a brand ethos.      That’s true. You're right about the ethos.

Honestly, Arthur, the state of things. It's just… disheartening, isn't it? Did you see that piece on the flooding up north? Absolutely dreadful. Families displaced, livelihoods ruined. Makes you wonder where it will all end.      Dreadful is putting it mildly, Margaret. I saw it. They’re blaming it on the usual suspects - climate change, lack of investment in flood defences… It’s a bit of everything, I suspect. Though, honestly, it feels like we’re just patching things up as best we can. No real long-term vision.      Exactly! Patching! That’s a perfect word for it. It feels like the government just reacts  after  the disaster, instead of trying to prevent them. It's the same with the NHS, isn’t it? Always in crisis mode. Though, speaking of crises... how are things at school? Still battling the budget cuts?      Don't even get me started. They've announced another round of reductions for next year. They’re talking about merging departments, reducing teaching assistant hours… It’s impacting the children, Margaret. The ones who need the most help are suffering the most. I feel like I'm spending more time filling out forms justifying everything than actually  teaching .      Oh, Arthur, that’s awful. You always put so much into your work. It’s a crying shame. Remember old Mr. Henderson, back in the seventies? He used to say teaching was a vocation, not just a job. Seems a long time ago now, doesn't it? It feels more like a battle these days.      It does. A constant battle. And the paperwork! You wouldn't believe the amount of box-ticking we have to do. It’s utterly soul-destroying. Anyway, enough about my woes. How are  you  coping? Still keeping busy with the garden?      The garden's… alright. It's not the same without George, though. He had such a knack for knowing what needed doing. I wander around it sometimes, and it just feels… empty. I've been trying to keep up with the roses, he always loved those ‘Peace’ roses. But honestly, sometimes I just sit and stare.      I know, Margaret. It's still so recent. You’re bound to feel that way. Don't pressure yourself. It's alright to just  be  for a while. No need to fill every minute.      It’s just… I used to be so busy. Teaching, marking, school plays, the garden with George, running the household… Now it’s just… quiet.

Honestly, this is exactly what I needed. December just…hits differently, doesn't it? The sheer  volume  of wanting to just hibernate. And then the pressure of Christmas looming. It's exhausting before it's even begun.      Tell me about it. The missus has already started on the gift lists. It’s colour-coded, apparently. Strategic gifting, she calls it. I just want a quiet pint and a decent Christmas film. Though, this spud  is  a thing of beauty. You’ve outdone yourself, really.      Strategic gifting! That sounds…intense. I’m trying to convince my family that experiences are the way forward. Concert tickets, a weekend away. Less clutter, more memories, that sort of thing. Though explaining that to my nan is a lost cause. She  needs  to buy everyone a scented candle.      Experiences are good. Though, give me the satisfaction of  making  something any day. I've been tinkering in the workshop, actually, trying to build a proper card table for all the inevitable board games. The old one's on its last legs. It wobbles something fierce.      Oh, that’s fantastic, Rhys! You always make the best things. Last Christmas your bird box was the hit. Did you manage to snag any more of that reclaimed wood you were talking about?      Aye, got a load from that demolition site near Llanelli. Proper stuff, been weathered for decades. Good for character, you know? Still, the cold snapping in makes working in the workshop a bit…brisk. I’ve got a little heater, but it’s barely making a dent.      You think  that’s  cold? Try getting up at five in the morning to go to the factory. It's like walking into a fridge! The heating’s always on the blink. Honestly, you’d think a manufacturing plant could keep itself warm. I'm starting to think about early retirement, just to avoid the winters.      Early retirement? That’s…ambitious! Though, I can see the appeal. My supervisor keeps hinting I should be thinking about ‘post-PhD life’, which basically translates to ‘funding is running out’. It’s a slightly different pressure, but still…the looming unknown is terrifying.      It is, isn't it? Thinking about the rest of your life feels enormous. My aunt recently retired, and she's completely lost without the structure. She’s taken up jam making, which is lovely, but I think she misses the intellectual challenge.

Honestly, your mam’s got a right collection of cutlery, hasn’t she? I swear every time I come ‘ere, there’s a different set on the table. Is this the ‘good’ silver, then?      Nah, definitely not the good silver. The good silver only comes out for Christmas and…well, pretty much Christmas. These are just the everyday fancy ones. She got them on a bit of a whim last year. Said they matched the new tablecloth.      Match the tablecloth? That’s dedication. My nan just uses whatever’s clean. And usually a couple of chipped mugs, if I’m honest.      Your nan’s a practical woman, lad. Nothing wrong with a chipped mug. Reminds me of my own mother. She’d have a drawer full of 'useful' things that no one else would touch. Old buttons, string, bits of foil…you name it.      Aye, my wife was like that. Never threw anything away. Said everything had a purpose. Drove our son mad, it did. He’d trip over piles of newspapers she was ‘saving’ for something.      Sounds familiar! Mum’s got a ‘maybe’ box in the attic. It's full of things she thinks  might  be useful one day. I'm convinced it’s a portal to another dimension.      A portal, eh? Ha! Well, at least it keeps the attic warm. Speaking of warm, this gravy’s lovely. Truly lovely. Your mam’s always been a good cook.      She is, isn’t she? I think she just genuinely enjoys looking after people. She’s always fretting if everyone’s eaten enough.      That’s a mother’s job, isn’t it? Fretting. Regardless of how old we get. My daughter called earlier. Asked if I'd had my lunch. I’m seventy-eight! I can manage a sandwich.      Seventy-eight…Time flies, doesn’t it? Seems like yesterday I was chasing after my own kids with a spoon full of porridge.      It’s nice having everyone together, though, isn't it? It feels like ages since we’ve all been in the same room. How are things with work, Liam? Still battling with that new project?      Oh, you have  no  idea. It’s a disaster, honestly. The client keeps changing their mind, and the deadlines are…ambitious, to say the least. I was up until midnight last night trying to sort out the budget.      Sounds stressful, love. You need to learn to say no sometimes.

Honestly, this day has been… one of  those  days. Old Mr. Henderson decided today was the perfect time to question the entire marketing budget, line by line. As if I don’t have enough on my plate with the skiing trip looming. Skiing! Is it soon? Will I get to wear my sparkly helmet? The one with the unicorn horn? It is soon, darling. About two weeks. And yes, you absolutely will. You'd lose the horn before you even got off the plane if I let you wear it  all  the time though, wouldn't you? Maybe. But it makes me go faster! Like a real unicorn zooming down the mountain. I sincerely doubt a unicorn horn improves your ski speed, love. It looks fabulous, though. Though, speaking of speed, have you been practicing listening to my instructions? No zooming off without telling me, okay? Last year was a bit… stressful. I listened last year! Mostly. “Mostly” isn’t really good enough on a snowy mountain, is it? It’s not like the park back in Milton Keynes. It’s proper slopes, lots of people… But I'm a good skier now! Miss Davies said so. She said I’m ‘showing great promise’. Miss Davies is a very kind lady. And you  are  getting better. But promise me you'll stay close. It's just... work's been completely mental and I really need a relaxing holiday. I need to not be chasing a small, sparkly unicorn down a mountain! Mummy, you always say work is ‘completely mental’. Is it always going to be ‘completely mental’? No, sweetheart. Not always. I'm hoping things will calm down once this Henderson situation is sorted. He just doesn't seem to understand the online campaign is performing well. It's all about data and reach these days, not just pretty pictures in a magazine! I spent hours putting that presentation together. What's a campaign? Is it like a battle? Do you fight people at work? No, no battles! A campaign is… well, it’s trying to tell people about something. Like, we're campaigning for everyone to buy our new widgets. It's not fighting. Though sometimes it  feels  like it. Widgets? What are widgets? Oh, you don’t need to worry about widgets. They’re boring grown-up things. More importantly, are you excited about the hot chocolate after skiing each day?

...Honestly, Mr. Davies is  killing  me with the Shakespeare. Like, I get it, it’s classic literature, but all the ‘thees’ and ‘thous’ just…blur into one massive headache. It feels like learning another language  within  English, you know?      Oh, tell me about it! I'm struggling too. It's not even understanding  what  he's saying, it's just decoding the language itself. Are you doing  Macbeth  as well? Because the witches are creepy, but trying to follow their rhymes while simultaneously figuring out what they mean… it’s a lot.      Yep,  Macbeth . It’s supposed to be all about ambition gone wrong, isn’t it? But all I’m ambitious about right now is finishing the essay on Lady Macbeth's guilt. It’s due Friday! Ugh. What about you? Anything interesting happening in your lessons?      Not really. Food Tech is still the highlight, obviously. We’re doing pasta sauces next week - I’m thinking a proper arrabbiata. Maybe even try to make my own chilli flakes. It's the only thing keeping me going, honestly. Maths is just…numbers. And Mr. Henderson is convinced we’re all geniuses if we can remember the quadratic formula.      Mr. Henderson thinks we’re all training to be rocket scientists. I swear he gets disappointed when anyone asks him to go over it  again . Speaking of things keeping you going… are you still properly smashing it in Spanish?      I think so? It’s the one subject I don't actively dread. Señora Rodriguez says I’ve got a natural ear for it, which is nice. I’m actually thinking… maybe I could take it for GCSE. I was leaning towards Art, but…      GCSE Spanish is a good shout! You’d be brilliant. Think of all the travel opportunities! You could actually  use  it, unlike, well, knowing all the kings and queens of England. Remember when we were little and you used to pretend to be a Spanish princess?      Oh my god, stop it! I was  five . Although, I  did  have a very impressive cardboard crown. Seriously though, I’ve been looking at what jobs people do with languages. It's not just translation, there's like…international business, working with charities, even journalism! What about you? Have you thought any further ahead than escaping Mr Davies?      I’m still really not sure. My mum keeps on about becoming a doctor, which is…a lot of studying.

…and honestly, darling, that ending. Utterly predictable. All that build-up for  that ? I mean, really.      Which one are you on about now, Gran? You've watched, like, three films since lunch.       The Crimson Tide . The one you recommended! Don’t tell me you actually thought that was a clever twist? The captain was obviously going to… well, you know.      Okay, okay, you got me. It wasn’t  Groundbreaking . But it’s a good solid thriller, isn’t it? And Denzel Washington is always good value.      Denzel's alright. Can’t fault the man’s talent. But it just felt…formulaic. Give me something like  Brief Encounter  any day. Now  that  was a film. Real emotion, proper acting. Not just explosions and shouting.      You and your black and white classics! I appreciate them, I do. But sometimes you just need a bit of escapism, you know? After a week of spreadsheets and production schedules, staring into the abyss of whether we’ll actually  meet  the delivery date for the new widgets… a bit of ‘sploding stuff is helpful.      Widgets? What  are  widgets anyway? You keep talking about them. Sounds terribly modern.      They’re… complicated. Let’s just say they’re small, plastic things that make other, bigger things work. I make sure enough of them get  made  and shipped on time. It's surprisingly stressful.      Sounds it. Still, it’s a long way from when I left school and started working at the bakery. Flour, sugar, a bit of jam… much simpler. Though Old Man Hemmings was a terror if you didn't get the icing  just  right.      Bosses are bosses, I guess, no matter the era. I’ve got one who’s obsessed with efficiency metrics. Honestly, I swear he thinks we’re robots.      Sounds dreadful. You need a good film to unwind. Have you seen the new one with Florence Pugh? The historical drama,  The Wonder ? I read a review, apparently it’s very good. Thought you might like it.      I've seen trailers! It looks a bit bleak, doesn’t it? But Florence Pugh is fantastic, so I’ll probably give it a go. Is it on one of those streaming things? I’m officially exhausted from the cinema. It was ages since I went, and the popcorn price nearly gave me a heart attack.      It's on Netflix, I think. And yes, the cinema is a rip-off these days.

Honestly, Mum, this traffic was  awful  getting here. Took me nearly an hour and a half from Hitchin. I swear, the M1 is just one giant car park these days.      Oh, you Southerners and your motorways! Always complaining. Birmingham traffic's no picnic either, you know. Though admittedly, today's been alright. Bit of drizzle, but nothing like that downpour we had last week. Did that flooding near your place ever clear up?      It did, eventually. Thankfully, we’re on a bit of a hill so we avoided the worst of it. Old Mrs. Higgins wasn’t so lucky, though. Basement completely flooded. Said her antique books were ruined. It’s just… everything feels so expensive lately. Repairing things, even just  living .      Tell me about it. Everything's gone up. Even a cup of coffee isn’t cheap anymore! And then there’s the heating… I'm dreading the winter bill. I was reading in the paper about the energy companies making record profits. It’s scandalous, it is.      It really is. It makes you wonder where all the money’s going. Speaking of scandalous, did you catch that case at court yesterday? The one with the property developer?      Oh,  that  one! The one trying to dodge paying his subcontractors? A right charlatan, he was. Tried to act all innocent, but the judge wasn’t having any of it. I've seen a lot come and go through that courtroom, love, and you can usually spot a liar a mile off. He had that shifty look.      I saw a bit of it on the local news. Sounds like he’s in for a long time. It’s good to see someone finally being held accountable, for a change. It’s draining, seeing people taken advantage of all the time, isn’t it? Especially at work. I had a student today trying to argue about his grade… utterly ridiculous.      Students! Always something with them, eh? You're a teacher, you'll know. Still, at least you’re doing something worthwhile. Teaching’s important. More important than building dodgy flats, that’s for sure.      That's kind of you to say, Mum. Honestly, sometimes I question it, though. The paperwork is endless. Anyway, enough about work. How’s Buster? Is he still chasing squirrels up old Mr. Peterson’s apple tree?      You know that dog! Absolutely. Mr. Peterson’s threatening to call the RSPCA, says Buster’s stressing the apples out.

Honestly, this air is… well, it’s not Norwich air, is it? But it’s a welcome change after a day of student essays. My head feels like it’s full of semi-colons and misplaced arguments. You and your students. You take their grammatical sins  personally . It’s endearing, really. Though I suspect it’s also why you need that extra large glass of wine tonight. It’s not just the grammar, it's the… the lack of  effort , you know? One student actually argued that ‘literally’ can mean ‘figuratively’. Literally! I nearly lost it. What was your day like, dealing with rebellious historians? Surprisingly quiet, actually. Mostly marking. Though old Professor Chen cornered me for twenty minutes about the merits of post-structuralism versus Marxist interpretations of the Tang Dynasty. It was… invigorating, in a slightly exhausting way. He really does thrive on debate. Oh, Chen. A force of nature. He’s brilliant, but definitely tests your intellectual stamina. Speaking of testing stamina, have you thought about what we're doing for dinner? I’m flagging a bit. Cooking feels… ambitious. I was thinking we could try that new place, ‘Silk Road Spices’? I walked past it earlier, smelled incredible. Apparently, they do a fantastic Xinjiang lamb dish. Xinjiang! Oh, yes please! That sounds perfect. Though… I really need to grab some proper teabags. I'm down to the final few Earl Greys, and honestly, a day without a proper cuppa is a day wasted. Right. Operation Teabags. We could swing by that little import shop near the university tomorrow? They always have a good selection, though it’s a bit pricey. Good idea. Maybe we should get a few different types. I’ve been meaning to try that oolong you were talking about. The one that smells of peaches? That's the one! It’s lovely. They had some in stock last week, but they go quickly. We might need a backup plan if they're sold out. Perhaps a trip to the Carrefour on Saturday? It’s not the same, but they have a reasonable selection. Carrefour it is, if we have to. Oh, and I need to remember to pick up some decent biscuits. I’m having a serious digestive craving. Shortbread, specifically. Not those awful sweet ones,  real  shortbread. You are a creature of habit, you know that? Shortbread and Earl Grey. It’s practically a national institution.

Right, okay. So, if I’m clear, Auntie Carol is picking Leo up from football on Thursday, and then  you  two are coming straight here?      Mmmhmm. And can we make cookies? Chocolate chip, please?      And sprinkles! Lots and lots of sprinkles! Ms. Davies said we used sprinkles at school and they were  amazing .      Amazing sprinkles, huh? Alright, amazing sprinkles are a definite. But we need to get a few things sorted first. I promised Sarah I’d try and meet her for a coffee Friday, but honestly, I’m feeling a bit frazzled thinking about everything.      Who’s Sarah? Is she bringing cake?      No cake, sadly. She’s just a friend from work. A grown-up friend. And I need to fit in a haircut too, I look like a scarecrow. Honestly, I haven't had five minutes to myself all week. Between lesson planning and, well,  life , it's been a bit much.      You look nice! Like Rapunzel, with long hair!      Oh, you charmer. It's less Rapunzel, more ‘desperate need of a trim’ but thank you. Okay, so Friday… if I can squeeze in the haircut, maybe a quick coffee. But mostly, I want to spend time with you two. We were talking about that photoshoot, weren’t we? For Grandma’s birthday?      The one with the silly hats? I want the sparkly one!      And I want to be a pirate! With a sword!      Sparkly hat for you, pirate for you. We can definitely do that. But we need to find a good light. The kitchen isn’t ideal. Maybe the garden, if the weather holds. It's supposed to be decent on Saturday.      Can we read a story after the cookies? A really long one? About a unicorn?      Absolutely. As many unicorn stories as you like. Though, might I suggest a slightly less sparkly one after all the sprinkle madness? Now, about dinner on Thursday when you come over... I was thinking spaghetti bolognese? Is that a win?      Yes! With loads of cheese!      Loads of cheese it is. Though, if you eat too much, you won’t have room for cookies. It’s a delicate balance, you see.      I  always  have room for cookies. It's a special tummy just for cookies.      Of course it is. You’re a clever one, you are. Right, everything seems to be falling into place. Auntie Carol, football, you two, cookies, sprinkles, spaghetti, a potential haircut…and a photoshoot.

Honestly, this canteen food is a crime against carbohydrates. Seriously, how can they mess up pasta? It’s, like, fundamentally difficult to ruin.      You say that every time, Liv. You  always  complain about the canteen. And then you still eat it.      Because I’m a student, Maya, and I'm perpetually broke! It's fuel, okay? Low-grade, depressing fuel, but fuel nonetheless. Besides, your salad looks…healthy. Threateningly so.      It’s not  that  healthy. There's a fair bit of halloumi in there. And a creamy dressing. Don't judge my life choices. So, what are you up to tonight? Any grand plans to escape the library?      Oh, you know, the usual. Drowning in readings on post-structuralism. It's fascinating, truly, but after about three hours my brain starts to leak out my ears. I was thinking of maybe hitting up Pryzm later, though. Zara's trying to get a group together.      Pryzm? Oh god. Last time I went there it was sticky floors and questionable life decisions all around. I think I lost a shoe.      You  lost  a shoe? Seriously?      I swear! It was that chaotic. I think someone nicked it. Or maybe I just tripped and it went flying somewhere. It was a blur. I'd rather a low-key pub, honestly. Somewhere we can actually, you know,  talk . Remember The Grey Horse? They do a decent mocktail.      The Grey Horse is good. A bit further out, though, isn’t it? Pryzm's literally on our doorstep. Plus, Zara’s promised to try and get us on the guest list, so free entry. Student discount and free entry… my bank account is weeping with gratitude already.      Okay, okay, you’ve convinced me with the free entry. But if I lose another shoe, I’m blaming you. And Zara. And the entire student population of Kingston. You’ve been ages since we properly went out, though. Feels like all we do is study.      Tell me about it. I’m pretty sure I've forgotten what sunlight feels like. How's your dissertation going, by the way? Still focused on Filipino migration patterns?      It is, yeah. It's…progressing. I'm hitting a bit of a wall with the primary research. Getting people to agree to be interviewed is surprisingly difficult. Everyone's busy. And a bit wary, I think. It’s a delicate topic.      That makes sense. It's good you're being sensitive about it, though.

…and honestly, the seagulls were  relentless . You’d be trying to eat your chips, and they’d swoop down like feathered bandits. It was terrifying, but also…kind of funny looking back on it. Sunderland seaside isn’t exactly known for its glamorous avian population, but South Shields takes the biscuit.      Sounds like a proper holiday experience then. Seagulls are the bane of any British beach, aren't they? My nan’s got a house in Whitstable, and it’s the same story. She spends half her time shooing them off the balcony.      The airborne pickpockets of the coast. It’s a national sport, trying to outsmart a seagull. Though, I’d rather be dealing with seagulls than the traffic down in London right now, honestly. I spent two hours just getting from Canary Wharf to my client’s office yesterday.      Two hours?! You’re joking! I’m glad I decided against a city break this year. Give me a bracing wind and a dodgy amusement arcade any day. Did you manage to catch any of that new series,  Taskmaster ?      I did, actually! Last night. Greg Davies is just… unparalleled. The tasks are so brilliantly stupid. That one with the marzipan and the blindfolds? I was crying with laughter.      It's good, isn't it? A bit chaotic. I missed the first episode, though. Was it crucial for understanding the overall arc of… well, whatever passes for an arc in  Taskmaster ?      Not really, no. It was just Ed Gamble attempting to build a miniature fortress out of biscuits. Utterly hopeless, naturally. It's the personalities though, isn't it? They're all so competitive, and so spectacularly bad at everything.      Exactly! It’s genuine ineptitude, not staged. Speaking of ineptitude, I attempted to make a paella last week. It was… an experience.      Oh dear. Paella’s a tricky one. You need the right pan, the right rice… it’s a whole process.      I skipped the right pan part. And possibly the right rice. It ended up tasting faintly of burnt sugar and despair. Sarah was very polite about it though.      Bless her. I've been on a bit of a baking kick lately, trying to replicate my grandma's shortbread. It’s  impossible . She never measured anything, it was all “a knob of butter” and “a handful of flour”. My attempts are consistently crumbly and slightly burnt.      That’s the secret, isn’t it?

…and young Thomas, bless ‘im, he’s already lookin’ at cars online. Says he needs somethin’ more reliable for gettin’ to that new job in Ipswich. Honestly, at his age, fiddlin’ about with eBay Motors...makes you wonder where time's gone, don't it?      Oh, Thomas is a clever lad. He always was good with machines. Remember when he took apart your wireless, Arthur, and actually  fixed  it? You were furious at the time, but…      Furious! I were without the cricket for a week! But aye, I suppose he did get it workin’ again. Still… spending good money on somethin’ you can’t see… I prefer a good auction, face-to-face. Used to be, you’d go to a local sale and know what you were gettin’.      Speaking of sales, have you two given any more thought to the house? The estate agent said interest is good, particularly from families needing space.      Well, Clive, it’s a big decision, innit? Fifty years we’ve been here. Imagine sellin’ all our memories…      It’s not the memories I’m worried about, Ethel. It's the bother of it all. Packin’, sortin’, lettin' strangers tramp through… and then where do we go? It wouldn't do to end up in one of those pokey flats, would it?      I understand your concerns, Arthur. But downsizing could free up a significant amount of money. We talked about that trip to Italy you always wanted to take, or maybe a nice, slow drive down to Cornwall? Staying in one of those youth hostels, remember you mentioning those?      Oh, Cornwall! I haven’t been to Cornwall in years. We took the kids down there once, stayed in a little caravan park. Lovely it was, even with the rain. Do they still have those youth hostels? I’d imagined they'd all be gone by now.      They do, Ethel, they do. Though I doubt I’d be climbin’ any bunk beds at my age. My knees aren't what they used to be. Remember old Dobbin, Ethel? Best horse I ever rode. Wonderful creature. We used to go out for miles, just me and him. Much simpler times. No eBay, no estate agents... Just horses and fields.      Oh, Arthur and his horses. You always did have a soft spot for them. Though I never understood it. All that mucking out! It smelled awful.      Dad, you used to tell me stories about Dobbin all the time.

...Honestly, the amount of unsolicited advice is just  relentless . Like, I appreciate people caring, but when your mum starts suggesting I dilute the expressed milk with water because ‘that’s what  we  did’ back in the 70s… it’s a bit much, isn’t it?      Oh my god, tell me about it! It’s like everyone suddenly becomes a child development expert the second you announce you’re pregnant. My aunt Brenda cornered me at Christmas and was going on about how I  have  to start solids at exactly four months, no later, otherwise Elsie will be behind. Elsie was three weeks old! I just nodded and pretended to be fascinated by the sprouts.      Sprouts, the perfect distraction tactic! I’ve perfected the art of the vacant nod. It’s the only way to survive. But seriously, the feeding thing… it’s just… overwhelming. I feel like I’m constantly second-guessing myself. Is she getting enough? Is she latching correctly? Is my supply good enough? It’s exhausting.      Exhausting doesn’t even  begin  to cover it. You’re doing amazing, by the way. Honestly. Little Leo seems so content after a feed. Mine… Elsie’s always a bit gassy. It’s probably something in my diet, but every article I read says something different. One says cut out dairy, another says it's perfectly fine!      Oh, the dairy debate! I’ve completely avoided it, just in case. Though I’m starting to crave cheese like it’s going out of fashion. I read something about hidden dairy in everything, even bread! It’s madness. How’s your mum coping with being a grandma again, by the way? Is she totally smothering Elsie with affection?      Smothering is an understatement. She's brilliant, don’t get me wrong, she's been a godsend with the washing and stuff, and she absolutely adores Elsie, but she wants to hold her constantly. Like,  constantly . And she keeps offering to come over every day. I love her, but I need a bit of space, you know? Especially now Mark's back at work.      Totally understand. Mum's been… Mum. She’s offered to move in, which is… a bit much. She keeps saying she wants to ‘help’ but I think she just wants to be here all the time. It’s sweet, I guess, but I need to figure things out for myself. It feels like everyone is trying to take over.

Honestly, this weather is  doing  my head in. One minute sunshine, the next it's threatening a downpour. Makes planning anything impossible.      Tell me about it. Apparently, it's a particularly volatile jet stream. All this talk about record temperatures last summer, and now we're back to needing cardigans in May. Climate change, you know? It’s a right mess.      Dad’s right, it’s a bit… chaotic. I was trying to book a picnic for Saturday, but every forecast is different. And Mum, you were talking about getting the hanging baskets up? Is that still on?      Well,  was  on. I was hoping to get them done this morning, before it gets any windier. But if it's going to chuck it down, what's the point? They’ll look like a soggy mess. Rosie’s already brought in half the geraniums from the patio, the clever girl. She knows.      Mornin' all. What's the doom and gloom about? Oh, the weather. Right. Sounds about right for England. Did somebody say geraniums? Rosie's got excellent taste, although she does try to eat the leaves occasionally.      Morning, love. Just lamenting the impossibility of a stable forecast. And yes, your mother-in-law is fretting about the hanging baskets.      Fret is a strong word, David! I'm just being… practical. And Rosie doesn’t  try  to eat them, she investigates. There’s a difference! Speaking of practical, have you remembered to take the bins out, dear? Recycling’s due.      Oh, blast. Completely slipped my mind. I’ll do it straight after breakfast. Anything else on the ‘to-do’ list for today?      I'm finishing up that article for 'Coastal Living' this afternoon, the one about dog-friendly beaches in Kent. It's surprisingly tricky to find good photos that aren't completely swamped with people.      Ooh, that sounds fun! I always think Kent has the best beaches. Although Margate's getting a bit… trendy now. Too many people with expensive cameras.      Trendy’s one word for it. Overrun is another. Actually, talking of Margate, Sarah called last night. Little Leo's got chickenpox. Poor lamb.      Oh, no! Is he terribly unwell?      Not too bad, apparently. Just miserable and itchy. She’s been up all night applying calamine lotion. They're worried about keeping him away from the playgroup.      Aw, that’s rough. Hopefully, it won’t last long. It’s always a nightmare with chickenpox, keeping them from scratching.

...Honestly, the physics test was  brutal . Mr. Harrison really went for it this time. I thought I’d revised everything, but then there were these questions about…induced currents? It was like a different language!      Oh,  no . Harrison’s the worst for that. He loves throwing in stuff he barely mentioned in lessons, just to ‘test our understanding,’ as he puts it. I was okay on the first half, mostly forces and motion, but then the electricity section… I just stared at the paper. Did you at least attempt the last question? The one about the transformer?      Attempted! Key word being  attempted . It was more of a hopeful scribble, really. And you? You're usually pretty good at physics.      Usually! I think I got some marks for the principle, describing what a transformer does, but the actual calculations… forget it. It’s just…so abstract. I much prefer art. Mrs. Davies is lovely, and we’re starting on landscapes now. Thinking of doing one of Grantchester meadows.      Ooh, that's a good idea! You're really good at capturing light. Mine always looks…flat. Speaking of landscapes, Grandad’s been going on about getting the garden ready for Christmas lights. He’s bought, like, a million different sets. It’s going to look ridiculous.      Honestly, your Grandad and Christmas. It’s a whole  thing . Remember last year when he tried to build that reindeer from old plant pots?      How could I forget?! It looked like a mutated garden gnome. Mum nearly had a heart attack when she saw it. He’s also trying to get me to help him with the new rose bushes. Apparently, 'proper pruning is a science,' which, knowing him, will involve a complicated spreadsheet.      Sounds about right. My Mum just wants to get the tree up and then forget about it. She's already planning the Christmas market trip. Are you going with your family?      Yeah, definitely. It's not Christmas without the Cambridge market and a questionable hot chocolate. Plus, I need to find presents… it’s the usual struggle. What about you? Any ideas? I’m completely stuck for ideas for Nana. She already has  everything .      I'm thinking about getting my little brother a new Lego set; he's obsessed with space. And for Nana… hmm, well, she collects those old stamps, doesn't she? Maybe a nice stamp album, or some particularly interesting vintage stamps?

...Honestly, Arthur, you wouldn’t  believe  young Maisie. She’s convinced that rat puppet is alive. Absolutely convinced! She carries it everywhere, talks to it, the lot. Calls it Reginald. Reginald!      Reginald, you say? A right proper name for a rat, that is. Though, I’ve always been more of a dog man myself. Never understood the appeal of rodents. Unless they’re in a trap, of course. Then they’re quite appealing.      It's a child’s imagination, Margaret. A perfectly normal phase. Though, I do agree, Reginald is…distinctive. It’s good she’s got something to focus on, keeps her occupied. Far better than staring at that blinking television.      Oh, I know, I know. It's lovely she's got such a vivid imagination. But she tried to feed it a biscuit yesterday! A digestive, mind you. That’s a fancy treat for a rat, even a puppet one. I had to explain, very gently, that Reginald doesn’t  actually  eat.      Bless her little heart. Reminds me of when young Thomas - that’s our grandson, you’ll recall - he used to have a stuffed badger he insisted on taking to church. Said Bernard needed to hear the hymns. The vicar, Reverend Davies, was terribly amused, he was.      Speaking of hymns and things… did either of you manage to get along to handbell ringing this week? I was tied up with a meeting regarding the village hall refurbishment. Absolute nightmare, frankly. Everyone has an opinion on the colour of the paint.      No, dear, I didn’t. My eyes have been playing up something dreadful. Everything's a bit blurry, you know? Thought I’d leave it, rather than risk misreading a note and causing a cacophony. Old Mrs. Higgins would never forgive me.      Eyes, eh? That’s something you ought to get seen to, Margaret. Don’t leave things like that. I put it off for years, I did. Thought it was just a natural part of getting on. Ended up needing rather strong spectacles. Now I can barely see  without  ‘em. I tell you what, trying to read the bus timetable is a challenge.      Arthur’s right, you really should. I can recommend a good optician in town. Actually, talking of buses… I attempted to get the number 27 into Norwich yesterday. Absolute chaos! They’ve rerouted it again, haven’t they? Took me nearly an hour just to figure out where to stand.

Right, so… museum this morning, then maybe wander down to Rialto this afternoon? Unless you've got a secret Venetian agenda, Auntie Brenda?      A secret agenda? At my age? Nah, love. Just hoping my legs hold out! Though, Rialto  is  good. Remember when we used to come here with your Grandad? It wasn't this… polished. It was proper bustling, fish market smells and everything. Not all these tourist shops.      Oh, I remember vaguely. I was little, wasn't I? Mostly remember Grandad getting me a ridiculously oversized gelato. It was bigger than my head! He insisted I finish it. Said a waste of good Italian ice cream was a sin.      That sounds exactly like him! He loved his gelato. And the cicchetti. Oh, the cicchetti! They didn’t have half the fancy stuff they do now. It was just simple, good food. Little sandwiches, fried olives, bits of mozzarella… proper working man's snacks, that. Not these prawn and avocado concoctions they’re selling now.      Seriously! I saw one with lobster on it. Lobster! On a little bread roll. It feels…wrong. I was hoping to try some proper Venetian stuff, though. Something authentic. Any recommendations?      Authentic, eh? Away from San Marco Square, that's your best bet. Find a  bacaro , a little wine bar. They’ll have proper cicchetti. Look for places frequented by locals, you’ll know it when you see it. And  sarde in saor  – sweet and sour sardines. It’s a bit of an acquired taste, but it's proper Venetian. Your Grandad adored them.      Sardines? Hmm. Maybe I'll start with something a bit less…fishy. What about the wine? I’ve heard Prosecco’s big around here, but is there anything…local?      Prosecco's lovely, but you're a bit away from the Prosecco region here. They drink a lot of  ombra  – it literally means ‘shadow’ because traditionally, workers would have a glass of wine in the shade after a day’s work. It's a local wine, usually a simple red or white. Often served in small glasses.      That sounds perfect. A little glass of wine, some simple cicchetti… Much more my style than lobster rolls. So, Rialto after the Peggy Guggenheim Collection, then? I booked tickets online, thankfully. The queues looked insane this morning.      Sounds lovely. Peggy Guggenheim’s a good choice, she had wonderful taste. Though, honestly, I prefer just getting lost in the backstreets.

...Honestly, the leg press felt impossible today. Like, genuinely questioning all my life choices during set two. Did you see Mark trying to spot Sarah? It was a disaster waiting to happen, he looked terrified he’d drop the weight on her head.      Oh my god, Mark  always  looks terrified when anyone asks him to spot! He's all bravado until there's actual weight involved. Sarah should know better than to ask him. Seriously though, you’ve been going consistently for… how long now? You must be getting stronger.      About three months really, properly. I felt like a newborn giraffe at first, completely uncoordinated. But yeah, I think I am. I managed to up my weight on the dumbbells a bit today, which felt good. It's just… motivation dips sometimes, you know? Especially after a long day at work. Coordinating the Henderson project is sucking the life out of me.      Tell me about it. Marketing at Bupa isn’t  exactly  thrilling every day either. It’s a lot of reports and ‘optimising engagement metrics’ which basically means trying to make slightly depressing health info look appealing. What even  is  the Henderson project? You never really said.      It’s a new data management system for the council. Sounds exciting, right? . It’s essentially moving everything onto a new platform. Endless meetings, endless emails, and everyone involved has a different opinion on how it should be done. It’s… draining. I need a holiday.      Oh, YES. A holiday is  essential . Have you started thinking about where you might go? I was having a browse last night and found some amazing deals to Crete. Think sunshine, beaches, ridiculously good food…      Crete sounds incredible! I was vaguely thinking maybe Italy, but I haven't really looked. Budget is the big problem, obviously. Everything is so expensive at the moment. I was hoping to go with Chloe and Emily, but they're both saving for… well, Emily's saving for a deposit on a flat, and Chloe's still talking about that disastrous relationship with Ben.      Ben! Honestly, I still can’t believe she went back to him  twice . He's awful. Speaking of awful exes, I bumped into Josh the other day.      Oh no. That's… unfortunate. Where?      Near the Grafton Centre. He tried to make conversation. It was deeply awkward. He asked how 'things were going' and I just mumbled about work and escaped into Boots.

...Honestly, the sheer arrogance of them to install those bollards  right  in front of Mrs. Henderson’s gate! She’s nearly 90, you know. Can’t get the bins out, can’t get her wheelchair turned around… it’s just… baffling. And when I pointed it out to the housing people, the new landlord's representative, all I got was, “It’s for security, madam.” Security from  what , exactly? Pigeons?      Bollards. Always bollards. A classic example of solutions searching for problems. Reminds me of some of the bureaucratic nightmares I uncovered when I was researching Philip of Spain. Extraordinary levels of pointless regulation. You wouldn’t believe the paperwork involved in moving a sheep in 16th-century Castile! I was at the Spanish archives for months, you know. Wonderful place, though dusty. The British Library, of course, is impressive, but doesn’t quite have the… the  atmosphere  of those old Spanish places.      You’re still working on that book, then? The one about Philip and Mary?      Oh, yes. It’s…slowly taking shape. A monumental task, really. Trying to disentangle fact from Tudor propaganda, Spanish bias, and plain old historical misremembering. It’s fascinating, but draining. I was reading about the Austrian battleship disaster, the  Szent István , the other day—just to give myself a break from the 16th century, ironically—and thinking about how even  contemporary  accounts can be so unreliable.      Goodness, that was dreadful, wasn't it? All those sailors. It's rather humbling, thinking about the scale of things. It puts bollards in perspective. Anyway, back to the housing association… I’m thinking of starting a petition.      A petition is a good start. Though, frankly, these new landlords seem utterly clueless. They've no concept of community. It’s all profit margins and efficiency reports. You know, it’s funny. People are always complaining about France, the bureaucracy, and the strikes… but their approach to property, to land, is so different. It feels… more rooted. Less transactional.      That’s interesting. I've only been to France a couple of times, mostly Paris, of course. It always struck me as a bit… chaotic. And the attitude to enterprise seemed rather… resistant. I remember a conversation with a chap in a bistro, complaining about how difficult it was to start any sort of business.      Oh, there's a resistance to  unfettered  enterprise, certainly. And there are anarchists, naturally, a perennial feature of French life.

Honestly, this is  way  better than the school canteen. Like, a million times better. Mrs. Higgins tried to pass off something grey and suspiciously circular as a ‘chicken nugget’ yesterday. I swear it moved.      You’re exaggerating, aren’t you? It couldn't have  moved . Though I did see Liam nearly lose his lunch over it. He’s got a weak stomach.      Weak stomach? Liam? The guy who ate a whole bag of those ridiculously spicy chilli crisps on a dare last week? That’s… selective weakness.      He regretted the crisps later, okay? It was a whole thing. He was bright red and couldn’t stop sweating. Mr. Davies almost sent him home. Speaking of Mr. Davies, did you guys hear he finally admitted he doesn't understand half of what we write in our English essays?      No way! Seriously? He always acts like he’s a literary genius. All that dramatic sighing after we hand them in…      It’s probably a tactic. Throw us off the scent. Make us think he gets it when he’s actually completely lost. It's psychological warfare.      He definitely marks based on how neatly you write. I swear, I could write absolute rubbish if my handwriting is perfect and get a B. Honestly, it's unfair. My cousin, Sarah, she’s at uni now, says the marking is much fairer there.      Uni sounds amazing. Freedom. No more compulsory PE. No more Mrs. Higgins' mystery meat. I'm saving up to get a decent graphics tablet, though, that’s a big expense.      What are you working on at the moment, then? Still doing those superhero comics? The ones with ‘Captain Calibration’ – brilliant name, by the way.      Yeah! I’m developing the whole backstory now. He was a…a data analyst before he got his powers. A really  boring  data analyst. Then an experimental algorithm went wrong, and bam! He can calculate probabilities faster than anyone else, hence the name.      That’s… actually kind of cool. A bit niche, maybe, but cool. Better than my attempts at writing a fantasy novel. I got stuck on page three. All about a gnome who collects bottle caps.      A bottle cap collecting gnome? That is niche. Though, there's a market for everything these days. My little sister is obsessed with collecting slime. It’s horrifying.      My mum’s trying to get me to eat healthier. No more takeaways, she says.

Right, well, this is…a project. Honestly, Nan, you’ve accumulated a  lot  of things over the years. Jonathan’s birthday is next week, and we really need to clear some space for people.      Oh, don't start, Margaret. It’s not clutter, it’s  memories . Every single one of these bits and bobs tells a story. And besides, where would I put everything if I got rid of it? It's perfectly organised chaos, you see.      She’s not wrong, Mum. It’s a museum of Kendal history in here. Though, I’ll admit, finding the biscuit tin requires an archaeological dig sometimes. Did anyone remember to order the cake? I was thinking chocolate, Jonathan always liked chocolate.      Yeah, Dad ordered it. Double chocolate, extra frosting. He said he got it from that new bakery near the station, "Sugared Bliss" or something. Sounds…intense.      “Sugared Bliss”? Fancy name for a bakery. Back in my day, it was just Mrs. Higgins and a plain sponge. Still tasted lovely though. Though, I do appreciate a good chocolate cake. Have we decided on the guest list, Margaret? Are we inviting all of Jonathan’s university friends?      We’ve sent invites to most of them, Mum. A few couldn't make it, commitments and all that. I was thinking we could have a buffet rather than a sit-down meal. Less formal, you know? And easier.      A buffet? At Jonathan’s birthday? That seems rather…common. He’s always appreciated a properly set table. Though, I suppose times have changed. Still, I'm making my potato salad. No buffet is complete without my potato salad.      Mum, relax. It’ll be fine. A buffet means more time chatting. Besides, remember last year when Great Aunt Mildred insisted on talking about her bunions for half an hour during dinner? A buffet avoids bunion monologues.      Oh, yeah! That was brutal. I thought I was going to fall asleep in my soup.      Mildred  does  like to talk. Still, she means well. Now, is anyone thinking about decorations? I've got some nice bunting somewhere…      I’ve got a few things, Mum. And I was thinking we could get one of those banner things with “Happy Birthday Jonathan!” printed on it. They’re quite cheap online. Though the branding on some of the websites is horrendous, honestly. All flashing colours and Comic Sans.      Oh, God, no Comic Sans. That’s a crime against design.

...Honestly, the PE teacher is  obsessed  with perfect duty. Like, it's the only thing she talks about! "Perfect duty, girls, perfect duty!" It's exhausting. I just want to play netball, not be scrutinised on how efficiently I collect the cones.      Oh, Mrs. Davies? She's the worst! I swear she thinks perfect duty is a life skill we  need  to master. Did you hear she gave Chloe a detention for…what was it? Apparently, the line of footballs wasn’t  quite  straight enough.      No way! Seriously? That's ridiculous! It feels like she's trying to turn us into robots. And all this adds to the GCSE stress, doesn’t it? I'm completely paralysed by choice. What are you thinking of dropping?      Ugh, don’t even get me started. I'm leaning towards dropping History. It's not that I  dislike  it, it just...feels like so much memorising. My mum keeps saying I need a good mix, but I’m thinking maybe focusing on the stuff I actually enjoy. Like, I’m pretty sure I want to keep Art.      Art’s good. You’re really talented. I’m torn about Music. I love playing the clarinet, I really do, but the coursework is… intense. Then again, I also don't know what I want to  do  with it. What about jobs? Have you thought about what you might want to be when you grow up? Everyone keeps asking.      Don't remind me! My aunt Susan cornered me at Gran’s last week, going on about being a solicitor. Apparently, it’s “stable and respectable.” Ugh. I’ve been watching loads of YouTube videos about… well, a bit of everything. There are people who make a living just being bloggers, you know? Like, beauty or gaming or even just talking about books.      Seriously? Really? That sounds amazing! Is it actually possible to  make money  doing that? I follow this one girl, Lexie, who does book reviews. She's got, like, a million subscribers. She seems to live a pretty good life.      Apparently, you can. It's all about advertising and sponsorships. It's a lot of work though. You have to be really consistent. My brother was trying to be a gaming YouTuber for a bit, but he gave up after like, two weeks. He said it was way harder than it looks.      Oh, Liam. He always bites off more than he can chew.

…Honestly, this weather’s been dreadful, hasn’t it? Not a proper summer day since… well, I can't rightly recall when. Used to be able to guarantee a good stretch of warmth in July, you know. Not anymore.      Aye, you're spot on, Arthur. Proper miserable. Reminds me of ‘66, though not as hot, thankfully. That year, the heat just… lingered. Couldn’t get a good night’s sleep for weeks. Still, at least we  had  heat. This is just damp and grey. Did you see that heron down by the river this morning, Arthur? A beauty, it was.      Oh, lovely! Herons are so graceful. I haven't seen one lately, though. I’ve been too preoccupied trying to get my new tablet to do what I want it to. Absolutely baffling, those things. My granddaughter, bless her, tried to show me how to video call, but I just…can’t get my head around it.      It does take a bit of getting used to, doesn't it? Mum, it's mostly about muscle memory – where to tap, swipe, things like that. I can always give you another quick tutorial when I’m back next week. I’ve just been updating some lecture materials, and the software keeps crashing. It's infuriating. They release updates constantly, supposedly “improvements,” but half the time they just break things!      Updates, eh? Sounds like a right palaver. Reminds me of trying to fix my old Austin Cambridge. Every time I'd get one thing sorted, something else would go wrong. A lovely car in its day, mind you. Built to last. Unlike these modern contraptions. All plastic and sensors. No soul.      You always did have a soft spot for those old British cars, Arthur. I remember when you got that Cambridge…bright blue, wasn’t it? And you spent more time under the bonnet than driving it, if I recall correctly!      A slight exaggeration, Dennis, a slight exaggeration! But it was a reliable workhorse. I once drove it all the way to Scotland, back in ‘78. Through Hadrian’s Wall territory. Now  that  was history! You could almost feel the Roman legions marching alongside you.      Scotland…that sounds lovely. I always wanted to see the Highlands. My father used to tell stories about his time stationed near Inverness during the war. He said it was bleak but beautiful. He found a ruined castle – apparently, it had a fascinating history connected to Bonnie Prince Charlie.

…and honestly, Doreen, the state of young Timmy’s handwriting! It’s like a spider’s been dipped in ink and let loose on the page. I popped down to the school yesterday, you see, just to see how he’s settling. Offered to help with reading, perhaps.      Oh, Arthur, you’re a dear. Always wanting to lend a hand. Timmy’s a lovely lad, a bit boisterous, mind you. My granddaughter, Lily, she’s in the same class. Says the new teacher, Miss Davies, is a bit… strict.      Strict? That's a polite way of putting it, I gather. My wife, Sarah, teaches at Northgate. She says Miss Davies is trying to impose order after… well, let’s just say the previous teacher had a rather ‘hands-off’ approach. Apparently, kids were practically running the place.      Running the place! Good heavens. Back in my day, a firm hand was all that was needed. A little discipline. Though, of course, things were different then. We didn't have all this… tweeting and TikTok nonsense distracting them. What  is  TikTok anyway? Sounds like a clock with a nervous tick.      Oh, Arthur, you’re a card. It's… well, it's little videos, mostly dancing and silly things. Lily spends hours on it. I try to get her to read a book, but it's like talking to a brick wall.      It's designed to be addictive, Doreen. Little dopamine hits every few seconds. It’s a nightmare for educators. Speaking of nightmares, did you hear about old Mr. Henderson down the road? Apparently, he’s taken to binge-watching those crime dramas on television and now suspects the deliverymen are casing the joint.      No! Not old Herbert? He used to be so sensible. Now he’s got a security camera pointing at his rhododendrons. Says he saw a suspicious-looking van. Probably just delivering his groceries! He's always been a bit of a worrier, Herbert. Reminds me of my Aunt Mildred. Always convinced the milkman was after her silver.      Oh, they all get like that eventually, don’t they? The world feels a bit more… uncertain. Although, I'll say, those delivery drivers are a bit haphazard sometimes. One nearly reversed into my rose bushes last week! I had a right word with him.      You always do, Doreen. You're a force of nature. Have you seen  Bargain Hunt  lately? It’s been terrible.

Honestly, this snow is relentless, isn't it? It’s beautiful for about five minutes, then it just becomes… problematic. Especially when you’ve got snowdrops just  starting  to poke their heads up.      Tell me about it. I was actually thinking about getting the raised beds sorted this weekend. Properly prepping them for the early veg. Now? It’ll be an ice rink out there. Maybe good for testing the structural integrity, though.      Structural integrity of your gardening? You’re a proper academic, you are. Serious about everything. Still, it  is  a good job we got those fleece covers, isn’t it? Saved the winter cabbages, at least.      Absolutely. Mum was right to nag me about them. She’d be out there wielding a spade even in this weather, the woman is unstoppable. Speaking of unstoppable… have you seen that new series of  Come Dine With Me ? It’s… aggressive.      Oh,  God . I caught bits of it last night. The passive-aggressive comments! The blatant sabotage! It’s entertainment gold, though, isn't it? Pure, unadulterated chaos. Better than most reality TV. I’m secretly taking notes, purely for research purposes, naturally.      Research purposes? Lay it on me. Are you planning a culinary coup? Perhaps sabotaging my dinner when it’s my turn to host?      Never! I would never dream of it. Though, honestly, your last attempt at paella… It was...ambitious.      Hey! That paella was a victim of circumstance! The hob was temperamental, the chorizo was… enthusiastic. Don’t remind me. Anyway, we should actually  plan  a proper dinner party soon. Not a  Come Dine With Me  battlefield, but a genuinely nice one. Before all this snow melts and everyone forgets what sunlight looks like.      I like that idea. We could invite Liam and Sarah. They haven't been up here since… well, ages. Actually, that reminds me… have you even started thinking about Daniel’s stag do? It's, like, next month.      Don't even. It’s a logistical nightmare. His brother wants paintballing, his other mates want a weekend in Prague… I’m trying to find something that doesn’t involve hypothermia or international incidents.      Prague sounds… risky. Maybe a nice brewery tour somewhere a bit closer to home? York, maybe? Or even Cambridge has some decent pubs.      York’s a good shout. Less chance of accidentally ending up in a questionable club. What about Sophie’s hen do?

Now, this is a proper roast, isn't it? Your mother’s always been a dab hand with a chicken. Though, truth be told, I miss a good bit of beef. Haven't had a proper roast beef dinner in… oh, goodness me, must be years. Used to be a Sunday staple back in Costessey, you know. Farmer Giles always had the finest cuts.      Oh, Arthur, you and your beef! You say that  every  time. It’s lovely chicken, though, isn’t it? And she made your favourite Yorkshire puddings, extra-large. Don’t pretend you’re not enjoying them.      Alright, alright, don't go twisting my words, Elsie. I  am  enjoying them. They're fluffy as clouds, I’ll give her that. Just saying, a bit of gravy on a proper Yorkshire… now  that ’s heaven.      It  is  a lovely meal, Mum. Thank you. It's so nice to be home. Though, I have to admit, I’ve been experimenting with a lot of vegan roasts lately for work. Trying to cater to vegan students, you see.      It's a challenge, isn't it? Convincing people a nut roast can be just as satisfying as the real thing. We had a debate last week about the textural differences. It got… heated.      Vegan roast? Now there’s an oxymoron if ever I heard one. Roast is  meat . Always has been, always will be. What’s the point? You can’t beat a bit o’ proper meat. Gives you strength, don’t it?      Arthur, dear, don't be like that. People have their reasons. And some of those vegan dishes can be quite tasty, I've tried a few when visiting Sarah. Though, nothing compares to your Mum's cooking, does it? She's always been a traditionalist.      It’s not about replacing tradition, Dad, it's about adapting to changing lifestyles and ethical concerns. Some students are really committed to reducing their environmental impact. And honestly, some of the vegan roasts are surprisingly good. There’s one with lentils and mushrooms that’s almost… meaty.      The key is umami, apparently. Getting that savoury depth of flavour. It's surprisingly scientific. I ended up down a rabbit hole reading about mushroom fermentation techniques.      Mushrooms, eh? Well, I suppose mushrooms  grow  in the ground… that's somethin', I suppose. But they don't  taste  like beef. Never will. Back in my day, if you were hungry, you ate what was put in front of you and didn’t complain.

…and then young Timmy, bless him, decides the gravy boat is a  boat . Full of gravy. Sailing it across the tablecloth, right into Auntie Brenda’s prize-winning begonias. Honestly, the look on her face!      Begonias, eh? Brenda always did favour a good begonia. Though, I always thought she fussed over ‘em a bit  too  much. Like they were royalty.      They were lovely begonias, Dad. Though, gravy on begonias does sound… dramatic. Here, have some potatoes, Ben. These are amazing, Mum. What’s your secret?      Cheers, Amelia. They  are  good. Mum's roasties are legendary. And dramatic gravy boat incidents aside, Auntie Brenda's plants were a bit much. Remember when she nearly had a fit when I accidentally kicked a football near them?      Oh, that was nothing. She’d have had a proper turn if it'd been one of her orchids! They were her darlings, those orchids. Speaking of darlings, how's that flat hunt going, Amelia? Still looking?      It’s…slow. Really slow. Everything's either ridiculously small, falling apart, or costs a king’s ransom. I saw one yesterday that needed a new kitchen, new bathroom,  and  the roof was questionable, and they wanted almost two thousand a month for it!      Two thousand? In  my  day, you could buy a house for two thousand. A perfectly good house! Not one of these new-fangled boxes they build now, mind you. A proper house, with character.      Times have changed, Arthur. Vastly changed. Inflation, you see. Everything’s gone up. Still, two thousand is a bit steep, even for London.      Yeah, Amelia, that's insane. Have you considered looking a bit further out? Like, maybe Hertfordshire? It’s commutable, and you might get more for your money.      I have, Ben. And Buckinghamshire. It’s just… exhausting. Endless scrolling, viewings that are a waste of time… I was hoping to be settled before Christmas.      Don’t get disheartened, love. It’ll happen. These things take time. Though, honestly, you young ‘uns are being priced out. It’s a disgrace. When I first bought my house…      Now now, Mary. Let’s not start on house prices again. It’ll only depress the girl. Amelia, your mum's right though. Don’t rush into anything. Better to hold out for something you really like.      I remember when  I  was looking for a place. Back in ‘58, it was. Found a lovely little terraced house in Salford.

…So, the thing that really struck me about that undergrad presentation yesterday wasn’t the content, honestly. It was  how  they presented. Just…flat. No energy. No connection to why any of this even  matters . It got me thinking back to that disastrous pitch meeting I had for ‘Bloom’ in its early days. Remember that?      Oh God,  Bloom . How could I forget? You were practically vibrating with nervous energy, and the prototype looked like something cobbled together from LEGO and duct tape. But you believed in it, absolutely. That’s what sold me, even before anyone else was convinced. The content didn’t matter so much as  you  believing in the content. Is that what you're getting at with the students?      Exactly! They knew their stuff, technically. But they weren't selling it. They weren’t telling a story. They weren’t making anyone  care . I was thinking…what if, instead of just ‘presentations,’ we framed the final year projects as ‘impact pitches’? Force them to think about the real-world problem they're solving, who benefits, the potential for scaling… the whole entrepreneurial package.      That’s… actually brilliant. It's a shift in mindset, isn’t it? From 'here's what I learned' to 'here's how this changes things.' It’s what I try to instill in my A-level students, but it’s harder at university level, everything becomes so theoretical. It would be a huge change to the curriculum though. A lot of the lecturers… well, they’re quite resistant to anything that isn’t the established way.      That’s the hurdle, isn’t it? But think about it - universities are constantly wringing their hands about employability. This  directly  addresses that. We could even bring in guest speakers, real entrepreneurs, people who’ve actually been through the startup grind. Like old man Hemmings, the guy who built that drone delivery company. He’s a bit eccentric, but he’s got stories for days.      Hemmings  is  eccentric. Last time I saw him he was trying to convince a group of primary school kids that drones were the future of beekeeping. But yes, bringing in practical experience would be invaluable. Perhaps a mentorship component too? Pair students with local startups?      Love it. That’s… that's going beyond just changing the presentation format. It's embedding that entrepreneurial thinking throughout the course. And imagine if some of those ‘impact pitches’ actually  got  funded!

Honestly, this risotto is fighting me. It’s supposed to be creamy and…well, it’s currently resembling glue.      Sounds…challenging. Risotto  is  a commitment. What are you even attempting, culinary genius? You usually stick to pasta.      I saw it on TikTok! It looked so easy. “Fifteen minutes, minimal effort!” Lies, all lies. And speaking of effort, how was your shift? Rough one with the autumn blues settling in?      You know it. Had a few particularly…animated patients. It’s that time of year, I think. Everything feels a bit heavier. Though Mrs. Higgins did brighten my day, insisting she’d seen a ghost in the dayroom. Said it was wearing a Victorian nightie.      Oh, Mrs. Higgins. She's a character. Makes a change from spreadsheets and project timelines, that’s for sure. This project… honestly, it’s just endless meetings about meetings. Remind me again why I signed up to coordinate the roll-out of a new coffee machine across three counties?      Because you wanted to 'gain experience' and 'build your skillset'? And because you’re secretly a coffee connoisseur. Don’t deny it. Which three counties are we inflicting fancy coffee upon this time?      Hampshire, West Sussex and… oh god, Kent. Kent is huge. I swear, every village in Kent has three different postcodes. Speaking of places, I was thinking about a weekend away. Somewhere… cosy. Any suggestions? I need to escape.      Ooh, yes! Definitely. We could do the Cotswolds? It's proper picturesque, all rolling hills and thatched roofs. I’ve always wanted to go to Bourton-on-the-Water. Apparently, it’s called the ‘Venice of the Cotswolds.’ A bit dramatic, but sounds lovely.      Venice of the Cotswolds… I’m sold. That actually sounds perfect. We could go leaf-peeping. Is it too early for Halloween stuff? I saw some decorations going up in the shops yesterday.      Never too early! I’m thinking of hosting a little party.
