Nothing too wild, just a few friends, spooky snacks, maybe a themed playlist. Are you in? Plus, you could redeem yourself for the risotto debacle by making some devilishly good Halloween treats.      Okay, okay, you've twisted my arm. I'll attempt baked goods. But if they end up looking like something from a horror film themselves, you're taking the blame. Although, thinking five years ahead – seriously weird to contemplate – I don't want to  still  be battling with a saucepan.

Honestly, darling, this place suits you. Really does. It’s…civilized. More than I ever managed, anyway. Remember the state of the kitchen in Essex when you were little? Perpetual chaos, I called it.      Mum! Don’t start. I distinctly remember  you  being the architect of most of that chaos. Flour everywhere from your baking attempts, Dad’s tools scattered...It wasn’t exactly pristine.      Oh, now, that's a bit harsh. I baked beautiful cakes. Sometimes. And your father… well, he was a man of practical pursuits, wasn’t he? Always fixing something. It was a  lived-in  kitchen, that's all. You wouldn’t understand, all minimalist furniture and perfectly curated bookshelves.      It's not curated, it’s just…organized. And I like knowing where things are! Work is stressful enough without coming home to a visual mess. Speaking of work, things are…interesting at the moment.      Oh? Interesting good, or interesting bad? You never tell me enough about this production controller business, do you? Sounds terribly important. All deadlines and spreadsheets, I imagine.      A bit of both, actually. We're launching a new line of…well, it’s complicated - sustainable packaging for a food company. Sounds good, right? But the entire supply chain is having issues. Suppliers are pulling out, costs are rocketing, and the marketing department wants everything done yesterday.      Oh, dear. Sounds like a right pickle. Always the way, isn’t it? People want things cheap and fast, and then wonder why things fall apart. I always said, good quality takes time. Used to tell that to Mrs. Peterson when I helped out at the flower shop, you know. “Patience, Mrs. Peterson, a good rose needs time to bloom.” She never listened.      You and your flower shop stories. It’s good to hear you're not stressed though. Retired life suits you. You seem…lighter.      Lighter is a good word. Although, full disclosure, I do miss the gossip. Old ladies know  everything . Still, being able to potter about in the garden, read a good book, without feeling like I'm constantly chasing my tail... it is lovely. Are you eating properly, by the way? You look a little pale.      Mum! I told you, I’m fine. It's just the stress at work. I grab something quick when I can. Last night it was a pot noodle. Glamorous, I know.      A pot noodle? At your age? Honestly, darling.

Right, honestly, this French is killin' me. I thought GCSE French would be enough for a week away, but nope. I asked for milk in my coffee this mornin’ and I’m pretty sure I accidentally ordered a small cow.      A small cow?! Oh, Chloe, you’re terrible! I’ve been alright, I think. Mum drilled ‘please’ and ‘thank you’ into me so relentlessly, I can at least manage basic politeness. Though, trying to explain the nuances of scientific methodology to the waiter when he asked if the steak was cooked to my liking…that was a disaster. He just blinked at me.      See! That's what I’m worried about! I’m tryin’ to explain to Madame Dubois that I'm studyin' biology, and she keeps lookin' at me like I've grown a second head. She thinks I’m talkin' about bean cultivation or summert. Biology, Madame! Cells and stuff!      Bean cultivation  is  biology, technically… but I get your point. It's just… different priorities, isn’t it? Cambridge prepared me for essays and debating, not… translating requests for dairy products. How’s uni goin’ anyway? Last I heard you were wrestling with organic chemistry.      Wrestling is a good word for it. It’s properly brutal. I’m startin' to think I should’ve just stuck with history. At least then I wouldn’t be spendin' every evenin' in the library smellin’ faintly of sulphur. You're doin' classics, right? That must be…manageable?      Manageable in a different way. Less fumes, more dead languages. It’s a lot of translation, actually - a surprising amount. Which, funnily enough, is why I'm finding this week easier than you. All that practice deciphering ancient Greek helps with even slightly wonky French. But honestly? I’m missin' proper Footy. Have you seen the latest results?      Oh, don't even  start  me on the football. Doncaster are… well, Doncaster. Still in League Two, still somehow managing to lose to teams I've never even heard of. It's tragic, honestly. I tried explainin' it to some lads in the pub last night – the offside rule, the passion, the sheer misery of supportin' Rovers – they just kept offerin' me more wine.      Classic. They probably thought you were performin’ some sort of elaborate ritual. Leeds did alright, though, didn't they? Snatching a win against…  checks phone  …Bristol City.      Aye, they did. Still not forgivin’ ‘em for what happened last season though.

…and honestly, I nearly jumped out of my skin. It was  huge , Sarah. Honestly, a proper huntsman spider. Right there, on the ceiling above the stairs.      Oh, you poor thing! Huntsman, you say? They're nasty, ain't they? Bigger than my hand, some of 'em. I had one in the bathroom once. Nearly gave me a heart attack, it did. Had to get my Derek to deal with it.      Derek’s a brave man. I… I tried to shoo it with a magazine. A  magazine , Sarah! It just… moved slightly, then carried on staring at me. It felt like a standoff. Eventually, I called my neighbour, old Mr. Henderson. He's a retired entomologist, can you believe it?      No way! Mr. Henderson? Always seemed a bit quiet. An entomologist… that figures, I suppose. Makes a lovely garden, though, doesn't he? Full of flowers. Probably attracts all sorts.      Exactly! Which is why I'm concerned. This spider feels like the beginning of an infestation. I swear, last week I thought I heard scratching in the attic.      Scratching, you say? Oh dear. Not mice, I hope. Now  they  are the worst. Spiders, you can… mostly ignore, right? But mice… they get into everything. I had a terrible problem with 'em in my old flat. Ruined a whole bag of flour, they did.      That’s what I’m afraid of! I’ve got a rather expensive box of biscuits upstairs. Shortbread, you know, the really buttery ones. And my grandmother’s quilt is stored up there too. I’d be devastated if they got to that.      Oh, that quilt! You showed me that a few Christmases ago, didn't you? Lovely work. You need to get some traps down, I reckon. The sticky ones. They're a bit grim, but they work. Or maybe one of those ultrasonic things? Do they work, d'you think?      I've read mixed reviews about the ultrasonic ones. I might try the traps. Though I hate the thought of… well, of what happens to them. It's terrible, really. But worse is them nibbling away at everything. It's just… nature feels rather  invasive  recently.      It does, doesn't it? It’s all coming inside with the weather changing. Speaking of invasive, you won't believe what's been happening with the birds in my garden.      Oh? What's that then?      A pair of magpies. They've built a nest  right  on top of my washing line.

...and honestly, tracing it back beyond my great-grandparents is a nightmare. All the records seem to disappear around the 1880s. It's frustrating! I’ve hit so many dead ends trying to get further back with the Pyms, my mother's side. She always said they were proper Dorset folk, farmers for generations, but proving it… that’s the hard part. Did your family stay put in Wales for a long time, Bronwen?      Oh, goodness, yes. Centuries, probably. My mother’s side, the Davies, were all from around Newport. Coal miners, mostly. Tough lives, I imagine. But they clung to the land, you know? My grandfather actually tried to move to Bristol for a while – that’s where I was born, oddly enough – but he couldn’t abide it. Said it lacked  hen wlad fy nhadau , the land of my fathers. Dramatic, he was! Your Pyms sound like they had a more… pastoral existence.      Pastoral until the Enclosures, I suspect. My mother did a bit of research before she… well, before she got ill. She found a mention of a Pym being evicted during one of those acts, losing a smallholding. It didn’t paint a very rosy picture. She became utterly fascinated with it all, actually. It was a good distraction, I think, in the early days.      That's… sad to hear about your mother. I only met her once, briefly at a family wedding, years ago. She seemed a lovely woman. What was it, eventually? You don’t have to talk about it, of course, if it’s too difficult.      No, it’s alright. It  was  difficult, but it’s been a few years now. It was vascular dementia. It just… stole her, bit by bit. The irony is, she was a librarian, used to words and stories, and then her own story just… fractured. It started with little things, forgetting names, then progressed until she didn’t recognise me at times. It was awful. That’s partly why I got so caught up in the family tree – trying to preserve something, I suppose.      Oh, darling. That  is  cruel. My own husband, Gwyn, suffered with Parkinson's. It's a different beast entirely, but watching someone disappear like that… it’s a special kind of heartbreak. We were both teachers, him and I. History, actually. He was brilliant with the kids, really brought it to life. He'd get them all excited about the Tudors, the Romans...

Oh, look! Another one. Honestly, it’s like Norfolk has become hot air balloon central this weekend. It's beautiful, isn’t it? Though slightly unsettling how low that one is coming down…      Stunning, absolutely stunning. And yeah, a  little  close for comfort. You’d think they’d have designated landing zones further from… well, everything. Makes you wonder about the logistics, doesn’t it? All that equipment, the fuel, the chase teams… must cost a fortune.      A fortune! Don't even get me started. I was reading an article about it - one flight can easily be several hundred pounds, and that's before you factor in all the ground crew. It's a very exclusive hobby. Makes our camping trips look positively frugal. Speaking of which, did we remember the extra pegs? I have a terrible feeling Winston tried to 're-home' a few yesterday.      Winston and his obsession with relocating tent furniture. He thinks he’s an interior designer, I swear. Yes, pegs are in the boot, don’t worry. I triple-checked after witnessing his architectural critique of our last setup. He was very vocal about needing more 'natural materials' incorporated into the design.      He’s such a character. And so convinced he's in charge. It's amazing, isn’t it, how a fluffy ball of chaos can hold so much personality? I saw a hare dart across the field a bit ago, too. A proper one, not a rabbit. It was so graceful.      I missed the hare. I was busy trying to avoid eye contact with that electric pylon. Honestly, they just ruin the view, don’t they? Such a blight on the landscape. I know they're necessary, but… still. It’s like a metallic skeleton stretched across these beautiful fields.      They do, don’t they? It’s a necessary evil, I suppose. Progress, and all that. It’s just… jarring. You wouldn't think power lines would bother me, coming from a city like London, but this is different. It feels  wrong . It’s why I love getting out here. Back to basics, you know?      Exactly. Back to basics. And further away from bills, for a little while at least. We’re lucky, we can afford these little escapes, but I was just looking at the price of everything recently… it's terrifying. Even tents are getting ridiculously expensive.      Tell me about it! I was looking at upgrading our sleeping bags, and I nearly choked on my tea.

...Honestly, the humidity is just  suffocating  today, isn’t it? It feels less like a pleasant summer afternoon and more like breathing through a wet flannel. Even the tennis felt harder than usual.      Aye, you’re not wrong there. Proper sticky, it is. Yorkshire weather prepares you for a bit of everything, but even I'm finding this a bit much. Not like a good, bracing drizzle, this. Just… clingy. How did your class go then? You teaching the beginners still?      I am, yes. It’s… rewarding, in its own way. Though trying to explain the nuances of present perfect continuous to a room full of people who are just trying to order a coffee in French is… a challenge. They all look at me like I've grown a second head.      Can’t say I blame ‘em! Languages weren’t my strong suit at school. Failed French miserably, and German was… well, let’s just say I still remember the shame. I was always better with practical stuff, you know? Getting people motivated, seeing results… that's what I like. That's what I do with the gyms, really. Bit different to conjugating verbs, eh?      Entirely different! Though, you’d be surprised how much coaching is involved in language learning, actually. It's not just about grammar tables. It's about getting people to overcome the fear of making mistakes, building their confidence… it’s about helping them find  their  voice.      That's interesting. I suppose it is. We do a lot of that with personal training, pushing people just beyond their comfort zone. Getting them to believe they can do more than they think. Sarah, one of my trainers down in Birmingham, she’s brilliant at it. Got a real knack for psychology, that one. Though she started as just a receptionist, you know? Worked her way up.      That’s fantastic! It’s so encouraging to hear about people progressing. I sometimes wonder if my postgrad degree was really necessary. It got me the job, obviously, but I often think practical experience – actually  living  in a country where the language is spoken - is far more valuable.      I reckon you’re spot on. I only stayed on at school ‘til sixth form, and honestly? I learned more running a team of people than I ever did in a classroom. Though, my mum was always keen on education. She always said it opens doors.

Right, well, that’s the shopping done. Honestly, young man, the price of a loaf of bread these days… it’s criminal. Used to be you could get a decent one for under a pound.      Yeah, everything’s gone up. Petrol’s ridiculous too. Mum’s moaning about it all the time when she has to drive me to training.      Petrol  is  a bother. Though I don't drive anymore, mind. Never really took to it, all that speed. Your grandfather, bless him, was a right lead foot, though. Always rushing, always late.      Aye, that’s true. He thought the roads were a personal racetrack. Once nearly ended up in Old Man Hemmings’ prize-winning marrows. Caused a right stir that did!      Oh, don't get you started on your stories, Arthur. They go on for hours! Though, it  was  a sight to behold, wasn’t it? Hemmings absolutely fuming.      Marrows? Seriously?      Oh, they were magnificent. Biggest I've ever seen. Your grandfather nearly took the whole patch out! Hemmings threatened to call the police, he did.      He wouldn’t have, though. Hemmings wouldn’t hurt a fly. Now, are you two sorted for Saturday? The theatre, remember? "Oliver!"      Yeah, Mum booked the tickets. I’m not massively keen, to be honest. Musicals aren't really my thing.      Oh, don't be like that! It'll be good for you. Get you out of your room. And it’s a classic. Besides, your grandmother's been looking forward to it for weeks. Haven't you, Margaret?      I have! I used to love that film when I was a girl. And it’s lovely to do something… nice. We don’t get out much these days, do we, Arthur?      Not as much as we used to, love. Bones aren’t what they were, you know. Getting down those steps to the car is a mission and a half. Still, I'll put a brave face on for “Oliver!” as long as there’s a decent cuppa afterwards.      You'll get a cuppa, Arthur, and a biscuit. Several biscuits, if you’re lucky. Right, back to more pressing matters. I was looking at the garden fence this morning, and it’s leaning something awful. I think the wind’s finally finished it off.      Can’t you just… fix it?      Oh, if only it were that simple, lad. It’s not just a few loose panels.

Honestly, this thing is taking us the scenic route  again . I swear, it thinks every B-road is a shortcut. Are you sure this is right for the gig, love? We're supposed to be there for soundcheck, aren’t we?      Give it a chance, Brenda. It recalculated after that roundabout. It  said  avoiding the A68 would save us five minutes. Which, frankly, sounds optimistic knowing these country lanes. And yes, soundcheck is at seven. We’ve got plenty of time… probably. Though knowing the band, they’ll be late regardless.      Five minutes? Five minutes crawling along past sheep and dry stone walls? I could've walked faster. And don’t even get me started on the state of the roads around here. It's a wonder the suspension on this car is still intact. Remember that pothole last year near Penrith? Nearly lost a tyre, we did.      How could I forget? You were convinced we’d have to call the AA and spend the night in a Kendal B&B. Dramatic, as always. Though, you  were  right about the state of the roads. They haven’t done a proper repair job in decades, have they? Seems all the money goes to London and then trickle-down economics… doesn’t trickle very far.      Exactly! It’s infuriating. Anyway, look, a buzzard! Over that field there. Aren’t they majestic? It’s amazing how they just hang in the air. I saw a proper hawk the other day, near school. Got rather excited, told Year Five all about it. They were more interested in their phones, naturally.      They are beautiful. Keeps you connected to something real, doesn’t it? Better than endless scrolling. Speaking of real, are you still knitting that scarf for young Thomas? He mentioned wanting something warm for the winter.      Aye, I am. It's a complicated cable knit, though. Takes ages. I got some beautiful Herdwick wool from that little shop in Hawes last week. Soft as anything. Reminds me, I need to get a move on, though. His birthday's next month. It's a good job I'm not teaching full-time anymore, I have the time for these things now. Retirement’s suiting me, I think. Even with the dodgy satnavs.      You definitely seem more relaxed. Being able to dedicate time to your crafts and… not dealing with teenage angst every day. Though, I miss your stories about school sometimes.

...Honestly, the exposed brick in that loft conversion was  trying  too hard. Like, "Look at me, I'm industrial chic!" It just didn't flow with the rest of the place, did it?      No, absolutely not. It felt…forced. Like they’d seen it in a magazine and just copied it, without thinking about the actual space. It’s always the way, isn't it? People get obsessed with trends. Did you manage to actually get a decent look at the structural integrity, though? I was distracted trying to politely avoid the owner's endless stories about her miniature dachshund.      Oh god, the dachshund! Yes, I did. Thankfully, the structure was sound, if a little…over-engineered. Which, alright, I’m not complaining about, but it does make our brief seem impossibly ambitious. Communal living spaces for students on  that  budget? It's a tightrope walk, isn't it?      Tell me about it. I was sketching some ideas on the train back, thinking about maximising space, and honestly, I ended up with something that looked like a particularly depressing Tetris game. Access to light is going to be the killer, I think. And student budgets… they’re legendary for being nonexistent.      They are. Still, it’s a good project, creatively. A proper challenge. Speaking of challenges, how’s Liam doing? I haven’t spoken to him properly since…well, since he started that new job. He seemed really enthusiastic about it initially.      Not good, actually. I had a pint with him last night. Apparently, the senior partner is a complete nightmare. A micro-manager to end all micro-managers. He’s questioning every single design decision, making Liam redraw things five or six times for the most trivial changes. It's apparently crushing his spirit.      Oh, that’s awful. Liam's brilliant. He's got such a natural eye for detail. It's just…a horrible environment, isn’t it? He needs to get out of there before it ruins him. Have you told him that?      I have. He’s worried about burning bridges, though. Said he feels like he  should  give it more time, prove himself. Classic Liam. He's too polite for his own good. I told him sometimes bridges  need  burning. Speaking of needing something… this coffee is lukewarm. I’m going to grab another one. What about you? More tea? Or are you feeling adventurous and going for a full English?

…and honestly, the roundabout at the A1 junction is just  asking  for an accident. People treat it like a suggestion, not a rule! I was nearly taken out by someone trying to squeeze in from the third exit when I was clearly already committed to the second. It’s madness.      Ugh, tell me about it. Driving around here is the worst. Everyone thinks they’re Lewis Hamilton. Did you see Sarah’s post about someone cutting her up on the High Street yesterday? She was  fuming .      No, I missed that. Sarah’s a sensible driver though, isn’t she? She's always complaining about people not using their indicators. It’s the basics, really. Common courtesy.      Yeah, she is. She said this guy just pulled straight out, didn’t even look. She had to brake really hard. It’s just… aggressive driving, isn’t it? Like everyone’s got somewhere massively important to be.      Always. And it's often not even important! Just someone rushing to get a latte. Anyway, enough about terrible drivers. How was your evening with Chloe and Liam last night? Did you go to that new Italian place?      It was good, actually! The Italian was lovely, really authentic. Chloe was going on about this guy at work, though. Apparently, he keeps ‘mansplaining’ everything to her.      Oh, not another one. Honestly, it never ends, does it? Is it the same Mark she was complaining about last month?      No, different one. This is David from Finance. Chloe said he just assumed she wouldn't understand the new spreadsheet software and started explaining it to her like she was five. She's brilliant with spreadsheets! She built one for the whole team last year!      Men. Sometimes I wonder…. Here you go. Strong, as you like it. It's just… they're so oblivious. They genuinely don’t realise how patronising it sounds.      Exactly! And when you  do  try to explain it, they get all defensive. It’s exhausting. Anyway, she vented, we had some pasta, and now she's formulating a passive-aggressive email response.      That sounds like Chloe! Smart girl. So, are you still on for that cinema trip on Saturday? They're showing that new Wes Anderson film. I know you love his stuff.      Oh, yes! Definitely. I’ve been looking forward to that. What time were you thinking?      How about we aim for the 2.30 showing? That gives us time for a leisurely lunch beforehand.

...Honestly, the ‘demonstrate initiative’ bit is what’s getting me. It feels so…corporate. Like I need to invent a problem just to solve it. It's for that producer role at Midlands Today, you know? The one we were talking about last week.      Aye, the one you’d be brilliant at! Don't overthink it, love. It doesn't need to be world-changing initiative, just something that shows you  saw  something needing doing and just…did it. Remember that time at the school fete when you single-handedly organised the raffle because nobody else would? That’s initiative!      That’s… a school fete, Sarah. And slightly chaotic initiative involving a lot of donated biscuit tins. I don’t think “successfully prevented a minor meltdown over missing raffle tickets” translates well to broadcasting.      Alright, alright, fair point. But the principle is the same! Think about your radio work. You always went above and beyond researching guests, didn't you? You’d find those little quirky angles nobody else bothered with. That's initiative. Did you mention that when you were interviewing for your current role?      I did, actually. But this feels…different. Midlands Today is a big step up. And the application form is designed to weed people out. It’s practically a personality test disguised as a job app. They want to know if you’re a ‘cultural fit’ which, frankly, feels terrifying.      Cultural fit is just code for ‘will you get on with Dave in accounts and not cause a fuss?’ Trust me, I've interviewed enough people to know. And you will! You're lovely, adaptable, and can talk to  anyone . What else is bothering you about it? Is it the competency questions?      Partly. Like, ‘describe a time when you had to work under pressure.’ I mean, every deadline is pressure, isn’t it? It feels so…formulaic. I want to tell them about the time the server crashed five minutes before the live broadcast and I had to improvise for ten minutes, but that sounds like a disaster, even though we salvaged it!      It  sounds  like a brilliant example of problem-solving under pressure! Focus on the ‘salvaged it’ part. Frame it as a challenge overcome. "Faced with unexpected technical difficulties, I utilised my quick thinking and broadcasting skills to maintain airtime, successfully engaging the audience until the issue was resolved." See? Sounds amazing. Avoid the word ‘disaster’ entirely.

Right, so let’s really nail down this ‘escape plan’. We’ve been talking about it for ages, but now we're actually  here , house-sitting in the sun, it feels… real. Less like a fantasy and more like a, well, a logistical challenge.      It does, doesn’t it? It’s scary and exhilarating all at once. And yes, logistical is the  perfect  word. Okay, so the core idea – you building bespoke furniture, me offering online tutoring in history – that's still firm?      Absolutely. I’ve been sketching designs every evening. Honestly, the inspiration here is incredible. All the textures, the wood… it's getting me fired up. I’m thinking we could specialize in reclaimed timber, give everything a real story. It feels more... ethical than buying everything new.      I love that! It taps into that whole ‘sustainable living’ movement which is huge right now. And the history angle… there's a real demand for personalized learning, especially post-pandemic. Kids need that one-on-one attention, and many parents are realising traditional schooling isn’t necessarily the be-all and end-all. I’ve already had a few enquiries from friends, even before we left the UK.      Good sign. But enquiries aren’t paying the bills, are they? Money is the biggest hurdle, obviously. We need to figure out a start-up cost. My workshop will be the biggest chunk, I reckon. Even a basic setup, with decent tools…      I’ve been looking at small business grants. There are some aimed at creatives, and others specifically for people starting businesses in regional areas – which technically this is, even though we’re relatively close to a city. We need to be careful though, grant applications are notorious for needing endless paperwork.      Paperwork… my nemesis. You're the organizational genius in this partnership. You tackle the grants. I’ll focus on the website. I've been playing around with some WordPress templates – something clean, showcasing the furniture. We need professional photos, though. That’s another cost.      We could barter. There's a photographer I know from a local art group here. She's always complaining she needs a new bookshelf! We could offer her a piece in exchange for a photoshoot. It's worth exploring.      Brilliant! You’re a lifesaver. See, this is why I need you on board. I have the creative side, you have the… the  practical  side. Do you ever regret leaving teaching full-time?

Honestly, Arthur, you’ve been cultivating that beard since… well, since before young Finnigan here even existed! It’s a magnificent thing, truly. Though, I suspect it hides a multitude of biscuits.      Accusations, Moira, pure accusations! It hides a lifetime of wisdom, perhaps, and a few crumbs, admittedly. But biscuits are for dunking in tea, not for hiding. And it keeps my chin warm, a vital function at my age.      It’s a lovely beard, Arthur, really. It just… makes you look even more like a very distinguished, slightly grumpy, Santa Claus. Finnigan seems to think so, anyway. He keeps trying to pull it.      Beard! Soft!      Soft it is, my boy, but not for grabbing! It’s a gentleman’s facial adornment, you see. One must respect the beard.      Speaking of respect, you two haven’t been out much lately. I know looking after a little whirlwind like Finnigan is a full-time job, dear, but you need to get out. Remember when we all went to that dreadful 40th birthday bash for Penelope’s husband?      Oh, don’t remind me. All that neon, and the DJ playing the same terrible song on repeat. I spent the whole evening trying to avoid small talk about mortgages and garden gnomes.      It was a symptom of the times, I think. The 40s are a fraught decade. Mid-life crises manifest as brightly coloured clothing and questionable music choices. But it’s good to  see  people, isn’t it? You're becoming housebound.      It’s not just the social side, is it? It's… everything. Finding a decent school place for Finnigan is proving impossible. Apparently, Cambridge is bursting at the seams. And the housing situation… don’t even get me started. It’s all just completely insane.      It’s the same everywhere, darling. Glasgow's no better. They’re building new estates constantly, but it's never enough. And the schools are packed. I taught for forty years, and I’ve never seen numbers like this. It’s partly this… influx, isn’t it? Not that I’m saying anyone shouldn’t be welcome, mind you.      The Polish communities have revitalised a lot of areas, Moira. Brought a tremendous work ethic, and wonderful bakeries. Though the council does seem to be struggling to keep up with infrastructure. It's the short-sighted planning, always.      It just feels like everyone is scrambling for the same limited resources.

...Honestly, the whole car park pass situation at the sports centre is a farce. They've changed it  again . Apparently, you now need a photo ID linked to it - like it’s Fort Knox! And Brenda from aqua aerobics was absolutely fuming, she’d just renewed hers last month. It’s always something, isn’t it?      Oh, don’t even  start  me on bureaucracy! It’s the same at the doctors. Jumping through hoops to get a simple appointment. They act like you’re trying to defraud the NHS, not just trying to get checked over. Speaking of which, how’s your mum doing? Last I heard she had that nasty cough.      She's…better, thankfully. Dr. Davies thinks it was a bit of a chest infection, nothing too serious. She's still a bit fragile, though. She keeps saying she wants to get back to her walking group, but I worry she's pushing herself too hard. She's stubborn, you know? Just like her father. Remember old George?      Oh, George! A character. Always had a story, didn’t he? And a twinkle in his eye. He used to tell me about his time doing National Service…all a bit hazy now, if I’m honest. It’s funny, isn't it, the things you remember about people. And your dad, too. Always tinkering with something, wasn't he?      Always. He’d have loved the piano, actually. I was thinking about getting lessons. Little Emily keeps having a go at it, banging away like a professional – or a very enthusiastic toddler, anyway.      That's lovely! It’s good she’s showing an interest. You always were musical, weren’t you? I remember you playing the recorder at school - dreadfully, if I recall!      Dreadfully?! I was quite proficient! Okay, maybe not concerto level, but I wasn't  terrible . And it got me out of double maths. What about you? You were always brilliant at sports day. Remember how you used to win the egg and spoon race every year?      That was down to sheer determination, no skill involved! I was just fiercely competitive. It’s probably why I ended up in sales. You have to be. It's tiring though, always 'on'. I’m thinking of reducing my hours when little Leo arrives. Sarah is due in October.      Oh, Sarah! That’s wonderful news! A baby! How exciting! You'll be brilliant aunties to Emily.

Aye, it’s good to get oot here, eh? Brucefield’s a good shout for switching off. Though switching  off  is proving…difficult. I’ve been trying to avoid Twitter, honestly. The whole thing feels…volatile these days.      Volatile is putting it mildly, Alistair. It’s a bear pit. I used to enjoy scrolling through it, purely for the nonsense, but even that's become exhausting. I’m finding myself checking it more for work, though, which is the frustrating part.      Exactly! That’s the problem. For me, it's supposed to be a tool for the comms team – gauging public sentiment, seeing what's trending, that sort of thing. But it’s a constant battle against the…noise. And the algorithm keeps trying to show me things I  don’t  want to see. It’s become less about 'sentiment' and more about 'outrage'.      Tell me about it. I’ve been using it a bit differently, though. Bit of a gamble, actually. I started a little ‘Ask a Director of Studies’ thread. Just answering student questions anonymously. It’s… surprisingly effective.      No way! Really? That's clever. You’re essentially bypassing the official channels, getting direct feedback and… managing perceptions, are you?      It’s not  that  calculated! Okay, maybe a little. It started because I was getting the same questions emailed to me fifty times a week. Now, I answer them once on Twitter and can just link students to it. Saves me a fortune in time, and it makes me seem, hopefully, approachable. Though I worry about getting dragged into a debate about essay marking…      That's fair enough! The debate potential is always there. I’ve considered doing something similar, a sort of ‘Ask a Comms Manager’ Q&A. But I’m worried about the potential for…misinterpretation. We’re dealing with a lot of sensitive information, you know? Public health campaigns, policy updates… one wrong tweet and it’s headlines.      Aye, that’s a completely different kettle of fish. I can operate with a bit more freedom. If I give a slightly ambiguous answer about referencing, it’s not exactly a national crisis. You’re playing with fire, Alistair. You’ve got to have iron-clad controls.      Iron-clad controls, and a team of lawyers vetted every 140 characters . It's a nightmare. I think I spend more time thinking about  how  to avoid saying something than actually saying something.

Honestly, this risotto is  fighting  me. I swear, every grain of rice is actively trying to avoid absorbing the stock.      Sounds… challenging. Rough weekend then? You seem a bit frazzled, even for a Monday.      Rough doesn’t even  begin  to cover it. Work was a disaster Friday, Sarah cancelled on us for Saturday – said she had a ‘family thing’ which, knowing Sarah, probably meant binge-watching reality TV – and then I decided I was going to become a culinary genius and attempt risotto. It’s a triple threat of failure, basically.      Oh, poor you. Work sounds… well, typical. And Sarah's a lost cause sometimes, isn't she? Though, realistically, we  all  have those weekends. What happened at work? Something with that Miller account?      Worse, actually. Mrs. Henderson decided, mid-project, that she wants  everything  changed. Like, the entire scope, the timeline, the budget… all of it. After we'd already gotten sign-off on the initial proposal! I spent the whole of Friday trying to placate her and re-jig everything. It was exhausting.      Ugh. People like that. Honestly, it's like they enjoy chaos. You’re too good at your job to let that stress you out that much, though. It's just a project, right? Not worth losing sleep over.      Easy for you to say, Miss Calm-and-Collected Mental Health Nurse! You deal with  actual  crises all day. My crisis is a spreadsheet that won’t cooperate. But you’re right. It’s just… it feels like I’m constantly running to stand still.      It’s still valid to be annoyed! And my 'crises' often start with spreadsheets, trust me. Patient notes, medication charts… it's all paperwork at the base. Speaking of which, I had a rather bizarre shift last night. Had a patient convinced they were a penguin.      No way! A penguin? That’s… incredible. Did they try to waddle?      Oh, absolutely! And demanded fish. Lots and lots of fish. It took three of us to gently explain the realities of indoor life to him. It’s moments like that when I wonder if I chose the right career.      See?  We all  have our days. Though, honestly, a penguin patient sounds a lot more interesting than Mrs. Henderson's demands. This risotto, however, is just consistently uninteresting. Maybe I should just order a takeaway.      Probably a good shout. You've earned it. Fancy pizza? We could invite Liam too, if he's free.

...Honestly, the kids were  exhausting  today. Year six are preparing for SATs, and it’s all anyone can talk about. Little Timmy was convinced the maths test was designed to make everyone fail. It’s heartbreaking, really. Anyway, enough about my woes. How was your morning, David? You were awfully quiet when I arrived.      Oh, you know, the usual. Just… thinking. About Arthur, mostly. Your brother. Still no firm date for his visit, is there?      No. He called last night, briefly. Said work’s been absolutely manic. Something about a huge contract being finalized. He sounded stressed, poor thing. He's leaning towards the weekend of the 18th, but he wants to confirm with the office first. He said he’d call back tomorrow.      The 18th would be good, wouldn’t it? Gives us a bit of time to get everything sorted. Though “sorted” with Arthur usually just means accepting chaos with a smile. Remember that time he tried to ‘help’ with the Christmas decorations?      How could I forget? The tree nearly ended up in the fireplace. He’s… enthusiastic. And speaks before he thinks. It’s always been that way. It’s just… with Mum and Dad gone, I feel a bit more… responsible, I suppose. Making sure he’s alright.      We all do, David. He's our brother. And he  is  under a lot of pressure at work. It’s just how he copes. Honestly, he’s probably more worried about disappointing us than anything else.      Speaking of arrangements, I was thinking about the meal for when he arrives. Should we do a roast? It feels… celebratory, you know? And Arthur always loved your roast potatoes, David. Even if he did try to sneak extra gravy when Mum wasn’t looking.      A roast sounds lovely, actually. Yes, I can do the potatoes. I’ve been experimenting with a new Maris Piper variety. Supposed to get wonderfully crispy. And maybe some Yorkshire puddings? I've perfected the recipe over the years… it’s the one thing I'm truly good at.      Oh, yes! Yorkshire puddings are essential! I can handle the vegetables, and Sarah, you could perhaps do the gravy? You make a fantastic gravy.      Perfect! Sorted. Although, thinking about it, his journey is going to be horrific. Coming all the way from London on a Saturday afternoon… the traffic will be dreadful.      He’s planning on driving, is he?

…and honestly, Arthur, this subjunctive mood is going to be the death of me. Honestly! I’ve been drilling ‘si’ clauses for a week now and it still feels…wrong. Like trying to put a square peg in a round ‘ole, y’know?      Well, now, don't get yourself in a state, Doreen. It  is  tricky. Spanish, for an English speaker, is a whole different beast. I’m still battling with ‘ser’ and ‘estar’. Honestly, they should just pick one, shouldn't they? It’s just…unnecessary complication, if you ask me.      Unnecessary! That's exactly it! We manage perfectly well without needing to differentiate between being and existing, don’t we? I mean, I taught English as a foreign language for thirty years, and  I  struggle with it. Imagine trying to explain that to a Japanese student!      Thirty years, you say? You'd think you'd have a formula for it all by now. A secret method, maybe? Because this Duolingo lark…it’s alright for vocabulary, gets you started, but it feels like learning to waltz by reading a list of steps. No feel for the rhythm, y’know?      Oh, Duolingo's a good starting point, but it's not enough. I’m trying a bit of everything. Rosetta Stone, some online classes, and I even found a little language exchange partner online, a young man from Madrid. He’s very patient…mostly. I think he secretly finds my pronunciation hilarious.      A language exchange! That's a good shout, actually. I've been thinking about that. Just talking to someone, hearing the natural flow of it. I tried one of those evening classes at the community centre, but it was all teenagers revising for their GCSEs. Felt a bit out of place, honestly. And they were all after the grammar, the rules. I just want to  speak  it!      Exactly! I remember with French at school… it was all conjugation tables and memorising lists. Never actually  using  it. It’s a shame, really. Have you ever thought about where people naturally pick up two languages so easily? Like in Catalonia, for example? They grow up speaking Catalan and Castilian, completely switching between them.      Catalonia, yes. I read something about that. And Belgium, with Flemish and French. Seems to be a lot of it around the Mediterranean, doesn't it? Maybe it helps with brain development when you're young. We Brits just tend to bumble along with our one language, expecting everyone else to understand  us .

Right, Dad, I think we’re getting somewhere. This lot looks like…utility bills from 2017? Seriously? Why do people keep these things?      Sentimentality, lad. Pure sentimentality. Your mother was like that. “You never know when you’ll need to prove you paid the gas bill in November 2017!” Honestly. Though, to be fair, she was quite meticulous. You get that from her, you know, being so organised… unlike some people.      Hey! I'm organised! Just… adapting to a different system. My flat is minimalist. Less stuff, less to organise. This…this is an archaeological dig. Speaking of systems, have you managed to scan that document I emailed you – the bank statement? It’s crucial for the flight booking.      Oh, that. No, not yet. Been a bit tied up with work, you see. Mrs. Higgins nearly had a meltdown because her broadband was down  again . Honestly, some people. It's always the same with them. But I'll get to it. What flight are we talking about again? Just reminding myself.      The one to Barcelona? For Sarah’s hen do? You promised to send me proof of address, and the bank statement is the easiest way. The airline is being ridiculously strict. It’s infuriating. All this because of…well, you know. Security.      Barcelona, right. Lovely place. Saw a picture of Kelly Brook there once, years ago, on the front of a magazine. Stunning. Anyway, I’ll scan that statement first thing. My printer's playing up a bit though, sometimes it doesn't recognise the feed. It's a miracle I got through customer services today without throwing it out the window.      You and technology, Dad. It’s a never-ending battle. Maybe I could have a look at it later? I’m fairly competent. Spent three years explaining the nuances of the present perfect continuous to teenagers, I can probably troubleshoot a printer. It’s all about patterns, really. Like…corpus linguistics. Identifying recurring errors.      Corpus linguistics? Is that…what you  do  all day with those students of yours? Sounds complicated. I just want things to  work . This printer is a menace. Actually, while you’re at it, have you seen that recipe for paella I printed out? I was thinking of making it when you're back from Barcelona. Celebrate.      Paella sounds amazing! Here it is, tucked inside a leaflet for double glazing. Seriously, Dad? Double glazing leaflets from 2012?

Honestly, this is ridiculous. Another one? We’ve stopped at, what, three petrol stations already? And they  all  have a queue stretching back to Newcastle.      Dramatic, as ever. It's a bank holiday weekend, Liv. Everyone and their dog is going somewhere. You knew it would be busy. Besides, I thought you were enjoying the drive? A bit of open road, wind in your hair…      Wind in my hair? I've got the window up because of the smell of petrol and desperation! And enjoying the drive is hard when we're crawling along, watching everyone else escape the city. It's not like we  need  petrol right now, is it? We were, like, three-quarters full.      We're doing a fair few miles to Mum’s, love. Best to top up when we can. And panic buying's started again, apparently. Saw it on the news. People acting like the world's ending because of a slight supply issue. Honestly.      Aye, well, people are daft. It's just… frustrating. Reminds me of when old man Hemmings used to fill every jerry can he could get his hands on whenever there was a hint of snow. Caused absolute chaos at the local station.      Oh, Hemmings! Now  there  was a character. Always said a bit of preparation never hurt anyone. Though I agree, his level of preparation was… excessive. Did you see that biker back there? The one in the full leathers, weaving between the cars?      Yeah! A proper speed demon, that one. Mad. Honestly, I don’t understand why people bike. It's just asking for trouble. All that wind and rain, and you’re basically a tin can on wheels for everyone else.      I think there’s something about the freedom of it, Liv. My cousin, Ben, is really into it. Says it’s the best feeling in the world. The connection to the road, the speed… He’s meticulous about safety though, all the gear and training.      Meticulous doesn’t change physics, does it? Still going to get flattened if someone pulls out on them. I’d be terrified. Though, I will admit, some of the bikes are gorgeous. Like, seriously works of art. That Ducati that pulled into the last station was  stunning . Red as anything.      See? You’re not entirely anti-bike. It’s the risk you object to. It’s the same thing with my job, really.

Right, so you've got your session with Ben on Saturday, have you packed your kit? Don't forget the new grips, we got those last week.      Yeah, Mum, it’s all in my kit bag. Honestly, you check like five times every session! I’m not  going  to forget.      He’s a conscientious lad, Sarah. He knows what he needs. Besides, you’re the one who usually ends up rummaging around for a water bottle he’s left somewhere.      That’s true, I am a bit of a bag-checker. Old habits. It's just…he's improving so quickly and I don't want anything to disrupt that momentum. Ben thinks he’s got real potential, you know.      Ben  always  says that. He’s a coach, it’s his job to be positive! But yeah, I'm feeling pretty good about my game. I managed to get my serve a bit more consistent this week.      That’s excellent. Consistency is key. Remember watching Alcaraz at Wimbledon last year? He wasn’t the biggest server, but his placement… phenomenal. He was making Sinner run all over the court.      Oh, absolutely! And the way he anticipates… it's like he can read their minds. He’s a bit of a Federer in the making, isn’t he? Although, I think Federer had a natural elegance Alcaraz doesn't  quite  match yet. It's more… explosive.      Alcaraz is just amazing. I saw a clip of him hitting a forehand return of serve, completely flat, down the line. It was insane. I tried to copy it in practice, nearly took Ben's head off!      Careful now! Ben's a good lad, and we need him to keep shaping your talent. Speaking of which, you've been watching a lot of these professionals, haven’t you? Are you analysing their technique or just enjoying the spectacle?      Both, really. I watch Djokovic a lot. His mental toughness is incredible. The way he can just… switch on when it gets tough. That’s what I really want to learn. Plus, his backhand slice is ridiculous.      It is. Remember when he and Federer played that five-set final at Wimbledon in 2019? An absolute classic. I was on the edge of my seat the entire time. That match had  everything .      I remember. I was working in London at the time and managed to catch the end of it in a pub.

Honestly, these napkins… they  do  look like tiny underpants, don’t they? I swear, Auntie Maureen picked them up thinking they were festive.      Nah, they're alright. Bit… peculiar, maybe. More importantly, are we talkin’ about dessert yet? I've saved room, obviously.      “Obviously.” You’ve already had two helpings of everything, Liam. You’re a menace. Though, I have to admit, the napkins  are  a choice. They remind me of something you’d find in a novelty gift shop.      Maureen's got a… unique sense of style. She meant well. Speaking of well, how’s the Christmas shopping going, love? Still battling the crowds?      It was a nightmare yesterday! The Arndale was rammed. Managed to get everything, though. Just hoping I remembered everything  on  the list. David's been dropping hints about a new golf club for months. It’s an expensive hint.      Golf clubs! Men and their toys. When your father wanted something, it was always a new book. A nice, quiet hobby. Though, he  did  try to learn the ukulele once. That lasted about a week.      A ukulele? Grandad? No way! Picture that. He'd have been proper terrible, wouldn’t he?      I can’t even begin to imagine. Dad, did you ever tell us about Grandad’s ukulele phase?      He never spoke of it. Buried it deep. Right, turkey’s good? Everyone happy with the bird? Always a bit stressful, getting it just right.      It’s lovely, honestly. Perfect. Better than last year. Remember when it was practically raw in the middle?      Don't remind me. I thought I was gonna need a dentist. This year's definitely better. So, anyone planning on any proper Christmas Eve traditions? I’m off to Jess’s place, her family do that whole carol singing thing, slightly embarrassing but fun.   Speaker_3  : Carol singing? That sounds… intense. My friends and I just have a massive movie night, usually something cheesy. Last year was  The Holiday  – total tearjerker.      Carol singing  is  lovely, though. Reminds me of when your father and I were first married. We'd walk around the village with the lanterns, singing at each house. Simpler times.      We used to go to midnight mass. Haven’t done that in years. What about you, Mum? Anything special planned?      Just a quiet night in, I think. Maybe watch  Downton Abbey , again. I'm obsessed. Though, I'm worried I've seen every episode so many times the characters will recognise me.

Honestly, this week has been  mental  at work. We’re trying to roll out this new project management system and everyone is just… resisting it. Like actively resisting. Old habits die hard, I guess.      Oh, don't I know it, love. Trying to get teenagers to embrace timed exams is a similar battle. They all think they work better under pressure, right up until they panic and draw a blank. It’s the same principle, really. People don't like change.      That’s the truth of it. I tried to explain the benefits of a new rotational grazing system to Old Man Hemmings last week. Nearly had a shouting match. Said his father did it one way for fifty years, and that was good enough. Stubborn as a mule, that one.      It’s just… frustrating. I spend hours researching the best way to do things, putting together training materials, and then it’s like talking to a brick wall. I had Brenda practically in tears because she can’t find the ‘status’ button anymore! It was right where it always was.      Bless Brenda. She’s always been a bit… technologically challenged. Remember when she thought a hyperlink was a type of magical portal?      Oh, I do indeed! She nearly clicked through to Narnia, she thought. Still, you’ve got to be patient, Daisy. They won't understand if you come at it all guns blazing. Little steps, that's what it needs.      I’m  trying  to be patient, Dad. But the deadline is looming, and the whole project is dependent on everyone using the system. My boss is already giving me ‘the look’. You know the one.      The ‘we need results, and we need them yesterday’ look? I know it well. Young Thomas at school is a master of that one. He thinks just glaring at us magically improves attendance rates.      Speaking of young Thomas, how’s your sister doing, Margaret? I haven’t spoken to her properly in ages. Is she still seeing that nice chap, David?      Oh, she’s good. Very good, actually. Things with David are… solid. They’re talking about moving in together, apparently. Sarah's thrilled, of course. Keeps asking if there's a wedding on the cards, though. You know how she is.      Oh, Sarah. Always planning the next big event. Last I heard, she was designing the seating plan for a wedding  she wasn’t even invited to .

Honestly, this risotto is taking  forever . I swear, every grain of rice is individually resisting being creamy. How was your day? Anything exciting happen at the office, beyond the usual paper mountains?      Exciting is… a strong word. Had my appraisal. Went… alright, I suppose. It was mostly just them saying all the things they  expect  me to be doing, which is fair enough, but feels a bit underwhelming when it's formally stated. You know? Like, "Yes, we noticed you’ve been doing your job." Riveting.      Oh, appraisals. The modern equivalent of a patronising pat on the head. Did you at least manage to subtly hint at a pay rise?      I tried! I brought up the increasingly complex reporting structures, the extra workload from Brenda’s maternity leave… the usual ammunition. They said they’d ‘consider it’. Which, translated from Management-speak, probably means ‘not a chance’. Fancy a pizza instead of risotto? I’m starting to crave something… less effortful.      Tempting,  very  tempting. But I’ve already got the stock bubbling. Besides, we’ve had pizza three times this week. Although, I did see Marks and Spencer are doing those stone-baked ones now. They looked… surprisingly decent. Speaking of M&S, did you see the new food hall layout? It's completely different.      No, haven't been in recently. They finally tackled that awful queuing system, I hope? It was always a nightmare getting a decent sandwich at lunchtime. And yes, their food is usually pretty good. They do a rather lovely duck confit. Although, conversationally, it feels wrong to talk about gourmet food when I'm reporting back on a mediocre appraisal.      Needs more parmesan. Look, don't dwell on it. You’re brilliant at what you do, and they’d fall apart without you. Honestly. Speaking of things falling apart… did you see that article about the horses being mistreated at that farm near Doncaster? Absolutely dreadful.      I did. Utterly sickening. It makes my blood boil. It's just… a lack of basic decency. Poor creatures. I’ve been donating to the equine welfare charity again. It’s not much, but…      Every little helps. Right, risotto almost there. You know, I attempted that cryptic crossword this morning. Got absolutely nowhere. Utterly defeated by a seven-letter word for ‘melancholy’.      Probably 'sadness'. Cryptic crosswords are designed to inflict pain, I’m convinced. I tried one on the train the other day and ended up just staring blankly at the paper, looking like a complete idiot.

Oh, honestly, I've been staring at my wardrobe for an hour. An  hour , and I still have absolutely nothing to wear. It's like, what even  is  the dress code for a Tuesday night at 'The Vault'?      Same, love, same. I’ve tried on about five different outfits and I just look… wrong in all of ‘em. I was thinking maybe the black jeans and a nice top? Standard, but it works, yeah? Though, thinking about ‘The Vault’… are we  sure  about heels?      Oh, heels are a definite no from me. Absolutely not. Last time I attempted heels and a night out, I ended up practically being carried home by Ben. It was not a cute look. I’m sticking to my chunky boots, thank you very much. Practical  and  stylish.      Boots are a good shout, yeah. I’m wearing my Doc Martens. Comfy is key, especially if we’re planning on being there 'til close. Plus, knowing us, someone will inevitably end up on the dancefloor and attempting moves they definitely shouldn't be attempting after a couple of cocktails.      You’re not wrong about the dancefloor attempts, are ya? I practically took out old Mr. Henderson at ‘Retro’ last month. Anyway, I think I'm gonna wear that floral dress - the one with the tiny straps. It’s a bit summery for October, but who cares? It’s pretty.      Oh, the floral one! Lovely! See,  you  have it sorted. I was thinking maybe something sparkly, but now I’m worried I’ll look like a right Christmas tree. And yeah, heels are debatable. I  want  to wear my red ones, they’re proper lovely, but I know I'll regret it after about half an hour.      Red ones are gorgeous, but you're right, ‘The Vault’ floor is always sticky. Sticky  and  slippery. Trust me, I've learned that the hard way. Plus, if we're having shots, balance becomes a…concern.      Shots are a  very  good point. We talked about doing tequila, didn't we? My stomach is already protesting just thinking about it. Though, if anyone’s gonna buy me a tequila sunrise, I'm not saying no.      Tequila sunrises are safer. Though, knowing Liam, he’ll try and get us all to do Jägerbombs. He’s on a mission to see how much he can make us regret our life choices.      Liam and his Jägerbombs.

…and honestly, the way Brenda from accounts just  assumes  I have time to rearrange her entire department’s Christmas social because she ‘forgot’… It’s just… exhausting. Some people seem to think ‘PA’ stands for ‘Personal Everything Arranger.’      Brenda, eh? Still wielding her organisational ineptitude as a weapon, I see. You'd think after five years she’d learn. It's that whole ‘bless her heart’ nonsense, isn’t it? A thinly veiled demand for you to fix her mess.      Exactly! It’s the ‘bless her heart’ that gets me. It's not endearing, it's manipulative! It made me think though… about soulmates. Do you think Brenda needs a soulmate who’s  really  good at logistics? Maybe that’s her karmic lesson.      A logistical soulmate. That’s a new one. I always thought soulmates were more about… resonance, you know? That feeling of finally  getting  someone. Not matching colour-coded spreadsheets.      Well, maybe there are different kinds. Like, a logistical soulmate is essential for blissful co-existence, and a deeper soulmate is for… spiritual growth and understanding the mysteries of the universe?      You've been reading those new-age books again, haven't you? The ones about past lives and energy fields.      Maybe. It’s just… I was thinking about our trip to Italy last year, and how effortlessly we navigated Florence. I mean, it was crowded and overwhelming, but with you, it felt…right. Like we’d done it all before, somehow.      Italy was lovely. Though I’m fairly certain we’ve never navigated Florence in powdered wigs and breeches. Speaking of which, I was imagining throwing a party, a proper Georgian affair. All candlelight and powdered faces. You’d look incredible in a pannier dress.      Oh, don't even  start . I'd trip over the panniers the moment I tried to move. And the hair! I can barely manage a decent ponytail, let alone a towering Georgian hairstyle! But… I do love the idea. Imagine the gossip. Who would we invite?      Oh, all the usual suspects, naturally. Austen, Byron, maybe a slightly cynical Dr. Johnson. And Cleopatra. She'd bring a certain… flair.      Cleopatra? Bit of a jump from Austen, don’t you think? Though, honestly, the drama would be  magnificent . I would want someone to play the harpsichord. And we  must  have a chocolate fountain. Even the Georgians deserve a chocolate fountain.      A chocolate fountain for Cleopatra.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork is getting ridiculous. They’re implementing this new compliance thing, and it feels like they just  want  us to fail. It’s all so… unnecessary.      Ugh, tell me about it. Government work is the same, just a different flavour of red tape. It’s like they actively avoid making things simple. My current project is all about streamlining benefits claims, and the irony isn’t lost on me – to streamline it, I have to fill out fifteen different forms  about  streamlining it.      Sounds about right. Though, I’m mostly battling sickness absence at the moment. Old Mr. Henderson's gone down with the flu  again . Honestly, I think he enjoys a day off. It's always just before a deadline, isn't it?      People take the mickey, don't they? Though, you can’t really blame someone for being genuinely ill. It’s just… the timing is always suspiciously convenient. Speaking of ill, how’s Mum doing with her knee? Has that physiotherapy helped at all?      She says it's a slow process. Still complains every time she walks the dog, but she’s managing. She’s already planning her summer garden, so I think she's feeling a bit more optimistic. She tried to get me to help with the seed ordering, said I have "a good eye for colour," which is just her being nice because I offered to make her a scarf.      Oh, the knitting! How’s that going, then? Is it turning into a full-scale operation? I swear last time I was here you had yarn overflowing from every surface.      It  was  a bit chaotic, wasn't it? I’ve calmed down a little since then. Started a proper project – a Fair Isle jumper for my nephew’s birthday. It's…ambitious. But I’m enjoying it. It's so mindful, you know? Just the rhythm of the needles. Completely different to spreadsheets.      I’ve always admired people who can knit. It looks so relaxing…and productive! I tried once, made a wobbly scarf that looked like it had been attacked by moths. It's a skill. You're very talented.      Nonsense! It just takes patience. Which, admittedly, is something I sometimes lack when dealing with clients. You'd think explaining simple contract terms wouldn't be so hard, but… you get all sorts. I had one chap last week who kept trying to barter with me for a discount using homemade jam.

Honestly, I'm starting to regret signing this lease. It's…cosy, yeah, but ‘cosy’ is code for ‘about to collapse in on itself’, isn’t it? And the heating! It’s either arctic or tropical in here.      Tell me about it. My room's above the bins. It’s…an experience. Though, on the plus side, I never have to walk  far  to take the rubbish out. Silver linings, eh? Did you hear back from Liam about Saturday? He was supposed to confirm if he could come to that gig.      Liam? Oh, he messaged me earlier. He can’t make it. Something about needing to work a shift to cover… well, he mumbled something about a "tax situation." Apparently, he forgot to register as self-employed when he started doing those freelance graphic design bits.       Tax situation ? Typical Liam. Always leaving things to the last minute. He's going to be stung, isn’t he? I swear, the amount of times I've had to explain basic things to him... like how to properly load a washing machine. It's baffling.      He's a creative, Liv. Logic isn't exactly his strong suit. Though, self-employment taxes  are  terrifying. I'm trying to avoid that whole world entirely. Mum keeps going on about how I should start a side hustle, but honestly, uni's enough of a hustle right now. Speaking of which, how's your dissertation going?      Don’t even  start  me on the dissertation. It's a complete disaster. I’ve got this massive writer's block. I’ve written and deleted the introduction like, five times. It's about post-industrial decline in Barrow, which sounds interesting until you actually have to  write  about it. It's just…grey and depressing.      Barrow? Oh, wow, that’s…intense. Actually, my grandma's from near there, Great Yarmouth. It’s had a similar thing happen with the shipyards closing down. You might find some interesting local history stuff if you look into it. It can make it less…grim.      Oh, that's a good shout, actually! I hadn't thought about local history specifically. I've been focused on the academic stuff, the theories and all that. Maybe a human element is what it needs.      See,  that’s  what I’m worried about with my project. It's all theory, all abstract. No real-world connection. I’m studying the semiotics of football chants, right?

Go on, lad, try this. It’s sea bass, beautifully fresh. Better than anything you get outta a freezer back home, eh?      Looks a bit…whole. Is there bones?      Oh, you soft thing! Yeah, there’ll be bones, but your Nana’ll show you how to get around ‘em. She’s a professional at fish dissection, remember? After all those years delivering babies, a few fish bones aren’t gonna scare her.      I’ve seen worse, believe me. Though I will say, dealing with a tiny little bone compared to… well, never mind. Anyway, this restaurant’s lovely, isn’t it? Proper little gem. Didn't think we'd find somewhere this good tucked away in Istria.      It is excellent. And the wine’s surprisingly good. A lot better than the stuff I usually end up with at those corporate dinners in London. All flash and no substance, usually. Speaking of substance, how's university going, Amelia? Still enjoying it?      It’s…it's good. Busy. I’m right in the thick of dissertation research now. It’s about the impact of social media marketing on small, independent businesses in the North West. Endless scrolling through Facebook, basically. Ironically.      Facebook, eh? All those young ‘uns glued to their phones. I still don’t get it, to be honest. Though I did see a picture of Buster – that’s Mrs. Higgins’ Yorkshire Terrier, remember? – on there last week. Wearing a little raincoat!      Buster! He's brilliant! He always tries to bite my ankles.      Sounds charming. Reminds me of my neighbour’s chihuahua. A tiny terror. I’d rather deal with complex spreadsheets, honestly. Which, unfortunately, is my life. What about you, Thomas? How’s school? Year 11, isn't it? Important year.      It’s alright. GCSEs are stressing me out a bit. Mr. Davies keeps saying we need to be revising  now , but it's ages away. Plus, Liam’s got a moped now. He keeps offering me rides.      Oh, Liam with the moped? Typical. Don’t you dare get on that thing, Thomas. You know your mum would kill him - and then probably me for not stopping you.      Absolutely not. They whizz around like maniacs on those things. Remember young Danny down the street? Broke his arm last summer on one of those. Dangerous. Stick to the buses, love. Safer. Though even  they  seem to drive faster in Bolton than anywhere else.

Right then. Cornwall. Proper job, that was. Though my knees are still tellin’ me about it. Not the walkin’, mind you, it was climbin' all those… steps.      Oh, don't start on the steps already, Arthur! You managed, didn't you? And you thoroughly enjoyed yourself, I saw the look on your face at Land's End. Honestly, you were like a little boy.      Well, it  was  Land's End, wasn’t it? Always wanted to see it. And that lighthouse… magnificent. Makes you feel… small, in a good way. Realised I'd never properly appreciated those things before, you know? Just took 'em for granted.      Speaking of appreciating things, I brought back a little something. Cornish fudge. Thought it might go down well with a cuppa. So, how  was  it? You two were rather vague on the details when you first got back, just lots of “lovely” and “exhausting”.      We were just a bit worn out, dear. It  was  lovely. Arthur was determined to do every coastal path he could practically get his hands on. And the YHA was… well, rather nice. Different. I wasn’t sure what to expect, volunteering like that.      Different’s good, Doris. Keeps the brain tickin’. Met some right characters at that YHA. A young couple doin' the whole of the South West Coast Path, on bicycles! Can you imagine? And a bloke tryin’ to cycle Yorkshire in a day. Yorkshire! Mad, absolutely mad.      Yorkshire in a day? Good grief. That sounds… ambitious, to say the least. Was the YHA busy? You were a bit worried about being stuck with hordes of teenagers, weren't you, Doris?      It wasn't too bad, actually. A mix of ages, mostly walkers and families. We were mainly helping with cleaning and making beds, the usual sort of thing. Although, Arthur did get rather involved in helping a little girl build a sandcastle. He's a soft touch, our Arthur.      She needed help with the fortifications! Had to defend it against the crabs, apparently. Little things like that, you know? They make the trip. Speaking of which, I took a shedload of photographs. Look at this one, taken near St. Ives. Beautiful, innit? Pity the light wasn’t quite right.      That  is  lovely. You’ve got a good eye for a composition, Arthur. Did you manage to get any of the lighthouses? You were going on about the lighthouses.

This shepherd’s pie is proper good, Liam. Honestly, miles better than anything I could knock up. You've outdone yourself, love. Though, it’s not quite  mam’s , is it? Nothing ever is.      Aye, well, I did follow a recipe. And your mam’s is legendary, isn't she? Everyone says so. Glad you like it, though. It’s a bit different from the building site dinners, that's for sure. Usually it’s a butty and a brew.      It  is  fantastic, Liam. Seriously. You’ve got the potato topping just right - nice and crispy. More interesting than my usual evening meal, which is…well, usually something I microwave after work. Production deadlines have been mental lately. It's all spreadsheets and shouting, honestly.      Spreadsheets and shouting, eh? Sounds thrilling, Esme. Though, I reckon a good bit of shouting would spice up conference organising, to be fair. It’s mostly just endless emails and placating speakers who want complimentary biscuits.      Complimentary biscuits? Seriously? People  demand  biscuits?      Oh, you wouldn’t believe. Especially the academics. They’re the worst. Think they deserve a whole buffet just for sharing their, well, sometimes quite dull, research. Anyway, how’s things going with Sarah, Liam? Still seeing her?      Yeah… we're still seeing each other. It’s…complicated. She's been a bit distant lately. I asked what was up, and she just said she’s got a lot on her mind with uni.      'A lot on her mind’ is code for something, isn’t it? My ex used that one  constantly . Always meant she’d met someone else or decided she hated the colour of my curtains.      Esme! Don’t fill his head with doom and gloom! It might genuinely be just uni. Though, I'll admit, that line's a bit suspect. Have you tried just… talking to her properly? Like, a proper date night, out of her usual routine?      I did ask her out last week. To that new Italian place, Bella Luna. She said she was swotting for an exam. It was a Friday night.      Ooh, dodgy. Bella Luna is nice though. They do a cracking tiramisu. She’s definitely avoiding you a bit, lad. Look, you’re a good bloke, Liam. Honest, hardworking… a decent cook, clearly. She’s lucky to have you.      She is. And honestly, don’t chase  too  hard. Let her come to you. It's way more dignified.

Oh my god, you will  not  believe the queues at security at Gatwick yesterday. Absolute chaos. Honestly, I think half of London decided to go to Barcelona at the same time as me.      Ugh, tell me about it. I had a similar experience getting back from visiting Mum. It was… lively. Barcelona though? How was it  really ? Pictures looked amazing on your Insta story. Did you manage to actually  do  anything besides queue and take photos?      It was…intense. Beautiful, obviously. The Sagrada Familia is just… breathtaking. And the food! Oh, the paella. I ate so much paella. But yes, there were a  lot  of people. Like, shoulder-to-shoulder on Las Ramblas a lot of the time. I did manage to get to Park Güell, which was worth fighting through the crowds for. And I spent an embarrassing amount of time just wandering around the Gothic Quarter, getting lost.      Sounds pretty exhausting, but good. I'm glad you had a good time, despite the hordes. I needed a weekend with Mum, a bit of quiet. She’s already planning my next visit and trying to set me up with the vicar’s son.      Oh, Mum’s still on the matchmaking train, then? Poor you. The vicar's son... doesn’t sound particularly thrilling. Speaking of thrilling… did you watch the finale of ‘The Serpent’?      Yes! Oh my god, gripping, wasn't it? I was on the edge of my seat. Truly terrifying to think that was all real. It’s just… sometimes I find all that true crime stuff a bit much after a day dealing with… well, you know.      Totally get that. It's a weird coping mechanism for some people, I think. But yeah, a bit draining. How was work anyway? Anything particularly… eventful?      It was okay. A new patient admitted, struggling understandably. It’s just… hard, watching people go through so much. It makes a weekend with Mum seem incredibly luxurious, in comparison. Anyway, enough doom and gloom. You mentioned paella. Are we ordering takeaway tonight? I'm feeling incredibly lazy.      Ooh, yes! That sounds perfect. I'm craving Spanish food again already. We could look for a decent tapas place. Actually, remember how we talked about going to Paris next spring? I was looking at flights earlier...      Oh my god, yes! Paris! I've been dreaming about Parisian pastries for months. Have you looked at hotels?

...Honestly, the whole thing was just a bit chaotic. Thirty Year Sixes, armed with paint and glitter, attempting mosaics. It looked less like ancient Rome and more like a particularly sparkly explosion in a craft shop.      Sounds…challenging. You’re a teacher, right? Primary school?      That’s me. History and a bit of art. Though, after today, I’m seriously questioning my life choices. It's rewarding, don't get me wrong, but the energy…it’s relentless. What about you? I remember you mentioning you ran your own business. What do you do?      I do. Well,  did , mostly. I sold it last year. Tech startup, actually. Software for small businesses, streamlining their invoicing and things. It was good while it lasted, a real rollercoaster. London-based, naturally. Difficult to escape the pull of the capital, you know?      Oh, wow. That’s quite a leap from mosaics and glitter! A tech entrepreneur. I can’t say I’ve ever known anyone who’s done that. Was it always the plan? To start your own thing?      Not initially, no. I did the whole graduate scheme thing at a big bank, utterly soul-destroying. Three years of spreadsheets and pretending to understand things I didn't. Then I met a couple of guys at a hackathon, we had a bit of an idea, and…well, one thing led to another. It was terrifying, amazing, exhausting, and ultimately, very lucrative.      I can imagine! It's rather brave to just…leave all that behind. I always considered teaching to be rather stable, comparatively. Though, sometimes I wonder if ‘stable’ is just a polite word for ‘stagnant’. Still, it pays the bills and I get the school holidays, and that's important. Being from Dorchester, I never really envisioned myself doing anything wildly ambitious.      Dorchester, right? Pretty countryside, I imagine? I'm a London boy through and through. Concrete and chaos are in my blood. But yeah, I get the stability thing. Actually, after selling the company, I felt…lost for a bit. Everything had been geared towards  building  something, and suddenly, it was done. I found myself just…drifting. Hence the trip to North Cyprus. Needed to recharge.      Oh, I understand that completely. When I have a particularly rough term, I daydream about running a little bookshop somewhere quiet. Just surrounded by books and peace. No glitter. No mosaic tiles.      Sounds idyllic. Much less stressful than chasing venture capital, I’d wager.

Honestly, I’m starting to think living with Liam and Chloe was a mistake. A  massive  mistake.      Woah, strong words, love. What’s happened now? Did Liam leave another mountain of dirty dishes again? 'Cause I swear, that lad thinks the dishwasher’s just a decorative feature.      It's not  just  the dishes, though that definitely contrib-… contributing. It’s everything. Chloe’s been having, like, full-on philosophical debates with the postman at 8 in the morning. 8! I was trying to study for my history essay. It's all 'the socio-economic implications of postal delivery' apparently.      No way! Chloe and the postman? That sounds… uniquely Chloe. But you know she gets like that when she's deep into something. Remember when she tried to explain astrophysics to Mrs. Higgins over the garden fence?      Aye, I remember. Mrs. Higgins looked absolutely terrified. But this is different. It disrupts everything. And Liam… he's just permanently glued to his computer, playing whatever game it is this week. He hasn’t seen daylight in three days, I swear. I asked him to take the bins out and he looked at me like I’d asked him to climb Everest.      He's always been a bit of a hermit, hasn’t he? But you two seemed to be getting on okay when we first moved in. What’s changed?      I think it's the pressure of Uni deadlines, to be honest. They’re both stressing about their postgrad stuff, and it’s making them both… odd. Liam’s become even more withdrawn, and Chloe’s just… more Chloe, but at a higher volume. It’s like the house is permanently vibrating with anxiety and philosophical questions.      Right. Postgrad life does do that to people. It's a different beast entirely. You were warned, weren't ya? I kept saying, ‘Don’t move in with postgrads, lass!’      You did! I ignored you. I thought, 'Oh, no, it’ll be fine, we're all friends!'. Silly me. Now I have to navigate a minefield of unwashed crockery, existential debates, and suspiciously silent gamers just to get to the kettle.      Well, you’re not stuck there forever, are you? It’s just for the rest of the term, right?      Aye, but it feels like a lifetime. And honestly, I don’t think I can handle another week of this. I'm running on caffeine and pure exasperation.

Right, that’s  that  done with. Absolute madness out there, I tell you. Madness! Couldn’t move for people.      Oh, was it really that bad, Arthur? I thought it was fairly quiet, considering it’s a Saturday. You’ve gone a bit red in the face.      Quiet? Quiet?! Margaret, you’ve got a selective memory, love. Remember old Mrs. Higgins with the shopping trolley? Nearly took my legs out from under me. And then the young lad on the scooter… Honestly, they shouldn’t  allow  those things in the market.      Now, now, Arthur. Mrs. Higgins is a bit unsteady on her feet, bless her. And the young lad was just enjoying himself. You exaggerate. Did you get everything on the list, at least? The apples for your crumble?      Apples are here. Bit pricey, they were. Nearly two pound for a pound of Coxes! Robbery, I tell you, absolute robbery. Used to be you could get a good bag for a shilling.      A shilling? Arthur, that was… well, a long time ago. Things change. And Coxes  are  the best for crumble. Remember your mother’s crumble? It wasn’t made with any old apple, oh no.      Aye, she made a good crumble, your mother-in-law did. Best in Norfolk, I reckon. Though I still maintain my recipe's getting pretty close.
