You think so, don't you? Be honest.      Of course, dear. It's almost as good. You put a little too much cinnamon in it, if I’m being  completely  honest. But a little cinnamon never hurt anyone.      A little? I use precisely the correct amount. It's a secret family recipe, you know. Passed down through generations... although, admittedly, mostly just from me to me.      That's right. Generations of Arthur. Did you manage to find that nice cheddar I asked for? The one from the farm shop?      Oh, bother. That’s right! The cheddar. I completely forgot. They'd run out, apparently. Some fancy food blogger had been in, and bought the lot for a photoshoot. A photoshoot, Margaret! For cheese!      Oh, Arthur. Honestly. A photoshoot. Well, we can manage without it. We’ve got that other block in the fridge, the mature one. That'll be fine for our sandwiches tomorrow.      It's not the  same . That farm cheddar’s got a proper bite to it. A tang. This other stuff’s a bit… bland. Still, at least I got the biscuits you wanted.

Right, well, that’s the garden mostly sorted for today. Just need to give the roses a good feed tomorrow, but they’re looking promising. Honestly, I think the slugs had a right party while we were away last week though. Young lad, you wouldn’t believe the holes in the hostas!      Hmm? Oh, yeah. Saw a massive one yesterday. Nearly stepped on it. Disgusting.      Disgusting? In my day, we didn’t call ‘em disgusting. We just called ‘em a nuisance! And you’d get out there with a bit o’ salt and sort ‘em out. None of this fancy slug pellet stuff.      Aye, salt was the answer. Good for the garden, good for the constitution, building character! Though I remember your mother, bless her soul, used to pick ‘em up and fling ‘em over the fence into old Mr. Henderson’s garden. Said he liked ‘em for his ducks.      Oh, don’t you start on your mother and Mr. Henderson’s ducks, Arthur! That’s a story for another day. Honestly, the things she got up to… Anyway, I was thinking, Michael, about the loft insulation. I had a look yesterday. It’s looking a bit thin, especially around the edges.      Loft insulation? Ugh. Sounds boring.      It isn’t boring, it’s important! It’s costing us money, lad. Heat rising, all that. I was thinking perhaps we could get someone in to have a look, give us a quote?      You always were sensible about things, Margaret. Never one to let pennies slip through your fingers. Though Arthur here used to think a penny saved was a penny… well, he’d just spend it on sweets.      A man’s gotta have his pleasures! Though I haven't had a good humbug in… well, a good while now, truth be told. Dentist wouldn’t be pleased.      Speaking of dentists, I’ve got mine next week. Dread it. They always tell me to floss more. It's a conspiracy, I swear. They just  want  to see me more.      Now, now, don't be silly. You need to look after your teeth. It’s just like looking after the roses – a bit of preventative care saves a lot of trouble later on. Do you two want another brew? I’ve just made a fresh pot.      Oh, go on then, Margaret. Just a little one. And maybe a biscuit? You always have those nice ginger ones.

Honestly, this wait is brutal. Thought this sports massage place would be more…efficient. My back’s killing me after hauling all those books back from uni.      Tell me about it. Dissertation life, eh? You Lincoln lot always seemed to have heavier reading lists than us Londoners. My shoulders are knotted from staring at a screen for twelve hours straight. Are you using one of those posture correctors? I saw an ad for one online. Looks… medieval.      Posture corrector? Sounds like something my nan would have. She's all about those magnetic bracelets for her arthritis. Swears they work wonders, though it's probably the placebo effect, innit?      Nan's are the best for that though, aren’t they? Mine thinks essential oils cure everything. Tried to get me to rub lavender on my exam papers for ‘focus’. Didn’t work, sadly. Didn’t even get a participation mark for the smell.      Alright, settle down, you lot. Tea will fix everything. Tea and complaining. Speaking of nan's, mine just got an iPad. She's convinced she’s a tech wizard now, sending me endless chain emails and questionable memes. It's terrifying.      Bless 'em. My grandad’s been trying to work out FaceTime for months. He keeps accidentally calling random people. Apparently, he spoke to a bloke in Australia for a good ten minutes thinking it was Uncle Barry.      That’s brilliant! Honestly, the older generation and technology… it’s a sitcom waiting to happen. I was showing my mum how to use TikTok the other day, and she genuinely thought all the dances were about cleaning.      Ha! My old man just uses the internet to look at fishing reports. Says it’s “vital research”. He’s got like, five different Facebook groups dedicated to rods and bait.      See, that makes sense. Focused interests. My dad's obsessed with vintage tractors. Hours spent on eBay. It's a whole world I don't understand. Though, you’ve got to admire the dedication, right?      Absolutely. It's nice they have hobbies. Keeps them busy. I'm just wishing I had that focus right now. This damn essay on post-structuralism is draining my soul. It's all just…words, isn’t it?      You and me both. I’m stuck on this theory about the commodification of nostalgia. Sounds clever, but it’s just circular reasoning wrapped in jargon. I was thinking of hitting the gym afterwards to clear my head.

Right, so, milk, bread, eggs… anything else anyone wants for breakfast tomorrow? I’m trying to get this shopping list sorted before I completely lose the will to live with this essay.      Ooh, get some of those little croissants, love. The ones from the bakery are lovely with a bit of jam. And don't forget butter. Proper butter, not that spreadable stuff.      Can we get some chocolate biscuits? The ones with the orange cream filling? PLEASE?      Always with the biscuits, aren’t you, lad? Alright, alright, chocolate biscuits are on the list. But not a whole packet each, understood?      Noted. Croissants, butter, chocolate biscuits…anything else food-wise? Oh, and speaking of things that are annoying…that wasp is back. It keeps buzzing around the light.      Oh, bother. It's probably desperate for sugar. I swear, they’re getting braver every year. I had one try and land  on  a mum in labour last week. Nearly gave her a heart attack!      Ewww! A wasp in a hospital? That's grim! Can’t you just…squash it?      Not ideal, son. Squashing them releases pheromones that attract more. Believe me, I read an article about it when I was doing some work with a hospital trust. It’s why they have those special traps.      So what  do  we do? I’m trying to concentrate and it’s doing my head in. Maybe a fly swatter? I think there’s one in the kitchen.      Fly swatters are a bit…aggressive. I’ve got some lavender oil somewhere. They don’t like that. I’ll have a rummage. It's a natural repellent. Safer than all those sprays, especially with your mum coming round tomorrow.      Mum’s coming?! Oh no. Does that mean we have to tidy up  properly ?      It does indeed. Your grandmother has standards, you know that. And frankly, so do I. We'll sort it out after the shopping list.      Speaking of things that sting… I think that mosquito bite I got on Saturday is getting worse. It’s all puffy and itchy.      Let me have a look. Hmm, it's a bit angry-looking. Have you put anything on it?      Just a bit of antihistamine cream. Didn’t seem to do much.      You should try some calamine lotion. It’s very soothing. Or even a paste of baking soda and water. That takes the itch out nicely. If it’s still bad tomorrow, you might need to get it checked, just in case it’s infected.

...and then Mr. Davies actually  said  that the reason I wasn’t getting full marks on the photosynthesis diagrams was because my leaves weren’t ‘aesthetically pleasing’! Honestly, aesthetically pleasing?! It’s SCIENCE, not art!      No way! Mr. Davies? Seriously? That’s… ridiculous. He’s always been a bit, well,  particular , hasn’t he? But aesthetic leaves? That takes the biscuit. Did you tell him that?      I tried! I was all like, “Sir, I understand the process, the chlorophyll, the whole thing!” and he just waved his hand and said, “Presentation matters, Amelia. It shows understanding.” I swear, he’s obsessed with neatness. It's a wonder he teaches science.      Ugh, that’s infuriating. It sounds exactly like something he'd do. Remember when he marked down Ben for his handwriting on the physics test? Even though Ben got all the answers right?      Oh god, yes! The handwriting saga! He just doesn’t get it. Anyway, enough about the nightmare that is Biology. What about P.E. today? Absolute chaos as usual, right?      Oh my gosh, don’t even get me started. Miss Harding made us do the bleep test. The  bleep test ! In this heat! I nearly died. I was definitely the first one out, I think. I just… collapsed.      You didn't! No way! Did you at least get a dramatic exit? Like, fall in slow motion?      Hardly! I just sort of… crumpled. It wasn’t graceful. Chloe was filming it on her phone, though. Said it was “peak Instagram content.”      Chloe is ruthless. She’d film a natural disaster if it meant getting likes. Speaking of Instagram, have you seen that new video from Saffron Barker? She’s doing a collab with a bunch of other school YouTubers. It’s all about revision tips.      Oh, yeah! I saw a snippet on my feed. It looks…intense. Like, colour-coded highlighters and perfectly organized notebooks intense. My revision space looks like a bomb went off. Mostly old biscuit wrappers and textbooks.      Same! My bed is basically a textbook graveyard. But seriously, maybe we  should  try some of Saffron’s tips? We've got the mocks coming up, haven't we? Actually, how are you feeling about those? Science is going to be the death of me after Mr. Davies' leaf debacle.      Honestly? Terrified. Especially Maths. I just…don’t get quadratic equations. It's like they're in another language. And then everyone else is talking about how easy it is, and it’s just… demoralizing.

Ugh, honestly, this cold is  dragging . I thought I’d shaken it off yesterday, but nope. Back with a vengeance. I feel like I've aged ten years overnight.      Aw, poor thing. You do sound dreadful. Here, drink this. Lemon and ginger, properly weaponised against the sniffles. Did you take any Lemsip this morning?      I did. And a paracetamol. It’s just… it’s really knocked my appetite. I tried to make some soup, thinking that would help, but the thought of food just makes my stomach turn a bit.      That’s not good. Remember that dodgy Thai takeaway we had last month? You weren't feeling brilliant after that. Is it anything like that?      No, no, not like that at all. That was… a full-on biohazard situation. This is just general bleurgh. More dreary than dramatic. Although, thinking about it, I did watch that episode of  Masterchef  last night, and Lloyd Grossman seemed awfully close to the food. Maybe he secretly inoculated everyone with a rogue chill?      Lloyd Grossman’s a health risk?! That’s a new one. He always seemed perfectly polished and…preserved. Honestly, though, getting sick always makes me think about vaccinations. Have you had your flu jab this year?      I did! Got it done in October. Which is probably why it’s ‘just’ a cold and not full-blown flu, fingers crossed. It’s just… inconvenient. I’ve got that big presentation on the body language recognition software at the end of the week, and I need to be on top form.      Oh, right, the one you’ve been stressing over? The bit about how the AI can detect micro-expressions? That sounds fascinating, actually. It’s amazing what they're doing with cameras and algorithms these days.      It is, but explaining it to non-tech people is the nightmare. And sounding confident while simultaneously feeling like death warmed up… that’s the challenge. I'm worried I'll be all shaky and red-nosed, giving away everything  I'm  trying to read in other people.      You'll be fine. You’re brilliant at presenting, even when you’re not feeling your best. Besides, a little bit of vulnerability can actually be endearing. People might even cut you some slack if you apologise for sounding a bit croaky.      You always know what to say. It’s just… I’ve been reading up on what happens when the system  misreads  body language, and it’s a bit terrifying.

Right. This is hopeless. Absolutely hopeless. I've got Q, X, Z… and a load of vowels. It's like the Scrabble gods are deliberately mocking me.      Oh, come on, Eleanor. Don't be so gloomy. You had a good turn last round with ‘JAZZ’. Though, I must admit, I was eyeing up that Z myself.      Don’t underestimate the power of a well-placed vowel, dear. Sometimes simplicity is key. Though, frankly, this board is a bit of a mess. You two are just flinging words down willy-nilly.      Now, now, Morag. A bit of strategic chaos never hurt anyone. Builds character, you know. Reminds me of my boys at school… utter mayhem sometimes, but brilliant, sparkling mayhem.      Sparkling mayhem? This is just frustrating! Honestly, I spent half an hour trying to decipher a word for these letters and came up with zilch. Reminds me of trying to navigate the Trafford Centre last Saturday. Gridlock. Absolute gridlock. Needed a forklift truck to get out.      You’re not wrong there. We went for those new walking boots for young Thomas and it was a nightmare. Honestly, you'd think everyone in Greater Manchester decided to shop simultaneously. Did you manage to get the rosemary for the lamb, by the way?      Eventually. After an age in a queue at the butcher’s. Old Mr. Henderson was holding court as usual. Talking about his prize-winning marrow. Honestly, the stories he tells…      Mr. Henderson and his marrows. A Manchester institution. Though I do find it slightly unsettling how much he anthropomorphises them. He was telling me last week that Beatrice, his largest marrow, was feeling “a bit under the weather”.      Oh, Morag, you’re terrible! He’s just a harmless old man with a passion for gardening. It’s good to have hobbies in one’s retirement. Speaking of hobbies, did you see that article in  The Wire  about the resurgence of vinyl?       The Wire ? I haven’t leafed through that in ages. Sarah was showing me some vintage record covers on Facebook earlier. All those psychedelic designs. Quite something. She’s become a bit of a social media fiend, our Sarah.      She posts everything, doesn't she? Breakfast, the cat, her feet… honestly, I don’t know how she finds the time. I tried posting a photo of my begonias last week, and I just couldn’t be bothered to write a witty caption.

Oh, this is a lovely little break, isn’t it? Honestly, all that talk of easements and rights of way… gives a body a headache. Fancy another biscuit, Arthur? They're rather good, shortbread, proper buttery.      Don't mind if I do, Margaret. Thank you. And yes, a blessed respite it is. All very important, of course, this preservation work the TME does, but intensely detailed. Reminds me a little of the precision needed in my line of work, really. Though, rather less mud involved, thankfully.      Precision? You and your inventions! Always fiddling with things, making them  better . You always did have a knack, Arthur. I remember you telling me, years ago now, about that first printing system you designed. Something to do with… offset lithography, wasn't it?      Offset, that’s the one. It wasn’t the first, of course, but I managed to streamline the whole process. Made it much more efficient for packaging, mainly. Before that, it was all rather cumbersome and slow. I patented a system for automatic plate changing, that was the key. That’s what got things moving.      Automatic… oh my. Sounds terribly complicated. I barely understand how my inkjet works these days, let alone the innards of a lithographic press! But it must have been immensely satisfying, seeing something  you  designed revolutionise an industry.      It had its moments. The real satisfaction came from marketing it, oddly enough. I spent a good portion of my career over in Germany, at the big trade fairs. Drupa, IGEM... those were something else. The scale of it all! Hundreds of huge machines, the air thick with ink and the smell of metal.      Germany! You always seemed so… at home there. I always suspected you enjoyed the efficiency, the orderliness. Quite the contrast to Somerset, eh?      Perhaps you're right! I did appreciate the German approach to engineering, certainly. Very methodical. And the exhibitors were… enthusiastic, shall we say. High pressure, but good fun. I remember one year, we had a massive demonstration planned – a live printing run of a full-colour catalogue. Everything was set, lights, cameras, action… and the plate-changing mechanism jammed five minutes before showtime.      Oh, dear! Disaster!      Near enough. But I'd built the thing, so I knew exactly where the fault lay. Climbed inside and managed to fix it  during  the demonstration. Didn’t miss a beat. The crowd went wild! They thought it was part of the show.

Honestly, Dad, this is  miles . Are we even halfway yet? Everything just looks…green. And fields.      Not quite halfway, love, but getting there. Another three, maybe four hours. More green is good, though, isn't it? Beats concrete any day. Thinking about uni applications already, though, distracting yourself from the scenery?      A little. Miss Davies keeps going on about needing a ‘personal statement’ that’s ‘unique and insightful’. Insightful about  what , though? I’m sixteen! What deep philosophical thoughts am I supposed to have brewing?      She's just doing her job, sweetheart. Don’t overthink it. Think about what you enjoy. Remember that debate you had with Mr. Henderson in English about whether language  shapes  thought, or thought shapes language? That was pretty insightful for a sixteen-year-old.      Oh god, that! He was convinced it was all Whorfian relativity, and I was arguing it was…well, both, I think? It was ages ago. It felt important at the time, but now… Is "Whorfian" even spelt right? I always mess up the 'o'.      It is. W-h-o-r-f-i-a-n. See, English is a nightmare, isn’t it? All these weird spellings. Why is ‘Leicester’ pronounced ‘Lester’? Makes no sense.      Exactly! And 'Worcestershire' sauce? It's a tongue twister  and  a geographical anomaly. It feels like someone just threw a bunch of letters at a wall. It’s fascinating, actually, the etymology of words. Where things  come  from. Like “quinoa”. It sounds so…new age, but it’s ancient.      Ancient indeed. From the Andes, wasn’t it? Trying to get you to eat it with dinner last night. You made a face like I’d offered you live worms.      It’s…bouncy. And a bit bland. I'm a creature of habit, okay? Give me pasta any day. Speaking of habits, do you think people are getting more pedantic about grammar? It feels like everyone's a self-appointed language police officer online.      Probably. Everyone’s got an opinion and a keyboard these days. It's always been changing though, hasn’t it? My dad used to complain about ‘the youth’ splitting infinitives. Now it’s about using ‘literally’ when you don’t mean literally.      Oh,  that . Drives me mental. It's like, people just lose the meaning of words! It’s weird. Oh, look! A service station! Do you think they'll have decent coffee?      One can only hope.

Right, so Dad reckons he can ‘supervise’ the gravy making this year. Honestly, it's more likely he'll just comment on how  I’m  making it wrong. He’s a right stickler, you know? “Needs more beef dripping, lass!” It’ll be the story of Christmas dinner, I swear.      Sounds…intense. My nan’s the same with the Yorkshire puddings. You wouldn’t  believe  the instruction. “Must be lard, never oil! And room temperature eggs, are you listening, Liam?” Like I’m deliberately trying to ruin Christmas.      Oh, they’re all the same, aren’t they? The older generation. Think they’ve got a monopoly on…well, everything, really. Your father, Amelia, sounds a bit like my wife was. God rest her soul. Always had an opinion on how the spuds should be peeled.      It’s just…it’s Christmas! Supposed to be relaxed. He hasn’t even offered to  help  with anything beyond critiquing. I’m coordinating the whole thing! Getting the turkey, making sure there’s enough Brussels sprouts…which, let's be honest, nobody actually  wants  but tradition, innit?      Brussels sprouts are a crime against vegetables, definitely. I'd happily swap 'em for, like, extra roasties. My mum just lets me get away with everything. She’s brilliant. Says as long as it tastes alright, who cares how I make it?      Your mother sounds a wise woman, Liam. Mine...well, she believed firmly in doing things  The Right Way . And The Right Way was always how  she  did them. It’s funny, though. I remember one year, she accidentally used salt instead of sugar in the pudding. Complete disaster. But we all laughed about it for years.      That  is  a good one. See, maybe a bit of chaos is good for Christmas. Though, I suspect Dad would consider salty pudding a personal affront. He’s a bit…particular. Did you two have a nice Bonfire Night? We had a little do up in Doncaster, but it was freezing.      Yeah, not bad. Went to a display with my mates in town. Loads of fireworks. Always a good laugh. Though it's expensive, all that. Struggled a bit with the cost this year, to be honest. Everything’s gone up, hasn’t it?      You’re telling me. Pension doesn't stretch as far as it used to. Used to be able to afford a proper Christmas, you know? Presents for everyone, a big roast, everything.

…and honestly, the worst part of the whole shift wasn’t even the rowdy stag do, it was explaining to someone why a Long Island Iced Tea  isn’t  actually just iced tea. You wouldn’t believe the looks.      Oh, bless them. People are wonderfully…uninformed sometimes, aren't they? It’s probably the name. It  sounds  innocent. Though, I get similar things with language. People assume if you speak one foreign language, you automatically know a dozen.      Exactly! Like, ‘Oh, you’re a bartender, you must know every cocktail recipe ever invented!’ No, mate, I know the ones on the menu and a few I’ve made up to get through quiet Tuesdays. So, how's the teaching going? Still wrestling with subjunctive moods and the perfect tense?      Always. It’s a constant battle. This term, I’m teaching a group preparing for their GCSEs. It’s…intense. They're convinced grammar is a personal attack. But it’s rewarding when it clicks, you know? Seeing them finally grasp a concept they've struggled with. It’s a bit like making a perfect cocktail, I suppose. All the elements have to be right.      A bit more pressure, though, isn't it? A bad cocktail just means someone has a slightly disappointing evening, a bad grade…well. I wouldn’t know, I tackled uni and then decided I preferred mixing drinks to, y'know, analysing Milton.      A sensible decision, perhaps! What  did  you study, anyway? I always meant to ask.      History, actually. Which is ironically useful for remembering customer orders. “Right, old Mr. Henderson? That’s like the Battle of Hastings, always a pint of bitter, predictable and reliable.” It’s a terrible joke, I know.      No, it's good! Though, I'm guessing remembering dates and monarchs doesn’t translate  directly  to pouring pints. You're from Birmingham originally, though, right? I've always thought it was a really vibrant city.      Born and bred. Though I did spend three years getting thoroughly rained on in York during uni. Best and worst experience of my life, probably. And yeah, Brum is alright. Bit rough around the edges, but it's got a heart. You down south, aren’t you? Hitchin, you said?      That's right. Hertfordshire. It's… a bit different. Quieter. Less character, perhaps. Though the commute into London is easy. I actually had my driving test last week.      Oh, really? How did it go?

Oh, bother. Look at the time! Tea break’s been and gone, hasn't it? We promised young Thomas we'd be ready with biscuits at half past.      Aye, time does fly when you’re…well, when you’re talkin’ about all sorts, doesn't it? Leastways, it does for an old fella like me. Are you having another cuppa, Marjorie? This one's lovely, bit weak, mind you, but lovely.      Actually, I was just finalising these for the fundraiser. I think we’ve got a good selection of photos for the banner – the bell ringing ones are particularly good, don't you think? Show off the tower nicely.      Oh, those  are  nice, David. Very patriotic looking. Though, are you sure about using that one of Arthur looking so… intense? He always pulls that face when he's concentrating. Might frighten the locals.      Frighten the locals? Nonsense, Marjorie! That’s Arthur bein’ Arthur! Seriously focused, he is. Best bell ringer in Norfolk, I reckon, though don’t you tell him I said that, he's got a big 'ead. But tell me, David, how’s that donation box comin' along? Remember we said we wanted something…distinctive?      It’s nearly finished. I’m varnishing it as we speak. I thought a nice, sturdy oak would be suitable. It's rather large, though, I hope it doesn’t take up too much room. I was picturing it near the entrance, perhaps with a little sign explaining it's for the Gambia project.      Oh, brilliant. The Gambia. Always loved hearing your stories about that place, David. Such a beautiful country, even with all the troubles. You really did a good thing, setting up that small medical clinic.      He did. A proper gent, our David. Though I still can’t get me 'ead around it all… helpin' folk out there when there’s need right 'ere, you know? Not that I don’t admire it, mind. It's just… I read an article the other day, about someone… well, pretending they was ill to get attention, you know? Munchausen’s Syndrome, they called it. Makes you wonder, doesn’t it?      That’s a rather abrupt jump, Arthur. From Gambia to a psychological disorder? I don’t see the connection.      Arthur, dear, don’t start on that now. It's a bit upsetting, isn’t it? Focusing on the good we’re trying to do is much more productive.

...Honestly, the jump scares in that new ‘Hollow Creek’ film were ridiculous. Like, aggressively predictable. You  knew  the creepy doll was going to move when the lights flickered, didn't you?      Oh, come on, Liam, you’re such a scaredy-cat! I thought it was genuinely unsettling. The atmosphere was brilliant, and I actually jumped a couple of times. Though, yeah, the doll was a bit cliché.      I haven’t seen it yet. Is it worth the stress? I’ve been trying to cut down on horror because it messes with my sleep. I downloaded this mindfulness app, ‘SereneScape’, though, and it’s actually pretty good. It has guided meditations and ambient noises.      SereneScape? Ooh, I need that. I've been trying to sleep properly for weeks. Work’s just been…a lot. New buyer is a nightmare, constantly changing her mind about everything. Honestly, it’s exhausting. What about you, Chloe? Still hearing good things about your new project?      Yeah, it's keeping me busy, which is good. A bit stressful too, deadlines are tight. But at least it's interesting. And speaking of stressful, did you hear back from Ben about Saturday? I thought you two were supposed to be heading to that new ramen place?      He cancelled. Said something about his nan needing help with her phone. Classic Ben, always ‘family emergencies’ when something better comes along. I’m starting to think I’m just someone to fill awkward silences.      Oh, Liam, that's rubbish! You're brilliant. He's just…flaky. Don’t let him get you down. Maybe we could all go out on Saturday instead? We haven’t done anything as a group in ages.      I’m in! I need a proper night out, something to take my mind off spreadsheets and demanding buyers. Although, ramen  does  sound amazing. Is that still on the cards?      Definitely. If Ben's too busy chatting to his nan, more ramen for us! Seriously though, I'm getting a bit fed up with his disappearing acts. It’s happened a few times now.      Tell me about it. It's just… irritating. It feels like I'm putting in the effort and he’s just…there. I saw Sarah and Mark last weekend, they were talking about their holiday to Greece. They sent me pictures. Turquoise water, white sand... it looked incredible. I need a holiday.      Greece sounds dreamy! I've been saving up for a trip to Italy, maybe next spring.

Honestly, Marjorie, this traffic was  brutal . Took us nearly two hours to get back from Ipswich, and half of that was just crawling along the A14.      Two hours, you say? Crikey. I remember when you could fly down that road. Used to get to Felixstowe in under an hour, no bother. What was holding you up this time, Arthur? Roadworks again?      Roadworks, of course! Always roadworks. And then, to top it all off, some clot decided it was a good idea to merge without looking. Nearly had a prang right in front of the Orwell Bridge. Gave me a right fright, it did.      Oh dear, Arthur! You must be careful. Your heart isn't what it used to be, is it? Though, knowing you, you probably gave him a piece of your mind.      I did lean on the horn, Marjorie. A good, long blast. I doubt he heard me over his own…well, let's just say lack of common sense. Honestly, the standard of driving these days. It’s appalling. All this rushing about.      They don’t have the patience, do they? Back in my day, you waited your turn. And you gave way to people. Now it's just everyone for themselves. Remember old Mr. Pye down the lane? He’d wave anyone through, didn’t matter what. A proper gentleman.      He did. A lovely man, Mr. Pye. Used to bring us gooseberries from his garden. Though I have to say, I’m rather glad I don’t  have  to drive anymore. The stress of it all…I’d rather take the bus, thank you very much. Even if it takes three times as long.      The bus, eh? You’re a braver woman than I am, Marjorie. Trying to navigate that bus timetable… it's a puzzle in itself. And don't get me started on the stops. They’ve moved half of them, haven’t they? I’d end up in Attleborough by mistake.      You and your sense of direction, Arthur! Never had much of one, have you? Remember that time we went to Cromer and ended up in Wells-next-the-Sea?      That was  your  map reading, Reginald! And I distinctly remember you saying “Turn left here, looks like a shortcut.” Shortcut to oblivion, more like!      Oh, you two are terrible! Always squabbling like an old married couple. Though I suppose you are, in a way. Lifelong friends, anyway.

Honestly, the M6 was a nightmare getting here. Absolute standstill for twenty minutes just south of Birmingham. I swear, every time I think about moving further north, I remember the roads.      Oh, you’ll get used to it, love. It’s never  not  busy, is it? Though, I do miss the relative calm of the Dublin roads. It was a different pace of life altogether. Though getting  to  Dublin Airport... now  that  was a trial.      Airports are the bane of my existence. I used to fly out to Azerbaijan regularly, for work obviously. The security queues, the delays… it aged me ten years, easily. Used to say I needed a holiday  from  the holiday.      Azerbaijan! Wow, that’s a long way. I’ve only really done European city breaks, mostly for conferences. Makes me appreciate a good train journey even more. No baggage restrictions, you can actually stretch your legs… though British rail isn’t exactly known for its punctuality.      Punctuality… a foreign concept. Even here, the buses are… optimistic with their timetables. Speaking of travelling though, have you two sorted out the logistics of the house move properly? It's a big undertaking, and you, Sarah, you are the organiser. Don’t let David get away with doing nothing.      He  has  been surprisingly proactive, actually. He's already booked the removal van and started decluttering. It's terrifying the amount of stuff we've accumulated. I'm more worried about convincing the solicitor it’s all going to go through smoothly. They’re… thorough, to say the least.      Solicitors. Don't even get me started. After retiring, I thought I’d finally escaped paperwork, but no. Dealing with pensions and all that carries its own brand of bureaucratic nonsense. It’s enough to give a man a headache. And my blood pressure isn’t what it used to be, you know. The doctor keeps harping on about cholesterol.      Oh, doctors… always harping on. Mine keeps telling me to take up gardening. Gardening! As if I haven't spent enough time weeding equations for the last thirty years. She doesn't understand the need for stillness, does she? Though, I suppose it's better than staring at four walls all day. Are you looking after yourself, David? Really looking after yourself?      As well as can be expected, Mary. I walk the dog, don’t I? That’s exercise. And I try to eat my greens, mostly because Sarah nags me about it.

Mum! You will  not  believe what Chloe posted on Insta. It's… well, it's just ridiculous. She's claiming she aced the history test without even studying, and she was totally panicking about it all week!      Oh, Chloe. Always needing to be the centre of attention, is she? Honestly, social media brings out the worst in some people. Still, better she’s bragging about a test than something worse. More importantly, though… I have news. Good news.      Yeah, well, it's all fake, isn't it? Everyone filters everything. What news? Is Dad bringing back fish and chips? Because I'm starving. College was  brutal  today, Mr. Henderson went on a tangent about the Magna Carta that lasted a full half hour.      No fish and chips, sadly. Though that does sound lovely now you mention it. This is much better news, actually. Remember my bike? The one that went missing last month?      Oh!  Your  bike! The red one? The really nice one you said was practically brand new? What about it? Don't tell me it turned up… covered in mud and with a flat tyre?      Worse, actually. And better. It was found. The police called this morning. Apparently, they raided a place in St Leonards, a bit of a known chop shop, and there it was. A little scratched, needs a new lock obviously, but otherwise… intact!      No way! Seriously? That’s amazing! I can’t believe it. That bloke who nicked it must be… well, he deserves everything he gets. I was so gutted for you, Mum. You loved that bike. You used to cycle everywhere.      I did, didn’t I? It was my little bit of freedom, and I was so annoyed with myself for leaving it unlocked, even just for a minute. I’d gotten so complacent. Anyway, they think it was part of a bigger operation, targeting bikes in the seafront area. It's good they caught them.      Still, I can’t believe they found it. That's proper detective work! So, when can you get it back? Can we go pick it up? I'll come with you! We could cycle along the promenade afterwards… once it's fixed, of course.      They said tomorrow afternoon. I’m planning on going then. And yes, you can definitely come with me. And a cycle  is  on the cards, though maybe a short one to start. It's been a while since I’ve been on two wheels, and I'm a little rusty.

Right, okay… if I take the gray route from Plymouth to Penzance… that’s seven, and then I can connect to… oh, brilliant! That completes my route to Bristol. Take  that , Rhys!      Easy there, Sarah! Don't get too cocky. I’ve still got a sneaky long route building up. It’s all about strategic discarding, you know. Keeps people guessing. Though, honestly, I’m mostly just hoping to block Gareth before he accidentally claims the entire Southwest.      Accidentally? I’m a master strategist! It’s a calculated expansion of my rail empire. Besides, someone needs to connect Wales to the rest of the country. You two are always ignoring us.      Now, now, Gareth. Don’t start a political debate over Ticket to Ride. It's meant to be relaxing! Though, speaking of connections… did you know the Hereford to Shrewsbury line used to be incredibly important for transporting livestock?      Oh, my Nan used to tell me stories about that, Dai. All the cattle markets. She said you could smell it for miles on a windy day! Not exactly pleasant, she added.      That's a vivid image, Bron! I grew up around farms in South Africa, so I know that smell. It’s…distinctive. But back to the game. Rhys, are you deliberately trying to make my life difficult? You  knew  I needed that blue route!      Me? Never! Merely exercising my right to efficient route planning. Although, I do recall you blocking me from Newcastle last time… retribution is a dish best served with little plastic trains.      He’s forgetting the time he completely cut off my access to Edinburgh. Pure malice!      You youngsters and your competitive spirits. Back in my day, we played games for enjoyment, not world domination. Though I remember one particularly fraught game of Monopoly… nearly ended a friendship, it did.      Oh, Monopoly can be  brutal . My sister and I haven't spoken properly since the great Park Lane incident of '98.      You’re all terrible. Honestly. Speaking of travel, though – remember that train journey we took through the Swiss Alps? The one where the scenery was so incredible, and the train barely moved?      How could I forget? It took us four hours to crawl twenty miles! But yes, the views… absolutely breathtaking. It was the most scenic, yet infuriatingly slow, journey of my life.      I spent the entire time trying to work out how the gradient worked.

Right, that  should  block you nicely. Unless you’ve got some devious card up your sleeve, of course. It’s funny how competitive we get over ‘Carcassonne’. Seriously, it's just laying tiles.      Devious is my middle name, darling. Though, admittedly, it's actually David. And you’re right, it  is  ridiculous. We’re both lecturers, capable of complex thought, and here we are, strategizing over medieval farmland. Though, I suspect it’s less about the farmland and more about not letting the other one win.      Precisely! It’s a principle. And honestly, your road-building skills are frightening. You're ruthless. Remember last time? You completed, like, three roads before I even had a single meeple out.      A good strategist anticipates their opponent. Besides, you were distracted by your mum offering another biscuit. It’s a cultural thing, you know? Norfolk hospitality. Endless tea and biscuits. Londoners aren’t quite so… generous with the baked goods.      Oh, don’t start on the London versus Norfolk debate. It’s a tired trope. Though you're not wrong about the biscuit situation. Mum literally hovers. Honestly, it's like a competitive sport for her. “Another shortbread, love? Just one more…” It’s a marked difference from your family’s approach, isn't it? Much more… reserved.      Reserved is a polite way to put it. My mum would offer you a choice of artisanal water. And then dissect its mineral content. It’s not a lack of kindness, it’s just… different. We didn’t really  do  casual dropping-in for tea and games. More scheduled visits, carefully planned three-course meals.      See? Totally different upbringing. Which probably explains why you get so perplexed by pub culture up here. You've still not fully grasped the nuances of a proper Norfolk pub quiz.      I’m trying! It’s just… the speed. And the depth of local knowledge. Last time, they asked about obscure medieval saints specific to this county. Medieval  saints ! In a pub! I felt utterly out of my depth. London pubs are more about… trendy cocktails and loud music.      Oh dear. It's a different beast entirely. And the drinking. It’s not about getting absolutely plastered, it's about… prolonged social lubrication. And trying to impress Old Man Hemmings with your general knowledge. It’s very performative.      Performative is a good word for it. It’s… a show. London drinking is more…functional.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of cardboard from unpacking is ridiculous. I thought I’d be feeling settled by now, but it’s still everywhere. It’s like living in a recycling centre.      Tell me about it! Moving is  always  worse than you remember. I thought after uni, I was done with that chaos. Turns out, life has other plans, doesn’t it? At least you've  got  somewhere. I'm still dithering about whether to actually look properly, or just stay put and rearrange.      Rearranging’s always a good option, love. Less upheaval. Though, you do get to a point where you just need a fresh start, don’t you? This gravy needs a bit more… well, everything, actually. Anyone fancy a taste test?      I'm good for a taste test, Kerrie. Fresh starts are good, but the  process ... that’s what gets me. Like, finding a decent removal company that doesn’t charge the earth. And then the council! The bin situation in Peterborough is… baffling. Apparently, my old address had recycling collected on Tuesdays, but the new one is Thursdays. How am I supposed to remember?      Oh, bins. A universal source of stress. In Wegberg, it was all colour-coded and incredibly strict. You got a warning for the  smallest  infraction. It's probably why I’m so anxious about getting it right here. And honestly, trying to compare councils... It's a full-time job!      It's a nightmare, isn't it? I spent a good hour on the phone with Swansea council trying to find out when they’re taking old white goods. Apparently, it’s a three-week wait, and they only collect on specific days depending on your postcode. It's easier to just hire a van and take it to the tip yourself, but my back isn't what it used to be.      Three weeks! That’s insane. I'm still waiting for British Gas to connect the gas. They said last Friday. Last. Friday. I’ve been cold showers all week.      Oh no! That’s awful. You'd think in this day and age, they'd be more organised. Speaking of organised… how’s your crafting going, Kerrie? Have you managed to get back to your pottery?      Slowly, slowly. I did manage to finish that birdhouse for old Mrs. Davies next door. She was chuffed to bits. Keeps me busy, you know? Something to do with my hands.

Honestly, this traffic is mental, innit? Feels like we’ve barely moved since we left Bethnal Green. You'd think heading  towards  the North Circular would be quicker, not slower.      Patience, Leo. It's Friday afternoon. Everyone’s escaping the city, or trying to. And remember what your driving instructor said about anticipating? You were always a bit… enthusiastic with the accelerator.      Enthusiastic? Mum, I was 18, had just passed my test, and that Vauxhall Corsa felt like a spaceship. This… well, this is sensible. A Volvo. Very… you.      Sensible is good! I’ve seen enough scrapes and near misses with your father’s various sporty choices over the years. Besides, a solid car for lugging presents to your Aunt Carol is vital. Speaking of which, did you actually  get  her something? Last year was… a bit of a disaster, wasn’t it?      Don’t remind me. The novelty socks were a bad call. I thought she'd appreciate the irony, being a librarian and all. She didn’t. This year’s sorted, though. Found a first edition of a Virginia Woolf essay she's always wanted. Proper little gem, online.      Honestly, Leo, that’s lovely. Really thoughtful. She’ll be over the moon. It’s the thought that counts, of course, but a bit of research helps. It’s like with the  TLS  - people don't appreciate the effort that goes into sourcing good copy these days. Everyone thinks they can be a critic.      The  TLS  is still going strong then? I always thought print was… well, you know. On its way out. Everyone’s reading everything on their phones now.      It is, surprisingly. There’s a resilience to it. A seriousness. People still want curated, thoughtful reviews. Though, admittedly, getting younger eyes on it is the battle. We’re trying to build up the digital side, podcasts, online pieces… but nothing quite replicates the feel of holding the paper, does it? It's a different experience.      Nah, you’re right. I get that. It's… slower. More considered. Like, scrolling through Twitter is just noise. A good book – or a good review in a weighty, prestigious journal – feels… important.      Exactly! It’s about slowing down. Something we all need to do a bit more of, frankly. Even  you , rushing around trying to save the world one essay at a time. How’s the dissertation coming along? Still wrestling with post-colonial narratives in the poetry of Ted Hughes?

...Honestly, the worst part wasn’t even the sunburn, it was the pigeons in Barcelona. Absolute  units  they were, brazen as you like, trying to steal chips right outta your hand. I swear one looked me dead in the eye and thought, "Yeah, you're not gonna stop me."      Oh, stop it, Liam! Pigeons? That’s your big holiday horror story? I was expecting tales of dodgy street performers or getting lost in the Gothic Quarter.      Aye, pigeons are proper cheeky, aren't they? Reminds me of that time down Runcorn Locks, and old man Higgins was feeding 'em… absolute chaos. They were landing on his head!      Oh God, I remember that! He didn’t even flinch, just kept scattering bread. You’d think he  wanted  it. So, Barcelona, then? Was anything actually good? Apart from the looming threat of avian larceny?      It was brilliant, actually! The Sagrada Familia… just breathtaking. And the food. Tapas, paella… I think I gained about half a stone just eating my way through the city. Bit of a shock to the system coming back to Mum's roast dinners.      Half a stone? Ambitious. I managed a full stone in Italy last year. All the pasta and gelato. No regrets. Speaking of Italy, remember Sarah’s trip a few years back? The one where she tried to order a pizza in pigeon Italian?      Oh, don’t remind me. It was mortifying! I was absolutely howling. She thought “pepperoni” was… something else entirely. Involved a lot of hand gestures and a very confused pizza chef.      She asked for a pizza topped with feathers, didn’t she? I'll never live that down. It was "peperoncino”, spicy peppers!      Feathers! That's brilliant. She’s always been a bit…direct, hasn't she? No filter whatsoever. Remember when she told Mr. Thompson, her headteacher, his tie was a terrible colour?      Oh yeah! Bold move. Actually, that's a bit like my Uncle Barry. He once told a posh waiter in London his soup tasted like dishwater. I thought we were going to get kicked out.      Honestly, this family. Always causing drama. I had a pretty tame holiday, all things considered. Cornwall. Rain most of the time, but the cream teas were superb.      Cornwall’s nice. A bit… gentle? I need a bit more  bang  for my buck, you know? Give me a chaotic city break any day. Though, cream teas are pretty persuasive.

...Honestly, the sheer  silence  is what gets me. You don’t realise how much constant noise there is until you’re properly away from it all. Even in the Highlands, near where my folks have their place, you get the road, or a distant farm… out wild camping, truly wild, it’s just… the wind. And maybe a stag roaring, if you're lucky.      A stag roaring, eh? Sounds a bit much for a relaxing weekend, Brenda. I mean, I appreciate a bit of nature, a good walk in Richmond Park, but  roaring  stags? Bit dramatic for my liking.      Dad, you’re missing the point entirely! It’s not about relaxation in the traditional sense. It’s a reset. A complete disconnection. It strips everything back. Think about the mental load everyone carries, the constant bombardment of information… being out there forces you to focus on the  essential . Finding shelter, staying warm, navigating. Your brain switches off the worrying, you know?      Exactly, Alistair. It’s… grounding. As a therapist, I see so many people utterly consumed by anxiety. They're living in their heads. But when you’re physically challenged, needing to actively  survive  – even on a very mild scale, like putting up a tent in a blizzard - it pulls you right into the present. It’s incredibly therapeutic, even if they don’t realise it at the time.      A blizzard, Brenda? You’re making it sound positively perilous! I thought you were talking about a pleasant weekend in the country. Sounds like a recipe for hypothermia to me. And I’ve got enough aches and pains as it is, thank you very much. I don't need to  add  to them by battling the elements.      It doesn’t  have  to be a blizzard, Dad. Though, yeah, I’ve done a few in a bit of a blow. It’s all about preparation. Proper gear, knowing your limits, respecting the conditions. It’s not recklessness, it's… calculated risk. And the rewards are immense. The views, the sense of accomplishment, the feeling of being completely self-sufficient…      He’s right, you know. It’s not just about the scenery, though the scenery  is  spectacular. The Hebrides in winter… well, it’s like nothing else. It’s about proving to yourself that you can handle something difficult. It's empowering. I’ve had clients who’ve come back from a weekend like that feeling completely transformed.

...Honestly, the whole thing just felt  pointless . All that build-up, all that hype, and for what? A beautifully shot, but ultimately, empty spectacle. I mean, did anything  actually  happen in that film?      Woah, hold on a second. Empty? I thought it was brilliant. Visually stunning, obviously, but the thematic layers… the exploration of isolation in a hyper-connected world… it was right up my street. What didn’t click for you?      Oh, don’t start with the ‘thematic layers’ now! It’s just…pretentious, isn’t it? It felt like it  wanted  to be deep, but didn’t actually  say  anything. Like the director was showing off how clever they were, rather than telling a story. It reminded me a bit of that novel, 'The Waves' by Virginia Woolf, all style and very little substance. Beautifully written, mind you, but utterly draining after a while.      That’s a harsh comparison! 'The Waves' is considered a classic. I get what you mean about style over substance sometimes, though. I guess I saw the isolation aspect as a really poignant reflection of modern life. Everyone scrolling through feeds, craving connection but only finding superficiality. And the ambiguous ending...that was the point, wasn't it? No neat resolutions, just…life.      Aye, maybe. But give me something with a bit more grit. Something like ‘Kes’, you know? Proper working-class story, raw emotion. That's film that  stays  with you. All this space opera stuff feels...distant. Like it's observing humanity rather than being  about  humanity. It's a bit like the difference between reading Zola and reading Tolkien. Both brilliant, obviously, but wildly different aims.      That’s a good analogy. I do agree there’s something powerful about films rooted in social realism. And 'Kes'  is  exceptional. But I think you're dismissing the emotional resonance of sci-fi. It can explore really universal themes, just using different metaphors. Look at 'Arrival' – that film hit me  hard .      'Arrival' was decent, I’ll give you that. Although, even  that  felt a little… overthought. Speaking of hitting hard, fancy grabbing a curry when we get back? I'm absolutely starving. All this film chat has made me crave something spicy.      Oh, absolutely. That sounds fantastic. Which place? That new Bangladeshi place on the high street, 'Spice Delight'? I’ve heard really good things. Apparently, their Rogan Josh is legendary.      Legendary, you say? Right, Spice Delight it is.

...and honestly, the way Mr. Henderson explained Excel to the Year 6s was  fascinating . He didn't just say "put the numbers in boxes," he talked about how it’s like building with Lego, but with information. Rows are the baseplates, columns are the bricks... It actually made sense to them, which is a miracle.      Lego is  way  better though. You can build spaceships! And castles! Excel just makes…numbers. Boring numbers.      Yeah! I built a spaceship yesterday! It had lasers and everything. It landed on Planet Bloop!      Planet Bloop sounds very exciting. It’s good to have a vivid imagination. But think of it this way – you could  record  all the details of Planet Bloop in Excel. How many aliens? What colour are their spaceships? How much Bloop-juice they drink!      Bloop-juice is green, and they drink  lots  of it. Like…a million gallons! You couldn’t fit that in Excel. It would go off the screen.      You might be right about the million gallons. It’s good to know its limits! Speaking of things that are a bit old-fashioned… I was helping Mum clear out the attic yesterday, and we found Dad’s old typewriter.      What’s a typewriter? Is it like a computer?      Not at all. It doesn’t have a screen or anything. You hit keys, and little metal arms with letters on them  bang  onto the paper to make the words. It makes a really satisfying  clack-clack-clack  sound.      Bang? Like a…fight?      No, not a fight! A gentle bang! It’s how the letters get onto the page. It’s very different than typing on a computer, or even on a tablet. It’s…permanent. You can’t just delete things easily.      Can you play games on it?      Hmm, not really. Although I bet you  could  write a story on it. A really exciting Planet Bloop story! It could be a proper, official document.      I’d rather play PlayStation. I’m getting really good at that racing game. I almost beat Dad yesterday.  Almost .      You will beat him, I'm sure. He pretends to let you get close, you know. It's a Dad trick. Remember that Brownie Promise evening on Tuesday?      Oh yeah! We learned the Brownie Promise! ‘I promise to do my best, to be true to myself and to develop my beliefs...' something, something. I forgot the rest.      You did brilliantly!

Honestly, Arthur, you look like you’ve slept in your clothes. Not that  I  mind, mind you, but Margaret would have a fit. You’re visiting her next week, aren't you?      Margaret? She’d just offer me another biscuit and tell me I'm looking ‘distinguished’. Though, she does fuss. No, I haven’t bothered with anything fancy this morning. It’s just you and me, Doris. Comfort is key at my age. Speaking of which, this toast is lovely. Where’d you get the bread?      From old man Hinchcliffe’s bakery, same as always. Best sourdough in Bradford. And don’t pretend you’re frail, Arthur. I saw you hauling those bags of compost in the garden yesterday. You were practically leaping over the flowerbeds! Though, you  were  wearing that awful gardening hat again.      It keeps the sun off! Practicality, Doris, practicality. Anyway, compost and horticulture… it reminds me of those fruit farms we visited in Kent, years ago. Remember? Miles and miles of orchards. Felt like being in a different country.      Oh aye, I do. Lovely it was. Though, give me Yorkshire countryside any day. Did you ever look into that thing I was telling you about, those deserted medieval villages around here? The one near Haworth?      The one you found a reference to in that dusty old book? I meant to, but then the roadworks started on the A650 and frankly, my brain went into lockdown. They've been going on for  months . It’s a complete and utter shambles. Absolute chaos. You'd think they were building a motorway, not patching a few potholes.      They’re always messing about with those roads. Makes you wish you could just take to the air. More coffee? I’ve got a new blend, Ethiopian Yirgacheffe. Slightly floral.      That sounds delightful, thank you. Though, honestly, I’m quite happy with my instant at the moment. Saves on washing up. You’re always experimenting with something new in the kitchen, aren’t you? Growing herbs now, is it?      Well, it’s handy. Fresh mint for my tea, basil for pasta… saves a fortune. And it’s satisfying. Unlike dealing with all this junk mail. It's relentless! And the phone calls. Scammers trying to get hold of my bank details. It’s a disgrace.      Tell me about it. I had one yesterday trying to sell me a timeshare in Florida! I don’t even  like  Florida!

Honestly, this Facebook algorithm is driving me mad. All Auntie Brenda’s cat pictures and political rants. It's relentless! I keep trying to unfollow her, but Mum would have my hide.      Brenda and her Mittens… a classic. You'd think after all these years, you’d be immune to her Facebook onslaught. Though I do find myself scrolling endlessly, which is probably a terrible habit.      Speaking of terrible habits, anyone fancy a biscuit? I made shortbread, trying to use up some of the Christmas butter before it goes off. And yes, the Facebook rabbit hole is  dangerous . I spent a good hour last night looking at travel blogs for Italy. Completely unrealistic, given… well, everything.      Oh, shortbread! Perfect. Thank you, love. Italy sounds lovely, though, doesn't it? A proper break. I haven't had a holiday since… oh, goodness, since before I started the extra shifts at the hospital. It’s relentless, this winter bug going around.      It is. I had a couple of my team down last week. Thankfully not all at once. Makes planning rotas a nightmare. Speaking of which, I’ve got a meeting about staff cover first thing Monday. Joy. Did you get everything sorted with your Mum’s medication, by the way? She was sounding a bit confused on the phone yesterday.      I did, thankfully. The pharmacist was brilliant. She’s put all her pills in a dosette box, labelled for each day. Seems to have made a huge difference. She was convinced she was taking double her blood pressure tablets before. Scary stuff.      That's good. Mum getting confused is always worrying. It's a sign, isn’t it? Of things… changing. Makes you think, doesn't it?      It does. It really does. Which is why I try and get away with her for a weekend every few months. Keeps her stimulated. We were talking about going to Brighton in February. Have you been lately, darling?      Ages ago! Not since we took little Timmy there when he was about five. He built the most enormous sandcastle, then a wave came and…well, you remember. Complete meltdown. He’s a grown man now, off travelling in Southeast Asia, completely unfazed by anything. Irony, isn’t it?      Oh, the irony! I remember that sandcastle. It  was  impressive. Speaking of travelling, did you guys get anything good for Christmas? I got a really nice leather journal, which I’m hoping will inspire some actual writing, rather than just scrolling.

…and honestly, Mum’s been on about me getting a ‘proper’ job again. Like copywriting isn’t enough. She keeps sending me links to teaching assistant roles. Teaching assistants! As if I'd willingly spend my days wrangling glitter and glue with seven-year-olds. No offense if you ever fancied that, by the way.      None taken! Though honestly, the thought gives me hives. Glitter is the herpes of the craft world. No, I’m quite happy buried in code and survey design, thank you very much. Though, being fair, Mum’s probably just worried. Copywriting  is  a bit…precarious, isn't it? Especially in this climate.      Precarious but brilliantly creative! And it pays the rent, mostly. Though ‘mostly’ seems to be the operative word these days. Everything is so expensive. Did you see the price of petrol this week? It’s daylight robbery. I nearly choked when I filled up the car to go visit last weekend.      Don’t even  start  me on petrol. I cycle everywhere, thankfully. Although, even  that  feels riskier these days with all the delivery vans whizzing about. It’s ridiculous. And the rent in London… it’s just insane. I’m practically living in a cupboard, and it’s still £800 a month! How are people supposed to save for anything?      Seriously! It's like they expect us all to be trust fund babies or something. I’m trying to squirrel away a bit for a deposit for a flat, eventually. But then something always happens. Car needs fixing, the boiler decides to take a holiday... It’s always something. How’s the PhD going, by the way? Still enjoying battling with algorithms?      Battling is a good word for it. It's…intense. I’m officially in the 'data cleaning' phase, which basically translates to 'staring at spreadsheets until my eyes bleed'. It’s soul-crushing, but apparently vital. I’m hoping to actually start writing up in the new year. I’m terrified, honestly. It feels like such a huge mountain to climb.      Oh, I can imagine. You're such a perfectionist, though. You'll nail it. Honestly, you always do. Remember that essay you wrote in uni about… what was it? Post-structuralist readings of children’s literature? It blew everyone away.      Oh, God, please don't remind me. I was fuelled entirely by coffee and anxiety for a week straight. But yeah, I guess.

...Honestly, the thought of another Zoom fitness class just fills me with dread. It's not the  exercise  itself, you know? It's the relentless positivity. "You're amazing! Feel the burn!" No, I'm quite aware of the burn, thank you very much, and I'm mostly feeling a desperate need for a biscuit.      Oh, I completely get that. Brenda's classes are…intense. She thinks shouting encouragement is a substitute for actual technique. I tried one with her last month. Lasted ten minutes. I was pretending I had a really important work call.      You’re both so lucky you  can  do Zoom classes. My internet has been atrocious all week. Keeps dropping out mid-plank, which is hardly conducive to core stability, is it? Though, to be fair, nothing really is conducive to core stability when you’re my age.      Oh, darling, don’t say that! You’re incredibly fit. You still walk miles every day.      I  huff  miles, more like. It's a slow, deliberate huffing process. And honestly, all this walking makes me think about house prices again. Ridiculous. Absolutely ridiculous. I was looking at a tiny cottage near Richmond Park, just a little one-bedroom, and it’s…well, it’s more than we paid for our  first  house, back in the nineties.      Richmond Park is prime real estate, though. It's beautiful there. But you're right, the market is insane. I was looking at flats in Edinburgh, just as an investment, and even there, it's escalating. It feels like nobody can afford to actually  live  anywhere nice anymore.      It’s frightening. I’ve been tentatively browsing in Guildford, thinking maybe a slightly bigger garden would be nice... but even something modest is eye-watering. I keep telling myself to just stay put, get the loft converted, and put up with the wonky plumbing.      The wonky plumbing is a legitimate concern. Though, honestly, I’d take wonky plumbing over a mortgage the size of a small nation. Speaking of which, have you both tried that new Moroccan tagine recipe I sent?      I did! Last night, actually. It was fantastic. A bit fiddly with all the spices, but definitely worth it. Fiona, you’re a culinary genius.      Oh, I haven't gotten around to it yet. It’s on the list. I've been stuck in a rut of shepherd’s pie and roasted chicken. So predictable.

...Honestly, the hydrangeas here are blooming  beautifully . Better than the ones Mam tries to grow, and she's got a proper green thumb, she does. Anyway, you were saying? Something about the project being a bit of a disaster zone?      Yeah, pretty much. It’s this flood defence scheme near Ely. The modelling was…optimistic, let’s say. Turns out the river’s behaving in ways the simulations didn’t predict. Massive re-think required, extra costs, angry landowners… the usual fun. I spent most of yesterday wading through spreadsheets trying to justify why we're already over budget.      Oh, that sounds  grim . Is it a ridiculous amount over? I mean, everyone's going on about the Budget and cuts and all that. Sunak’s trying to look all sensible, but it just seems like everyone's a bit worse off.      Ridiculous is an understatement. We're looking at a potential 20% increase, and that's  before  factoring in the extra work. It’s infuriating, because it's not a lack of effort, it's just… bad data initially. And now it’s all political. They want to be seen doing something about flooding, but they don’t want to be seen spending loads of money doing it. It's a proper Catch-22. They’re probably hoping for a dry winter.      That’s… incredibly short-sighted. It’s that kind of thinking that  causes  the problems, isn’t it? My job is all about data, but it’s the clever  use  of it, the checking and validating… that’s the bit they skip, to save time and money. I’m a Corpus Administrator, remember, basically making sure language data is all tagged properly. Sounds dull, but it’s vital. If the data’s rubbish, the AI is rubbish, the research is rubbish– everything falls apart. Sounds a bit like your river modelling, actually.      Exactly! It's the same principle. Someone just wanted a quick, cheap solution. They didn't bother to thoroughly investigate the existing river behaviour, relied on outdated information… it's just frustrating when you  know  it’s going to bite you later. Still, at least your work sounds…cleaner. No wellies required?      Definitely no wellies! Mostly just a lot of staring at screens. It's pretty draining in its own way, though. You start seeing patterns in everything. Actually, talking of things that require effort... have you seen  Wicked ?

Right, that’s a good covering, wouldn’t you say, Alan? Though I swear, this paint smells like me nan’s attic. All dust and…optimism, strangely enough.      Optimism? You’re readin’ too much into it, lad. Smells like cheap paint to me. But yeah, good coverage. Needed doin’, this fence. Been lookin’ a right state. Still can’t believe the council are tryin’ to push through that development down the road.      Tell me about it. Another block of identikit flats. No character, all glass and angles. It’ll ruin the whole streetscape. Remember old Mrs. Higgins’ garden? They’re planning to build right over it. She spent  decades  on that garden.      Aye, a tragedy, that is. She grew the best tomatoes you ever tasted. And she always had a biscuit for the kids. Now they're talkin' about 'regenerating' the area. Regeneratin' right out of existence, more like. It’s all about profit, innit? No thought for the people who already live here. Speaking of thinkin', did you ever get round to watchin' that film I told you about,  The Third Man ?       The Third Man ? Oh, the Orson Welles one? I did, actually. Last week. Very noir, very atmospheric. I was struck by the use of shadows, actually. Reminded me of some of Hopper’s paintings. The loneliness, the alienation. Powerful stuff. You’re right to recommend it, Alan. Though, I must say, all that Vienna underground looked a bit claustrophobic.      Claustrophobic! That's Vienna for ya! But Welles...he was a genius, wasn’t he? Proper actor. I reckon I coulda been an actor, you know. Had a bit of a go at the amateur dramatics when I was younger. Played a convincing villain, apparently.      I can picture that. You've always had a…presence, shall we say. What role was it? I can’t imagine you playing the romantic lead.      Nah, never. I was Iago in  Othello . Now  that  suited me down to the ground. All scheming and whispering. Got a good review in the local paper, too. Though, the wife said I brought some of that back home with me for a few weeks afterwards.      I believe it. Anyway, back to more mundane matters. I was thinking about replacing the guttering. It’s starting to sag in places, causing a bit of a damp patch on the back wall. You wouldn’t happen to know anyone reliable, would you?

Oh, look at that field of poppies. Absolutely stunning, isn't it? It's a shame the light isn't quite right for a photo, though. Everything looks a bit washed out.      It  is  beautiful. Proper rolling Polish countryside. Much nicer than the M6, that’s for sure! Are we still on track for Tarnow around lunchtime? I’m starting to think about pierogi already.      Should be, if we don't stop  too  often admiring the scenery. Though, honestly, a little break wouldn't go amiss. My back's starting to ache from this driving. How much did we spend on diesel in Slovakia, by the way? I've lost track.      About 80 euros, I think? I made a note in the spreadsheet. Honestly, the fuel costs are the biggest worry. I was hoping we'd be doing better on mileage, but this little beast isn’t exactly fuel efficient, is she?      No, she’s a charming beast, but greed isn't one of her virtues. Still, worth it for the freedom, eh? Remember when we talked about doing this five years ago? I was convinced this trip would never happen. I was… well, I was stuck in a rut, to put it mildly.      Stood still, more like! You were practically growing roots in Cambridge. Glad you finally decided to sell half your china collection and just  go . It's been amazing. And seriously, did you really need seventeen Royal Doulton figurines?      Don't remind me! Sentimental nonsense, the lot of it. My mother would have had a fit, but honestly, they were gathering dust. Better someone else appreciated them. It's liberating, isn't it? Realising you don't  need  all that stuff. We're travelling with everything we need right here.      Exactly! Though a slightly bigger fridge would be nice. Seriously, we’re living on biscuits and apples again. I saw a hitchhiker back there, a young lad with a massive backpack. Should we have stopped?      Oh, I don’t know about that. It felt a bit… risky. You read such awful stories. And honestly, with the space already at a premium… Imagine trying to have a conversation with someone crammed in here!      Fair enough. Probably best avoided. It’s just… I remember backpacking around Europe when I was 18, and relying on the kindness of strangers. I'd hate to think of him struggling.      You always were a soft touch, Lizzie.

Honestly, this traffic is  mental . Thought getting out of St Anne’s would be easier on a Tuesday.      It’s always like this heading towards Preston, love. Especially near the docks. Remember what happened last time we tried to go this way on a Saturday? We were stuck for nearly an hour!      Aye, I remember. Little Maisie was proper having a meltdown, wasn’t she? Screaming for those bloody Haribo sweets. Said she  needed  them.      She still does, Dad. Just… quieter about it now. Speaking of needing things, did you manage to find that ridiculous history textbook? The one Mr. Henderson said is essential for the essay?      Nae, not yet. Bookshops in Preston are a bit hit and miss. I was hoping Waterstones would have it, but they often sell out of the Sixth Form stuff, don't they? You checked online at Blackwells?      Yeah, it’s on order, but it won’t be here till next week. Honestly, the exams are looming, and I feel so unprepared. It’s all these strikes as well, disrupting everything. They're talking about more train strikes next month now. How are people supposed to get to revision sessions?!      It  is  chaotic. Honestly, I’m starting to miss the days when things felt a little more… predictable. Remember when the biggest news was the Queen’s Jubilee celebrations? It feels like a lifetime ago.      Aye, a grand do that was. The whole street had a street party. Old Mrs. Higgins made her famous Victoria sponge, bless her. She’s not been herself lately, though. I popped round to see if she needed anything, and she’s just… not the same. Bit confused, you know?      Oh dear. Is she okay? Maybe she just needs a check-up. It's worrying when older people start getting like that. It reminds me of Gran when…      Don't dwell on that, darling. But you're right to be concerned. I’ll give her a ring later, see if I can offer to take her to the doctor’s. Speaking of needing help, has anyone had a look at the quotes for moving house? It's terrifying how much it all costs.      I did, last night. It's a robbery, honestly. Trying to find a reputable company that won’t smash all our belongings to bits is proving difficult too. Remember that time Uncle Barry moved and everything arrived in a million pieces?

Honestly, Mum, you shouldn't have. Appearing like this, out of the blue…it gave us both a fright! Though, a pleasant one, admittedly. Thirsk isn't exactly Kendal, is it?      Pleasant frights are the best kind, love. And Thirsk is… nice enough. A bit flat, perhaps. Kendal has the hills, you see. You can  feel  the history in the stones there. This feels… newer. I needed a change. And honestly, I was getting rather bored staring at the garden gnome.      Gran? You weren't… dealing with things again, were you? Like, feeling really down? You didn't say anything when I called last week.      Oh, Leo. Always so perceptive. No, not "dealing with things" precisely. Just… a bit listless. It’s a silly age, this, you know. You start sorting through things. Not just physical things, but memories. And some of them are… heavier than others. I started going through old photographs. Found some of your Grandad when he was a young man. Quite dashing, actually. It made me… thoughtful.      Thoughtful can easily slip into… other places for you, Mum. We worry. Remember what the doctor said about keeping busy? And routine? A sudden trip to Yorkshire isn’t exactly routine.      Doctors. Always wanting to medicate. A change of scenery is far more effective. Besides, I told Mrs. Higgins I was going to visit a friend in Leeds. She won’t suspect a thing. Though, she  did  ask if the friend had a cat, as she's always trying to offload Mittens.      You told Mrs. Higgins you were visiting a  friend ? Gran, you’re brilliant! She thinks everyone’s a potential cat-sitter.      One has to maintain a certain mystique, darling. Now, tell me about school. Everything alright? You haven't been spending  too  much time on that… what do you call it? TikTok?      Gran! It’s not just TikTok. It’s how everyone keeps in touch. And yeah, school’s okay. We’re doing Shakespeare. It’s… actually alright. Mr. Davies makes it funny. He does all the voices.      He’s a good teacher. He really tries to engage them. It’s a tough job these days, keeping their attention with all the screens vying for it. Speaking of which, have you seen the new robot dog they’ve developed? It’s controlled by neural impulses!      Neural impulses? Good heavens. Sounds like something from a science fiction film. Though, I suppose everything does these days.

Right, so you’ve had a proper play with it then, Liam? What’s the verdict on the new beast? Honestly, I was a bit worried I’d splashed out on something that wouldn’t actually  do  what I need it to.      Nah, it's solid, mate. Seriously. The speed is a huge step up from your last one, isn’t it? I booted up that video editing software you were on about – the one that kept crashing – and it barely blinked. No lag, no stuttering. You’ll be rendering stuff in your sleep.      Rendering what exactly? Still doing those weird digital paintings, Ben? Look like someone threw a rainbow at a broken washing machine, if you ask me. No offence.      Artistic expression, Alex! You wouldn’t understand. And yeah, mostly that. But I'm trying to get into some motion graphics, little animated bits for YouTube. Want to expand the skillset, you know? That's why I needed something that wouldn’t die halfway through.      It's more than capable, honestly. The graphics card is pretty decent. Have you looked at setting up dual monitors? Would be a game changer for editing. Plus, thinking about storage, have you backed everything up from the old laptop? Don’t want to lose all your stuff.      Good shout on the backup. I meant to do that last week, totally slipped my mind. And dual monitors... tempting. But then I’d need a bigger desk. This flat’s already crammed, as you both know. Speaking of cramped, did you hear about Old Man Hemmings next door? Apparently, he's building a shed the size of a garage.      No way! That bloke? He barely leaves his house. What does he need a massive shed for? Hiding from the postman?      Probably storing all the garden gnomes he’s obsessed with. Remember that time he complained about your climbing rose, Alex, saying it was encroaching on  his  airspace?      Don't remind me! That was a nightmare. Still reckon my rose looked better than his plastic flamingos. Anyway, back to the laptop. You getting any decent clips on YouTube these days, Ben? Anything besides cat videos?      I try! Mostly just tutorials for artwork, little speed paints. Gets a few views. But it's slow going. I was watching this Korean guy on YouTube the other day, doing incredible digital art. Seriously talented. Made me feel like I need to go back to art school.

Honestly, this place is a revelation. Tarnow needed something like this. Not another  pierogi  place, bless them, but somewhere…a bit more cosmopolitan. The decor is really quite lovely, isn't it? All that exposed brick. And they actually understand what a flat white is!      It  is  good. I was a bit dubious when I heard it was opening, you know? Another place aiming for ‘Instagrammable’ and delivering…mediocrity. But it’s really pulled it off. And you're right about the coffee. I nearly wept with joy getting a decent brew. It’s the little things, isn’t it? Especially after a day wrestling with twenty teenage Japanese students trying to master the present perfect.      Oh, the students. Still doing the TEFL occasionally then? I thought you’d fully committed to the Polish schools now.      I am, mostly. But the private classes pay better, and honestly, it keeps my brain ticking over. It’s… grounding. Something solid. You know, after everything.      After everything? Sounding a bit cryptic, darling.      Just… the past couple of years. Losing Gran. Then… well, you know. Liam. It felt like I was constantly chasing something, trying to  be  someone, and completely lost sight of who I actually was. I turned to… well, let’s just say unhealthy coping mechanisms.      Oh, sweetie. I did know. Mom told me. You were so good at keeping it all bottled up. And Liam… that was a mess. A thoroughly awful mess. Are you… are you still struggling?      Not like I was. I’ve been going to meetings, therapy… it’s slow. It's about figuring out what  I  want, not what other people expect. Which is terrifying. I always defined myself through relationships – good student, girlfriend, teacher… Now I'm trying to dismantle all that and just... exist. Kind of ironic, really, to be finding my identity in Poland.      I can see that. It's a good place for reinvention. Nobody knows your history here, you’re a blank slate. Although, you’ve always been incredibly resourceful, even when… even when you were making less-than-ideal choices. Remember that disastrous attempt to open an online vintage clothing shop?      Oh, God, don’t remind me! "Retro Revival" – the irony. It lasted about three weeks and involved a lot of sequins and questionable polyester. I thought I was going to be the next Alexa Chung. I was… focused on the wrong things, I suppose.

Right, so the Dorset Steam Fair. It  looks  amazing, doesn’t it? All those old tractors and engines… Honestly, a bit lost on me, but Dad’s been going for years. Are you sure you'll be alright with the crowds, though, Grandad?      Crowds don’t bother me, love. Been in bigger scrapes in London, believe you me. It’s getting  to  the crowds that’s the bother these days, with my knees. Is there decent access for… well, for someone who needs a bit of a sit down every ten minutes? That's the main thing. And a loo that isn't a mile walk.      They usually have mobility scooter hire, don’t they, dear? I remember Auntie Margaret used one a couple of years back.
