Old Man Hemmings was practically  giving  it away, knowing it’s been a thorn in the side of the council for years. And the transport links are surprisingly good. A-26 access, mainline station...it’s not as isolated as you seem to think.      Transport links are one thing, accessibility for those who  need  us is another. What about the communities in, say, Tonbridge, or even down towards Crowborough? They’ll face a real challenge getting here reliably, especially families without cars. Have we truly mapped that out in the business case? Because I recall a rather…optimistic projection regarding public transport usage.      The business case, as you know, is based on reasonable assumptions. And the projections  do  account for a phased increase in transport provision, contingent on funding. We’ve already had preliminary discussions with Kent County Council about expanding the local bus routes. It’s a ‘build it and they will come’ scenario, to a degree.      ‘Build it and they will come’ sounds dangerously like wishful thinking when we’re talking about end-of-life care, Richard. People aren't going to travel long distances for convenience; they need proximity. And speaking of building... have you had any further dialogue with the local hospices? St. Michael’s, for example? We don’t want to duplicate services, but complement them. Their catchment area overlaps significantly.      Absolutely. I had a very productive lunch with their CEO last week. They're supportive, genuinely. They’re struggling with capacity, as are most hospices. This isn't about competition, Penelope. It’s about expanding access to high-quality palliative care. They see us filling a gap, particularly in specialist nursing for complex cases.      Good. That’s reassuring. Because specialist nursing  is  crucial. The feedback I’ve been getting from clinicians is that there’s a real demand for more holistic support; not just managing pain, but addressing the emotional and psychological needs of both the patient  and  their families. That needs to be reflected in the staffing model. Are we budgeting adequately for that?

Oh, goodness me, look at this one! Southport Pier, 1998. You were sporting quite the…interesting moustache, darling.      Don't you dare, Sarah! That was a  sophisticated  moustache. I thought it gave me a bit of George Clooney about me. It was for a work do, actually. Trying to impress old Mr. Henderson. Didn't work, obviously. He just kept asking if I’d accidentally glued a caterpillar to my face.      Oh my god, I wish I'd seen that! Seriously, Dad, a caterpillar? That's brilliant. This album is gold. Remember when we all went to Royal Ascot with Auntie Brenda? She insisted on that enormous hat…      Oh, Brenda. Bless her. That hat was a hazard to air traffic. And she was convinced she’d spotted the Queen winking at  her . Honestly, the woman lived for a bit of royal glamour. Speaking of glamour, how did your interview go today, Liv? You were awfully quiet on the drive back.      It was…okay. It’s a really competitive role, you know? Lots of other grads with polished portfolios. I think I stumbled a bit on the question about brand voice consistency. I said something about "vibes," which I now deeply regret.      Vibes? Oh, love. They want precision, not vibes. They want to know you understand the technicalities. But don't beat yourself up about it. You’re a fantastic writer. Remember that campaign you did for the local bakery? That was brilliant!      Absolutely. Everyone was talking about those posters. You've got a real knack for it, Liv. And you’ve only just started, don't forget. Sometimes it just takes finding the right fit. Did they ask about your experience with social media marketing?      Yeah, a little. I talked about the university projects, but I think they were looking for someone with more agency experience. It's just… frustrating. All my friends seem to have landed amazing jobs already.      Don't fall into that trap of comparing yourself, darling. Everyone’s journey is different. Remember when I was first starting out at the council? I spent six months filing paperwork and making tea. Six  months . It built character, apparently.      It certainly did! You were a very patient man, then as now. Oh, look at this picture – Kemsing village fete, 1985! We were so small! And Mum was trying to win that giant Teddy bear. She never did, did she?      She always went for the biggest prize, didn’t she?

Right, I’m officially regretting suggesting a double feature of ‘The Descent’ and… whatever  else  you picked. My nerves are proper shot to pieces already, and we’ve only been through the opening credits of ‘The Descent’!      Oh, come on, El. It’s good though, isn’t it? Properly claustrophobic. And honestly, the caving scenes are beautifully shot, even if they  are  terrifying. You said you wanted scary! I thought you were brave.      Brave and stupid are two different things, aren’t they? I thought I was brave when I suggested it, now I’m thinking I’ve fundamentally misjudged my tolerance for things crawling out of dark holes. It's just... realistic, isn’t it? Like, could actually happen.      That's the point! That's what makes it good. All those jump scares would be horrifying if you thought it was genuine. Speaking of, did you notice how they built the tension with the sound design in the first five minutes? It's brilliant. So subtle at first, just drips and echoes...      Don’t! Don’t analyse it! You’re making it worse. I’m trying to just… exist, and hope nothing reaches out and grabs me through the telly. Honestly, I’m looking at shadows now. Our living room was never this ominous before. And you, you're dissecting the soundscape!      Sorry, sorry! Old habits die hard, I suppose. Film studies brain, you know. I just appreciate the craft, even when it’s making me hide behind a cushion. What's the scariest bit you've seen so far?      Don’t ask. Don't even. It was when… well, when she shines the torch and you see  something  moving in the distance. That was it for me. I didn’t even need to  see  what it was. The implication was enough. You Cambridge lot are all about implication, aren't you? Very subtle scares. We in Yorkshire, we like things to  leap out  at you.      That’s a massive stereotype, El. Though I will admit, our horror tends to be more psychological. We don't do blood and guts quite like… well, like a lot of other places. Don't worry, the second film is a bit more gothic. Victorian ghost story. Less crawling things.      Gothic is good. Ghosts I can handle. It's the things that  live  that bother me. Especially things that live underground. It’s just… unnatural.

...Honestly, Grandad, you wouldn’t  believe  the email I got today. It was another one trying to get me to ‘upgrade’ my security software. Honestly, they’re getting more and more convincing. You’d fall for it, wouldn't you?      Oh, don't you patronise me, love. I was an accountant for fifty years. I’ve seen more scams than hot dinners. Though, admittedly, they weren't usually delivered  through  the ether like these things are now. It's all a bit… wizardry really. Still, I wouldn’t click on anything I wasn't expecting. That's the golden rule.      Wise words! I  didn’t  click, of course. I just deleted it. It’s just… exhausting keeping on top of it all. It makes me appreciate a proper book even more. Speaking of which, have you finished that biography of Churchill your daughter got you?      Almost. It's a hefty one, that. My eyes aren’t what they used to be, you know. I wish I'd gotten one of those… what do you call them… iPads? You’re always fiddling with yours. Might make reading easier.      An iPad? You’d be a natural! I could set it up for you, download the Libby app – that’s where you get library books digitally. It’s brilliant. Though you would need to be careful about… well, you know, the scams.      Scams, everything’s a scam these days! I still don't understand why anyone would rent out their house to strangers. This Airbnb business, it’s madness. What if they damage the place? Or just have a wild party?      Well, they do have insurance, and reviews are a big thing. Mum and Dad used one in Italy last year, and they said it was lovely. Saved them a fortune compared to a hotel.      Italy, eh? Good for them. Your mother always did like a bit of sunshine. Though, I prefer a good pizza at home, myself. Have you ordered one yet? I'm feeling a bit peckish.      Not yet, but I was thinking about it. Pepperoni and mushroom, your usual?      You know me too well. Though if they’ve got one with olives… Oh, and tell them extra garlic. I’m not bothered about my breath at this hour. What's been keeping  you  busy today, apart from dodging digital villains? Anything interesting at school?      Just the usual chaos, Grandad! Year 5 are rehearsing for a play.

Aye, this is the life, eh? Brucefield’s a good shout for gettin’ away from it all. Though, escapism's all well and good, but it does make me think… you remember that tiny bookshop we stumbled into in Prague? The one crammed absolutely full o’ first editions?      Och, how could I forget? ‘U Knihkuptce’, wasn’t it? Like stepping back in time. Dust motes dancin’ in the single shaft o' light. And that smell…old paper and somethin’ else, like cloves maybe? I spent a good hour just runnin’ my fingers over the spines. Found a rather beautiful, battered copy of Rilke’s  Letters to a Young Poet  there. Still treasure it.      Aye, Rilke. Good choice. I was torn between that and a first edition o’ Conrad’s  Heart of Darkness . Ultimately, the price tag on the Conrad kept me from bein’ foolish. Though, I  did  get that wee collection o’ Czech folk tales. Remember? The illustrations were incredible. Bit macabre, some of ’em, but beautiful.      Oh, the folk tales! With the woodcut prints, right? That was a good find. You were determined to learn some Czech phrases to try and haggle with the owner, weren't you? Disasterous, mostly. All you managed to say was “My grandmother likes potatoes.”      It’s true! My linguistic skills are notoriously… selective. But it was worth it for the stories. It made me think about travel differently, that shop. It wasn’t about tickin’ off landmarks, it was about findin’ these wee pockets o’ culture, these hidden gems. Like that little cafe in Florence, remember? Not the tourist traps, but the one tucked away behind the leather market.      The one where the nonna made the best ravioli I've ever tasted in my life. And spoke absolutely no English, just gestured wildly and kept refillin’ my glass with wine. That's what it’s all about, isn't it? The unplanned moments. It's funny, you know, readin’ about other people's travels is great - I’m currently workin' my way through Paul Theroux’s  The Great Railway Bazaar  – but it never quite compares to bein'  in  it.      Theroux, eh? Good man. A bit cynical at times, but a brilliant observer. I’ve been re-readin’ Bruce Chatwin lately.  In Patagonia  still blows me away, even after all these years. The way he weaves history and myth together…and his fascination with shoes!

Honestly, Mum, I’m starting to think I’m delusional applying for this. It’s…a lot.      What is, love? Still on that Foster & Partners application? The Shard designers? Give yourself a break, you’ve got a fantastic portfolio. You  should  be applying for things like this.      I know, I know. Logically, I get that. But reading the job description again… “Experience leading complex BIM projects, demonstrable understanding of sustainable design principles at a large scale, proven ability to manage client expectations…” It feels like they want someone with ten years under their belt, not someone who’s barely been a qualified architect for a year.      Oh, don’t you start with that self-doubt now. You did brilliantly on your Masters, didn’t you? Remember Mrs. Davies saying your dissertation on green infrastructure was the best she’d seen in ages? And you absolutely shone on that community centre project - leading the design team, dealing with all those different opinions…      That was a modular build, Mum. This is…a potential high-rise in the City. Different league. And managing a small team of student volunteers is  not  the same as managing a team of experienced engineers and contractors.      No, it’s not, you’re right. But it’s a starting point, isn’t it? Everything is. And they wouldn’t put the advert out if they didn't think someone relatively new could be a possibility. Application criteria are always wish lists. They’re fishing, darling. You need to be the brightest fish.      Brightest fish, eh? You always know what to say. It’s just…the deadline is next week, and the supporting statement feels impossible. I’ve rewritten it three times already.      Well, show me then. Let’s have a look. I may not know anything about BIM, bless me, but I’m pretty good at spotting when someone is underselling themselves. And I know you, better than anyone.      Okay, brace yourself. It’s currently a very polite, very vague apology for not being the perfect architect.      Oh dear. Yes, you’re right. “A willing and eager learner…” That’s what you tell your boss when you accidentally spill coffee on the filing system, not when you’re applying to a world-renowned firm! You need to highlight what you  can  do, not what you haven't done yet. Talk about your strengths. Your design flair, your problem-solving skills, your passion for sustainability.

…and honestly, Doreen, this new roundabout on the A47 is a disaster waiting to happen. Utterly baffling design. They’ve narrowed the approach lanes, you see, and the signage… well, it’s just optimistic, isn’t it? Optimistic that anyone can actually navigate it without ending up in a ditch.      Optimistic is a kind word, Arthur. Downright daft is more like it. I went that way last Tuesday, taking Betty to the doctor in Norwich, and nearly ended up in a hedge. Honestly, they spend all this money on these fancy roundabouts, but they don’t seem to understand the basic principles of traffic flow. Remember the old Dereham bypass? Simple, effective, never a problem.      Oh, you two and your roads. Always complaining about the roads. Though, I must admit, I avoid the A47 whenever I can these days. It’s not just the traffic, it's the  drivers . So many young ones glued to their phones, completely oblivious. It’s terrifying.      It’s not just the young ones, Doreen! I saw a bloke in a BMW practically reading a newspaper yesterday. Honestly, the entitlement! Back in my day, if you were behind the wheel, you  were  driving. No distractions.      Aye, those were the days. And the cars! Built to last, they were. None of this flimsy plastic nonsense they make now. My Austin Cambridge... that was a car. You could hit a brick wall in that and barely scratch the paint.      You always did have a fondness for a solid motor, didn't you, George? I remember when you got that Cambridge. Looked like a battleship! Always said it was over-engineered for Norwich, but you were proud as punch.      Speaking of Norwich, have you heard anything more about young Emily? She was saying she's struggling to find anywhere affordable to live there. Says the rental prices are through the roof, even for a tiny flat.      It's a disgrace, that is. How can young people get a foothold on the property ladder with prices like they are? When I first started out... well, you could buy a perfectly decent house for a few thousand pounds. It's completely unrealistic now. And the government's supposed to be doing something about it, but frankly, I've lost faith in politicians.      Don't even get me started on the government, George. A complete shambles, the lot of them. Pledges and promises, all hot air.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of requests for the art studio space this month is startling. I’ve had three definite bookings and two very firm enquiries already. It's exceeding all projections, which is wonderful, of course, but it means we  really  need to get that back room sorted.      Yeah, you mentioned that. It’s looking a bit… chaotic back there at the moment, isn’t it? I’ve been meaning to get a proper look. Are we still thinking a full conversion, or just a tidy and some better lighting?      A full conversion, absolutely. It needs to feel…professional. These aren't just hobbyists we’re attracting, Mark. One woman’s a ceramicist selling in Liberty! We need to match the quality of their work with the space. That means proper storage for materials – essential, really - decent flooring, and a washbasin, at the very least. I was thinking about a sink donated from the refurbishment of Mrs. Patel’s kitchen, if she’s still happy to part with it.      Good thinking about Mrs. Patel! She's always keen to help. I’ll chase that up tomorrow. Flooring… that’s going to be the big cost, isn’t it? We’re a charity, after all. Could we look at recycled options? There are some places around Peckham that do reclaimed wood flooring, relatively cheap.      That's an excellent suggestion. Reclaimed wood would be perfect, fits the aesthetic too. More ‘Brixton’ than polished concrete, wouldn’t you say? We also need to think about furniture. Proper easels, storage cupboards… are we budgeting for new, or trying to source second-hand? I spotted a rather lovely set of vintage stacking chairs at a market last week, but they needed a bit of TLC.      Vintage is good, but TLC adds time and potentially more cost. I’ve got a contact at a liquidation place – they often get furniture from closed-down offices. I could see what they have. It might not be  vintage chic , but it’ll be functional and affordable. Speaking of affordable… how are we doing with the yoga studio income? Has that picked up since we started advertising on those local Facebook groups?      It has, actually. Surprisingly well. We’ve had a consistent stream of drop-ins, and a few people have signed up for block bookings. It’s not going to make us millionaires, but it’s definitely contributing. Keeps the lights on, so to speak.

Right, these spuds are  dangerously  good. Honestly, I think I’ve eaten my weight in them already. Anyone else feeling the potato-induced slump coming on?      Oh, you’re telling me! I think I’ve officially entered a food coma. Though, to be fair, everything’s incredible. You’ve really outdone yourself this time, Rhys.      Glad you think so, Anya! It’s a bit of a family recipe, really. My nan’s roast potatoes were legendary, and I’ve been trying to replicate them ever since. Secret’s in the goose fat, obviously. And the rosemary.      Goose fat, eh? Always a winner. Makes everything taste… sinfully good. You know, growing up, we didn’t have goose fat. Mum always used sunflower oil. Perfectly good, but... not  this .      Oh, sunflower oil! Bless her. She did her best with what she had, didn't she? I remember she used to try and make a Yorkshire pudding, but it always came out flat as a pancake. Such a laugh.      Ah, yes, Eluned and her Yorkshire puddings. A constant source of amusement. But she made the best gravy. The  best . No amount of goose fat could compensate for her gravy, I tell you. It was magic.      Gravy  is  a key component, I’ll grant you that. Though I like to think mine holds its own. Used a splash of cider in there, actually. Adds a bit of tang.      Cider? Interesting! That’s a clever touch. It does give it a lovely depth of flavour. You’re a master chef, Rhys, you really are. Much better than anything I could rustle up after a day wrangling teenagers.      Don't try and flatter my chef, Anya! He'll get a big head. Though, he  is  rather good, I suppose. It’s a good job he left teaching, honestly. The kids at that school were… a handful.      He was always more artistic, anyway. Remember that time he tried to sculpt a life-size dragon out of mashed potatoes at university?      Oh, don’t  remind  me! The flat was a disaster zone. Potato everywhere! We were finding bits of it for weeks.      In my defence, it was a very ambitious project. And I was fuelled by late-night curry and a genuine desire to impress a girl. Didn't work, by the way.      Sometimes the ambition is the reward, my boy. Besides, a dragon made of mashed potatoes...that's a story worth telling.

...Honestly, the traffic on the A19 was mental. I swear, every lorry driver in the country decided to take a holiday today. Took me nearly an hour just to get from Washington to Boldon.      Ugh, seriously? That sounds dreadful. I took the A1 and it wasn’t  pleasant , but definitely better. Though, seeing as you deal with language data all day, did you notice that new advert for that breakdown cover? The one with the talking car? It's… something.      Oh, aye, the one with the really posh voice? It's awful, isn't it? Trying to be quirky and it just comes across as deeply unsettling. And the script! Basic as you like. I probably analysed it subconsciously while driving, actually. “Need help? Beep beep! Call us!” Honestly. My job is occasionally rewarding, but then I encounter adverts like that and question everything.      Exactly! It's the forced personality that gets me. They just slap a vaguely humorous tone onto a fundamentally stressful situation. I’d be more reassured by a calm, efficient voice. Remember that old AA advert with the guy in the flat cap?  That  was good.      Oh, aye! Proper reassuring. Now  that  was an advert. Listen, about Saturday… are we still on for that new Italian place in Ouseburn? I was talking to Sarah – you remember Sarah from uni? – and she said it's brilliant, really authentic.      Ouseburn sounds amazing. Saturday's good, yeah. I’ve been meaning to explore that area more. It's completely different to Harpenden, isn’t it? All that gritty industrial heritage. My hometown feels… well, it feels like a catalogue showroom sometimes. All perfect lawns and semi-detached houses.      Ha! Aye, Sunderland's a bit rougher around the edges, that’s for sure. But that's what I like about it. It's… real. And Ouseburn's changing, becoming a bit of a hub for artists and everything. It’s good to see. Have you heard anything from your mum and dad recently? They were thinking about a holiday, weren't they?      They were talking about going to Italy actually! Tuscany, I think. They're proper tourists, my parents. Little guidebooks, pre-booked tours, the whole nine yards. It’s sweet, though. They deserve it. They were asking about us, said they were wondering if we wanted to join them.      Oh, wow! Italy… tempting. But I think we already booked those tickets for that film festival in Newcastle.

…and honestly, the whole thing with Aunt Margaret just felt so  sudden . One minute she was complaining about her knees, the next… well, you know. It’s the speed of it that's got me rattled, I think. We were only talking last month about her trying that new grapefruit diet.      Oh, bless her. Grapefruit diet, though? Sounds… punishing. My Doris, she’s always on some new thing. Last month it was kombucha, before that, apple cider vinegar. Says it’s ‘cleansing’. Honestly, I think it just makes her flatulent. But going back to your Aunt Margaret, sudden is awful. My Dad, it was quick too. One day seemingly fine, the next a stroke. Didn’t even get to say a proper goodbye.      Exactly! You just think you have more time. And the funeral arrangements… it’s all so overwhelming. My brother, David, is being very ‘practical’. Which is his way of… not dealing with it, I suspect. He’s already booked the celebrant and chosen the hymns. Efficient, but…cold.      Men, eh? They bottle it all up. My George was the same after his mother went. Just threw himself into sorting everything, like a military operation. Didn’t shed a tear, not a single one. I practically had to drag the emotion out of him. He needed it, you know? Holding it in just eats you up inside.      That's precisely what I'm worried about with David. He's always been like that. Controlled. Mum keeps trying to get him to talk, but he just says everything is "under control" and changes the subject. She's really upset, poor thing. She and Margaret were so close, practically sisters. She's lost weight already, I swear. She’s always been a bit… robust, but now she barely touches her food.      Oh, that’s classic. Grief does funny things to your appetite. Or lack of it. Doris lost a stone when her sister passed and she wasn’t exactly small to begin with! She said she couldn’t face food, it just felt… pointless. It's heartbreaking watching them. Has your Mum seen a doctor about the weight loss? It's not just the grief itself, you want to make sure nothing else is going on.      I’ve suggested it, but she just waves me away. Says she’s just “not feeling up to things”. She’s always been fiercely independent, Mum.

Right, that was a really lovely dinner. Thank you, David. The lamb was excellent. And honestly, just… nice to sit and chat without phones buzzing every five seconds.      My pleasure, Sarah. Glad you enjoyed it. I’ve been meaning to try that rosemary and garlic marinade for ages. It definitely paid off. So, how’s the freelance life treating you this week? Still battling rogue apostrophes and questionable comma placements?      You know me too well. It's relentless, David. Honestly, I spend half my life explaining the Oxford comma to people who  insist  it’s unnecessary. It's the small victories, I suppose. I actually landed a new client today – a small brewery needing help with their social media. Which is a nice change from academic proofreading, even if I do secretly enjoy spotting a misplaced semicolon.      A brewery? That sounds cool. Do they give you free beer?      Not yet, Leo, not yet! But I’m hoping to negotiate that as part of the contract. Think of the marketing possibilities… "Proofread by a professional, brewed to perfection!"      You should be the taste tester then. You're the expert.      Hey! I’m a discerning beverage enthusiast, thank you very much.      You’re both ridiculous. Sarah, that’s a clever angle with the brewery, clever indeed. It's all about finding the unique selling point. I’ve got a team meeting first thing tomorrow about streamlining our logistics. It’s… exciting, in a deeply bureaucratic sort of way.      Oh, dear. Sounds thrilling. Anything exciting happening with you two? Any thoughts on work experience for the summer, boys?      Dad said he might be able to get me something at the garage. Sorting spanners and… things. It's not ideal. I was hoping for something a bit more…computer-y.      I’m still trying to convince Mr. Harris, my science teacher, to let me help him with his experiments. He does that stuff with the rockets, remember?      The rockets! That  does  sound good, Leo. That’s excellent experience. Have you spoken to him properly about it?      Yeah, but he said he’s worried I’ll blow something up. Said I have a "healthy enthusiasm for combustion."      "Healthy enthusiasm for combustion"! That’s brilliant! I think maybe the garage is the safer option, Ethan. For everyone’s sake.      Speaking of things blowing up, remember that ski trip we took to Austria a few years ago? When David decided he was a professional downhill skier?

Oh,  this  one. Look at us. Absolutely dreadful fashion choices all round. Japan, 2015, right? Remember how determined I was to look like a rugged explorer, even though we spent most of our time in Tokyo train stations?      Rugged explorer in cargo shorts and a… was that a safari hat? Honestly, darling, you looked like you were about to lead a guided tour of a garden centre. And me, attempting ‘quirky tourist’ with that oversized floral scarf. We were so young and blissfully unaware of how silly we looked.      Blissfully unaware is the key phrase. I think I genuinely thought the safari hat was subtle. It was my attempt at blending in, you see. I’d read somewhere that Japanese men often wore hats...it didn’t quite translate. Did we even make it to Kyoto? I have a vague recollection of temples, but mostly, I remember the vending machines.      Kyoto, yes! We spent a lovely day there. Remember the tiny tea house, hidden down that little alley? The one with the incredibly grumpy cat? And you tried to order tea in Japanese, and it went  spectacularly  wrong?      Don’t remind me. I asked for hot water with a side of… badger. Or something very close to that. The waitress looked utterly horrified. I think she thought I was a mad foreigner.      You absolutely did! It was ‘badger’ and she’d asked if you wanted sugar! Sugar, not… a wild animal. It's still one of my favourite travel stories. It perfectly encapsulates your approach to international communication. Bold, confident, and utterly inaccurate.      Hey! I  tried . And it’s not my fault Japanese and English sound nothing alike. Speaking of wildlife though, have you seen any badgers around here lately? I was checking the trail cam this morning and nothing but foxes and the occasional deer.      Not recently. Old Man Hemmings down the lane swore he saw a whole sett forming near the woods last spring, but he also claims to have seen Elvis buying groceries in Dereham. So, take it with a pinch of salt.      Point taken. Hemmings is… a character. Still, I’d love to get some good photos of badgers. They’re so wonderfully striped, and so elusive. I've been practicing with the long lens, though mostly on squirrels. They're less dignified subjects.      Squirrels  are  rather frantic, aren’t they? I remember you spent an entire afternoon trying to get a decent shot of one eating a nut, then realised it was just a slightly blurry orange blob.

…Honestly, the Guinness in Galway was something  else . Proper creamy, you know? Not like the stuff you get on tap back here, feels like they just…water it down. I swear, I spent half my trip just wandering around pubs, "researching" the local breweries.      Oh, you and your "research," Liam! You always find a way to justify a pint. Ireland sounds lovely though. I’ve always wanted to go. Was it…rainy? Everyone says it’s always rainy.      Always. It’s a defining characteristic. But the scenery makes up for it. I went a few years back, before I opened the café. Found this tiny little village…completely postcard perfect. Though, the pub quiz questions were  brutal .      Brutal, huh? Sounds intense. I reckon I'd be useless. My geography peaked at knowing where Sydney is. Speaking of intense… anyone else ever gone skinny dipping? I did it once in a billabong back home. Utter madness. Water was freezing, and then a cow started staring at us.      A cow? Seriously? That’s… peak Australia. We didn’t get cows, thankfully. Just a few curious sheep. And a rather aggressive seagull. No skinny dipping for me, though - too cold, even in Ireland. I’m a wimp.      A cow! Oh, Darren, you have the best stories. I've considered it, actually, skinny dipping. Once, at a beach in Cornwall. But then I remembered about jellyfish and abandoned the idea. Too sensible, I suppose.      You're both mad. Don’t need jellyfish  or  cows judging your life choices. Speaking of sensible, how’s the bakery, Chloe? Still churning out amazing croissants?      Pretty hectic, actually. Wedding season is kicking off and everyone wants fancy cakes. I'm considering hiring someone, but finding reliable bakers is proving…difficult. Although, I did manage to perfect my rugelach recipe! It's based on one from Claudia Roden. You know her? Jewish-Egyptian cookbook author. It's incredible.      Claudia Roden? The name rings a bell. Mum used to have a few of her books. Proper authentic recipes, right? My Nan makes a mean cholent, though. That's about the extent of my Jewish culinary knowledge.      Cholent? What’s that? Sounds…substantial. Is it the kind of food you need to fortify yourself for, like, a zombie apocalypse?      Basically. It’s a slow-cooked stew. And yes, absolutely apocalypse-worthy. It’ll keep you going for days. Though, Liam’s snoring might attract the zombies  before  the stew keeps you alive.

...Honestly, the sheer audacity of it! He just  assumed  I hadn't checked my bag properly. Like I’m some sort of… peanut smuggler!      Right, the customs officer at Stansted? Still fuming about that, then? I thought you said you explained you were bringing them for my mum. She  loves  peanuts. A very specific brand, if I recall.      Loves them and will hunt you down if you bring the wrong ones. And I  did  explain! I said, “They're for my mum, she has a… peanut preference.” He just stared at me like I was trying to import endangered species. And then the pat-down! Honestly, Mark, a pat-down for  peanuts ?      Border security is a bit twitchy these days, isn’t it? I was reading something about increased surveillance at ports, all linked to… well, everything going on. But a peanut preference? That’s a new one for them, I imagine. Still, speaks volumes about your mum's dedication, doesn't it?      Dedication bordering on obsession, you mean. Anyway, it made me late meeting Professor Davies. I ended up rambling about airport security instead of focusing on the research data. He gave me  that  look. You know the one.      The ‘you need to get your life together’ look? Yeah, I know it well. He’s a good bloke, but a stickler. Speaking of needing to focus…I finally cracked that level in ‘Eldoria Online’. The one with the three-headed griffin? Absolute nightmare.      Oh, good for you! I haven’t had time to game lately. Work’s been manic. And Professor Davies keeps adding more to my plate. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I’m living and breathing spreadsheets. Did you see that new Marvel film? Was it any good? Distraction therapy, needed desperately.      It was… okay. A bit too much CGI and not enough plot, if I'm honest. Felt like they were trying to one-up the last one instead of telling a good story. We should just go to Alton Towers next weekend. Properly switch off. Rollercoasters and sugar-filled snacks.      Alton Towers… Now  that's  talking. Nemesis Reborn is supposed to be terrifying. Though, knowing my luck, I'd probably get stuck at the top and become a human weather vane. They'd be questioning  me  about airport security again, but this time from a significantly greater height.      You always manage to find the worst-case scenario.

Honestly, this is exactly what I needed. Proper fish and chips after a week of… well, after a week of trying not to capsize.      Rowing’s proving a bit trickier than you anticipated then? I knew you were fairly fit, but there’s a knack to it, isn't there? It’s not just upper body strength.      It’s  everything . Core, legs, timing… and a complete disregard for dignity when you inevitably end up looking like a floundering seal. I thought kayaking was hard, and it has its moments, especially in a bit of a chop, but rowing feels… more sophisticated in its difficulty. More… precise.      I can believe it. Kayaking's more forgiving, I think. You can just sort of wobble your way through. Remember that time we went down the Avon, and I nearly went under that low branch?      Oh,  please . You didn’t  nearly  go under. You elegantly ducked, whilst simultaneously emitting a small scream. It was practically a performance piece. But speaking of getting wet… I need serious waterproofs. Everything I own is soaked through after an hour on the Cam. Any recommendations? I’ve looked online, but it’s all so confusing.      Oh, I’ve become something of an expert on waterproofs ironically! All this tutoring outdoors, rain or shine you know. Cotswold Outdoor did me well a couple of years back. Good quality, but pricey. Though, honestly, worth it if you're going to be regularly drenched. What sort of jacket are you thinking? Something breathable, definitely.      Breathable, yes. The current one makes me feel like I’m rowing in a plastic bag. It's almost worse than being wet. It was a bit of an impulse buy from a supermarket, I confess. Actually, this all reminds me… I finally met Cousin Brenda’s daughter, Chloe, last month.      Oh, really? Brenda’s daughter! I’d almost forgotten Brenda  had  a daughter. You always said she was quite… distant.      Distant is putting it mildly. Brenda and my Mum had a falling out years ago – over something ridiculously trivial involving a prize-winning marrow at a village fete, if you can believe it – and they barely spoke for decades. Chloe reached out on Facebook, completely out of the blue. Said she'd been trying to find us for ages. It was lovely, but awkward. Trying to fill thirty years of lost family history in a coffee shop…      That must have been.

Honestly, Dad, I’m  stressed . Results day is looming and I feel like my brain’s just… emptied. It’s like trying to recall Morse code after not looking at it for months. Remember when you tried to teach me?      Aye, I do. You weren't keen, were ya? Kept saying it was a waste of time when we had texting. "Why bother with dots and dashes when I can just send a thumbs-up emoji, Dad?" I remember that clear as day. Still, a good skill to have in a pinch, eh? Though I suppose learning to navigate Vodafone customer service is a more useful modern survival skill, honestly.      It is! Honestly, getting through to someone who understands what "data roaming" even  is  feels like cracking an unbreakable code. But university… it just feels so big. I walked around the campus last week and I got completely lost. It’s massive.      That’s natural, lass. It  is  a big step. Manchester University's a proper maze, isn't it? Reminds me of trying to find a parking space at the Trafford Centre on a Saturday. Pure chaos. Did you get a map? I could have printed you one. I’ve got that new printer, remember? The one I got on eBay after the old one decided to pack in after, like, two weeks.      Yeah, I had a map, but it didn’t help much. Everything looks the same! And everything’s so… organised. Like, the library is this huge, imposing building and I just felt… intimidated. I’m worried about managing my money too. Student finance is a nightmare to figure out.      Right, money. Always the tricky bit. Look, don't panic. We'll sort it. We've been saving, you know, a little each month. And your nan’s promised a contribution. It won’t be a fortune, but it'll help. And remember, I'm still here. I can help you budget. We’ll get you a good set of stationery too – proper pens, not those flimsy ones they give you at school. Good pens make all the difference to motivation.      That’s nice of you, Dad. I do have a weakness for a good gel pen. And I really need new shoes, my trainers are falling apart. Amazon did a delivery today, but it wasn’t them. It was just Mum’s new glass water bottles. She’s really trying to go plastic-free.

…Honestly, mate, this essay is killing me. Absolute death. Professor Davies is expecting a dissertation on the socio-economic impact of…wait for it… algorithmic trading. Algorithmic  trading . Like I even know what that  is  beyond vaguely sounding important.      Davies, yeah, he loves his niche topics, doesn’t he? Sounds proper dry. I'm wrestling with data analysis for my dissertation. Feels like I’m staring into the abyss of spreadsheets, innit? But algorithmic trading… that's a new level of obscure. You thinking of going to the library, or just trying to bluff your way through it?      Bluffing feels increasingly tempting, to be honest. I’ve skimmed a few articles, and it’s all just…numbers. And jargon. I was hoping to bounce some ideas off you, actually. You're always good at simplifying complicated stuff. Plus, you just  seem  to know everything about everything.      Nah, man, that's just a front. I spend half my time Googling things while pretending I knew them all along. But hit me with it. What’s giving you the biggest headache? And before you get into it, you gotta promise me we’re taking a break later and ordering that new ramen place on Brixton Road. I’ve been craving it all week.      Deal! Ramen sounds amazing. Right, so it's the scale of it, I think. How algorithmic trading impacts…everyone. Davies wants case studies, and I'm just thinking ‘Wall Street wolfs making money’ feels a bit… shallow.      It  is  shallow! You need to think broader, yeah? Think about how it impacts pension funds, insurance companies, even just everyday investments. It’s all connected. Actually, it reminds me a bit of something I was reading about Tokyo.      Tokyo? What's Tokyo got to do with dodgy trading algorithms?      Hear me out. I was looking at some travel blogs, 'cause I'm seriously thinking about doing a gap year after we finish, maybe teaching English over there. And a lot of them were talking about how incredibly advanced their tech infrastructure is. Like, they’re completely reliant on automated systems for everything - traffic control, the stock exchange, you name it. It’s all algorithms. So you could maybe structure your essay around how different countries are  adapting  to this sort of thing? Japan as a case study of embracing it, maybe contrast with a country that’s more hesitant?      Woah. That's…actually brilliant.

...Honestly, Mum, the photos from Buckfast Abbey are lovely, aren’t they? I've just been scrolling through them on Facebook, trying to figure out which ones to actually print. It’s just… so  brown . Everything's brown! But the stained glass was spectacular.      Brown is a good description, dear. It  is  rather…monochromatic, isn't it? But peaceful, though. Very peaceful. And you got a good shot of the monks, didn’t you? Old Mr. Henderson at the book club was fascinated – said he used to know a monk there, years ago. Apparently, they make a surprisingly good nettle tea.      Nettles! Reminds me of the war. We used to make soup from nettles. Wouldn't touch 'em now, of course. Too much bother. Though I must say, that Abbey looks a sight more impressive than it did when I was a lad. All polished up. They’ve done wonders with the gardens.      It  was  well-maintained. I was thinking, maybe next year we could look at doing a bigger trip? Something a bit…further afield? I was looking at cruises, actually.      Cruises? Oh, now you’re talking! I’ve always fancied a cruise. Somewhere warm, preferably. The Mediterranean? I've heard good things about the Greek islands.      Cruises are for people who are afraid to get their feet wet. Give me a train journey any day. You see the country, you talk to people…crises on the open ocean, no thank you. Though I suppose if they’ve got a good buffet…      Dad, you’d love a cruise. Endless buffets! And entertainment. We could go somewhere to see the Northern Lights? Or maybe the fjords? I’ve always wanted to see Norway.      Norway sounds lovely, but all that cold… and think of the insurance! Travel insurance is a nightmare these days. Especially with my dodgy knees. I had to fill out such a lengthy health questionnaire just to get covered for Devon!      Mum, you’re thinking about insurance already? We haven’t even decided  if  we’re going!      Insurance… It's all a fiddle, you know. All these companies. Reminds me of David Cameron and those tax avoidance schemes. Now  there  was dodgy dealing. Proper fiddle that was. Getting richer while the rest of us…      Oh, don't start on politics, Arthur. It'll ruin the afternoon. Besides, it's all a bit above my head, to be honest. I just want to enjoy my tea and biscuits.

Honestly, you two look  relaxed . Properly relaxed. Did Belgium really work its magic? You both seemed so stressed about driving over there beforehand.      Relaxed is putting it mildly, love. It was… an experience. More of a comedy of errors, if I'm being truthful. Your mother’s insistence on navigating with that ancient sat nav was the start of it all.      Ancient is a bit harsh, Arthur! It got us  mostly  there. It just… had a very strong opinion on roundabouts. And narrow cobbled streets. Frankly, it tried to drive us into a canal at one point.      No way! A canal? Seriously? I told you to download a proper app on my phone. I could've set it up for you before you went.      Well, your mother doesn't trust these 'fancy apps', says they drain the battery. Plus, she's convinced the sat nav 'knows the real routes'. Honestly, it was like arguing with a brick wall. We ended up adding an hour to every journey.      It wasn’t  that  bad! And we saw some lovely countryside getting lost. We stumbled upon this gorgeous little market in Bruges, full of lace and chocolates. Did I tell you about the waffles? Oh, the waffles. They were heavenly.      You mentioned waffles, yes! But heavenly is a strong claim. Were they better than the ones we had in Ghent a couple of years ago? Because those were life-changing.      Oh, easily. These were… authentic. And the vendor used real Belgian chocolate, not that powdery stuff they sometimes give you. And the market itself! So vibrant. I even bought a little hand-painted ceramic tile as a souvenir.      She spent a fortune in that market, she did. I was trying to keep track of the budget, but she just kept finding 'bargains'. I think we brought back more chocolate than clothes.      Sounds like Mum. Though, honestly, a market sounds amazing. I've been meaning to go to one here in Brighton, but work’s been so hectic. How was the cycling? You mentioned you were hoping to do some.      We did a bit! Arthur didn't fancy it too much, he said his knees weren't up to it. But I hired a bike for a day and cycled along the canals near Ghent. It was beautiful. Very flat, luckily. I'm not built for hills.      Flat is an understatement. It was like cycling on a billiard table.

Right, I  think  this is enough chilli powder. Honestly, it always feels like a guessing game. Do you remember Auntie Margaret's chilli? It wasn't spicy at all, just… flavourful. She used to say the secret was cinnamon.      Cinnamon? Margaret and her eccentricities! I vaguely recall something about nutmeg as well. She was a wonderful cook, though. Always made you feel utterly stuffed and then offered you another scone. This smells good, by the way. Not subtly cinnamon-y, thankfully. I'm not in the mood for something sweet with my dinner.      Good! Because there’s absolutely no cinnamon going in this. Just a healthy dose of… well, hopefully healthy, chilli. It’s just, I was scrolling through Facebook earlier, and old school friends keep posting photos of their perfect meals, all beautifully plated and… I don’t know. It makes me feel inadequate.      Facebook. The highlight reel of everyone’s lives. Don't compare yourself to that nonsense, love. You're a brilliant cook. Remember that pheasant you did last Christmas? Absolutely superb. And believe me, I’ve seen  their  cooking. Remember Brenda’s attempt at a soufflé? Collapsed before it even hit the table.      Oh, God, yes! Brenda and her soufflé disasters. Still, they always  look  so put together. And they’re all posting about their fancy hand creams and perfumes. It's a whole thing. Speaking of perfume, have you tried that new ‘Midnight Bloom’ everyone’s raving about?      Midnight Bloom? No, doesn’t ring a bell. I’m resolutely stuck in my ‘Vetiver’ phase, you know. Anything too floral gives me a headache. It's probably my Scottish upbringing. We’re a practical bunch. Roses are lovely to look at, but give me a sturdy heather any day. Though, admittedly, the lilies you got last week  did  brighten up the place. They’re still going strong, actually, aren't they?      They are. I put them in the living room. It makes the fireplace look a little less… sad. It needs a good clean, doesn’t it? It's been ages since we’ve lit it.      It does. We should tackle that next weekend. Maybe after that charity shop rummage you were talking about. I'm hoping to find a decent record player. I’ve been on a vinyl kick recently.      Ooh, good idea! And I’m trying to declutter. Although, I always end up bringing more in than I take out.

...and honestly, the heat in Queensland nearly did for me. Not used to it, you see. Manchester prepares you for a bit of drizzle, maybe a damp chill, but not  that . It’s a different kind of oppressive, isn't it?      Oh, absolutely. I spent a summer in Sydney, teaching English as a Foreign Language. Lovely country, magnificent beaches, but the sun… I’m from just north of Bristol, Almondsbury, and we get our fair share of sunshine, of course, but it’s a gentler heat. Queensland sounded… bracing, even from what you’re saying. Did you go for work, or just a holiday?      Bracing? That's a polite way to put it! I’ve been to Cairns a couple of times, conference work mostly. It hits you like a wall. Though, I find the people are wonderful. Very welcoming. And down to earth. I'm from Sheffield, and we're generally considered pretty grounded folk ourselves.      Work, yes. A bit of a consultancy gig, sorting out some issues with a local mining company. Tidied up their accounts, mainly. So many of them, all in these terribly expensive suits, strutting around like peacocks. You’d think they were running the Bank of England, not digging holes in the ground! I always found it a bit…much. And the ties! Don’t even get me started on the ties.      Oh, the suits. Yes, I noticed that during my time teaching abroad, in various places actually. Even in France, the business attire was significantly more formal than anything worn back home. I found it rather amusing, to be honest. A bit stuffy. I was always more comfortable in sensible shoes and a cardigan. Though, trying to explain that to my students sometimes was… challenging. They expected a certain ‘teacherly’ look, I suppose.      Sensible shoes are a good choice, believe me. I've spent years on my feet lecturing, and comfort is paramount. What did you teach, if you don't mind me asking? And where  all  did you teach?      Mostly English grammar and pronunciation. I liked helping people dismantle those tricky little rules! I worked in Spain, France, Italy… and, as I said, a summer in Sydney. It’s a very rewarding profession, though can be tiring. The bureaucracy around visas was always a headache. Trying to get a bank loan to cover the travel sometimes felt like a bigger challenge than teaching subjunctive clauses!

Honestly, this pierogi is surprisingly good. I was expecting… well, I don’t know  what  I was expecting, being a vegan place in Poland, but it’s really quite delicious. Though, I still can't quite get my head around a pierogi without potato and cheese.      Tell me about it! It's a cultural adjustment, even for me. And coming from someone who actively  chooses  to eat this way, that's saying something. Anyway, you wouldn't believe the rabbit hole I fell down on TikTok last night. Some influencer doing a ‘day in the life’ as an English teacher in…Kazakhstan, I think?      Kazakhstan! Good heavens. Sounds a world away from Bury, doesn't it? You’re always glued to that thing, aren’t you? I try to avoid it. Too much… curated perfection, I find. Makes me feel thoroughly inadequate. I did dabble with Instagram for a bit, mostly to look at pictures of gardens. But then I realised I was comparing my pathetic little balcony herb garden to Capability Brown landscapes and promptly deleted it.      Yeah, it's a minefield. But sometimes it’s useful for picking up teaching tips, you know? Seeing what other people are doing. And the Kazakhstan one was genuinely fascinating. Apparently, the students are  obsessed  with British slang. She was trying to explain ‘taking the mickey’ and it was hilarious. Did you see that new drama on BBC,  Happy Valley ? Everyone was talking about it.      Oh,  Happy Valley ! Yes! I did, actually. Brilliant. Sarah Lancashire is just phenomenal. Though rather grim, isn’t it? All that Yorkshire bleakness. I’m a bit of a sucker for a good crime drama, if it's well-written. I haven’t really watched much TV recently, though. I've been getting into podcasts again.      Oh, which ones? I try to listen to one on my commute – helps me block out the screaming children on the bus. . I’m currently obsessed with this true crime one… it’s morbid, I know, but so well researched.      I'm listening to a history one at the moment, about the Tudors. It's lovely. Proper storytelling, very BBC Radio 4. I used to listen to a lot of those when I was, well, when I was working. Before… all this. It fills the time, you know? Makes me feel a bit less… adrift. Do you ever feel like that?      To be honest, yeah, sometimes.

Right, so, Pippy said she  really  wants to try and get a photo of us all with her for her Blue Peter badge application. Apparently, she’s performing with ANON’s Travelling Circus next week, and that’s her evidence of ‘doing something amazing’.      I want to be  in  the picture! Can I wear my sparkly swimming costume? The one with the mermaid tail?      Can I have a biscuit? I'm hungry. And can I wear my pirate hat? It's  amazing .      Okay, okay, we can discuss the outfits. Sparkly mermaid tail sounds… festive. Pirate hat is good. But first, we need to figure out logistics. This circus… it’s down near Cambridge, isn’t it?      Yes! Pippy said it's a  real  circus, with elephants and lions and everything! Well, maybe not lions. She said they're a bit scary.      I want to see an elephant! Do we need our passports?      No, darling, we don’t need passports to go to Cambridge. It’s still in England. Remember when we talked about needing them for France? Different country.      Oh. Right. But what if Pippy flies on a trapeze? Does she need a passport for  that ?      I think she'll be alright without it for the trapeze. It’s all happening under the Big Top, remember? Speaking of Pippy, she was telling me she's twelve. Can you believe it? Seems like yesterday she was barely taller than you, Leo.      Twelve? Wow. That's… a big number. Bigger than my age. How much pocket money do twelve-year-olds get?      That's a good question! Each family does it differently, sweetie. Probably more than you get. Now, about this circus… It’s Saturday, and I thought we could go swimming first? We promised you both.      Yay! Can we go to the big pool with the wave machine?      And can I use my inflatable shark?      Absolutely. Swimming, then circus, then maybe fish and chips for dinner? It’ll be a busy day.      Did you know Pippy said her Grandad eats really weird things? She said he eats  really  old eggs! Like, super old!      Old eggs, you say? Well, that’s… interesting. Apparently, in some parts of China, they have a delicacy called century eggs. They preserve eggs in clay, ash, and quicklime for  months .      Eww! That sounds disgusting.      It’s an acquired taste, apparently. Definitely not something I’ll be trying anytime soon.

Right, so… this is awkward. Proper awkward. But I needed to tell someone, and you're the only one I feel I can, y’know?      Awkward how? You look like you've seen a ghost, love. What's up? You can tell me anything, you know that. Is it uni stress? Something with your mum?      No, not that. It’s… it’s about Mark. And, well… it’s a bit embarrassing. It's about… us.      Mark? What about Mark? Did he… did he do something silly again? He's a good lad, but sometimes his impulses…      No, it's not  him  doing something silly. It’s… he’s been struggling. With… getting, well,  things  working, if you catch my drift.      Oh. Oh, right. You mean… erectile dysfunction?      Yeah. That. I didn’t even wanna say it out loud. He told me last night. He was proper mortified, bless him. Said he’s been worried about letting me down.      That must have been awful for him to tell you. It's a really vulnerable thing to admit. And good on him for telling you, honestly. A lot of blokes would just… bottle it up.      I know, right? He was proper upset. He kept saying it wasn’t my fault, that he felt like less of a man, all that. I tried to reassure him, but I just… I didn’t know what to say. I've never even  thought  about anything like this before.      It’s okay to not know what to say. It's a really common thing, honestly. Stress, anxiety, even just being tired can cause it. It doesn’t define him, and it  definitely  doesn’t mean he's failing you. Has he seen a doctor?      He’s hesitant. He’s worried about what they'll think, about having to… explain everything. He’s a bit old-fashioned like that, y’know? Thinks it's a sign of weakness.      Ugh, that's the worst. That stigma is so damaging. You need to gently encourage him to go. There are so many solutions now. Medication, therapy, even lifestyle changes can make a huge difference. It’s about getting to the root of the problem, not just feeling ashamed.      I tried to say that, but he just brushed it off. He said he doesn’t wanna be “one of those” that needs pills to… perform.      Right. Okay. This is where it gets tricky.

Honestly, this Slimming World lark is exhausting sometimes. I’m trying to figure out if I can have a biscuit with my tea without completely blowing my syns for the day. It's just…a biscuit!      Oh, don't even  start  on the biscuits. It's a minefield. Are you thinking a proper chocolate digestive or just one of those weird fibre ones? Because those fibre ones…they're a psychological betrayal, aren’t they? Pretending to be biscuit-like.      No, no, a proper one. A tiny, tiny one. But I was looking at the Healthy Extra options, and the rules are so vague! Can I actually  have  a biscuit, or do I have to choose between bread  or  a biscuit? It feels like a trick.      It is a trick! They want you to feel slightly deprived. Right, okay, tiny biscuit… probably worth a few syns, but honestly, if it keeps you on track, then a couple won’t kill you. Especially if you're good all week. Speaking of good, did you see that Sainsbury’s has the best Quorn range at the moment? I got some of the mince to make chilli tomorrow.      Oh, really? I’ve been meaning to stock up on Quorn. Honestly, it's the only thing keeping me sane and still able to have ‘meat’ meals. And you’re right about the syns. I’m agonizing over everything! Even the 0 calorie syrup feels…suspiciously artificial.      It  is  artificial. Let’s be real. But it’s 0 syns, and sometimes you just need something sweet with your porridge, right? I'm just hoping it doesn’t give me headaches. We’re proper grown-up now needing to weigh up these things! Anyway, we need to nail down 'treat day' on Saturday. What are you fancying?      Oh, Saturday! I was thinking… maybe a roast? I've been craving proper roast potatoes. And I've got a recipe for cauliflower cheese that's surprisingly good. We can Free Food the cauliflower, obviously.      Cauliflower cheese sounds amazing! Roasted veg alongside it…perfect. We need to have a plan of attack though. We don't want to just fall face-first into a pile of chocolate. Maybe pre-portion some things?      Good thinking. Portion control is key. Although, I swear, my scales are completely unreliable. One minute I’m down a pound, the next I’ve gained three. It's infuriating.

Honestly, just thinking about two weeks in Cornwall is already making this week bearable. I’ve been looking at cottages with fireplaces… imagine, roaring fire, books, walks along the coast. Bliss. Are you still leaning towards surfing lessons?      Absolutely. I'm determined to at least  attempt  to stand up on a board this time. Last time was… humbling, let’s put it that way. More time being  in  the water than  on  it. Though, actually, that wasn’t so bad. It was surprisingly warm. Are we definite on St Ives? I was reading about Padstow. Apparently, the foodie scene is incredible there.      Padstow  is  tempting, but St Ives feels…right. It's got that artist vibe I like. Plus, the beaches are a bit more sheltered. Though, realistically, I suspect we'll spend a good chunk of time just pottering around antique shops. You know me.      Of course. And I’ll be the designated carrier of all your treasures. Speaking of treasures, did you get anywhere with that short story you were working on? The one about the lighthouse keeper?      A little. I hit a wall with the ending. It felt… contrived. I keep trying to force a dramatic reveal, but it just doesn’t feel natural. It's so frustrating. Maybe I should just scrap it and start something new. It’s not like anyone’s paying me to write the next great novel.      Don’t be so hard on yourself. You’ve got a real knack for describing atmosphere. Remember that piece you did about that abandoned chapel? That was brilliant. Maybe the lighthouse keeper doesn’t  need  a dramatic reveal. Maybe the story is just about the loneliness of the job.      Hmm, that’s a thought. Maybe you’re right. It’s just… I feel this pressure to write something ‘important’, you know? Especially with everything going on in the world. This political mess is infuriating.      Tell me about it. I was reading an article earlier about…well, I won’t bore you with the details, but it felt like another brick in the wall of nonsense. It’s exhausting. Honestly, sometimes I think I’d rather just live off-grid.      You’d last five minutes! You’d miss your gadgets and your internet. And your perfectly organised spreadsheet of all the football scores.      Fair point. Though, I did see a documentary about a guy who built his own house out of reclaimed materials.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of heather was breathtaking. Didn’t quite capture it on the postcard, did I? It just…flattened it all out, you know? Too much purple. Sent it to Margaret, she’ll likely stick it to the fridge with a magnet. Margaret and her magnetic gallery. She’s a good one for that. I got yours this morning, by the way. Lovely picture of the castle. Though, it does look a bit…windswept. Reminds me of your hair after a particularly bracing walk. Windswept is generous! It was practically horizontal. Anyway, postcard aside, we really ought to fix something for Fiona’s birthday. It’s the 27th, isn’t it? Seems to creep up on us every year. The 27th it is. Goodness me, already. I was thinking a little gathering here? Not a huge affair, she's not one for fuss. Perhaps a nice roast, we could invite the Millers... and maybe David and Sarah? Sounds lovely. The Millers would be good. And yes, David and Sarah, though Sarah's been terribly busy with that new project at work. Might need a bit of prompting. Do you think she’d appreciate a lemon drizzle, or is she still on that gluten-free kick? I believe the gluten-free is still in effect, sadly. Though she does occasionally ‘slip up’, according to David. He relayed a tale of a rogue biscuit last week. We'll need to remember that. What about the weekend  after  Fiona's? I was rather hoping we could finally get up to that steam railway museum. You’ve been talking about it for months. Oh, the railway museum! Excellent idea. Depending on the weather, of course. It's hardly a pleasant outing in the pouring rain. Though, a bit of drizzle wouldn't deter me, given the chance to see those engines. Right. I'll keep an eye on the forecast. Speaking of forecasts…have you been following this latest rumbling about Scottish independence? Seems they're stirring things up again. Oh, don’t even get me started. Honestly, it’s exhausting. More division, more uncertainty. I spent a summer lecturing in Edinburgh years ago. Wonderful city, beautiful people, but the whole thing feels… deeply unresolved. I know. It's a complex situation, to say the least. They've got legitimate grievances, haven’t they? But splitting up the country... I'm not convinced it's the answer.

Right, so we’ve got the flowers, and… what are you two drawing now? It looks suspiciously chair-shaped.      It  is  chair-shaped! It's for the people coming to stay. The Syrian people.      Yeah! A really comfy chair. With… with springs! So they don't feel bumpy.      Oh, that’s lovely, you two. Very thoughtful. It  is  a good chair design. Bit ambitious with the springs for a drawing, mind you. But the sentiment is perfect. We talked about them needing a welcoming space, didn't we?      Mummy, will they be sad?      They’ve been through a lot, darling. Leaving their homes and everything behind is a very sad thing. But they’re very brave, and they’re coming to a safe place. And hopefully, we can help them feel a little bit happier here. That’s why we’re trying to make our house nice for them. And why you’re drawing such wonderful chairs.      So, what kind of chairs  do  they have in Syria? Are they different?      That’s a good question. They’ll have all sorts, just like we do here. Some old wooden ones, some newer plastic ones, maybe some really fancy ones if they had a lot of money. Different countries have different styles, you see. We’ve got these comfy armchairs, and those kitchen chairs… and that really wobbly one in the attic that Great-Grandma used to have.      The wobbly one! It tries to eat you!      It does have a personality, doesn’t it? We're thinking of setting up the spare room with a proper desk for the older boy – he's about your age, actually, Speaker_3 – so he can do his schoolwork. It's a bit daunting starting at a new school, isn’t it? Especially when you don't speak the language very well.      Will he have tests? I  hate  tests.      He will, eventually. But not straight away. They'll focus on helping him learn the language first. It’s not about showing what he  doesn't  know; it’s about learning what he  needs  to know, to feel settled. It's very different from some of the tests you get at school, isn’t it? More about figuring things out, not just remembering facts.      He needs a really,  really  bouncy chair for thinking.      A bouncy chair! That’s a brilliant idea. Maybe we can find one. Though I’m not sure the one in the attic is bouncy enough.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of tiny clothes is terrifying. I keep thinking, “They grow out of it  so  quickly!” It's a mountain of miniature outfits. You're already fully in ‘nesting’ mode then, I see. It’s a good kind of terrifying, though, right? A happy terrifying. And massively impractical. I vaguely remember my sister going through this. It  is  happy. Just…overwhelming. It makes me think about Sarah, actually. I haven't heard from her in ages. Last I knew, she was still trying for a second. Oh, that's right. Poor Sarah. She was so gutted when the first attempt didn’t work out. How long has it been? Months? It must be nearly six, I think. I feel awful that I haven’t reached out. It feels… presumptuous, you know? Like asking about it will just reopen old wounds. I get that. But Sarah’s not the type to be offended. She’s always been incredibly open. Maybe just a quick text checking she's alright, not necessarily focusing on babies? Something about work, or something completely random? That’s a good idea. Work. Yes. We could talk about the absolute chaos of the new intake. Honestly, they're bright, but their referencing skills are… questionable. I spent half of yesterday helping a student find a peer-reviewed journal that wasn’t a blog. Oh, bless them. It’s the same every year. They come straight from school thinking Wikipedia is gospel. I had one argue that TikTok counts as academic research last week. No! Seriously? The world is officially losing its mind. Though, to be fair, TikTok  is  a massive repository of information… mostly misinformation, obviously. But it’s symptomatic, isn’t it? This whole erosion of critical thinking. It is. It feels like we spend half our lectures trying to teach them  how  to learn, rather than the actual subject matter. It's exhausting. Although, I did have a good session with Ben today. Remember Ben, the one who was struggling with the essay structure? Vaguely? Tall, wears those awful patterned shirts? That’s the one! He actually nailed it today. Completely restructured his argument, clear, concise… I think he finally clicked. That’s why I still enjoy the teaching, you know? When you see that little moment of understanding. Absolutely. Those moments make all the referencing disasters worth it. It’s a shame it’s so rare!

Honestly, this is  exactly  what I needed. London feels… suffocating sometimes, doesn’t it? All that noise and rushing. It’s lovely just to hear birdsong for a change.      Absolutely. Though I think I’d start missing a decent coffee shop after a couple of days. Pure countryside is beautiful, but a little  too  pure for this London boy. You really do appreciate the small things, like a flat white, when they’re gone.      You and your coffee! It’s a serious affliction. Reminds me of Old Man Hemmings from my village growing up. He refused to leave Norfolk, swore the London water would give him the vapours. Utterly convinced.      The vapours? That’s brilliant. People are wonderfully superstitious, aren't they? Especially the older generation. My nan used to insist on throwing salt over her left shoulder if a black cat crossed her path, even  inside  the house! Sent salt flying everywhere once during dinner with our American cousins. They were… bewildered.      Oh, my auntie’s even worse. She thinks policemen can smell if you’ve done something wrong. Literally believes they have some sort of sixth sense for guilt. She was practically apologising to a traffic warden for  thinking  about parking slightly over the line.      That’s fantastic! I wonder if they get training for that. "Advanced Guilt Detection." Imagine the syllabus. Though, funnily enough, I did have a run-in with a policeman a couple of weeks ago. Nothing serious, just a parking ticket near the university.      Oh dear. Anything interesting happen? Did they at least have a good story to tell?      Not really. Standard issue - slightly grumpy, slightly bored. But it did get me thinking about the university's reputation in the local paper. Apparently, they’re trying to get more positive publicity, focusing on our research. They asked if I had any “human interest” stories I could pitch.      Ah, the PR machine. Always hungry for a feel-good narrative. What did you suggest? Hopefully not your parking ticket escapade.      No, I managed to avoid that one. I mentioned some of the outreach work you do with the local schools – the history workshops. That seemed to go down well. Honestly, you're much better at that stuff than I am. You have a knack for making it accessible and engaging.      Well, they’re lovely kids, and Norfolk has such a rich history. It's easy to get enthusiastic.

Honestly, Dad, this new update is  infuriating . They’ve completely redesigned the layout. It took me fifteen minutes just to find where to change my notification settings.      Notifications, eh? Sounds like a load of fuss to me. Back in my day, a notification was someone knocking on the door. Much simpler. What are you even needing notifications  for  all the time?      Everything! Work emails, messages from friends, reminders for uni…it's how everything happens now. It's just annoying when they keep changing things. Speaking of annoying, have you sorted out a van for moving the shed stuff over to Mum’s?      Nearly. Called a few places yesterday. Prices are ridiculous. Everyone's trying to rip you off, the lot of them. Found a fella down in Ashford who'll do it for, well, still a bit steep, but it's the best I've managed so far. £180 for a Luton van for the afternoon.      Ouch. That  is  a bit pricey. Maybe we should look at hiring a trailer instead? Would that be cheaper? I can drive the car, we just need to figure out how to attach it.      Nah, too much faff. And all that lifting. Remember your back, love. Luton van’s the way to go, even if it hurts the wallet. Anyway, speaking of faff… did you manage to get hold of Uncle Barry? I wanted to know if he was coming to the Great Dorset Steam Fair.      I texted him earlier, haven’t had a reply yet. He’s terrible at checking his phone, honestly. He still thinks texting is a newfangled miracle. He’ll probably turn up anyway, you know he loves that fair. Says it reminds him of his childhood.      Aye, he’s a sentimental soul, your Uncle Barry. Reminds  me  of my childhood, actually. All that steam and noise. Wonderful. Better than these…computer games you youngsters are always glued to. What  is  it you’re playing now? Still that…Fortnight thing?      Fortnite's a bit old news, Dad! I'm playing Baldur's Gate 3 at the moment. It’s… complicated. A role-playing game, really. Lots of choices, lots of story. It's completely absorbing.      Sounds exhausting. I’d rather be down on the riverbank, rod in hand. Had a good session last week, down by the old mill. Pulled out a decent sized chub. Nearly as big as my forearm!

…and honestly, the sheer audacity of it! Demolishing the library? It’s been there since  forever . My grandmother used to take me there when I was little. Remember when we used to spend hours in the children’s section, Mark? Absolutely. The smell of the old books… and Mrs. Higgins, always shushing everyone with a kind smile. It’s a cornerstone of the community, isn’t it? What’s the council’s reasoning this time? "Regeneration"? That’s what they always say. Regeneration! It’s code for ‘building overpriced flats no one can afford’. Apparently, the land is ‘prime real estate’. Honestly, prime for what? More soulless glass boxes? I’ve been looking at the plans online, and it's dreadful. It’ll completely change the character of the High Street. I saw a snippet about it in the  Guardian  online. They mentioned something about a petition? Have you signed it? Signed it, shared it, badgered everyone I know to sign it! I've even emailed the local councillor, although I’m not holding my breath. They rarely reply to anything unless it involves council tax. Speaking of which, are you still wading through those spreadsheets for work? Sadly, yes. Endless spreadsheets and form-filling. It's… stimulating. Honestly, sometimes I feel like a highly paid paperclip. Anyway, back to the library. Did you see the photos that old Mr. Henderson posted on the village Facebook page? The ones from the 1920s? Oh, yes! The ones showing the original facade. It used to have that lovely stonework, didn’t it? They stripped it off in the 70s, said it was crumbling. It’s such a shame - they could have restored it. It's always easier to just knock something down and start again, isn’t it? It feels like this town is losing all its character. Precisely. It’s the same with the old bakery. They're talking about turning that into a… a vape shop. A  vape shop ! That beautiful building, with all the original tiling still intact, reduced to selling flavoured smoke. It's depressing. It is. You know, I was thinking about the sofa... We need to actually  decide  on a fabric. I was looking at that website you showed me, and there are just  so  many choices. I’m leaning towards something durable, you know, with the dog and everything. Right. Practicality wins. I do like that Harris Tweed, though.

Oh, this is a good one. Bit of Fleetwood Mac. Always does the trick on a long drive, doesn't it? Remember when Sarah was obsessed with them? She'd play  Rumours  constantly.      Ugh, yeah, for like, a solid month. It was… a lot. Though, I do secretly love ‘Dreams’ now. Don’t tell her I said that, she thinks it's  so  mainstream.      It  is  a classic, though. It’s hard to dismiss. Speaking of classics, has anyone thought about a present for Uncle David yet? His birthday is looming, isn't it?      It is next week. I was thinking another one of those ridiculously oversized, novelty socks. He seems to appreciate them. Last year’s lobster ones were a hit.      They were brilliant. Though I think he nearly tripped over them walking the dog. I was considering a new gardening gadget. He’s always going on about needing a better hedge trimmer.      He has  so  many gardening things. Honestly, his shed is like a museum of tools he's used once. Maybe something… less practical? Like, a record? He used to be really into jazz, right?      That's a good shout, Chloe! A nice vinyl. Maybe something by Coltrane? It would be a bit more thoughtful than another garden implement. I found a really nice limited edition on Discogs the other day, but it was a bit pricey.      Discogs? Is that still a thing? I thought everyone just streamed music these days.      Some of us still appreciate a bit of physical media, Richard. And Sarah’s right about jazz. He used to spend hours listing to it. It was a phase, but a long one!      So, a record it is then? I can have a look online later. I'm pretty good at finding deals. Actually, I've been meaning to ask, Alan – you're good with computers and stuff, aren't you?      Relatively. I deal with data all day. What’s up?      My laptop's been acting weird. It keeps freezing, and I think I might've accidentally downloaded something dodgy. I’m terrified I've got a virus. It's how I book all my appointments at the salon, and I’d be totally lost without it.      Ooh, that sounds stressful. You should definitely get it checked out. Don’t try fixing it yourself, Chloe, you’ll just make things worse.      Absolutely. You don't want to risk losing all your client details.

Right, so this one…the Skoda Octavia Estate. Looks a bit sensible, doesn’t it? But practical. And with the boot space, we could actually  fit  everything in for a proper holiday, not just squeeze it.      Sensible is…an understatement, Mum. It looks like something Mr. Harrison from History would drive. No offence to Mr. Harrison.      None taken. Mr. Harrison’s a perfectly good driver, I’m sure. But you’ve gotta think, lad. Old Bessie’s on her last legs. She’s starting to sound like a bag of spanners rattling down the street, and the insurance…well, let’s not even  start  on the insurance.      Yeah, that's the killer, isn’t it? Even though she's ancient, they still charge a fortune ‘cos…well, because I’m me. 17, a new driver...apparently, I'm a high risk.      Exactly. Which is why I’m trying to be sensible about this. A newer car, with better safety features,  should  bring the insurance down a bit. And we need to think about what’s going to be best for you, driving to and from college next year.      But a Skoda? Seriously? I was looking at… well, maybe not a sports car, but something with a little…attitude. Like a Ford Focus ST. They look cool.      Cool doesn't pay the bills, love. And "cool" comes with a hefty insurance premium. I’ve been having a look at some quotes – and honestly, a Focus ST, or anything remotely sporty, is astronomical for you. We're talking needing a second mortgage astronomical.      Right, yeah, I figured. I punched in my details on Compare the Market, just for a laugh. Nearly choked on my tea. But what  makes  the insurance so bad? It's just a car, innit?      It's not  just  a car. Insurance companies look at everything. Your age, your driving experience – no experience is the biggest factor, naturally. Where you live – crime rates in the area affect it. The car itself - how powerful it is, how likely it is to be stolen, how expensive it is to repair. And, sadly, statistics show that young drivers are more likely to be involved in accidents. They're using data from…well,  years  of claims data.      So, it's all down to statistics? Feels a bit unfair. I’m a good driver! Apart from that little… bump in the supermarket car park.

There ya go, lad. Fuel for the gaming. You’ve been quiet all evening, though. Everything alright? Not stressing over school, are ye?      Nah, school’s…school. Just thinking. It’s weird, innit, how much stuff seems to pile up? Like, even  thinking  about homework feels stressful.      Oh, don't I know it.
