Heath Robinson, you say? Aye, a bit. Looks sturdy enough though, Arthur. Though a squirrel’ll have it dismantled within the hour, mark my words. They’re clever little buggers, squirrels are. Remember Old Man Hemmings’ bird table? Gone in a weekend, utterly demolished.      Honestly, you two! Always the doom and gloom! It’s lovely, Arthur. Really thoughtful. And much better than that rickety old thing you had before. This cake needs finishing, by the way – I made a little extra. It's low sugar, you know, for both your sakes.      Low sugar, is it? Well, that’s decent of you, Doreen. Though I sometimes think this diabetes business is blown all outta proportion. My father lived to ninety, and he ate treacle toffee by the bucketload!      Your father was a hardy soul, that’s true. But he didn’t have the lifestyles we do now, Arthur. Sitting around more, less exercise… it all adds up. Plus, he probably had good Norfolk genes!      It's not just the sugar, Arthur. It’s everything. I read an article about the importance of fibre, for maintaining good gut health as you get older. And proper hydration, that’s key. Honestly, you two need looking after! You’re both heading towards seventy-five, you know. It creeps up on you.      Seventy-bloody-two, thank you very much! And I feel perfectly alright, considering. Though my knees do complain a bit on damp days. Speaking o' complainin', did you see what the blackbirds are buildin’ in the hawthorn? A proper fortress, it is.      I did! Absolute chaos. Seems like they're using everything but the kitchen sink. Got some bits of plastic ribbon woven in there, I noticed. Nasty stuff that. Not very natural.      It's a sign of the times, isn’t it? They’re adapting to what’s available. I was thinking… I have those old puppets in the attic. The ones the grandchildren used to play with. Might be nice to get them out and put on a little show for the great-grandchildren when they visit.      Puppets, eh? Now  that’s  an idea! I used to be quite good at voices, you know. Could do a cracking seagull. Used to torment Mrs. Higgins with it when we were courting.

Right, I think I’m going to go for the  sheftali . Apparently, it's a Cypriot speciality – minced pork with herbs, wrapped in caul fat. Sounds… interesting. Have you decided, Arthur? You’ve been staring at that menu for a good ten minutes.      Hmm? Oh, yes, sorry. Getting a bit deaf in my old age, you know. Though this little gadget helps, most of the time. No, I think I’ll have the  kleftiko . Lamb, slow-cooked… can’t go wrong with lamb, can you? Reminds me of your brother, David. He always said a good roast lamb was a sign of a civilised society.      That sounds like David, alright. Always had a firm opinion on everything, didn’t he? It's strange, isn't it, thinking about him? It’s been almost five years now. Still feels… raw sometimes. Especially with Mum not being well.      Aye. That woman's a fighter, your Mum. But this… this lymphoma… it’s a nasty thing. How is she, truly? Last I heard she was struggling with the chemo.      She’s… managing. The chemo’s finished now, thankfully, but she’s so weak. She's back home with Aunt Carol. Carol’s been a saint, really. She’s even been trying to learn some Turkish phrases to use when we visit the shops here. She reckoned it might cheer Mum up. Trying to count to ten, she is! Apparently  bir, iki, üc  is quite a mouthful for a woman of eighty.      Good for her! That’s the spirit. Always finding a way. You know, when my Stella – my wife – was ill, it was the little things that kept us going. Just making a cup of tea, reading to her… It’s remarkable what small kindnesses can do. Speaking of kindnesses, look at that woman over there, trying to feed the stray cat under the table. Bold as brass, that cat!      Oh, yes! He's a handsome fellow, a proper ginger tom. It’s nice to see people caring for them. We've got Barnaby, haven’t we? Our ridiculous dachshund. Total chaos in a furry package. He’d have a field day with that cat, I reckon.      Dachshunds are characters alright. Remind me of old Mr. Higgins down the road back in Sedgeley. Short, stout, and with a stubborn streak a mile wide. He used to say he was a natural dowser – could find water with just a forked stick.

Honestly, Mum, this living room still feels exactly the same. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing, it's just…comfortingly unchanging, isn't it? It’s good to be back though. A proper break from spreadsheets and project timelines.      It is lovely to have you, darling. And yes, it  is  the same. Your father refuses to let me change a thing! Says it's perfectly functional. Though, functional doesn't always equate to…stylish. He's still got that awful rug.      Now, now, Margaret. That rug has history! Saw me through many a rugby match. Speaking of which, did you see England yesterday? Absolutely brilliant!      I caught a bit, Dad. Was mainly trying to ignore the notifications pinging on my phone about work, to be honest. It’s hard to switch off. They’re already asking about Q1 projections. It’s January 6th!      Oh, they always do. You work too hard, Emily. Honestly. Is that new firm treating you alright? You were a bit quiet about it last time you were here.      It’s...fine. It's a step up, career-wise, which is the main thing. More responsibility, coordinating bigger projects. But the office culture is…intense. Everyone's constantly trying to impress the boss. It's exhausting.      Sounds like a typical London office, then. I remember dealing with similar nonsense when I was climbing the ladder. Just keep your head down and do good work. Can’t go wrong with that. What kind of projects are you working on?      It’s mostly digital transformation stuff for a client in the finance sector. Very corporate. It’s a far cry from my uni dissertation on community arts projects! Remember that?      Of course. Your grandmother was so proud of that. Speaking of Gran and Grandad…they were asking after you both, of course. Said to send their love. Grandad’s been reminiscing about his time at Norwich High School for Boys – apparently, he knew a chap who… oh, it’s a long story.      Involved a stolen cricket bat and a very angry groundskeeper! We’ve heard it a hundred times, Margaret.      Well, it’s a good story! Anyway, we were thinking about the kitchen renovation. We started getting quotes today. It's going to be more expensive than we thought, naturally.      Oh really? What are you thinking of doing? Completely gutting it?      We’re hoping to open it up into the dining room, create a bit more space.

...Honestly, the lengths people will go to, eh? It's just… mental. I was scrolling through TikTok last night, and stumbled on this whole saga about a lass who'd been chatting to someone for  months , fell head over heels, and then found out the person she was talking to was actually her geography teacher. Like, a sixty-year-old man pretending to be a ripped surfer dude!      Oh,  now  that's a belter! A geography teacher? You can’t make it up, can ya? Sounds like prime Jeremy Kyle material, that does. Straight to the lie detector, I reckon. Did she send him money or anything? They always send 'em money, the poor loves.      It's awful though, isn't it? The emotional damage. It’s not just about the money, although that's bad enough. It's the betrayal, the lying, building a whole relationship on a foundation of…nothing. I saw something similar on Reddit, a bloke catfishing someone as a soldier serving overseas. So predictable.      She didn't send him money, thankfully. But she’d told him  everything . She’d confided in him about her anxieties, her family problems… He’d even been giving her… advice. It's just creepy. Proper creepy. And the worst thing is, she was feeling really vulnerable because she'd just come out of a tough breakup. Easy target, I suppose.      Aye, that's the sad bit, innit? People preyin' on vulnerability. It’s disgusting. Makes you wonder what goes through their heads. What do they  get  out of it? Attention? An ego boost? I remember bein’ on Facebook years ago, and gettin’ messages from weird blokes pretending to be someone else. I blocked ‘em all, obviously, but it’s still unsettling thinkin’ about it.      I think it's partly a power thing. They get a kick out of controlling the narrative, manipulating someone else’s feelings. It’s pathetic, but real. I’ve heard they sometimes even create whole fake lives – photoshopped pics, fabricated stories… it’s a lot of effort for something so malicious.      Right? It's almost a full-time job being a catfish! And the audacity! This geography teacher – apparently he’d even sent her poetry, all this flowery stuff. And when she finally confronted him, he just…denied it. Then tried to spin it as if  she  was the one in the wrong for questioning him!      Denied it?!

…Honestly, Nan, this ham and pickle is  elite . You’ve outdone yourself.      Oh, don’t be silly, darling. Just a bit of butter and good bread makes all the difference. So, tell me more about this Paris trip you’re planning with Theo. You haven't given me the details. Just a vague ‘we're thinking about it’.      Right, yeah. Well, Theo’s uncle has a little flat just off the Canal Saint-Martin. He’s offered it to us for a week over Easter. Dead cheap, basically free. We're trying to figure out if I can get the essays done before we go. The Classics department are  brutal  with deadlines, you know?      Classics? Still at it then? Good for you, a solid grounding, that. Though heavens, it sounds stressful. Reminds me a bit of art school, actually. Always a looming deadline, a blank canvas… or a papyrus scroll, in your case. Paris, though! It’s been…oh, decades since I was last there. It used to be my favourite city. Do you speak any French?      A bit. Did French GCSE, which is…mostly remembering how to order a baguette and complain about the weather. Theo's much better, he took it to A-Level. He can actually  converse . I'm hoping to brush up a bit before we go - Duolingo’s my friend, for now. It’s a shame you haven’t been back in ages. You used to tell me stories about living near the Louvre.      Ah, yes. A tiny, rather damp apartment. But the location… incomparable. And the light! One could paint for days just looking at the way the light hit the buildings. I mostly spoke German back then, to be honest. It was easier to get around the art circles. My German’s probably dustier than my French now, though. My mother, you know, she was Viennese. A very proper Austrian lady. She insisted I remain fluent.      You always drop little hints about Vienna, it sounds amazing. A bit different from…well, South London. Did you go back much after you left? I’ve always wanted to visit Italy, actually. It’s on the list, a slightly longer list than Paris.      Italy...Oh, Italy! We’d go every summer when I was a girl. My grandfather had a little vineyard in Tuscany. The smell of the grapes ripening… it's etched in my memory. Though, truthfully, I haven't been back since my husband passed.

Honestly, Dad, you were right. Leaving this early was a complete waste of time. It's just…solid. And it’s starting to spit with rain now, isn't it?      Told ya. People think getting a head start means anything when everyone else has the same idea. Dorset's lovely, mind, but getting  to  Dorset… that’s the rub. And yes, feeling a bit damp already. Reminds me of Blackpool, honestly.      Oh, Blackpool ain’t so bad. A bit…brash, maybe. But you can get a good fish and chips there. Speaking of which, are we stopping anywhere for lunch? This journey's going to take forever.      We can stop at that services near Salisbury, Mum. It's not gourmet, but it’ll do. I’m just… stressed about getting everything sorted at Auntie Carol’s. The solicitor is being a nightmare.      Solicitors  are  nightmares. Always have been. Robbing you blind for writing a couple of letters. Remember old Mr. Henderson, down the street? Spent a fortune on him when he tried to sell his house. Never understood a word the man said, but paid him handsomely for the privilege.      Honestly, it's the principle. Carol worked so hard for that little bungalow. And now having to deal with all that legal stuff… it's exhausting. Are you sure you've everything you need, love? The deeds, the will…?      Yeah, I triple-checked. It’s just…they’re asking for  so  much detail. And every phone call to them costs a fortune, even on my mobile. You'd think in this day and age, everything would be digital. Remember when you used to have to call and wait on hold for ages just to change your address?!      Ah, those were the days! Proper hold music, too. Not this synthesized rubbish they play now. And speaking of phones, they're all so complicated. I tried to update my Sat Nav map the other day and nearly threw the thing out the window. It kept asking me about Windows 8! What's Windows 8 got to do with finding my way to Weymouth?      It’s just… everything’s integrated now, Dad. It’s all software. Annoying though, isn’t it? I'm supposed to be writing my dissertation on the social impact of digital technology, and yet I spend half my time battling with it. It's ironic, really.      What  is  your dissertation on, exactly, darling?

Right comfortable this is, isn't it, Doreen? Rain batterin’ against the window, good brew… can't ask for much more, can ya?      Not a bit, Arthur. Absolutely lovely. Makes a change from that blasted sunshine we had all last week. Positively  scorching , it was. You’d think we were in Spain, not Norfolk.      Spain! Aye, I remember Spain. Blackpool it weren’t. Though, mind you, I’ve never been to Spain. Just see it on the telly. They all seem to be sunburnt and drinkin’ sangria. Looks a right carry-on.      It’s not all sangria and sunburn, Arthur. Though, I did see a programme once about a little village… very peaceful. But Blackpool has its charms, doesn't it? We had some good days there, didn't we? Remember the illuminations?      Oh, the illuminations! That's a memory. Used to take little Timmy, bless him, he’d be glued to ‘em. Eyes wide as saucers. All those lights… expensive things to run, I expect. Probably cost the council a fortune.      Everything costs a fortune these days, Arthur. You wouldn’t believe what a ball of wool costs now. It used to be a bob or two, now it’s… well, I don’t even  look  at the prices anymore. It’s depressing. This is for young Emily, you know. She's expecting, poor love.      A cardigan, is it? Lovely. She’s a good girl, Emily. Works herself to the bone, she does. Just like her mum, always lookin' after everyone.      She gets it from her grandmother, more like. Though I wasn't exactly 'working myself to the bone' running a childminding business. It was a pleasure, mostly. Just… tiring. Remember little Thomas, the one who used to hide all the biscuits?      Oh,  that  one! Cheeky little imp. Would find them anywhere, he would. Under the sofa, in your handbag… everywhere! You were forever lookin' for those biscuits.      Forever! And then he’d just grin at me, all innocent-like. They’re all grown up now, those children. Makes you wonder where the time went. I still get Christmas cards from a few of them. Keeps you feeling connected, doesn’t it?      It does. Though I don’t hold with all this social media business. Facebook and whatnot. All nosey parkin’, if you ask me. No privacy left in the world.      Well, it's how Emily keeps in touch with everyone.

This is lovely, honestly. You’ve really outdone yourself with the roast, Ben. Though, I’m pretty sure I requested Yorkshire puddings as a direct condition of coming over.      And a perfectly reasonable condition it was, Liv. Wouldn’t dream of depriving you. Though, I am slightly offended you think I’d  forget  the Yorkshire puddings. It’s practically a national scandal. How was your day? Anything exciting happen in the world of…research managing?      Oh, you know. The usual. Endless spreadsheets, people wanting things yesterday, and a constant feeling that I’m drowning in data. Though, I did manage to wrestle the funding application for the biodiversity project into  something  resembling coherence. It's a beast, that one. Honestly, sometimes I think I preferred writing my dissertation. At least  that  was just  my  chaos.      Ugh, funding applications. The bane of every academic’s existence. I’m still chipping away at mine - the one for the field work in Scotland. It's…challenging. Trying to convince people that tracking badger sett activity for a year is vital to national ecosystem health. They seem to favour things with more…immediate impact. Like, curing cancer or something.      Tell me about it! They always want the flashy stuff. Biodiversity is  important ! Speaking of important things, did you hear back from Ethan about Saturday? He messaged me asking if you were still up for that gig.      Ethan! Oh, brilliant. Yes, I replied. I am absolutely in. It's been ages since we last saw him. I’m really looking forward to it. He said they’re playing that new jazz club down by the river?      Aye, The Blue Note. Apparently, it’s supposed to be amazing. Proper intimate setting. It'll be good to catch up. He hasn’t changed a bit, has he? Still relentlessly optimistic, even when his band is having a total disaster on stage.      Not a jot. Though, I think his bassist is new. Apparently, she's phenomenal. He was raving about her skills when I spoke to him last week. Said she's a proper prodigy. Reminded me a bit of…well, a younger version of Isla, actually.      Really? Isla  is  a genius on the bass. Speaking of Isla, did she ever get around to starting that vegetable patch she was talking about? Last I heard she was interviewing different types of compost.      Oh, Isla and her compost. It’s a serious undertaking with her.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of applications I had to sift through for that Research Assistant role was  mental . You wouldn’t believe how many covered the basics, looked okay on paper, but just… lacked that spark. It’s disheartening, really, seeing so many bright people struggling to get a foot in the door.      Tell me about it. It’s the same in academia, only amplified by approximately a billion. I was talking to Ben at the department the other day – he finished his PhD  last year  and is still on a temporary research contract, bouncing between projects. He's applying for lecturer positions, of course, but the competition is… savage.      Savage is the word. And it's not like everyone's come straight outta uni all bright-eyed and bushy-tailed either. I had a candidate yesterday, properly qualified, solid experience, but he'd been made redundant from his previous role six months ago. Six months! That does things to your confidence, doesn't it? You start questioning everything.      Absolutely. It’s the gap. Employers see a gap and immediately assume… what? Laziness? Lack of initiative? It’s ridiculous. Especially now, with everything going on economically. It’s not a lack of skills, it’s just… a flooded market. Remember when we were worrying about tuition fees back when  we  were applying? Feels almost quaint now, doesn't it?      Quaint and privileged, probably! We were moaning about nine grand a year, which felt apocalyptic. Now it’s… well, it’s even worse. And the expectation that you have to do internships, volunteering, build a ‘portfolio’… before you even  start  looking for a proper job? It's exhausting. My little sister’s just finished her A-levels, and she's already stressing about all of that.      It’s a system designed to benefit those who can afford it, isn’t it? Those who have parents who can subsidise unpaid internships, or keep them going while they ‘find themselves’. It’s just… unfair. Speaking of stressing, you wouldn't believe the deadline looming for my funding application. Honestly, I'm pulling my hair out. It feels like my entire academic future hinges on a 30-page document.      Oh, that's awful! You'll smash it, though. You always do. You're brilliant at that kind of thing – so methodical, so…precise. Distraction is needed, though. We  need  to talk about something less soul-crushing.

This is… well, it's a bit chaotic, isn't it? All these animals having a party. Bit much, even for a five-year-old.      It  is  a bit loud visually, isn't it? But Leo loves it. He gets completely absorbed. It's the repetition, I think. “The bear wore a hat, the bear wore a hat, the bear wore a hat!” He can practically recite it.      Repetition is good for learning, you know. I used to use rhymes all the time in the classroom. Little ones latch onto patterns. It's how they make sense of the world. Though, honestly, some of these modern children's books… where’s the story? It's just…noise.      Exactly! And it got me thinking… I was sketching earlier, and I had this idea for a book. It’s not  about  parties, but… it's about family. Not like, 'mum and dad and 2.4 children,' but…a different kind of family.      Oh? Do tell. Is it about Leo’s family? He's always asking about his half-brother, Finn. He doesn't  quite  understand why Finn lives with his dad now and not with us all the time.      Kind of. It's more… a grand family. Like, everything mixed up. There's a badger who's adopted by a family of foxes, and a squirrel who’s step-dad is a hedgehog. And it’s all about how they’re all different, but they  are  a family. I was thinking maybe illustrations showing their family tree, but a really wonky, sprawling one.      A wonky tree. I like that. My own family tree is…complex. Generations of Scots moving around. My father’s side were staunch Glaswegians, mind you, but my mother’s family scattered like dandelion seeds. Stories galore though. Your uncle Hamish, now  he  had a tale for every occasion.      You always had the best stories, Gran. You used to tell me about your brother, Alistair, who ran off to sea. Mum never liked hearing about him, said he was a bit of a rogue, but  you  made him sound exciting. Actually, thinking about it, maybe there's a bit of Alistair in Finn’s dad, Ben. Always chasing some new adventure.      See? That's the kind of stuff I want to get into! It’s not about judging anyone, just… showing that families come in all shapes and sizes. It’s hard for kids to understand broken families, or blended ones, when all the books show perfect little units.

Right, honestly, this job is killin’ me. Not  killin'  me killin' me, but it’s…monotonous. Shelf-stacking at Tesco's ain't exactly stimulat’n, is it? Especially when half the customers look at you like you've personally offended them by being there.      Oh, no way! Still at Tesco’s then? I thought you were gonna start lookin' for somethin’ different after the Christmas rush. It sounds absolutely draining. I’m still doin’ shifts at the library, which is…quiet. Too quiet sometimes, actually. I ended up alphabetising the entire biography section last week just to feel somethin’.      Quiet sounds heavenly right now, to be honest. I've had three people complain about the placement of biscuits today.  Biscuits . And yeah, still at Tesco's. Applyin' for other stuff, but not much luck so far. It just feels like everyone wants experience, but how are you supposed to  get  experience without a job? It's a right catch-22, innit?      It is! Seriously. It’s infuriating. Everyone wants a mini-adult with a fully formed CV at nineteen. Listen, I saw a posting for a research assistant thing at the university – super basic admin stuff, but it’s  at  the university. Might be worth a look? I can send you the link.      Ooh, yeah, that’d be brilliant! Anything to escape the biscuit brigade. Thanks, love. Speaking of escaping… I was thinkin’ about… well, I was lookin’ at booking a weekend away, just the two of us. Somewhere with a bit of scenery.      Ooooh, that sounds lovely! Where were you thinking? Anything in mind? And… this is random, but I’ve been puttin’ off dealin’ with this for ages…      Anywhere really. Just a change of pace. Somewhere we can walk and… not talk about biscuits. What's up? You look like you're about to confess to a crime.      Not a crime, exactly. It’s…my legs. It's nearly summer, and I haven't shaved in like, three months. I'm proper furry.      Oh, go on! A bit of fluff never hurt anyone. You look perfectly fine. I honestly hadn't even noticed. I've not shaved  mine  in ages either. Feels liberating, doesn't it?      Liberating… until I try to find shorts, and then I panic slightly. My mum’s been subtly hinting she's got a razor ready for me whenever I go home. She’s obsessed with smoothness, she is.

...Honestly, it's just baffling, isn’t it? Like, how did the Cyrillic alphabet even  develop  from Greek? It feels so…different. I was reading about it for a project at work, trying to understand the evolution of data encoding, and ended up down a rabbit hole of linguistic history.      Different is an understatement. It’s beautiful though, isn’t it? All those curves and loops. My grandma used to write to her cousin in Bulgaria using it, or at least  attempts  at it. Apparently, learning it as an adult is… a challenge. Though, I suppose anything is compared to learning Mandarin, right?      Aye, fair point. Mandarin looks like a whole different universe. It’s just… Greek seems so logical, so foundational. Then you get to Cyrillic and it’s like, "Okay, we took a left turn somewhere." Speaking of logical, this pint  is  logical. Needed this after that meeting. Old Mr. Henderson was going on about KPIs again.      Tell me about it. Headaches guaranteed. Though, I’m aiming for precision engineering here, not KPIs. Trying to finish the literature review for my thesis is basically a full-time job. And to distract myself from the impending doom, I’ve started watching boxing again.      Boxing? Really? You always struck me as more of a… bookish type. No offence!      None taken. It’s a weird stress reliever, actually. All that controlled aggression. It's strangely compelling. Though it does remind me of that time… remember when Liam tried to learn to box at uni?      Oh, God, Liam. The most uncoordinated human being on the planet. He lasted about five minutes before accidentally punching the instructor. Proper disaster. He swore he saw stars. And then cried.      Cried! It was glorious. And then tried to blame it on the instructor “holding back.” Speaking of bad decisions, have you seen the comments sections on football forums lately? It's… vile. The racism is just out of control.      Don’t even get me started. Saw something absolutely disgusting online about Saka after the Euros. It's heartbreaking, isn't it? And it's not just online, is it? You hear it in the stadiums too, sometimes. It's a stain on the game. It feels like we haven't moved on at all.      Exactly! I was talking to one of my friends, a social anthropologist, about it, and she said it’s deeply rooted in historical power dynamics.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for the Heritage Lottery Fund is enough to put anyone off. I spent nearly a week just compiling the initial application for Oakhaven Manor, and that was  before  I even got to the detailed costings. It's a beautiful building, don’t get me wrong – gorgeous Jacobean detailing – but the roof… the roof is a nightmare.      Oh, Oakhaven. Yes, I drove past it last month. Seen better days, definitely. And you’re preaching to the choir about the HLF. They're becoming increasingly bureaucratic. It feels less about preservation and more about ticking boxes. Did you include a full structural survey, of course? They’ll pounce on anything missing there.      Naturally. Everything. Condition reports, photographic evidence, historical research dating back to the Domesday Book almost! I even managed to track down a descendant of the original family who wrote a lovely supporting statement. Still, I'm worried the scope is too ambitious. I've proposed a full restoration of the east wing, which is largely derelict,  and  a small visitor centre…      Ambitious is good, Beatrice, but it needs to be  realistic . They want to see sustainable plans. A visitor centre is fine, if it’s demonstrably linked to the building’s historical narrative. Don’t pitch it as a tea room with a few portraits on the wall. They’ll dismiss it instantly. What’s the current usage of the east wing? And more importantly, what  will  it be?      Well, at the moment, it's… largely inhabited by pigeons. I envision it as an education space, workshops for traditional crafts – things that resonate with the building’s history. We could run courses on wattle and daub, maybe even lime plastering. It’s a fantastic opportunity to breathe new life into dying skills.      That's much more like it. Focus on the skills angle. The HLF are very keen on funding projects that offer training and employment opportunities. And make sure the business plan clearly demonstrates how the workshops will generate income  after  the funding period ends. They’re not interested in perpetual dependency. I had a similar issue with St. Ethelreda’s church a few years ago. I proposed a restoration and a small museum, but they wanted proof that the museum wouldn't just be a money pit.      That's exactly my fear! The income projections are… optimistic, let’s say. I was considering applying for a smaller grant from the Pilgrim Trust as well, to specifically cover the roof.

Right, honestly, this data is  killing  me. It's just…messy. Like trying to herd cats, only the cats are linguistic variables and they’re actively trying to disprove my hypotheses. Sounds familiar. Welcome to the wonderful world of research, eh? What’s the biggest headache right now? Is it the accent identification, still? You were saying last week it wasn’t quite…crisp. It’s not crisp! It’s more like a blurry watercolour painting where everyone speaks vaguely ‘Northern’. I can distinguish Yorkshire and Lancastrian alright, but anything further north… it all blends into this… something . And especially when you get into areas like Sunderland – my hometown, naturally – things get really complicated. Sunderland, aye. You’ve mentioned the specific nuances there before. Something about influence from Scots and a slightly different vowel shift, wasn't it? That's fascinating. It highlights how regionally specific things truly are, even within a relatively small geographical area. Birmingham's got its own quirks, you know. People always assume it’s just a generic ‘Midlands’ accent, but there's a lot going on under the surface. Exactly! That’s what frustrates me. People lump everything together. It's not just about broad regions, it's about hyperlocal dialects, sociolects… the subtle shifts that happen generationally. My fieldwork team are good, don't get me wrong, but translating that subtlety into quantifiable data is the real challenge. They’re struggling to consistently differentiate between, say, a Wearside accent and a Durham one. That’s tough. It’s almost a ‘you know it when you hear it’ kind of thing, isn’t it? And that’s the problem with trying to codify something so naturally fluid. Maybe you need to refine your criteria? Focus on a specific phonetic feature – a particular vowel sound or consonant cluster – that's demonstrably present in one and absent or altered in the other? I've tried. Honestly, I've tried everything. We’ve looked at /r/ dropping, vowel length, diphthong realisation… it all overlaps! It's a dialect continuum, and trying to force it into neat categories feels…wrong. It feels like I'm doing a disservice to the actual linguistic reality. It's making me question the whole methodology. Don't beat yourself up about it. That's what research  is  – constantly questioning your methodology. It's healthy. Speaking of questioning, have you thought about a break? You've been obsessing over this for weeks.

...Honestly, the amount of food they  waste  at school is criminal. I saw trays coming back practically full yesterday. Little bits of everything barely touched.      It’s ‘cause the gravy’s too lumpy. And Mrs. Higgins makes funny faces when you ask for no peas.      Yeah! And Charlie Thompson swapped his sausage for my carrot, and then  ate  the sausage! It wasn’t fair!      Oh, the dramas of the dinner hall. Right. Well, it’s just… we need to make sure you’re both actually eating  something  nutritious. You’re growing boys and girls. Not exactly thriving on crisps and chocolate biscuits, are you?      I like the biscuits! Especially the ones with sprinkles.      Me too! Can we have some when we get back from tennis practice?      We’ll see. First, we need to talk about the money for the tennis tournament. It’s £15 each, and… well, things are a bit tight this month.      Fifteen pounds? That's loads! What does it even  pay  for?      It covers the court hire, the little medals for everyone who participates, and some drinks and snacks during the breaks. It’s a big tournament, you know, lots of schools taking part.      Can’t we just… not have the medals? I don’t really need a medal.      That’s sweet of you, darling, but it’s not really how it works. It's a package deal, unfortunately. Listen, maybe if you both helped around the house a little more – a bit more tidying up, maybe emptying the dishwasher without being asked – we could earn a bit towards it. What do you think?      Ugh, chores?      I’ll empty the dishwasher. But only if I can be a clown afterwards.      A clown? Where did  that  come from?      I was thinking… if it’s hard earning money for tennis, maybe we could join the circus instead! I could be a really funny clown. I do a good silly walk.      I could be the tightrope walker! I’m really good at balancing. Remember at Granny’s when I walked along the garden wall?      I remember Granny nearly having a heart attack. And that  was  a very wobbly wall. But a circus… that’s quite a leap from school tennis, isn't it?      But imagine! We could travel the world! And we wouldn't need money for school dinners because we'd have all the food with the circus!      And maybe there’d be lions!

Honestly, Dad, you’ve barely touched your dinner. You said you were hungry! And you were raving about the roast when I said we were going to the cinema first.      Oh, it’s alright, love. Just thinking. That film… rather unsettling, wasn’t it? All that revisionism. Reminded me of that debate at Cambridge University last week.      Unsettling is one word for it. Manipulative is another. They really did gloss over… well, a lot. But that Cambridge debate - I heard snippets about it on the radio. Something about the national curriculum, wasn’t it? All the fuss about  how  we teach history?      That's right. A lot of the points raised in the film mirrored the arguments I heard. It was the historian, Dr. Anya Sharma, speaking, advocating for a more thematic approach, less about dates and kings, more about societal impact and… well, the lived experience.      Lived experience! Sounds a bit touchy-feely for history, doesn't it? When I was at school, it was all about knowing your battles and your monarchs. And understanding the causes and effects. Blunt, perhaps, but it certainly worked for me. Got me through my degree at Reading, it did.      But did it give you a true  understanding , Dad? Or just the ability to regurgitate information? Because that's the crux of it, isn't it? My daughter's learning about the Tudors now, and it's all about power dynamics and social structure, not just 'Henry VIII had six wives'.      Exactly. And honestly, the current curriculum, while attempting to be more inclusive, feels… fragmented. Like a patchwork of topics thrown together. It needs cohesion. When I was training, there was a real emphasis on historical methodology, understanding source criticism… that feels lost now.      Source criticism? When  I  was at school… …we were just grateful to have textbooks! Things were simpler then. Less debate. Less… political correctness.      Simpler, maybe, but no necessarily  better . Look at the state of politics now! Educated people, presumably, making decisions based on… well, questionable historical interpretations.      It's connected, I think. A lack of critical thinking skills, a reliance on simplified narratives… it all impacts our political discourse. Which leads me to… …the constant tinkering with higher education.      Oh, don’t even get me started. I was speaking to a university Dean last week, and they’re tearing their hair out. The focus on student ‘experience’ over actual academic rigour is astonishing.

Right proper drizzle out there, innit? Reminds me a bit of France, actually. Not the sunshine bits, mind, but them grey, damp days. Spent a bit of time over there during… well, y'know. National Service.      Oh, you did, Arthur? I always forget about that part of your life. You don't talk about it much. Harrow was alright in the fifties, never saw much rain like this though. More smog, if truth be told. London’s breath on us, always.      Smog was terrible. My father used to complain about the soot getting  inside  everything. Said it coated your lungs. He worked in the City, you see, right in the thick of it. Progress, I suppose, even if it was grim progress. Changed things, eventually.      Biscuits anyone? And you’re right, Dad. Grandad used to say he could taste the coal dust in his tea. Can’t imagine that now. Though this rain  is  persistent. It’s been going on for days. Makes you think of trenches, doesn’t it? All that mud.      Mud, aye. That’s a good word for it. Endless mud. And the cold. Went right through you, it did. Not like this damp, this is just…unsettling. We were lucky, though. Didn't see any proper fighting. Mostly guard duty, shifting paperwork. Though even  that  was stressful, worrying about what was happening elsewhere. Seen lads come back…not the same.      Poor things. It’s awful, war. Makes you think about your ancestors, doesn’t it? My grandmother, bless her, she lived through both World Wars. Never talked about it much either, just always seemed… resigned. Said her father, old Mr. Henderson, fought in the Crimean War. Can you imagine? A different world entirely.      The Crimean War… that's a long way back. My family history seems fairly mundane by comparison. Factory workers, shopkeepers… mostly in Middlesex. Although, apparently, we had a bit of a black sheep ancestor who ended up transported to Australia. Something to do with sheep stealing, if the family legend is to be believed.      Sheep stealing! Goodness. That’s a story. Makes our lives seem rather tame, doesn’t it? Though I did have a rather heated exchange with the police about parking the other day. Not quite on the level of transportation, admittedly.      Police, eh? Always nosy, them. Back in Costessey, old Sergeant Miller knew everything. Everyone's business was his business. Couldn’t move without him knowing.

Honestly, Dad, it feels really…weird. Knowing this is the last time we’ll be doing this drive for a while. Mum's house feels so empty already.      I know, son. It’s a big shift. Fifty-eight years in that house, you don’t just…walk away from that lightly. Still, Northamptonshire will be nice. A bit quieter, a bit more space. And closer to your Auntie Carol, which she’s thrilled about, naturally. She’s already planning visits.      Auntie Carol plans visits regardless of proximity, Dad. She’s a force of nature, that woman. Speaking of which, have you sorted out the mortgage stuff with the new place? Everything okay with that? You sounded a bit stressed on the phone yesterday.      It's…complicated. The solicitor is being a bit slow, dragging his heels. Apparently, there's something about the deeds and a right of way. Honestly, it’s all a bit beyond me. I keep asking him to explain it in plain English, but he talks in legal jargon. Makes my head spin. You, being the English Language Instructor and all, maybe you could decipher it for me if it comes to it?      I can certainly  try . Though ‘legal English’ is a whole different beast from teaching conversational stuff. I doubt my skills would be particularly useful in a court of law! But yeah, send it over, I’ll have a look. How’s your cough, by the way? You were hacking something fierce last week.      Oh, it’s lingering. Doc says it’s just a chest infection, gave me some antibiotics. Doesn’t seem to be doing much good, to be honest. Just makes me feel a bit…fuzzy. Still, I’m used to being a bit under the weather. Reminds me of your Grandad, he had a similar cough for years. Stubborn man, wouldn’t go to the doctor.      You should really push for a follow-up appointment if it's not getting better. Don't be like Grandad. Mum would kill me if anything happened. She's already convinced moving will be the death of you.      Your mother always was a worrier. Though, to be fair, she’s got a point about the upheaval. It's just…everything's changing all at once. Leaving the house, selling the business… it feels like closing chapters.      I know. But new chapters too, right? And you deserve a rest.

...Honestly, I'm still wrestling with the seating plan. Gran keeps saying she wants to be next to Chloe, but Chloe will just spend the entire evening talking about her new boyfriend and Gran won’t hear a word anyone else says! It's a lovely problem to have, I suppose, but a problem nonetheless. And Dad, well, he seems to think he  should  be at the head of the table, which... isn't really how we do things.      Oh, classic Dad. Always needing to be in charge. Though, to be fair, he probably just wants to make sure everyone’s got enough to eat. He's like a well-meaning, slightly bossy, food guardian. Have we definitely gone with the roast beef? I was thinking maybe a salmon en croute, a bit fancier, you know?      Salmon en croute is a  lovely  idea, but Gran…she’s been a bit fixated on roast beef. And honestly, simplifying things feels good. Less stress. Besides, I remember last year she specifically requested it, and I feel awful when I mess up those little preferences. It's just... sometimes it feels like they slip away so quickly, those little things she remembers. It’s a reminder, isn’t it?      It is. It's scary, isn't it? Seeing little changes. But she seemed really bright when I saw her on Tuesday, telling me all about the fishmonger. Apparently, Mr. Peterson had a particularly good delivery of haddock. She was very specific about the colour of the eyes!      Oh, she  always  judges the fish by the eyes! That’s her benchmark of freshness. I’ll have to make sure we get the beef from that butcher in Stamford, then. He always has the best cuts. Speaking of which, I've been meaning to rearrange the cupboards in the kitchen. I found a box of old photographs while I was looking for the good tablecloth.      Oh, brilliant! Photos are always a good distraction. Are there any of Gran when she was younger? She always tells such amazing stories about living through the war. I bet there are some gems in there. I’m happy to help sort through them, though be warned, I'm terrible at putting things back where they belong.      Plenty! And a lot of embarrassing ones of Dad as a teenager. I was thinking we could put a few in frames around the dining room for the party.

...Honestly, the pain is just  ridiculous . I keep poking at the hole with my tongue, which I know I shouldn’t, but it’s just… there! Like a cavern in my mouth.      You and your wisdom teeth. You’ve been moaning about them since we landed in France! Is it getting worse, or is it just… consistently awful? I swear, if I hear another description of the “cavern” I’m going to start charging you rent.      Consistently awful, leaning towards spectacularly awful. It’s not the actual pulling that bothered me, it's the  hole . They said it’d be a few days, it’s been nearly a week! And the taste… ugh. Like old socks and something metallic.      Sounds delightful. Seriously though, have you been keeping up with the salt water rinses? Mum always went on about salt water when I had mine out. Though, knowing Mum, she probably insisted on using sea water collected personally from Brighton beach.      I’ve been doing ‘em! It helps for like, five minutes, then it’s back to feeling like someone’s lodged a tiny gravel pit in my jaw. How are things back home with your parents? Did the moving go alright? Last I heard, they were wrestling a sofa up three flights of stairs.      Don’t even  mention  the sofa. Dad’s still muttering about it. Apparently, the previous tenant had measured the doorway wrong. It was a whole saga. They finally got everything in, though. They think they like it, mostly because it's a bit closer to the shops. Mum’s already planning how to repaint the entire flat.      Classic Mum! Always a project on the go. My folks are driving me mental too, but about uni. They keep ringing, asking about re-enrolment, asking if I’ve thought about postgraduate options… like, can a girl just enjoy a week of sunshine and mild pain without existential questioning?      Tell me about it. They’re already subtly pushing me towards applying for Masters programmes. I haven’t even finished my undergrad! It's like they think the moment we get our results, we automatically morph into discerning scholars.      Exactly! It’s so draining. I just want to get back, sort my teeth, and then just…  be  for a bit. Before being pressured into further education, or a career, or… adulthood.      Maybe we should both run away and join the circus.

Right, so, lactose-free chocolate chip cookies are… a challenge. They just don’t  quite  hold their shape the same way. Honestly, sometimes I think the dairy is doing more structural work than the flour.      Are we making cookies for the kindness things?      We are, darling. We’re making cookies to deliver to Mrs. Higgins next door. Remember? We talked about doing little things to make people happy. It’s almost Chinese New Year, and that’s a good time to be kind, don’t you think?      Can I be in charge of the money for kindness?      Money? What money, love?      These! We can use the checkers and draughts pieces! The black ones are a pound, the red ones are fifty pence, and the little wooden ones are ten pence! I told Leo.      That's a good idea! But what if we want to buy something  expensive  for kindness? Like... a really big box of chocolates?      That  is  a good idea, actually. Clever thinking. We might need to supplement your system with real money for anything truly substantial. But for buying, oh, a little bunch of flowers, or a card, it's perfect. So, you two are in charge of ‘Kindness Currency’?      Yep! I'm the banker! Leo can be my assistant.      I want to be the kindness chooser! I decide  who  gets the cookies!      That sounds fair. Alright, kindness chooser and banker. Excellent team. Now, thinking about Chinese New Year… I was reading about all the traditions. Apparently, red envelopes with money are really important.      Like my draughts pieces? Red is lucky, right?      Exactly! Red is very lucky. But we don't give draughts pieces as gifts, sadly. Although… it’s the  thought  that counts, isn’t it? Speaking of red, I was thinking of dying my hair.      Red?! Like a mermaid?      Maybe not quite mermaid, darling. More of a… deep burgundy, perhaps. Or maybe even a dark plum. I'm feeling a bit…bold.      You already dyed it blue once! Remember? It looked like a Smurf!      Don't remind me! It was a phase! A very short-lived, slightly regrettable phase. This would be more sophisticated. Anyway, back to kindness. What other ideas do you have? Besides giving cookies and expertly managing our draughts economy.      We could draw pictures for the people at the care home! Old people like pictures.      And we could help Dad with the garden! He hates weeding.

Honestly, Mum, it was  so  embarrassing. Mr. Henderson practically had to peel me off the dashboard.      Oh, darling. You're okay, though, aren't you? No broken bones? Just a bit shaken? Tell me everything, from the beginning. And try not to dwell on Mr. Henderson, the man thinks a slightly overgrown rose bush is a health hazard.      I’m fine, mostly. Just…bruised. And mortified. I was practicing my driving, you know, going really slowly around the quiet bit near the Old Town, and I just...didn't see the bin. A wheelie bin, Mum! Not even a big one! And then…bump. It didn't hurt, just…the noise. And the look on Mr. Henderson’s face.      Oh dear. Well, everyone bumps into things learning to drive. It's a rite of passage, almost. Remember when  your  Grandpa George reversed into Mrs. Miggins' prize-winning hydrangeas?      Yeah, you’ve told me that story about a million times. Though hydrangeas are definitely more impressive than a bin. Still, it's awful. I feel so clumsy. It’s making me think I’ll never pass my test.      Nonsense! One little bin doesn’t define your driving abilities. Speaking of things that feel a bit…unstable, did you read the article I sent you about the AI-generated  Alice in Wonderland  illustrations?      The really weird ones? Yeah. Some were genuinely creepy. Like the Cheshire Cat looked like it was glitching out of reality. It's amazing what computers can do, but it just doesn’t have the  feel  of John Tenniel's original designs, does it?      Exactly! It lacks soul. It’s all…technical perfection, but no heart. It reminded me of that production of  Alice  we saw at the Brighton Dome a few years back. The costumes were incredible, though. Remember the Mad Hatter’s outfit? All mismatched fabrics and repurposed teacups?      Oh, yeah! And the Queen of Hearts' dress was amazing, so red and...threatening. I was thinking about costumes actually. I need to start brainstorming for the school play. They’re doing  A Midsummer Night’s Dream .      Oh, lovely! Are you hoping for a part?      Maybe. I’m not sure. I’m kind of terrible at memorising lines, which is a bit of a problem for theatre. I spend hours on the internet trying to find memory tricks. It's a black hole of useless information, honestly. One minute I'm looking up mnemonic devices, the next I'm watching videos of seagulls stealing chips.

...and honestly, Harold, the look on young Emily’s face last night was just  desperate . They’re facing a wall of solar panels, stretching across Farmer Giles’ best pastureland. It's just…wrong. I spent the evening trying to explain the nuances of a Section 106 agreement, and I could see her eyes glazing over after about five minutes. Bless her, they’ve only just started.      It’s always the detail, isn’t it, Margaret? They think it’s simply a case of shouting “No!” and the council will listen. They haven’t encountered the machine yet. I remember when we were fighting the turbines near Ramsgate. Years of meetings, endless paperwork… it saps your soul. Did you point them towards the Planning Portal? It’s a rabbit hole, but essential.      Essential, yes, but it’s not enough. Paperwork and procedure – the council  loves  that. It gives them cover. They hide behind process. What they don’t want is a genuine challenge to the fundamental logic of these things. They’re being pushed, you see. By government targets, by energy companies throwing money around…      That’s exactly what I was trying to get across to Emily. It’s not just about the visual impact, although that’s certainly important. They need to understand the planning gain, the financial incentives for the council, who benefits, and  how  they benefit. It’s all connected, isn’t it? It’s a grubby web of interests.      Absolutely. And the planning appeal process… don't even get me started. We went through that with the turbine issue. A barrister, a lot of expensive reports… and ultimately, they still approved it. The inspector paid lip service to our concerns about bird migration and visual amenity, but the energy company had a slick presentation and a neatly-packaged ‘community benefit’ fund.      And that’s the problem, isn’t it? It’s all about energy, energy, energy. Renewable or not, the focus is solely on  producing  it, not on  storing  it. They pour billions into wind and solar, but a pittance into battery technology, or better grid infrastructure. It’s shortsighted. If we could store it efficiently, a lot of this landscape desecration wouldn’t be necessary.      You’re spot on, Arthur. I was reading an article just last week about some fascinating research into flow batteries. Apparently, they're much more scalable and sustainable than lithium-ion, but the funding… it’s nowhere near comparable.

…and honestly, Eleanor, I still think you’re rushing this driving business. It’s not like when I learned, you know. Roads were quieter then. Fewer boy racers.      Dad, we’ve been over this. I’m nearly thirty-eight, not eighteen. I've been wanting to do this for years. And honestly, the logistics of teaching without a car are getting… challenging. Plus, Mum's been hinting she'd like a break from being the family chauffeur.      She has, bless her. Although, secretly, I think she enjoys it a bit! She likes feeling useful. And honestly, a bit of peace and quiet on the school run will be lovely.      Useful is one thing, but the insurance! Have you looked at the insurance quotes, Eleanor? Absolutely scandalous. For a woman your age… even with a clean license, it's going to be considerable. I remember when I got my first car, a Morris Minor, insurance was a pittance.      I have, Dad. It  is  pricey, but I'm shopping around. I’ve been looking at telematics boxes, the ones that monitor your driving, see if they can bring the cost down. And I’m thinking about a smaller engine, something reasonably economical. No sports cars here, promise.      Sensible girl. And a smaller car is easier to park in Birmingham, believe me. Speaking of sensible, have you thought about where you'll practice? I know you're near that industrial estate near your school… might be a bit quiet on a Saturday morning.      That's the plan, Mum. And Mr. Henderson, the instructor, said he'll take me out on some proper A-roads once I'm confident. I'm a bit nervous about roundabouts, actually. They seem to just… come at you.      Roundabouts! Don’t even get me started on roundabouts. Utter chaos. Everyone thinks they’re Formula One drivers. Just remember, give way to the right. Simple as that. Although, these modern ones, with multiple lanes… it’s a nightmare.      Your father's slightly exaggerating. They're not  that  bad. Though I did see a rather spectacular pile-up on the Hagley Road roundabout last year. Thankfully, no one was seriously hurt.      Right. Well, that’s reassuring! Speaking of stressful situations, are we still on for Cornwall next month? I booked the cottage ages ago, and I was thinking we could visit St. Michael’s Mount.      Cornwall… yes, that should be nice.

Honestly, Dad, this parking situation is  criminal . I spent twenty minutes circling just to get a space near Mum’s this morning. It’s getting worse and worse, isn’t it? Everything’s so crammed.      Criminal? That's a bit strong, love. Though I do agree, it's a right pain. Back in my day, in London, you just...found a space. Had to be quick about it, mind you, but it wasn’t this constant frustration. People just didn’t  have  so many cars. Everyone walked, or took the bus.      Well, things are different now. Everyone  needs  a car. Or feels like they do. Especially if you want to get out to the countryside, which is what I was trying to do today, to get some decent veg. Gillingham market is alright, but it's not the same as a proper farm shop. Thinking about it, Brighton has some really lovely ones... maybe that's a sign.      Brighton, eh? Still on about moving, are you? Don't you reckon it's a bit…frivolous? All that upheaval! And the cost? It’s already expensive enough living down here. I’ve seen those seaside prices, you know. They’re sky high.      It’s not frivolous, Dad! It’s…a chance. A change. I’m finishing my Masters soon, and I’m starting to think about what I really  want . And Brighton feels…right. More opportunities, a bit more life. And maybe I could actually cycle to work, rather than being stuck in traffic all the time.      Cycling to work? Sounds exhausting. And all those hipsters… I saw something on Facebook about Brighton. Terrible parking, apparently. Ironically. Though, speaking of Facebook, I keep getting notifications. Hundreds of them! I don't understand it. All these people wanting to be my 'friend'. Do I even  know  half of them?      Oh, Dad. Facebook. It’s a bit of a time sink, isn’t it? I can help you sort out the notifications. You can turn most of them off, you know. It's in the settings. It's probably just people from school or old work colleagues.      Settings… sounds complicated. I just click on things until they stop annoying me. Reminds me of fixing the wireless when you were little. Bang it hard enough, and it usually worked. Different times, eh? We didn’t have all these… digital distractions. We had each other, and a bit of telly if we were lucky.

...Honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Mr. Henderson to mark down my essay for "lack of original thought" when I literally quoted Shakespeare! It's baffling. He probably just wanted to justify his existence.      Henderson, eh? Sounds about right. The man's a walking thesaurus of passive aggression. Did you at least  try  the sarcasm route? You know, subtly undermine his authority with a cutting remark disguised as a polite query?      Considered it. Vigorously. But I was already on thin ice after questioning his interpretation of Hamlet’s soliloquy. Apparently, "existential dread" is too… modern a lens for the Bard. Honestly, the man needs to get out more.      Right? It’s Shakespeare, not sacred text. Speaking of getting out more, how’s the golf going? Still attempting to "win" at a sport designed to actively frustrate you?      Don't even  start . It was a disaster. I spent three hours chasing a little white ball around a field, and finally managed to hit it directly into a pond. A  lily pond , of all places. It looked genuinely offended.      Oh, that’s brilliant. Truly poetic justice. You’re destined to be a tragic figure, aren’t you? Like a golfing Hamlet, perpetually contemplating the inevitable splash.      Very funny. You, on the other hand, are suspiciously quiet about your summer job. Still stacking shelves at the Co-op?      No, thankfully. Escaped that particular purgatory. I’m helping out at my uncle’s garage now. Turns out knowing the difference between a spark plug and a… well, another spark plug, is surprisingly useful. It’s messy, though. I’m constantly covered in grease.      Ah, the glamorous life. At least it's a change of scenery. My part-time at the library is… predictable. Though Old Man Fitzwilliam did try to convince me my surname was actually “Fitz-Exeter” due to my birthplace. Said it sounded more “distinguished”.      Fitz-Exeter? That does sound rather… upper-crust. He’s a character, that one. My grandma always insisted on calling me “Nottingham-boy.” Gets right on my nerves. Like I’m some sort of local landmark.      It’s the nicknames, isn't it? They always stick. My auntie keeps trying to get me to respond to “Willie,” even though my name is openly Alistair. Willie! I feel like a Victorian chimney sweep.      Horrific. Reminds me of Uncle Barry, who goes by “Baz.” Baz! Honestly. He thinks it makes him sound cool.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of bunting required for this corporate away-day is just… criminal. Like, who needs that much pastel pink? They wanted ‘uplifting’, I gave ‘em a Pepto-Bismol explosion.      Sounds… stressful. Bunting? Serious business, that. I was shifting pallets all day. Proper graft. Nothing pastel about it, believe me. Just grey concrete and the smell of… well, you don’t wanna know.      Oh, don’t even  start  on pallets, Liam. I had a nightmare trying to get a shipment of component parts released this afternoon. The paperwork was a disaster, apparently someone logged the quantity as "a smidge". A  smidge ! How am I supposed to build a production schedule around a smidge?      A smidge?! That’s… that’s just daft, innit? Honestly, people. It’s like they actively  try  to make my life harder. Though, I suppose it beats last week’s request for a ‘medieval banquet’ theme. In a modern conference centre. With vegan options.      Medieval vegan… now that’s a challenge. What did you come up with for that? Did they want like, lentil stew in a wooden bowl?      Precisely! And a ‘dragon’ made out of balloons. It was… intense. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if I should just pack it all in and open a tea shop back in Doncaster. Less stress, more scones.      Don’t do that, Anya! You’re brilliant at what you do, even if they throw ridiculous requests at you. Cambridge needs your event-planning skills. And frankly, Doncaster probably has enough tea shops.      You always know what to say, Chloe. You’re a good friend. But honestly, living in Cambridge… it's expensive and I'm still sharing a flat with two students. They're lovely, they are, but their idea of cleaning involves shoving everything under the bed.      Tell me about it. I’m still living with me Mum. Saving up for a deposit is a joke these days. Every week feels like two steps forward, one step back. Though, Mum’s cooking is pretty good, gotta give her that.      I’m lucky, I managed to snag a small flat near the Science Park about six months ago. It’s tiny, and the only view is a brick wall, but it's  mine . Though, the heating bills… oof. We should all start a collective fund to keep warm this winter.      Good idea! Seriously. I’m trying to eat better to combat the stress, but it’s hard when the shop around the corner does a cracking deal on chocolate biscuits.

…and there you are, both of you! Good to actually  see  faces, even if it is through this blasted thing. Honestly, Maureen, you look positively blooming. Have you been pottering about in that garden of yours all morning?      Blooming? More like battling bindweed, Arthur. It’s a constant struggle, I tell you. Though, I did get the runner beans in. Hopefully, a good crop this year. And hello to you, Doreen. You’re looking well too. Still got that new hair colour?      Hello, both! Yes, Reginald, I do. A little bit of sunshine in these grey old days, don't you think? Arthur, you haven't changed a bit – still looking like you've got a problem to solve, even on a lovely afternoon. You were telling us about the eclipse last week, weren't you? Did you manage to get a good view?      Managed? I practically  lived  in the garden for the duration. Had all the proper filters, the works. Remarkable, absolutely remarkable. Makes you think, doesn’t it? About how small we are, floating about on this… this little speck. Then you start reading about black holes and the beginnings of space… it’s all a bit much for a retired civil engineer, I tell you.      Black holes, eh? Sounds a bit frightening. I prefer a good wildlife programme. Did you see that one about the cosmos on Tuesday? Lovely pictures, that one. Though everything’s so… politically correct these days, isn't it? They're always careful  how  they describe things. Not like David Attenborough in the old days.      Oh, Reginald, you always say that! It’s just being sensitive to different viewpoints. Though, I did find it a bit much when they referred to ‘non-human animals’ instead of just ‘animals’. It feels a bit…stilted. Speaking of gardens, Arthur, I saw you were moving some plants around. You and your rearranging.      Just trying to get a bit of order, my dear. And I'm thinking… it’s ambitious, I know… but I'm considering moving the bamboo. It’s spreading like wildfire, honestly. Right across the fence line with old Mrs. Higgins. And she's already giving me daggers about it.      Mrs. Higgins! She’s a right one, isn’t she? Always complaining. Though, I suppose she’s right about the bamboo. It’ll take over everything if you let it. Did you finish putting up that owl box?

...Honestly, the traffic on the A19 was mental. I swear, every single person from Newcastle to Middlesborough decided to go for Sunday dinner at the same time. It took me nearly an hour just to get to the A1.      Sounds about right. That stretch is always a nightmare, isn't it? I'm glad I convinced you to meet me  here  rather than trying to navigate into York itself. Parking would have been… a biblical undertaking.      You were spot on. I’d have been circling for ages. And then walking miles. Honestly, driving’s stressful enough without adding that to the mix. Still, at least we made it to this little pub. Have you been here before? The Black Swan, right?      Yeah, a couple of times. Good food, decent beer. Not overly fancy, which is what I was after. I was picturing you needing a proper sit down and a roast after that drive.      You know me too well. A proper sit-down is  exactly  what I needed. I was starting to fantasise about abandoning the car and catching a bus, but then I remembered Stagecoach's… reliability. Or lack thereof. Back home, in Sunderland, they’re always late, or just don’t bother turning up.      Oh, don’t remind me. My mum lives near Durham, and she complains about the buses constantly. Says it's like playing Russian Roulette with your schedule. It's better down south, I’ll admit, but even around Harpenden things aren't perfect. Less… dramatic, though.      Dramatic feels like an understatement for the North East transport system. Anyway, back to more pressing matters: food! I'm starving. Are you thinking roast or something else?      Roast sounds good. Though I was reading about this new Italian place that's opened near the Minster. Apparently, it’s brilliant. Really authentic, not one of those tourist traps.      Ooh, the Minster… I've not been inside for years. It’s massive, isn’t it? I remember school trips, feeling absolutely dwarfed by everything. It’s probably changed loads. And an Italian sounds nice, but maybe another day. I need comfort food after that drive. Yorkshire pudding is definitely calling my name.      Fair enough. We can try that Italian next time we're up here. I was thinking about houses too, actually. Have you seen what's available around here? Properly ridiculous prices for what you get.      Oh, don't even start.

Aye, listen to that one, Brenda. Lovely bit o’ song this mornin’. Think it’s a robin, but I’m always second-guessin’ myself. I used to be right good at identifyin’ ‘em, but me ears aren’t what they were.      Oh, it  is  nice, isn't it? Yes, sounds like a robin to me. Though, honestly, they all sound a bit the same after a while. I’m more attuned to the sound of my alarm clock these days, unfortunately. Dreadful thing. Beeps like a malfunctioning heart monitor.      Ooh, I hate those digital ones. Give me a proper bell alarm any day. Wakes ye gently, like. Though, mind you, even that can be a shock to the system at six in the mornin’. I was thinkin' o' gettin' one o' those sunrise alarm clocks. Supposed to be good for yer mood.      I’ve heard about those. A bit pricey, aren't they? More money than I’m willing to spend on a gentler wake-up. Speaking of mornings… I’ve noticed the sparrows are back in force at the feeder. Little gluttons, they are. I’ve had to refill it twice already this week.      They are greedy, aren't they? I put out a nyjer seed feeder just for the goldfinches, but the sparrows try to squeeze onto it anyway. Little acrobats! I feel awful when it's cold, though, knowin' they're relying on us.      It’s a good feeling, isn't it? Helps to feel useful. Though, it’s a bit like running a hotel for feathered friends! Reminds me, I need to book a dentist appointment. Mine's been putting it off for months, says he’s ‘terribly busy’. I suspect he just doesn’t  want  to deal with my teeth.      Oh, dentists. A necessary evil. I had a right fright last year. Had a nosebleed that just wouldn't stop…scared me half to death. Thought it was somethin’ serious. Turns out it was just a dry nose and a bit o' pickin'! I felt a right fool.      Oh dear! That  does  sound alarming. I get those occasionally too, especially in winter with the central heating on. Actually, talking of health… old Mrs. Higgins from down the street – you remember her, always impeccably dressed? – she’s not been well. Apparently, it’s throat cancer.      Oh, no. Poor Margaret. I do remember her. Such a proud woman.

…and honestly, the comments section on that article about single mothers by choice was  brutal . Just…layers of judgement. You’d think people had nothing better to do. It reminded me a bit of the IVF forums, actually. A lot of well-meaning, but ultimately, incredibly painful, opinions flying around.      Oh, don’t even get me started on online forums. It’s a minefield. I understand the need to connect with people going through similar things, especially with something like IVF - it  is  isolating. But the negativity… it’s really damaging. Did you… are you still thinking about it? About IVF, I mean?      It feels like a lifetime ago now, doesn’t it? Five years. And no, not actively. The window feels… closed. Not that I’m entirely at peace with it, mind you. There’s always a little pang. But I’ve found other things to focus on. You know, the yoga’s been a lifesaver. Completely clichéd, I know, but it really has. Grounding. Less… spiralling.      Oh, I'm glad to hear that. I keep meaning to get back into it. Work is just…constant. The caseload is insane. And everyone’s trauma seems to be amplified these days. It’s exhausting. But genuinely pleased yoga is helping. You always were a bit of a worrier, weren’t you?      Still am, just a slightly more mindful worrier! It’s forced me to slow down. And actually, that slowing down has allowed space for something rather unexpected. I’m…writing a book.      No way! Seriously? That’s fantastic! About what? You always had a knack for storytelling. Remember those elaborate tales you’d spin for the kids when we were younger? Always ending with a rogue badger, if I recall.      You have a good memory! It’s… well, it started as a distraction, really. During lockdown. It’s a historical fiction, set in Dorchester, actually. A bit about smuggling and local folklore. It's utterly bonkers, but I’m enjoying it. It's a massive change from marking GCSE essays, that’s for sure. Though, funnily enough, some of the research feels just as intensive!      Dorchester! That’s lovely. You’ve always been so connected to your roots. I’ve been thinking about a bit of a change myself, actually. Not writing a novel, not quite  that  ambitious! But I’m looking into retraining. Maybe something in counselling, specifically for adolescents.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of marking I had last week was ridiculous. Seventeen essays on the French Revolution! Seventeen! And half of them felt like they’d been written by someone who’d only  heard  of France, let alone its history.      Sounds familiar, love. Though mine were usually about Shakespeare. The things they’d pull out of thin air… completely inventing plot points! Still, at least it kept me busy. Retirement’s… quieter, to say the least. Too quiet, if I’m honest.      I can imagine. It’s a huge shift, isn’t it? I’m only just starting to see how much free time people have when they aren’t dealing with lesson plans and parent-teacher meetings. Though 'free time' is a bit of a myth with a toddler running around, to be fair. Little Leo’s just discovered the joy of emptying the biscuit tin.      Ah, yes. Tiny terrors. I remember my Sarah going through that phase. Biscuits, crayons on the walls, the usual. My wife, bless her, had the patience of a saint. She’s… not with us anymore, sadly. It’s been five years now.      Oh, I’m so sorry to hear that, Anon. That must be incredibly difficult. I didn’t realise.      Thank you, dear. It is. Still, life goes on, doesn't it? Keeps me busy enough just trying to remember where I’ve put my glasses. Speaking of which, have you noticed things seem to be getting a bit… rough around here lately? I saw young Darren from number 14 getting shouted at by a couple of lads near the park yesterday.      I did hear something about a spate of petty thefts. My neighbour, Mrs. Henderson, had a flowerpot stolen off her porch! Of all things. It feels different now, doesn't it? I’ve lived in Hitchin all my life, and then moved down here two years ago, and it feels… less safe than I remember. It's a real shame.      Birmingham’s changed a lot over the years. I’ve lived here all my life, you see. Used to be a proper community spirit, everyone knowing everyone. Now… well, people keep themselves to themselves more. And the opportunities have dwindled for the young ‘uns. Makes them desperate, I suppose. It's not an excuse, mind you, but it explains some of it.      It’s a complicated issue, isn't it? I try to instill a love of learning in my students, hoping it gives them options, but it feels like an uphill battle sometimes.

Right, so I’m officially stating it. Curry night next week is non-negotiable. We haven’t ‘ad a proper curry since… well, since before Christmas, hasn't we? And Leeds does ‘em best, naturally. None o’ this poncey, watered-down stuff you get down south.      Oh, here we go. The Yorkshire curry supremacy debate begins! Honestly, Ben, you act like they don’t  have  spice in Hertfordshire. And I’m siding with Cambridge actually, there are some cracking Indian places here. Besides, I’m the one doing the cooking, so I get a say.      Technically, you're not  doing  the cooking, Amelia. You’re assembling pre-prepped ingredients from the deli. Let's be honest. And I agree, curry is a good shout. Though, I was thinking after that horrifying rom-com we watched last night, we maybe deserve something lighter. Like… tacos?      Tacos are good. Although, Rom-coms are a guilty pleasure. Don’t look at me like that, Amelia. It’s research! For understanding the female psyche… or something.      ‘Research’? Honestly, Felix, you were humming the theme tune this morning. And Ben, don't even  start  with that "Leeds curry" nonsense. It’s all subjective! I just feel like after a heavy curry we’ll all be slumped and miserable. Plus, I found a recipe for these amazing mango salsa tacos, it’d be really quick.      Slumped and miserable is a small price to pay for authenticity, lass. Mango salsa? Sounds a bit…fruity. Curry proper should ‘ave you sweatin’ and reachin’ for a pint o’ lager. It's a ritual! It's practically a religious experience!      He’s not wrong about the pint, actually. Though, maybe a good pale ale with tacos wouldn't go amiss. Felix, what are you listening to? Something tragically upbeat, I presume?      Nope. Actual music. Been diving into some German post-punk. It's surprisingly good. Really driving basslines. You wouldn’t get it, though. It’s not on the BBC Radio 6 Music playlist.      Oh dear god. Anything but German post-punk. Please. My ears beg you. Ben, any musical recommendations to counteract that impending doom? Something… less angular?      Aye, well, I’ve been listenin’ to a bit o’ Sea Shanty stuff lately. Sounds daft, I know, but it’s proper catchy. Makes you want to sail the high seas, it does. Not very Cambridge, I suppose.      Sea shanties? Honestly, you lot.

…and honestly, the traffic getting  into  Cambridge was a nightmare. Rain coming down sideways, everyone driving like they’d lost a bet. Nearly took out a cyclist.      Oh, typical Cambridge. It always feels ten degrees colder there, even in summer. Did you manage to find a parking space alright, Liam? I'm starving, and I need coffee.      It’s actually quite pretty, though, isn’t it? All the old buildings glistening with the rain. Very…atmospheric. Though I do agree about the cold. I swear my bones are permanently chilled from living in this country.      Atmospheric until you're trying to navigate cobblestone streets in the pouring rain with a dodgy sat nav. Speaking of which, have we even decided  where  we’re going for this kids’ camp scout? Anna mentioned a few places, but I’ve lost track.      Right, the camp. I think Anna was leaning towards that place near Bury St Edmunds, the one with the outdoor climbing wall? Said it’s got decent reviews. Parking’s probably going to be a pain too, though. It's always the way, isn't it?      Oh, that one! That sounds good, actually. My little nephew went there last year and loved it. Said the instructors were brilliant, and they kept them busy all day. It’s just…getting everyone coordinated. My sister's perpetually late, you know?      Classic. Someone always has to be the logistical nightmare. I’m happy to take one of the younger ones if needed. My weekend’s pretty free, apart from needing to finish editing a particularly dreadful piece on competitive ferret-legging.      Competitive  ferret-legging ? Seriously?! That sounds…intense. I’m avoiding any responsibilities involving small children and potential animal-related injuries. I need to focus on finishing the sound design for this new level. It’s driving me mad. So much tweaking.      Sounds stressful, Ben. You need to hit the gym, mate. Blow off some steam. You looked a bit pale last time we saw you.      Liam's been on a gym kick, you know. He's become a total fitness fanatic. He's been trying to get me to go with him for weeks.      It’s good for you, Sarah! Honestly. I feel so much better since I started. It's not just about the muscles, it’s about the headspace, you know? Plus, they’ve got that new functional training area – ropes, tyre flips, the whole nine yards.

Oof, that looked nasty. Honestly, these tackles are getting more and more reckless. You'd think with VAR they'd clamp down on it a bit more, wouldn't you?      VAR’s a bit patchy, isn't it? Sometimes feels like they only intervene for the really obvious ones, and leave all the sly stuff. Plus, it breaks the flow of the game, doesn’t it? Ends up being more frustrating than helpful. Still, it’s a good match, tense stuff. Bit different from watching Sunderland these days, eh?      Don't even  start  on Sunderland. I haven't subjected myself to that particular brand of torture in months. Honestly, watching paint dry would be a more exhilarating experience. This is… marginally better. At least it's a derby, so there's  some  passion. Although, knowing my luck, the team I’m rooting for will just crumble in the last ten minutes. It's a Northern trait, I think - expecting the worst.      A Northern trait? You're probably right. We Midlands folk are more… cautiously optimistic. Or just resigned. It’s about the same thing, really. Speaking of things ending badly, did you manage to get all your Easter eggs hidden? Little Leo was asking about the Easter Bunny non-stop yesterday.      Oh, that was a mission. He's getting so clever, honestly. I had to employ some seriously strategic hiding places. Behind the radiators, inside your hiking boots… places he’d never think to look. Although, knowing him, he’ll probably find them all within five minutes of being allowed to start the hunt. And then demand more.      Sounds about right. He takes after you, the negotiator. Remember when he wanted the dinosaur costume  and  the fire truck for his birthday? It took a solid hour of explanation and compromise. What are we doing for Easter Sunday itself? Your mum still up for coming down?      She is! She's bringing her famous roast potatoes. I’ve already warned you, you're not allowed to comment on how much butter she uses. It’s a family tradition.
