And we'll probably watch some awful Easter themed film. Remember that one with the talking bunny that becomes a detective?      Don’t remind me. That film was… a choice. Still, Leo loved it. Anything for the kid. I've been thinking though, once the Easter madness is over, we should actually try and see a film in the cinema.

Oh, look at this one! Little Leo, absolutely  covered  in blue paint. I’d forgotten about that fun fair in Blackpool. He insisted on winning one of those ridiculously oversized stuffed animals.      Blackpool, now  there’s  a memory. The price of those stuffed things… robbery, I tell ya. But the look on his face! Worth every penny. He was only… what, six? Seven?      Seven, I think. He told me about it last week. Said it was bigger than him!      He always  was  a wee scamp. Full of beans, your Leo. Reminds me so much of his Da at that age. Always getting into mischief.      Oh, you're right, Nan. Definitely his father’s son. Though Leo’s got a bit more… determination, maybe? Remember when Mark tried to run the London Marathon?      Don’t  even  bring that up. The blisters! I had to practically carry him to the finish line. He swore he’d never run again. He was moaning for a week.      He did, though, didn’t he? Ran it again last year. He’s a bit competitive, Dad. Saw some photos on his Insta.      He’s a stubborn man, that’s what he is. But proud of him, I am. He's actually thinking of doing Iceland next year. Some crazy ice marathon or other.      Iceland?! Good heavens! That sounds… cold. Are you going to go and support him this time?      I might. I’d need a serious winter coat, that’s for sure. And a flask of something warming. It’s a long way to go just to watch him suffer.      He gets his resilience from my side of the family, you know. We Scots are used to a bit of a chill! Though an ice marathon does sound a bit extreme, even for us.      I think he likes the challenge. He keeps going on about seeing the Northern Lights while he’s there.      Oh, that  would  be incredible. We should all go, shouldn't we? A family holiday to Iceland.      Iceland? With me trying to keep up with your son? I think I’ll pass, thank you very much. I’m more of a cinema and a quiet pint kind of man these days. Did you see that new film, with… what’s her name? The one with the dragons?      “Emberwing”? Yeah, it was okay. A bit long.      I haven’t had a chance to go to the cinema in ages.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of ebooks I’ve downloaded recently is bordering on ridiculous. I keep thinking, “Oh, this looks good,” and then it just sits there, taunting me from the Kindle. It’s like digital hoarding.      You’re not alone there, definitely. I've got about five on the go - which means I've properly finished  none  of them. Though, to be fair, work has been a bit… intense. It’s just constant fire-fighting these days. Between HR issues and trying to get everyone back into a routine after the holidays…      Fire-fighting, you say? Sounds a bit like when your father used to try and sort out the garden shed. Everything was a crisis! Though his fires were usually started by piles of old newspapers.      Oh, goodness, you're right! He  did  have a tendency to let things accumulate. Remember that time he tried to build a bird table out of spare parts and it collapsed during Mrs. Higgins' garden party?      Oh,  don’t  remind me! Poor Mrs. Higgins nearly had a heart attack! And the bird table ended up landing in her prize-winning roses. It’s a small world, isn't it? She practically raised me, being next door, and still brings me over rhubarb from her garden every year.      It really is. I was thinking about that earlier, actually. I was chatting to a client in Bristol yesterday, and his sister went to the same primary school as I did! Boston, remember? Tiny little school.      Boston! Right. I’ve heard you mention it. So different to Peterborough, isn't it? More…rural?      Vastly. And everyone knew everyone. We spent our entire childhoods building dens in Farmer Giles’ field. Do you remember building dens, Mum?      Oh, yes. We weren’t allowed in Farmer Giles’ field. Too dangerous, your grandpa said. We built ours in the orchard, using old apple boxes and sheets. Horribly wobbly things. We mostly played 'House', though. Endless cups of pretend tea and arguments over who was the baby.      I remember those! I always wanted to be the mum. It meant I got to boss everyone around! Though, my brother always made me play with his Dinky cars instead. He had this amazing collection.      Dinky cars! Yes! I was more of a Sindy girl, myself. Though I always secretly wished I had his cars. Talking of childhood, I found a box of my old knitting in the attic last week.

… Honestly, Doreen, this coronation… all this fuss. It’s a bit much, isn’t it? Feels like we haven’t had a real good fuss in ages, and now it's  this . Not that I’ve got anything against the young lad, Charles, mind. Seems a decent sort.      Decent sort, yes. Though I can’t say I followed his… endeavours with Camilla all that closely. Still, well, he's the King now. And a bit of colour does brighten things up, doesn’t it? We’ve had a grey patch, haven’t we? Not just the weather, everything.      Grey is putting it politely. More like… well, you remember when the Queen Mother went. That  was  a moment. Proper national mourning. This…it feels different. More like a party. A very expensive party. And the costumes! All that gold braid.      Oh, you’re a grumblepot, Arthur. Always have been. It's tradition, dear. The pomp and ceremony. Reminds one of history, doesn’t it? I did enjoy seeing all the carriages. Though I think I preferred it when they actually  rode  horses, rather than going in those fancy motorised things.      Fancy motorised things, she calls 'em. Waste of money, I tell you. Could’ve put that towards… well, anything, really. Proper funding for the NHS, perhaps. Speaking of which, young Michael was telling me the wait for Mrs. Higgins’ hip replacement is still… well, it's considerable, apparently.      Poor Ethel. She’s been in pain for ages with that hip. It's a shame, isn’t it? Always so cheerful, despite everything. You’d think someone of her age would get prioritised, but… No, forgetting my manners. More tea, Arthur? It’s getting a bit lukewarm.      Go on then. Just a splash, mind. Too much and I’m up all night. It’s funny, isn't it? When we were younger, a coronation was something  we  were living through. Something… monumental. Now it's just… something on the telly. Like a historical drama.      That's life, Arthur. Everything changes. Do you remember when we first got a television? Black and white, of course. Mr. Peterson next door practically built us the aerial. Said it was essential for keeping up with the news. And then colour came along... changes, constantly changing.      Peterson. Now  there  was a character. Always tinkering with something. And the news! Used to be proper news, reporting on things that mattered.

…and honestly, little Timmy tried to argue with me that a comma  was  a full stop. A full stop! I nearly choked on my biscuit. Honestly, where do they get this stuff from? It's like they actively try to misunderstand grammar.      Oh, bless him. Kids are brilliant at that, aren’t they? My Year 2s were convinced ‘because’ was spelt ‘bekuz’ for a solid month. It’s adorable, and also incredibly frustrating. How’s teaching going otherwise? Still loving the little ones?      Most of the time, yeah. It’s rewarding, properly. Though the parents... that’s a whole other story, innit? Had a right palaver last week with one who thought their darling boy should be reading chapter books already. He’s  six . Honestly! Makes you question everything. What about you? Still battling the teenage hordes?      Sadly, yes. Year 10s are just…a mood. All dramatic sighs and eye rolls. I’m teaching Shakespeare, and they seem genuinely offended by the concept of iambic pentameter. I tried breaking it down with a beatboxing analogy. Didn’t land.      Shakespeare and teenagers? Sounds like a recipe for disaster. Though, honestly, beatboxing Shakespeare... that  is  quite inspired. You’re a better woman than I am. I'd have just given up and played them a TikTok about it.      Oh, you’d be surprised what they respond to! Though TikTok is a slippery slope. I try to keep it to educational stuff, but they find a way. Anyway, how’s the copywriting going, Chloe? Still churning out brilliant ad copy?      It’s…keeping me busy. Mainly writing about dog food and insurance at the moment, so not exactly Oscar-winning stuff. But pays the bills. I'm trying to pitch a campaign for a travel company, though. A proper getaway, you know? I need a holiday desperately. Anywhere good you guys have been recently?      We went to Cornwall last month. Proper lovely. Bit rainy, naturally, but stunning coastlines and cream teas make up for it. Needed a break after dealing with GCSE results. Honestly, the stress! My boyfriend’s car decided to pack in on the way home, though. Total nightmare.      Oh, no, that's awful! What happened? Proper breakdown, or just a bit temperamental? My uncle Dave's a mechanic, if you need a recommendation. He’s down in Bristol, but might know someone in London.      It was the alternator, apparently. Thankfully, we were near a garage.

…and honestly, the state of some of the gardens on Barlow Street! It's a right mess, isn't it? Remember old Mr. Henderson? His was always immaculate. Roses, everything trim. Now it looks like the jungle's taken over.      Ah, poor Mr. Henderson. Gone too soon, that one. And you're right, Barlow Street  has  gone downhill. People just don't take the same pride these days. Though, mind you, everyone's got their own struggles. It’s hard to keep on top of things.      It's not just Barlow Street, is it? It feels like the whole area's changed. More empty houses, more…well, you see things you didn’t used to. I was walking back from the bus stop last night, and there was a group of lads hanging around the corner of Upper Parliament Street acting a bit dodgy.      Mum! Did you know Sirius Black was framed? Professor Lupin explains it all! It’s brilliant!      That’s lovely, love. Finish your homework first, though, yeah? Honestly, Harry Potter, he lives in that book. You’d think he’d be having a rest by now!      It's a good distraction, isn't it? A world away from… well, from everything else. Speaking of which, I was reading an article the other day about the impact of social media on teenage anxieties. Quite alarming.      It  is  scary. My little cousin’s always on TikTok. She’s only ten! I worry about what she's seeing, y’know? And the pressures.      It is worrying. But what can you do? You try and talk to them, but…they just roll their eyes. Though, honestly, some of the things  I  hear about from volunteering at school…it’s not just TikTok. It's everything. Kids dealing with stuff no child should have to think about.      It’s a different world now. It reminds me, actually, of some research I was doing on the anxieties surrounding the industrial revolution. A similar sense of rapid, unsettling change. Though, of course, this is on a completely different scale. Have you heard anything about that new housing development they’re planning on the old docklands?      Oh, don't even get me started. They’re saying it’s going to ‘regenerate the area’, but it’ll just price everyone out. All those flats, all that fancy stuff… it’s not for people like us.      Exactly! They’ll build these shiny apartments and then wonder why the community spirit’s gone.

...Honestly, the gluten-free options at the Village Shop are appalling. They’ve got one brand of bread, and it tastes like sawdust. You’d think in this day and age, they’d make more of an effort. Though, to be fair, the sausages are lovely. Proper Gloucester Old Spot, you know? Not that processed rubbish.      Oh, I agree about the Village Shop. I popped in for a loaf the other day and was deeply disappointed. Berkeley’s Farm Shop is much better for that sort of thing. They do a decent gluten-free range, and their local produce is fantastic. Though it  is  a bit pricey, isn't it? Still, better than sawdust bread. You going to Nepal, you’ll be needing to think about all this, won’t you? How’s the planning going?      It is pricey, the Farm Shop! But worth it for a treat. And Nepal… oh, the planning is a headache! So many forms, so many vaccinations. And trying to figure out food! I’m worried about allergies and just… everything being different. I remember when  we  went backpacking in the 70s, you just… went. No fuss. Bit of a dodgy curry now and then, but that was it!      Dodgy curry! Oh, the stories I could tell! I went to Greece with a friend in '78 and we ate something… questionable. Honestly, I thought I’d never recover. But you’re right, it was simpler then. This Nepal trip is… daunting. My daughter did all the initial research, but she’s so focused on the trekking aspect, I have to keep reminding her I need to  eat  too! And I don’t want to offend anyone with dietary requirements.      Your daughter, she’s the Iron Man one, isn’t she? The one who cycles everywhere? Fantastic achievement, completing one of those. I saw the Tour of Britain go past the other day, right through Wotton-under-Edge. It was a bit chaotic, but exciting. Really brought the community together. You and Geoff must be so proud of her.      It’s incredible what she does! Truly. Geoff's been making her these power bars, all gluten-free and packed with goodness. He’s become quite the chef, actually. It’s wonderful watching him enjoy it, especially after his job. Remember how he used to complain about the long hours at the bank?      Complain?! He  moaned  for years!

…and honestly, the feedback forms for the agricultural tech conference were  brutal . Brutal, I tell ya. Apparently, the canapés weren't 'artisanal' enough. Artisanal! It's a conference about tractors, not Michelin stars!      Oh, you’re kidding! People actually complained about  canapés  at a tractor conference? That’s a new level of… entitlement. My week's been less about fussy food and more about chasing down a supplier who’s decided, mid-production run, that he’s ‘re-evaluating his life choices’.      Re-evaluating his life choices? During a production run?! Sounds…dramatic. Is it holding everything up?      Massively. We’re talking a potential two-week delay on the new product launch. My manager is not pleased, to put it mildly. I've spent the last three days on the phone acting as a negotiator, a therapist, and a glorified babysitter.      Oh, bless you. Reminds me a bit of dealing with Mr Henderson at the solicitors office last month. Wanted everything in Comic Sans.  Comic Sans  on legal documents! I had to gently…suggest alternative fonts.      No way! Honestly, some people! It's the little things that grind you down, innit? I spent an hour yesterday trying to explain to a delegate why the Wi-Fi password wasn't ‘WelcomeToFarming2024!’ – it was a security thing, obviously.      It's the constant problem-solving, isn't it? It’s not the big crises, it's the endless stream of tiny fires. I’m starting to feel like a professional fire extinguisher. Are you still enjoying the events coordination, though, despite the canapé-related trauma?      Most of the time, yeah. It's just… draining. Especially when you put so much effort into making everything perfect, and then someone complains about the font size on the signage. Although, I did get a lovely thank you from the speaker at the keynote. Said I was a ‘lifesaver’ getting his presentation sorted at the last minute. That's what makes it worthwhile, I suppose. How are you finding things, being a Production Controller? Still enjoying the fast pace?      It’s definitely fast-paced. And stressful. Actually, I'm starting to wonder if I’m in the right career. It’s all spreadsheets and suppliers and deadlines. I did my Masters in Art History, remember? Sometimes I just want to… look at paintings, not production schedules.      You always were brilliant at art. Remember that exhibition you curated at university?

...Honestly, the sheer audacity of it! Demolishing the Plumstead library? It's the  only  decent community space left around here. And they want to put luxury flats in its place, of course. Another block of overpriced boxes no one local can afford.      I know, I saw the plans online. It’s absolutely ridiculous. They always go for the easy win, don't they? A quick buck from developers, and to hell with the residents. Are you seriously thinking of starting a petition?      I am. I’ve started drafting something, actually. It feels… futile, a bit? But we have to  try . Mrs. Higgins from the book club said she’d definitely sign, and old Mr. Patel practically begged me to do something. He uses the computers there every day – says it’s the only way he can keep in touch with his grandkids in India.      Good. Futile or not, doing nothing is worse. I’ll sign it, of course. And I can help with getting signatures. I’m on a pretty good footing with a few of the shopkeepers on the High Street. They’re usually up for supporting local causes. Do you want me to print some copies for them?      That would be amazing, thank you. Honestly, you’re a lifesaver. I was panicking about getting enough momentum. They’ll just say ‘low usage’ and ‘cost-cutting’ again, won’t they? It's always the same tired excuses.      It will be. That’s why we need to hit them with numbers. Show them how many people actually  use  it. And we need to frame it right. Not just ‘we like books,’ but access to computers, free learning resources, a safe space for kids after school… you know, the practical stuff.      Exactly! I’ve tried to include all that in the wording. It’s just… trying to translate all that into a concise, impactful petition feels like a transcription nightmare. Trying to capture the  essence  of the library’s importance! It's harder than transcribing a mumbled legal document, I tell you.      You and your transcriptions! Still at it, then? Same soul-destroying work?      Sadly, yes. Still churning through audio files. Though last week I had a particularly bizarre one – a lecture on the history of Victorian taxidermy. Honestly, you wouldn’t believe the detail.      Oh, wow. That  does  sound… niche. At least it’s interesting. I’m stuck in admin hell.

…and honestly, Doreen, I still don’t understand why they keep coming round. Not that I mind a chat, mind you, but these Jehovah’s Witnesses... persistent, aren't they? Young lad this time, very polite, but going on about the end of days, the New World… all a bit much over a cuppa, wouldn't you say?      Oh, Arthur, they’ve been at it for yonks, haven’t they? Remember old Mrs. Grimshaw down the lane? She took it all to heart, joined 'em for a good few years. Drove poor Bertie mad, she did. He was a man of routine, and all that talk of upheaval… well, it wasn't for him.      It’s a comfort to some, I suppose. People looking for answers, for something to believe in. Though I do agree, it can be a little overwhelming, especially when they keep popping up. My niece, Sarah, she got involved for a while. Then her Michael convinced her it was all a bit… controlling.      Controlling is a good word for it, Doreen. They were asking about young Thomas, if he’d considered reading their literature. He’s only just started university, bless him! Trying to tell him the world’s about to end when he’s trying to pass his exams… it’s ridiculous.      Speaking of Thomas, how  is  he settling in? Heard he’s doing engineering, like yourself, Arthur? Good lad. Always was a bright spark.      Doing alright, doing alright. Says it’s hard work, naturally. A lot more theory than practical, he says. I tried to offer some advice, practical stuff, but he just rolled his eyes. “Grandad,” he said, “it's all different now.” Different! Still, makes a man feel old, doesn’t it?      Oh, they always say that, Arthur! It's the way of things. Remember when you were telling me about that new bridge design you saw? You were describing it like it was magic! It  is  different, but built on the foundations of what came before.      Foundations. That's what I always say about marriage, isn't it? Gets a bit wobbly sometimes, needs a bit of patching up, but the foundations have to be strong. Fifty years, and I still look at Eileen and think… how did I get so lucky? She’s at the WI today, learning how to make miniature flower arrangements. Honestly.      Miniature flower arrangements! That sounds very Eileen.

Honestly, this mashed potato is  divine , Anon. You’ve always had a gift for it. Not like some people I know, who manage to make it gluey.      Oh, Mother, you always were a harsh critic in the kitchen! It’s just a bit of butter and cream, really. Nothing fancy. Though, I did find a lovely little antique shop on the way back from picking up those logs. You’d adore it. All sorts of…well,  things .      “Things” is a generous description, I suspect. Likely a collection of dust-catchers, judging by the shops I’ve seen these days. Still, good on you for supporting local businesses. Though, everything seems to be going the way of online these days. Even the upholstery quotes I got for that chair… all wanting to outsource the finer stitching to India! Can you imagine?      That’s… a bit worrying, isn’t it? The quality control. I mean, I deal with outsourcing at work all the time, but usually it's more straightforward data entry. Delicate work like upholstery? That feels different.      Indeed. It's a race to the bottom, isn’t it? Everything sacrificed at the altar of the budget. Remember when things were  made  to last? This new generation doesn’t even understand that concept. It’s all disposable. It’s reflected in the schools now, too. All these academy conversions… it takes away the heart of the community.      It does. And it’s not just the schools. Old Mrs. Higgins next door was telling me she’s worried sick about the new restaurant going in on the High Street. Apparently, they’re planning to do ‘small plates’ and charge a fortune for it. She says it’s forgetting what people actually  want .      Small plates… bah! Give me a proper roast and Yorkshire pudding any day. Though I must say, that trip you two took to Tokyo last year… did you find much good food there? Beyond the small plates, naturally.      Tokyo was incredible. The food was… an experience. Everything was beautifully presented, a real art form. And the variety! We had a fantastic little place, a ramen shop tucked away down a side street – absolutely authentic. Nothing like what you get here.      Ramen, you say? Is that anything like noodles? I’m not much for foreign food, you know. Give me a nice piece of Scottish tablet or a good fudge any day.

…Honestly, Marjorie, this council tax is getting ridiculous. Every year it creeps up, and for what? The roads are still full of potholes, and the bins only get emptied when they feel like it.      Tell me about it, Arthur. Back in my day, you could rely on things being…reliable. Now, it’s all computer says no. They sent me a letter this year, said I hadn't paid, when I  know  I’d sent a cheque. Took three phone calls and a strongly worded letter to get it sorted.      Oh, don’t even  start  me on the council tax, Reginald. It's daylight robbery, pure and simple. They claim it's for services, but I can't see what services we're getting for our money. It’s just…gone. Disappears into a black hole somewhere. Though, I suppose it’s no different from the pension contributions, is it? In you go, and what comes out is always less than you expected.      That's the truth, Marjorie. I was looking at houses, you know, just browsing online. Thinking of maybe downsizing, something a bit…easier to manage. And the prices! You need a winning lottery ticket just to get a garden shed these days.      Downsizing, eh? Whereabouts were you looking, Arthur? Still Norfolk, I presume? Can’t see you going far after all these years.      Aye, mostly around here. Maybe Dereham, somewhere like that. I saw a semi-detached for… well, I won’t bore you with the figures, but it was extortionate. And the estate agent was going on about 'excellent transport links'. The only transport link is a single-track road and a bus that runs twice a week.      Estate agents! They could sell sand to the Arabs. They're all the same, promising the earth. Remember when we were looking at places back in the seventies, Reginald? Honest descriptions, decent prices…those days are long gone.      Speaking of getting around…I tried using one of those Sat Navs the other day. My granddaughter, Chloe, she set it up for me. Said it would take me to the garden centre in Wymondham. It sent me down a lane narrower than my Morris Minor! Ended up reversing for half a mile.      Oh, Reginald, you and technology. It's not a natural fit, is it? I’ve got one, but mostly I just ignore it and go the way I remember.

Right, that was a good bit of grub. Though I still think your fajita sauce is the best, love. Beats anything I’ve tasted, even down in Texas.      Oh, stop it, you flatterer! It's just a bit of chili powder and some clever blending. Though, I  am  rather proud of it. Speaking of clever blending… how’s the computer coming along? Still wrestling with that warranty?      It’s a right headache, honestly. I’ve spent the last two hours on the phone with them. They’re saying because I opened it up to check the graphics card, the warranty's void. Can you believe it? I wasn’t messing about, just trying to figure out why it was overheating.      Opening it up? Didn’t you say it was all clicky and stuff? Like, no screws?      It  was  mostly clicky, but there were a couple of sneaky screws hiding under the rubber feet. Needed to get to the fan, see if that was clogged up. They’re sticking to their guns though. "User tampering" is what they called it. Pure gobshite, I tell ya.      That’s ridiculous! You're an IT manager, you know what you're doing. Honestly, these companies… Did you mention you’re a professional?      I did, several times. They didn't seem to care one bit. They just kept reading from their script. I’m thinking I might just rebuild it. I’ve got a spare processor and some decent RAM kicking around.      Can I help? I’ve been learning about CPUs in school. Mr. Davies is really good at explaining it.      You know what? That'd be grand, lad. Maybe after dinner? We can have a look. Though, no promises it won’t involve a bit of cursing… technical terminology, of course.      Wonderful. Just steer clear of the swearing in front of little Leo here. Speaking of little Leo, have you seen his ears? They really  stick out  with that new haircut. I swear they're getting more prominent.      Ah, now, they’re grand ears. Character! Besides, he gets them from his mother's side of the family.      Oh, don't try and blame my family! They're perfectly respectable ears on my side, thank you very much. Anyway, what about tomorrow? Have you organised anything for yourselves?      I was thinking we could take Leo swimming. The wave pool at the leisure centre. He loves that, doesn’t he?

Honestly, this is perfect. Simple, cheesy pizza after a chaotic day. What do you two think? Is it the  best  pizza ever?      Mmmhmm! Best  ever ! But… can we have garlic bread next time? With loads of cheese?      And pepperoni! And can we build a fairy garden  tomorrow ? A really, really big one? Like, bigger than the table?      Woah there, slow down soldier! One thing at a time. Garlic bread is a good shout, sweetheart. Pepperoni, definitely. And a giant fairy garden… we'll see what space we have. Leo, please don't fall and take the fruit bowl with you.      I almost did it! It's hard!      I can do a handstand! But only for… three seconds.      Well, that’s fantastic! Practice makes perfect, doesn’t it? You’re both so full of energy. It’s lovely to see. It reminds me... Auntie Susan asked if you two had picked out outfits for Millie’s party on Saturday.      Ooh! I want to wear my sparkly dress! The one with the unicorns!      I want to be a pirate! I have a pirate hat! And an eye patch!      A pirate and a unicorn. Sounds like a rather adventurous party. Now, listen, something Sarah mentioned today at school got me thinking. She was saying how difficult it can be getting children to  explain  what's bothering them. She’s got a little boy who just clams up.      Clams up? Like a… a shell?      Kind of. Like he shuts down and doesn't say anything. I was trying to explain to her how sometimes, you both just need someone to  listen  without jumping in. Do you understand that?      Like when I’m telling you about a really long dinosaur and you don’t say “Oh, that’s silly!”?      Exactly! That’s a brilliant example, Leo. Sometimes, just letting someone finish their thought is the most important thing. Even if it's about a very, very long dinosaur.      Or a monster! Like the Loch Ness Monster! Do you think it’s real?      That’s a question people have been asking for centuries! Some people believe it is, others don’t. Imagine though, a giant monster living in a lake in Scotland!      It would need a really big pizza! Like, fifty pizzas!      You’re probably right. Fifty pizzas. And lots and lots of garlic bread. You know, thinking about ideal meals… if you could design the perfect menu, what would it be?

...Honestly, the mussels were incredible. I haven’t had mussels that fresh since… well, since that trip to Whitby years ago. Did you manage to try them, Liam?      Nah, I went for the pizza. Proper good pizza, that. Proper cheesy. Though I think I saw Gran trying to wrestle a shell with her fork. Looked a bit of a battle.      Oh, Mum! You know mussels are a nightmare for you. You always end up needing about ten napkins and looking like you’ve been in a fight.      It’s a principle, love! I refuse to be beaten by a shellfish. Anyway, it  was  worth the effort eventually. This Istrian wine is lovely too, isn’t it, David? A bit lighter than what you usually go for, I reckon.      It is, actually. Very refreshing. I was expecting something a bit… bolder, given the heat. But this is perfect with the seafood. Croatia is doing something right, clearly. Much nicer than some of the dreary business lunches I’ve had in London lately.      Tell me about it! Everything feels a million miles away from uni stress right now. Although, I’m already stressing about my food tech project. We’re supposed to be designing some sort of new food product.      Food tech? What, like inventing a pizza that delivers itself?      Something like that! It's terrifyingly open-ended. I was thinking maybe some sort of pre-prepared, nutritionally balanced meal for students, but it all feels a bit…beige.      Beige isn’t good. People eat with their eyes first. Remember that, as a midwife. Presentation is important, even if it’s a plate of scrambled eggs. It encourages appetite.      She’s right, you know. It's all about the user experience. Think about Steve Jobs - he didn’t just sell computers, he sold an  experience . What's the experience you want your food product to deliver?      Hmm, good point. An experience… easy, convenient, healthy… maybe something… personalised? Like, you could tailor the nutrients based on your activity levels? It sounds ridiculously complicated, though.      You could make those weird edible water bubbles! I saw a video of them. Like, a whole drink in a little plastic-free bubble.      Now  that  is an invention. Though I can just imagine the mess. Speaking of inventions, did you see that thing on the news about them trying to develop a rapid test for Ebola? Terrifying stuff, that.

Right, that were a good bit o’ lunch, wasn’t it? Another slice o’ that ham, Doris? You always do make a lovely ham.      Oh, go on, Arthur. You say that every time. It's just a simple ham, nothing special. Though, I did get a good price on it from Mr. Henderson at the butcher's. He was telling me about his grandson, started university this term.      University, eh? Costs a fortune these days. I was reading an article in  The Spectator  about student debt… absolutely crippling. Young people starting their lives already owing tens of thousands. It’s a disgrace, frankly.      It is. And the PPI claims… well, the banks made a killing off mis-selling, and now they begrudge paying out. I had a chap on the phone yesterday, very insistent. Claimed I’d been mis-sold something twenty years ago. I just put the phone down. Waste of time.      Oh, they’re a nuisance, them callers. Always trying it on. I had one last week, saying I was due a refund. Refund for what, I asked him? He couldn’t even tell me! Just wanted me to give him my bank details. Nearly had a heart attack, I did.      You have to be so careful, Arthur. They’re getting cleverer all the time. Did you manage to get the TV sorted, by the way? You were wrestling with the remote yesterday.      Aye, I did. Roy – that's your son, Harold, he's a whizz with that sort o’ thing – he came round and fiddled with it. Said something about the HDMI cable. Honestly, it’s all Greek to me. Just glad I can watch  Songs of Praise  again. I do love a good hymn. Especially the ones they sing at the Abbey. The acoustics in there… spectacular.      You’ve got a good voice yourself, Arthur. Remember when you led the singing at St. Margaret’s for that village fete? Brought the house down!      Oh, did I? I've no recollection of that. Probably had a bit too much elderflower wine. Though I always enjoyed a good singin' session. It's just… haven’t felt up to it lately. This dodgy knee, you know.      Speaking of things you're not feeling up to... Dorothy, are you still planning on driving to see Emily next month? It's a long drive to Cornwall.      I am, yes. Though I am a bit apprehensive, I don’t mind admitting.

Honestly, that was a…spirited session. Young Mr. Davies clearly hadn’t grasped the concept of ‘reasonable force’ when defending his garden gnomes.      Och, garden gnomes, you don’t say? They get passionate about their ornaments, folk do. I’ve seen arguments over less. Though usually it's handbags, not… whatever he was wielding. A watering can, was it?      A rather hefty one, yes. It's amazing what people will escalate to. It does make you think, though, doesn't it? About justice, and what's  really  fair. He was clearly frustrated, his neighbour’s cat had been…relieving itself on his prized petunias, apparently.      Aye, well, a cat will be a cat. Though I can see why he'd be upset. Still, court's not always about fairness, is it? It's about the law. And a watering can counts as an offensive weapon these days, sadly. Still, beats some of the things I’ve seen walked through those doors. Remind me never to mess with anyone’s patio furniture.      Quite. It’s such a strange little microcosm, isn’t it? A snapshot of everything that goes wrong. And the variety of people... Honestly, I spend my days trying to explain the nuances of the subjunctive to teenagers, and then I come  here  and learn more about life.      You're a teacher then? I remember you mentioned something about languages. Good for you. A lot of good needs doing in education. My grandson, wee Jamie, he’s struggling with his maths. Says it just doesn’t  click .      I teach French and Spanish, actually. And I completely agree. Education is vital. Maths can be tricky, though. It’s all about building that foundational understanding. Maybe extra tutoring would help Jamie? It’s expensive, I know… everything is.      It is. Everything's gone up, hasn’t it? Even a simple loaf of bread feels like a luxury these days. And the petrol! Don’t even get me started. Makes you wonder how folks manage. I used to get the bus into Solihull, but they’ve cut back the routes where I live. It's just not practical anymore.      It’s scandalous, really. Public transport should be readily accessible, especially for those who can't drive or can’t afford a car. I try to cycle when I can, but the roads aren't always the safest, and sometimes the weather… well, you know.

Mummy, if I had  all  the sparkly stickers in the world, would I be happy? Like,  really  happy?      That’s a very good question, Lily-Rose. A  very  good question. And Leo, what about you? Would a mountain of LEGO make you massively happy?      A REALLY big mountain? Bigger than me?      Bigger than you, even. Yes. Would that make you super-duper happy?      Yeah! Definitely! I could build a castle! A spaceship! Everything!      But… would it make you happy  forever ?      Clever girl. That's what we need to think about. Okay, so, imagine you both have all the sparkly stickers and LEGO in the world. You've built your castle, Leo, and you’ve covered everything in sparkles, Lily-Rose. Then what?      Then… I'd build another castle! A bigger one!      And then?      And… and then a robot to help me build!      And then you’d get… bored? That's what happened with my dolls last week. I had ALL of them out, and then I just wanted to draw.      Exactly! Having lots of things – sparkly stickers, LEGO, even lots and lots of money – can be fun, it can make you smile, but it doesn’t  always  make you happy forever, does it?      So money doesn't buy happiness? I heard Mrs. Davies say that at school!      You did! Mrs. Davies is a wise lady. It's a bit of an old saying, isn’t it? But it's true. Happiness comes from different things. It comes from… well, what makes  you  happy, Lily-Rose, when you don't have sparkly stickers?      When we read stories! And when you tickle me! And when Leo doesn't sneak my crayons!      Hey! I only sneak them sometimes!      Sometimes is enough! See? Happiness is listening to a good story, feeling loved, and having someone you care about not pilfer your art supplies. It is friends and family. Things you  do , not things you  have .      So, if we had loads and loads of money, and we didn't have time to read stories with you, would we be happy?      No, my loves. We wouldn’t. All the money in the world wouldn’t make up for missing out on time together. That's the most important thing, isn’t it?      Like when Daddy's working late? You always make pancakes to cheer us up!      That's right. And those pancakes, and the story we read afterward, and even a little bit of a grumble about missing Daddy – that’s all happiness.

...Honestly, the whole thing feels a bit ridiculous. My uncle keeps going on about investing in rare earth minerals. Says China’s got a stranglehold on them and it’s the future. Like I even  have  money to invest!      Rare earth minerals? Sounds… niche. Is that, like, stuff for electric cars and stuff? I did read something about that. Apparently, they're key for all sorts of tech, not just batteries. Which makes your uncle’s point kinda valid, actually. China  does  control a massive chunk of the supply.      Exactly! He's presenting it like he’s some kind of financial genius, predicting the world’s needs. But it just feels like a get-rich-quick scheme. He showed me a patent application he's thinking of filing – some kind of filter for extracting them more efficiently. Apparently, he’s been tinkering in the shed for months.      A patent? Wow. That  is  ambitious. Is it any good? Like, actually feasible? My dad’s always going on about inventing things, too. He had a brilliant idea for a self-stirring mug, but then someone already patented it. Turns out, the world is full of people who want self-stirring mugs.      He claims it’s revolutionary. Lots of complicated talk about magnetic fields and nano-particles. Honestly, it went right over my head. He keeps saying it'll be bigger than the internet. I just roll my eyes. Though, if it  did  work… imagine the money.      Yeah, imagine. But even if it works, getting it to market is a nightmare, isn't it? All the manufacturing and distribution. It's not like he can just build them in his shed. Which, thinking about China again, is their advantage, right? They can manufacture stuff at a scale no one else can touch.      That’s what I said! He dismissed that, saying Western innovation is superior. I'm like, ‘Uncle, logistics matter!’ It's not just about  having  the idea. It’s about making it real. It reminds me of Mr. Harrison in Physics. All theory, no application.      Haha, yeah, Mr. Harrison is a bit like that. He could explain quantum entanglement for an hour but couldn't fix the projector. So, what have  you  been thinking about, career-wise? Away from rare earth minerals and ambitious uncles?      Honestly? I’m completely lost. Everyone's talking about AI and coding and stuff, and I'm not sure I’m cut out for that.

Honestly, I think I’ve eaten my weight in carbs already this week. But after that black run this morning… I  needed  it. My legs were screaming!      Tell me about it! My quads are still burning. I hadn't realised how out of practice I was. It’s been… what, five years since we last did this?      At least! Maybe six. Remember that disaster in Austria? Colin nearly took out a ski instructor.      Don’t remind me. He was so smug about it too, saying he’d ‘taken control of the situation’. The instructor didn’t see the funny side. Speaking of Colin, how are things with him and Mum? She seemed a bit… strained on the phone last week.      Oh, you noticed too? It's the retirement, I think. She’s driving him mad wanting to redecorate the whole house, and he just wants to sit and watch football. Classic Mum and Colin. He's trying to be supportive, bless him, but he’s a man of simple pleasures. It’s just…a lot for him all at once.      It always is. She’s endlessly energetic, isn't she? I worried she’d fall over herself with boredom if she stopped working. But maybe he needs a bit of peace now and then too. And how's little Leo coping with the new school?      He’s finally settled, thankfully. First few weeks were rough, lots of tears and clutching at my leg, but he's made a friend - a boy called Sam. Apparently they’re obsessed with dinosaurs. Honestly, it’s all I hear about now. He even tried to convince me the ski instructor was a T-Rex.      Oh, that's lovely! It’s good to hear he’s finding his feet. It’s hard, starting a new school. I remember being absolutely terrified when we moved primaries.      I know. It’s a big transition. Anyway, enough about family drama and anxieties. We’re supposed to be relaxing! Are you up for another run this afternoon? Maybe something a little gentler? I fancy exploring that blue run near the gondola.      That sounds perfect. My pride can recover while my muscles do. Before we go though, have you managed to get hold of Sarah? I texted her yesterday, but haven't had a reply. I was hoping we could all go for dinner tonight.      I tried calling her this morning, no answer.

Oh dear, a little… enthusiastic with the layers there, wasn’t I? Honestly, Arthur, sometimes I feel like I’m back in primary school, wielding safety scissors and hoping for the best.      Don’t worry, Margaret, it’ll grow out. It’s a… bold stripe, that’s for sure. Though, I did feel a  twinge  just then. Are you absolutely certain you know what you’re doing back there? It felt awfully close to my earlobe.      Perfectly certain! Well, relatively. Distracted, perhaps. I was just thinking about the racket strings. If we’re going to actually  do  this, properly, we need a robust solution for the breakage. Not just a quick re-string.      You mean beyond just… replacing the broken string? Because that’s what I was picturing. New string, tensioned correctly, job done.      No, no. Think preventative! Players break strings, especially at that point near the frame. What if we reinforced it? Some kind of… bracing. I was thinking small cable ties, woven into the string bed  before  stringing. A little network of support.      Cable ties? Margaret, that sounds…agricultural. Wouldn’t they just add weight and interfere with the feel of the racket? Badminton’s a game of finesse, remember, not brute force.      That’s what we need to  test . Thin cable ties, properly positioned. We’re not talking strapping whole planks of wood on, Arthur. Think tiny, clever reinforcement. And strategically placed, of course. Maybe centering on the point where most breaks happen – according to young Thomas, it’s always around the 3 and 9 o’clock positions, right?      Thomas did mention something about that when he was complaining about his third broken string last month. Still, cable ties… It feels like a rather… limited ‘fleet’ of solutions, doesn’t it? We need options. What about a specialised adhesive? Some kind of polymer reinforcing spray?      Adhesive’s good, but durability might be an issue. Cable ties are… inexpensive. We could get a pack of a hundred for under a fiver. Testing material cost is a big factor, you know. This might actually be a viable little sideline.      A sideline. That’s what you said about the birdhouse business. And the knitted tea cosies. And the… Actually, never mind. Okay, cable ties. How would we market this? “Margaret and Arthur’s String Savers - Guaranteed to withstand even the most ferocious smash!”?      We  could , but no. More professional. “String Shield: Proactive Badminton Racket String Reinforcement.”

Now, that one… that's a bit much, innit? All those… swirls. Feels like lookin’ into a washing machine on full spin.      Oh, Arthur, you say that about most modern art. You preferred landscapes with cows, didn't you? Lovely, predictable cows.      Predictable is good, Doris! At least you  knew  what you were lookin’ at. A cow. A field. A bit o’ sky. None of this… abstract nonsense. What’s the point, eh?      It’s not about  point , Grandad. It's about evoking a feeling, or exploring a concept. It’s about the artist’s internal landscape, rather than replicating what’s externally visible.      Internal landscape? Sounds a bit pretentious, don’t it? Back in my day, a landscape was what you saw from the window!      But think about Impressionism, Arthur. Monet didn’t try to paint exactly what he  saw  – he tried to capture the  impression  of light and colour. That was a huge shift in how people thought about art. It wasn’t about perfect representation anymore.      Impressionism… yes, I ‘spect I’ve heard of that. All blurry, wasn’t it? Like someone needed their glasses.      You and your glasses, Arthur! Everything’s blurry to you if it’s not black and white on the telly.      It’s a stepping stone to these more abstract pieces, really. Think about Kandinsky, or Malevich. They were stripping art down to its most fundamental elements – colour, shape, line. They weren't trying to  show  something, they were trying to  feel  something and translate that onto the canvas.      And it's not just about feeling. A lot of abstract art is a response to the world around them. Malevich's ‘Black Square’ for instance, was a reaction against traditional artistic values, a rejection of representation after the turmoil of WWI. It's a statement.      A statement? What's it statin’? "I can't paint a decent picture?"      Not quite! It's stating a belief that art can exist independent of depicting the physical world. It's about pure artistic expression. It's not necessarily  easy  to understand, and it’s okay to not  like  it, but there’s usually a lot more going on than meets the eye.      I think sometimes the problem is people expect art to be…pleasant. To look nice over the fireplace. But art isn’t always about being pleasant, Arthur. It can be challenging, unsettling, even shocking.      Shockin’?!

...Honestly, the audacity of Chloe to turn up  late  to pre-drinks, then complain she was tired. Like, girl, you chose the chaotic energy of a Friday night! It’s just… exhausting being around people like that.      Tell me about it. My shift today was 90% managing someone else's emotional fallout because they couldn’t handle a slightly critical comment from their mum. Honestly, adults. It’s draining. It's like everyone's perpetually stuck in secondary school drama.      Ugh, mums are the worst sometimes, aren’t they? My own was texting me about needing help with her printer at 8pm. Like, can it wait until tomorrow? I’m trying to relax! It's infuriating. And then she’ll say I never call. You can’t win.      Absolutely. It's a no-win situation. Though, dealing with heightened emotions all day does give me an… appreciation for the sheer illogicality of human behaviour. Like, the way people  construct  arguments. It’s fascinating and frustrating.      Speaking of illogical, have you noticed how much the English language is just… falling apart? “Impactful” as a verb? Seriously? My boss used it in a meeting today. I almost choked on my coffee.      Oh god, don't even get me started. “Utilise” instead of “use”. It’s pretentious nonsense! It's like people are trying to sound clever by using unnecessarily complicated words. It makes my brain hurt. I have patients trying to articulate their feelings, and I'm having to filter out the jargon they’ve picked up from…where  do  they even hear this stuff?      Social media, probably. And influencers. Everything’s “vibes” and “literally” now. Literally everything is literally something. It’s exhausting. Right, I’m officially procrastinating cleaning by bitching about the state of the world.      A very valid distraction technique. To be fair, this place  is  looking a bit… lived-in. We promised we’d do a proper clean this weekend.      I know, I know. I just… I'd rather scrub toilets than look at another spreadsheet. Work was relentless this week. That new project is a total mess. Everything’s constantly changing, and no one seems to actually  know  what they’re doing. I'm basically herding cats.      Sounds familiar. My unit is short-staffed  again . So, already stretched thin, with added pressure, and then a manager breathing down your neck asking why patient progress isn't… faster.

Honestly, this day has just  vanished . One minute it was 7am, the next it's nearly nine and I’ve barely had a moment to breathe. Mr. Henderson wanted that report re-formatted three times, then asked for a completely different set of data to be included. It’s exhausting.      Sounds like a typical Tuesday with the Henderson machine. He’s brilliant at the big picture stuff, isn’t he? Absolutely hopeless at the detail. That’s where you come in, saving the day, as always. Did you at least manage a decent coffee break?      A snatched ten minutes, fuelled by lukewarm instant. Luxury! It got me thinking, though… he’s incredibly  intelligent , you know? Proper brain box. But sometimes I wonder if he has a shred of common sense. It's like, the higher the IQ, the lower the ability to just… function normally.      That’s a good point. I see it with some of my clients, actually. All the certifications in the world, can design and build the most complex systems, but ask them where the nearest petrol station is and they’re lost. It’s not the same as being  wise , is it? Common sense is just… accumulated life experience, I suppose. Knowing what usually happens if you do something stupid.      Exactly! It’s knowing not to touch a hot stove, not calculating the thermal conductivity of iron. Though, knowing you, you likely  would  calculate it.      Don’t tempt me. Old habits, you know? Speaking of habits… I had a cigarette with Dave at lunch. Don't look at me like that!      Oh, here we go. One cigarette. That's always how it starts. After all the promises, the patches, the gnashing of teeth...      It was just  one . And stressful, alright? Old mate Dave is going through a divorce. Needed a distraction. And frankly, I needed a distraction from thinking about Henderson’s endless email chain. It’s not like I’m back on a pack a day.      No, but it does make me worry. You know the impact it had on your dad. It's a slippery slope. And honestly, sometimes I think you use stress as an excuse.      That’s harsh, Sarah. Look, I'm aware of the risks. I just… sometimes I need something. It’s the same with a glass of wine in the evening, isn't it? You and your Pinot Grigio.

Right, who wants pasta shapes? I’m thinking dinosaurs, because, well, everyone loves a dinosaur. And after the escapades at the farm today, maybe we all  feel  a bit prehistoric.      Dinosaurs! Yes, please! But can I have the green ones? Those are the Brachiosaurus, and they’re the biggest.      I want the red ones! Those are the T-Rex! They bite!  Roar!       Careful now, soldier. No biting at the dinner table. Honestly, you two were  full  of energy at Farmer Giles’ today. More energy than the actual sheep, I think. Especially you, Leo.      But the piglets were  so  cute! And they were squeaking! I wanted to pick one up.      I know, darling, they were. But Farmer Giles said they were a bit sensitive, and we need to be gentle with animals. You were a little…enthusiastic. Mrs. Peterson sent me an email about your "enthusiasm" in class today too, actually.      Oh.      What did Leo do?      Apparently, he was demonstrating how a dinosaur would chase a… well, a classmate. A very loud, dramatic chase, involving a lot of roaring and flapping.      But I  was  a dinosaur! And Ethan was running away! It was fun!      I’m sure it was fun for  you , Leo. But it scared Ethan, and it disrupts the learning for everyone else. We need to keep our roaring for farm visits, okay? And maybe limit the flapping.      I was really good at the farm. I helped feed the chickens.      You were brilliant, Lily-Rose. A very responsible chicken feeder. And you even remembered to wash your hands afterwards, which is a massive win. How was school for you today, sweetheart?      Okay. We did painting. I painted a rainbow. But Thomas splashed paint on my picture.      Oh, dear. That’s not very kind of Thomas. Did you tell your teacher?      Yes, Miss Davies cleaned it up. It still looked a bit…smudgy.      Well, even smudgy rainbows are beautiful. Right, pasta’s almost ready. We can watch a DVD after dinner. What do you fancy? Something with dinosaurs, maybe? Although, after today, I think I might need a nice, calming nature documentary.      Can we watch ‘Land Before Time’? The one with the Littlefoot? He’s a Longneck, just like the Brachiosaurus!      ‘Land Before Time’ it is, then. Though you might have to promise to behave like Littlefoot – friendly and helpful – and  not  like a rampaging T-Rex.      I think we should watch ‘Finding Nemo’.

…and honestly, the whole thing with that actor, you know, the one from  Bridgerton ? It's just… ridiculous. Apparently, he's taken up competitive knitting. Proper, judged knitting.      Luke Newton? No way! That's… unexpected. Though, I suppose it's a good way to unwind from all the screaming fans and whatnot. Better than, I don’t know, competitive ferret legging.      Don’t even  say  that. Ferret legging sounds horrific. But knitting? I mean, I've been stuck into this fair isle jumper for ages – it’s proving a proper headache, actually. The colour changes are killing me. It's nothing like his little scarves he showed on that talk show.      Right, the chunky scarves. He made it look so… effortless. Though knowing how much time these things take, 'effortless' is probably a generous description. Is it for someone special, the jumper?      It  was  for me, originally. But honestly, looking at it… it might end up being a very expensive cat blanket. I started it before the Olympics hype kicked off, thinking I’d have loads of downtime. Turns out, managing the data from that new study is more all-consuming than I anticipated.      Tell me about it. I thought being a PhD student meant lots of contemplative reading and pondering the mysteries of the universe. It’s mostly just… hours of staring at spreadsheets and trying to convince software to cooperate. Thinking about the Olympics feels like a proper escape, though. Did you see that incredible gymnastics routine last night?      Oh, the Romanian one? Stunning. Absolutely stunning. Makes my hands cramping over a dropped stitch seem… trivial, to say the least. It's just amazing what the human body can do. Brings a bit of joy to everything, doesn’t it? Especially after… well, after last Easter.      Yeah. That was… rough. Least said about Auntie Brenda’s ‘performance art’ interpretation of the Easter story involving a papier-mâché lamb and a smoke machine, the better.      She honestly thought she was bringing a new dimension to the resurrection. Mum was mortified. I’m still finding glitter in the flowerbeds. Are we doing anything… less avant-garde this Easter? Maybe just a nice walk?      Definitely less avant-garde. I was thinking we could go to that new exhibition at the Fitzwilliam. The pre-Raphaelites? I know you’re a fan.      Oh, brilliant! That sounds perfect. All that glorious detail, the colours... considerably more inspiring than a tangled ball of yarn, I imagine.

Right, love, so we’ve got the tube map here… Honestly, London transport is a nightmare even  with  a map. I still reckon getting across town feels like navigating a plate of spaghetti. You sure you're up for all that walking though, Arthur? Your knee's been giving you gyp lately.      Oh, don’t you worry your head about my knee, Margaret. It’s a bit creaky, alright, but nothing a bit of strong tea and a good sit-down afterwards won’t fix. Besides, I’m determined to see that Egyptian exhibit at the British Museum. Been wanting to go for months. And  you  wanted to go to the Science Museum, didn't you?      I did, aye. But I was thinking… we could do both, yeah? But it’s a fair distance between ‘em. Or… maybe we pick one, and then fancy going to see that new IMAX film? The one about the deep sea creatures? I read a review, said it was absolutely stunning in 3D.      IMAX, eh? Now  that  sounds good. Though I remember last time we went to one of those 3D showings, I nearly lost my lunch. Everything felt… wobbly.      Oh, you and your sensitive stomach! That was that space one, wasn’t it? Too many spinning planets, I reckon. This one’s underwater, gentle movements, supposedly. Anyway, the British Museum is free, eh? The IMAX is a bit of a splurge, but if we skip one of the museums, that balances it out. What do you reckon?      Hmm, a fair point. And free is always good. Though honestly, I’m a bit fed up with the crowds at the British Museum these days. Packed solid, it always is. Makes it difficult to actually  see  anything, let alone enjoy it.      You’re not wrong there. It’s always teeming with tourists. Though I do love the Rosetta Stone. Always fascinated me, that. Still, maybe we go early? Get there for when it opens? Beat the rush a bit?      That’s a thought. Though getting up early on a Sunday... now  that's  a sacrifice! Still, better than being elbowed in the ribs by a school trip. What about getting the tube to Russell Square for the museum, then a bus towards the South Bank for the IMAX? It’d break up the walking a bit.      Russell Square sounds good. And a bus is definitely preferable to trying to change lines a dozen times.

…and honestly, the student who asked if Dickens was still alive? You couldn’t make it up. It’s been a  long  semester, hasn't it?      Tell me about it. I had one genuinely ask me if Confucius invented the internet. Confucius! I almost choked on my water. Though, to be fair, they were all very enthusiastic. Just…lacking a tiny bit of historical context. So, Christmas. Are we still on for the usual debacle at my place?      Debacle is a strong word, old boy. It’s  festive chaos . And absolutely. Unless you’ve had a sudden aversion to my Aunt Mildred’s questionable Brussel sprout creations?      Questionable is…a diplomatic assessment. But no, I’m bracing myself. It wouldn’t be Christmas without them looming, would it? And honestly, it’s good to have a bit of ‘home’ while we’re three thousand miles away from the real thing. Have you managed to get hold of everyone? Any updates from back in Blighty?      Yeah, spoke to Mum last week. She's already started knitting everyone hideous Christmas jumpers. Said she’s attempted one for little Mei’s cat. Apparently, it didn’t go well. The cat was…unimpressed. Your side of the family?      Oh, my sister’s threatening a full-blown Christmas themed light show this year. Apparently, she’s been watching  Christmas Vacation  on repeat and taken it as a personal challenge. And Dad’s already started stocking up on sherry. It’ll be a typical Mancunian Christmas at their place – loud, bright, and involving a lot of questionable dance moves.      Sounds…thorough. Speaking of movies though, have you seen that new one,  Argylle ? Been getting a lot of buzz.      No, not yet. I’ve been meaning to, but between marking and prepping lectures, my evenings have been rather consumed. Is it any good? Worth venturing out into the frankly terrifying Beijing traffic for?      It’s…a lot. Very stylised, very meta. Think spy pastiche with a healthy dose of absurdity. It's definitely not subtle. You'll either love it or hate it, I suspect. It reminded me a bit of those old Austin Powers flicks, actually.      Hmm. Maybe. I'm more in the mood for something comforting this time of year. Perhaps another re-watch of  Love Actually . So predictable, but it always makes me feel a bit Christmassy.      Don't tell anyone, but I secretly love  Love Actually  too.

Right, I’m officially logging off for the night. Twitter’s just… a void tonight, innit? Endless scrolling, endless outrage. Needed to tell someone before I completely succumb to sleep deprivation.      Tell me about it. I was attempting to look at cake decorating ideas, ended up down a rabbit hole of people arguing about sourdough starters. Honestly. It’s exhausting. My brain feels properly fried from dealing with customers all day, I don’t need that on top.      Oh, customers. Don’t even  start  me. I had a woman today who genuinely tried to argue that a full English breakfast should be £3.99. Like, seriously? And then when I politely explained the rising costs of… everything, she wrote a one-star review saying “rude staff, overpriced breakfast.”      Blimey. That’s harsh. Online reviews are the worst. You can spend years building something, and one disgruntled person can just… wreck it. I saw a restaurant in Margate got absolutely savaged recently, despite everyone saying the food was brilliant. Apparently, the chairs were ‘uncomfortable’.      Oh Margate's interesting isn't it? Such a vibe. I was thinking about a little pop-up bakery there next summer. Just for a few weeks, see how it goes. I've been sketching some ideas for the shopfront, all pastel colours and… I dunno, a bit Wes Anderson.      Ooh, that sounds lovely, Liv! You’d be perfect for Margate. It's all that quirky, vintage stuff. It would do  brilliantly . But online reviews would still be a pain, even there. People just want something to complain about.      It’s true. It's like they think they’re professional food critics or interior designers suddenly. I was reading this thread about cafe design, and everyone had  opinions  on everything, from the lighting to the placement of the sugar.      It’s always the sugar, isn't it? Apparently, if it's not in individual packets, you're automatically a monster. I swear. But yeah, Margate... I'm just feeling a bit stuck here, you know? Everything in London feels so… saturated. And expensive. Plus, the rent. Don't even get me started.      I get that. Sometimes you need a change of scenery. I’ve been thinking about doing a little revamp of the cafe, actually. Nothing major, just… freshen it up. Maybe some new artwork. I’m terrible at design though, honestly. It all feels a bit overwhelming.

Honestly, this is lovely, Sarah. You really  do  make the best tomato sauce. Though, Oisin is treating his like it’s some sort of archaeological dig, painstakingly separating the pasta from everything else.      It's… red. And slippery.      He's a connoisseur, Mum. A very discerning one. At least he's eating  something . I swear, getting him to eat anything green is like pulling teeth.      You get that from your father, you know. He used to hide his peas under his napkin. It's a genetic trait, I'm convinced. Speaking of genetic traits, have you seen the bird's nest in the apple tree? It's huge! I think there are eggs, but I haven't dared get close enough to look.      Oh, really? That’s wonderful! We must try and spot what kind of bird it is. Though, with your fear of anything flapping, I'm not sure  you  getting close is a good idea, darling.      It's not a fear, it's a healthy respect! They swoop! And the noise... Anyway, it's nice to think something's nesting and thriving, isn't it? Especially after that disaster with the gerbils last year. Remember?      Please don’t remind me. The Great Gerbil Escape of ‘23. That was chaos. They got  everywhere . Behind the sofa, under the fridge… even in your shoes, Mum!      They were surprisingly agile little things. Though, not so agile at avoiding being stepped on, thankfully. Honestly, I thought I’d found one nesting in a bag of pasta once! It was a rogue pea.      Did the pea have babies?      No, sweetie, peas don’t have babies like gerbils do. They grow from seeds. We can talk about it when we’re in the garden tomorrow, maybe after we pick some raspberries? I think they're starting to ripen.      Raspberries sound good. Anything’s better than revising for this history exam on Thursday. It’s all dates and kings and battles. Utterly pointless.      Now, now, history is  not  pointless. It helps us understand the present. And helps you pass your GCSEs, which is a rather important thing, wouldn’t you say?      He’s right, you know. It's all a bit dry, though. Speaking of which, I was thinking, once the exam’s over, we could all go for a bike ride down by the coast. And  then  ice cream. Lots and lots of ice cream.

…and honestly, the state of my eyebrows is a disgrace. I really need to book an appointment with Brenda. It’s just… finding the time, you know? Work is relentless at the moment with the Johnson account, and then trying to juggle everything else…      Oh, Brenda’s good, isn't she? Does a proper job. You look frazzled, love. You’re working yourself into the ground. I always say, a tidy brow makes all the difference. Makes you look more awake, at least! I had mine done last week. Felt right as rain afterwards.      Awake? You always look bright as a button, dear. Though I agree about Brenda, she’s a clever girl. Reminds me of my sister, always had a good eye for detail. Though my sister was more into arranging flowers than eyebrows, mind you.      It's the Johnson account, Mum. They're demanding. Constant changes, wanting things done yesterday, and frankly, their spreadsheets are a nightmare. Still, it pays the bills. Speaking of which, I need to do a food shop. I’m aiming for Saturday morning. Want to come along, Carol? We could grab a coffee afterwards?      Saturday’s good. I’m free. I’ve finished at Mrs. Higgins’ by then. Though honestly, the amount of dust in that house… it’s criminal! She’s a lovely woman, but she just doesn’t  see  it. And she still tries to offer me a cigarette! Honestly, after all these years…      Oh, don't I know it! Old habits die hard. Your father, bless his soul, tried to quit twenty times. Ended up sneaking them in the shed! He said the smell of the tobacco reminded him of his dad. Sentimental, he was.      That's… something. Right, no smoking discussion, please. It’s a trigger for everyone! Anyway, Mum, are you managing alright? You haven't been out much lately and I worry.      Oh, I’m fine, darling. Just taking it easy. My knees aren't what they used to be, you know. And the telly's got everything you need these days! Though I did fancy a nice meal out. Haven't been to The White Hart in ages.      Oh, The White Hart! They do a lovely roast. And their sticky toffee pudding is to die for. Actually, I went there with Derek a few months back. He… he insisted on having a smoke outside, even though they’ve got that little smoking shelter now.

Honestly, this is bliss. Just…quiet. Apart from the occasional gurgle, of course. He’s such a good baby, isn’t he? Even with the weaning drama.      He  is  a good baby. And the weaning drama is…developing, shall we say? He’s decided pureed carrot is an affront to his dignity. Which, frankly, coming from someone who used to happily gum on his own feet, is a bit rich.      Oh, they’re little divas, aren’t they? It’s all about control at this age. I remember with you, it was the sweet potato you refused. Absolutely  refused . We ended up hiding it in everything for weeks.      You hid vegetables in my food? I thought Mum was the sneaky one!      Your Mum and I were a team! A strategic alliance against vegetable aversion. It worked eventually. Anyway, how did the sign language class go last night? Did you pick up anything new?      It was good, actually. Really positive. We learned ‘milk’ and ‘more’. Which is…insanely useful, considering. He already seems to  understand  ‘milk’ when I sign it, even if he can’t reciprocate yet. It’s just…amazing, seeing how quickly they pick things up.      It  is  amazing. I remember reading about it, and thinking it sounded a bit…faddy. But then seeing how well it worked for Sarah’s little boy, I was completely converted. Does it feel natural to you, though? I worry I’d look utterly ridiculous.      Honestly? A little silly at first. Flapping your hands around like a demented bird. But you get used to it. And the teacher's brilliant – she's really good at making it feel approachable. Plus, it feels…empowering for him, even before he can sign back. Like you’re giving him a voice before he has words.      That’s a lovely way to put it. Maybe I should look into it. Although, my schedule is a nightmare this week. I’ve promised to help Dad with the garden, and then there's Carol's birthday on Wednesday.      Oh, is it Carol’s birthday? What are you getting her?      I’m still deciding! She’s so hard to buy for. She's got everything. I was thinking maybe a voucher for that spa she likes? Or perhaps a nice bottle of wine.      The spa sounds good. She deserves a bit of pampering. Are you all going out for the evening?

Honestly, it’s just… different, isn’t it? Coming from London, even just for a weekend, you forget how  flat  everything is there. It’s all straight lines and buildings. Here… it's gentle. Even these little rises feel like mountains. Mountains might be pushing it, love. But you’re right. It's a subtle landscape. London just assaults you with its scale. Norfolk… well, it whispers. It takes a bit to notice the nuances. I grew up with it, so I probably took it for granted for years. That's what I mean! It’s a deceptively beautiful place. When I first told my mum I was moving here to teach, she was…underwhelmed, shall we say? She pictured endless fields of cabbages. Oh, mums. Always practical. Though, to be fair, there  are  a lot of cabbages. And turnips! It’s farming country, after all. Still, it’s more than that. Look at those trees lining the field, the way they’re all leaning slightly… that’s the wind, you know? Constantly shaping everything. I’ve noticed. It’s almost… sculptural. I’ve been trying to explain it to my students. They’re mostly city kids, haven't really  seen  a proper landscape. They think a hill is something you find in a park. They’d probably be shocked to hear Norfolk folk arguing over whether something is  actually  a hill. It's rather subjective around here. Anything over fifty feet above sea level is considered a significant elevation, apparently. Fifty feet? That’s… barely noticeable! We were walking up Primrose Hill last week, and that's probably more than fifty feet! Different perspectives, I suppose. It’s all relative. And the villages… they’re so distinct. Each one feels like it’s grown organically, rather than being planned. See that one in the distance, with the church spire? That’s Burnham Market. It's become quite…  posh  in recent years. Oh, I’ve driven through there. It’s full of Range Rovers and weekenders. A bit too much for my liking, honestly. I prefer the ones that feel a bit… lost in time. Like Creake Abbey. That was lovely. Creake Abbey is special. They do a good farmer's market there, too. It’s one of those places where you can get genuinely local produce, not just stuff shipped in from somewhere else. My grandmother used to take me there when I was a kid.

...Honestly, the sheer  audacity  of some cyclists, ya know? Just sailing through red lights like they own the place. Saw one nearly get flattened by a bus on the High Street yesterday. Gave me a right fright.      You and your cyclists, Liv. It’s a perpetual battle for you, isn’t it? I think they just get so used to zipping through gaps, they forget everyone else is operating on slightly different rules.      It's not just that! It’s the attitude. Like we’re inconveniencing  them  by being in a two-tonne vehicle. And then they get all huffy if you give them a little beep.      Okay, okay, I get it. You've had a near-miss trauma. Though, to be fair, some drivers aren’t exactly considerate either. Remember old Mr. Henderson trying to overtake a tractor on that bend near the village?      Oh, don’t even  start  on Mr. Henderson! That was another level of reckless. Anyway, speaking of stressful jobs… how's Ben taking the new role at the council? He seemed a bit… overwhelmed when I spoke to him last week.      He is. It’s a massive step up, going from working on individual projects to managing a whole team and dealing with planning permission nightmares. He’s already aged ten years, I swear. He's constantly on calls, even at dinner. It’s a shame, really. We haven’t had a proper catch-up in weeks.      That sounds rough. He always seemed so good at the detail, the actual  doing  of things. I can imagine the politics of it all would be draining. Does he have a good support network there?      He’s got Sarah, one of the senior planners, who’s being really supportive. She used to be in his position, so she gets it. But he’s also a bit of a perfectionist, you know? He’s trying to fix everything at once and it’s just… unsustainable.      Classic Ben. Always trying to save the world. He'll burn out if he’s not careful. Maybe suggest a proper holiday? Somewhere with no signal.      I’ve tried. He just laughs and says he’d be thinking about work even on a beach in the Maldives. Changing the subject slightly – did you see that new Wes Anderson film?  Asteroid City ?      Oh, aye! I went last week with Maya. Visually stunning, as always, but… I don’t know.

Honestly, it's  gorgeous , isn’t it? That brilliant yellow. Though, I always feel a little bit guilty enjoying it, knowing it’s basically a giant cash crop.      It  is  stunning. Like a sea of sunshine. And you’re right to feel a bit conflicted. It’s a beautiful sight powered by… well, the economics of cooking oil and animal feed. It’s amazing how much of our landscape is shaped by demand, isn't it? My research touched on agricultural subsidies a while back, really opened my eyes.      It’s funny, isn’t it? You spend your life studying language – the seemingly intangible, the beautifully abstract – and then you come out here and  everything  is about practicality. Money. Yield. The best time to sow. It's grounding, I suppose. Though I prefer to just appreciate the colour! Do you know what those little purple flowers are over there? The ones dotted amongst the grass?      Orchids, I think. Common spotted orchids. They like the undisturbed grassland. Good sign for biodiversity, even in a farmed landscape. You're the botanist of the two of us, though. Pretty sure I'd just wander past them cheerfully unrecognising.      Hardly a botanist! Just… observant. And my grandmother had a phenomenal garden. She instilled a love of knowing what things  are . It feels important. More important, sometimes, than knowing the intricacies of post-structuralism, let’s be honest.      Don't let your colleagues hear you say that! They'd have your hide. Though, I do get it. All that theory can feel…distant. Speaking of important things, how’s the research grant application going? Still wrestling with the methodology section?      Oh, don’t even. It’s a beast. They want me to somehow quantify the impact of dialectal variation on children’s reading comprehension. Like I can reduce something so fluid and culturally embedded to a series of data points. I keep getting stuck on the ethics of it all, frankly. Are we just reinforcing societal biases by trying to 'correct' for differences?      That’s a really good point. It sounds like they’re asking you to prove something that’s inherently...not provable in that way. Have you pushed back at all? They’re usually pretty receptive to feedback.      I’ve hinted. Subtly. Being academic, you know. It’s hard not to sound like a complete troublemaker. Though honestly, I'm tempted to include a section on the inherent limitations of applying quantitative methods to qualitative phenomena.

...Honestly, the parking situation near the tennis club is mental. I spent twenty minutes circling yesterday, and ended up half a mile away and practically sprinting to get there on time for Sarah's match. It's worse than trying to find a space at the Metro Centre on a Saturday.      Right? Absolutely bonkers. You'd think for a place that  hosts  events, they’d have sorted the parking out properly. Is it just the club itself, or the whole area around it? I used to get stuck trying to visit Mum when she lived near there.      The whole area really. Loads of new flats are going up, see, and everyone’s got a car. They haven’t built enough spaces to cope. It's just a free-for-all. It reminded me a bit of trying to park near the Angel of the North on a busy day, just… less dramatic. Though at least with the Angel, you kinda  want  to be there, risking a parking ticket.      Haha, true! You wouldn’t be heading to the Angel specifically to battle for a space. Speaking of flats, have you had any luck looking around? You said you were thinking of moving closer to work?      A little. It’s a nightmare, isn’t it? Everything’s either tiny, overpriced, or both. I saw one in Heaton, looked decent online, but when I went to view it, it was like a shoebox. And the estate agent kept going on about “cosy” which is just a polite way of saying “you can touch both walls at once.”      'Cosy' is estate agent code for 'bring a hard hat.' I’ve had similar experiences. They try to sell you on the 'vibrant community' whilst conveniently overlooking the fact it’s next to a dual carriageway. Still, it’s a good shout to look in Heaton, isn't it? Easy enough for you to get into town.      Aye, it is. It’s just…finding something  nice . And affordable. You and Amelia found a good place, didn't you? That flat near Harpenden Common?      We did. Bit of luck, to be honest. Someone pulled out last minute. It's a bit further out than we initially wanted, but with the train link, I can get into London pretty easily. Although, talking of getting places easily... how’s the new car treating you? Honestly, it's a lovely bit of kit.

Honestly, it’s just… bizarre, isn’t it? The whole thing with that actor. Accusations flying left, right and centre. You’d think with all the money and advisors they have, they'd be more careful.      You mean the one on the telly? The one with the posh voice? It  is  a bit of a mess, innit. Seems like they all get into trouble eventually, don't they?
