Moving down here to Gloucestershire in '68 felt like another planet. Everything was so different from Ramsgate. We rented for years, of course. Buying wasn't even on the cards. Mortgage rates were astronomical.      Different planet is right. Coming from Manchester, everything  south  of Birmingham felt… refined. And expensive! I was offered a lectureship at the university, and frankly, finding a place was a nightmare. The university accommodation was dreadful – tiny rooms, shared bathrooms… I ended up in a converted Victorian house share with a bunch of art students. It was... lively.      Art students, eh? Sounds colourful. I was interviewed for this practice in, oh, '65 it was. Drove down from Birmingham. Lovely drive, even then, but I remember thinking, "Good Lord, this is a long way from my mum!" Got the job, thankfully, but then the real panic began – finding somewhere to live. That house I mentioned… it was on the Hagley Road.      Hagley Road? That’s changed a lot! Used to be quite leafy, wasn’t it? Though, everything’s changed, hasn’t it? When I came for my interview at the school, it was a bit of a trek. The school was up on a hill and I arrived absolutely drenched. Didn’t make the best impression, I can tell you. Though, they still offered me the job! They must have been desperate.      Desperate times! I remember when we started looking, estate agents were… different. Not like now, with glossy brochures and web portals. It was a little advert in the local paper and hoping for the best. And the condition of some places! They’d just slapped on some wallpaper and hoped you wouldn't notice the structural issues.

…and honestly, the porcelain dolls were the bane of my existence for a good ten years. People  adore  them, you know? Collect them. But dusting them? Utterly fiddly. And the price they fetch isn’t always worth the effort, especially the really delicate ones. Though, a good Meissen… now  that’s  worth something.      Oh, I can imagine! The detail on those things is incredible. You must have seen some beautiful pieces over the years running the gallery. It sounds a fascinating… and rather demanding… life. I always admired people who had that entrepreneurial spirit. I was far too cautious, I think.      Demanding is putting it mildly, dear. It wasn't so much the work, though there was plenty of that. It was the people! Trying to judge what they  really  wanted versus what they  thought  they wanted. And the haggling! Lord, the haggling. Still, it kept the brain ticking, didn't it? What about you? A speech therapist… that must have been profoundly rewarding.      It was. Truly. It wasn’t always easy, of course. Some cases were heartbreaking. Children struggling to find their voice, adults recovering from strokes… it takes a lot of patience. I specialised in working with children with cleft palates, mostly. It's amazing, the progress they can make with the right support. And it's a privilege to be a part of it. Though, I wouldn’t say I was entrepreneurial. I worked for the NHS for most of my career. Safe and steady.      Safe and steady has its merits, that’s for certain. I always felt a bit… at sea, without something to build. My father, he was a farmer, stubborn as an old mule. Expected me to marry a farmer, naturally. But I had other ideas. Always loved to draw, even as a little thing. Spent hours down by the River Tone sketching.      The River Tone! That’s lovely. I spent a lot of my childhood by the water too, though it was the Pacific Ocean, back in Sydney. It's… strange, isn't it? Growing up so far away. My parents emigrated when I was very young, just after the war. They thought Australia would be a better life.      Australia! Oh, my. That  is  a long way. Always pictured it filled with sunshine and kangaroos. Was it a big adjustment for them?      A massive one, I think. Mum especially missed her family terribly. Dad was more pragmatic, focused on building a new life.

Right, okay, so I think we're good on the garlic. Honestly, this smells amazing already. Though, honestly, I'm still slightly traumatised by Aunt Carol’s attempt at Christmas dinner last year. Seriously, rock solid sprouts.      Oh god, don't even  mention  Aunt Carol’s sprouts. They were a biohazard. It's a miracle nobody lost a tooth. Speaking of miracles, this dough is behaving itself, which is a minor victory. How’s your arm doing, by the way? Still a bit sore from the… artistic endeavour?      Yeah, a bit. It twinges. It wasn't  that  bad, though. Worth it. You should’ve seen Leo’s face when I showed him. He was proper gobsmacked. He kept saying it looked 'sick'. Which, I think, is a good thing.      'Sick' is  definitely  a good thing coming from Leo. So, the phoenix is complete? Is it fully coloured? Bit brave getting something like that on your forearm, innit?      Fully coloured, yeah. Took six hours. It's... ambitious. But I'm buzzing with it. Reminds me of uni, that feeling of just… going for it. Anyway, enough about my questionable life choices. What are we having  with  this amazing smelling pasta? Are we doing the fancy cheese thing again?      Fancy cheese is always a good idea. And I've got some of those little candied orange peels I made earlier, that’d be rather lovely sprinkled on top. Sort of festive, doesn't it feel autumn-wintery even though it's only October?      Candied orange peel? You're spoiling me. And yeah, it does. Speaking of festive, have you even  started  thinking about Christmas? I'm already stressing. I need to book the train tickets and… everything.      Please don’t even bring up Christmas. It's a logistical nightmare. My nan already wants to know what I want for Christmas and it's barely Halloween. And the bakery is going to be insane. I swear, pumpkin spice everything until January.           Alright, you two! Smells heavenly in here. What culinary magic are you concocting? And don’t tell me you started discussing Christmas already. I refuse.      Hey, Chloe! We were just lamenting the impending doom of December. And slightly gloating about my new tattoo.      Ooh, a tattoo! Let me see! Wow, that  is  impressive! A phoenix? Bold choice. Right, Christmas, though. Look, I’m already planning the café's Christmas menu. Gingerbread lattes are a must, obviously.

Right, Cambridge is properly in the rearview mirror now, eh? Feels…weirdly quiet already. Like a bubble burst.      It always does, doesn’t it? That place has a way of absorbing you. Such a strange, beautiful little world. You’ll miss the punting, I suspect. Though, perhaps not the early morning supervisions.      The punting, maybe. The supervisions… less so. Honestly, Mum, being able to sleep past seven without feeling guilty is a genuine luxury. How much further you reckon? Traffic looks… optimistic, shall we say.      Optimistic is putting it kindly. Probably an hour, maybe more. Depends on what happens near Junction 15. Speaking of luxuries, have you given any more thought to what you're doing after you hand in the thesis? Still thinking about that research fellowship?      Yeah, the fellowship’s still the plan. Applied to a couple at Oxford, actually. Bit cheeky, going across the divide, isn’t it? After three years staunchly defending Cambridge’s honour.      Oh, don't be ridiculous. A good researcher follows the opportunity, not a flag. Besides, a little healthy rivalry never hurt anyone. Though your Grandad would be spinning in his grave. Cambridge through and through, he was. What’s the thesis looking like, by the way? Still on track for a December submission?      Mostly. Just… the final chapter’s being a right pain. It’s all converging, everything needs to  click , and it’s currently resolutely un-clicking. But yeah, December’s the goal. It's just... then what? That's the bit that’s starting to freak me out a bit.      Well, the fellowship if you get it, obviously. But even if you don't, it's not the end of the world. You’ve got options, Tom. You’re a bright lad. What about…living arrangements? Are you still thinking of staying with Aunt Carol and Uncle David for a bit while you figure things out?      That was the idea. They’ve offered the spare room, which is brilliant, honestly. But it feels…temporary, you know? And they're talking about downsizing, potentially moving out of London altogether. It's a lovely offer, but I don’t want to be a burden if they’re uprooting their lives.      They wouldn't see you as a burden, darling. But I understand. It’s sensible to think about alternatives. Have you considered… perhaps looking at flat shares? There are some quite nice areas, even within a reasonable commute to the university, that wouldn't break the bank.

...and honestly, the train was  packed . You’d think on an Alumni Day, they'd put on extra services, wouldn't you? Especially coming into Cambridge - it’s always busy, but today… chaos. I ended up standing all the way from Peterborough.      Oh, dreadful! I drove, actually. Thought it would be easier, preempting exactly that. Parking was a nightmare though, circling for about twenty minutes. Still, at least I wasn’t squashed like a sardine. Are you an alum yourself then? What did you study?      I am, yeah. Did my Masters here in Linguistics. Now I work as a research coordinator, mostly dealing with dialectal variations. It’s fascinating, really. You?      Similar! I'm a research administrator, also in the Linguistics department. Graduated a couple of years ago. It's good to be back, though. Feels…different. More grown-up, I suppose.      Grown-up, you say? Hmm. Cambridge has that effect. I've been affiliated with this faculty for… oh, goodness, too many years to count. Lecturer in History of Law, myself. And I’ve seen a lot of ‘grown-ups’ pass through these doors.      Oh, hello! Lovely to meet you. I’m Alice, and this is Chloe.      Hi! It's a pleasure.      Arthur. Retired now, mostly, but still dabble in a bit of guest lecturing. Fascinating to hear you both are still involved in linguistics. What sort of variations are you looking at, Alice?      At the moment, I’m coordinating a project looking at the impact of migration on accents in the southeast. We're focusing on areas around Aylesbury, actually – where I’m from originally. It's incredible how quickly things shift, how subtle pressures can create new pronunciations. It reminds me a bit of archaeological digs, in a weird way. Layering and change over time.      A rather apt analogy, my dear. I spent some years excavating a small village in Shropshire, near Oswestry, where I grew up. Incredible what you unearth. Not just artifacts, but the echoes of voices, the patterns of daily life. We found evidence of surprisingly sophisticated trade links with Arab culture – dating back to the 9th century, you understand. Completely upended our understanding of the period.      Wow, that’s incredible! I didn’t realise there was such a strong connection then. We did a brief module on historical linguistics that touched on Arabic influence on Iberian languages, but nothing like that domestically.      It's fascinating how languages travel and intermingle.

Right, so you’re  still  doing overnight bakes for that influencer, then, Liv? Honestly, the lengths people go to for a bit of online clout. Saw her latest video – a six-tiered rainbow cake, all for a ‘get ready with me’ backdrop. It’s… a lot.      Tell me about it, Leo! It’s exhausting. But it pays. And honestly, she’s not a bad client. A bit… demanding about the shade of lilac, but pays on time. It’s better than struggling, yeah? I mean, trying to make a living as a baker in London is  hard . Real hard.      You’re telling me. Running the café… it’s a constant hustle. Especially with the cost of, well,  everything  going up. I reckon half my profit just disappears on electricity bills. Seeing stuff like that cake Liv's talking about online just… feels a bit removed, doesn't it? Like another planet.      It is, isn’t it? That whole influencer economy… it’s fascinating, and a bit worrying. I was scouting locations for a new shoot today, talking to a couple of young guys who are hoping to make it as travel vloggers. They’ve basically put their lives on hold, just chasing views. It’s a pressure cooker.      Precisely! And it feels like everyone's expected to  have  a side hustle now, doesn't it? Like, having a 9-to-5 just isn't enough anymore. I'm doing research for my masters, which is… something. But even  that  feels like I should be monetising it somehow. Content creation, or whatever.      Don’t even get me started. My mum keeps asking when I'm going to "utilise my degree," whatever  that  means. I've got a perfectly good degree in history, but it doesn't exactly translate to… making sourdough. It’s a bit frustrating, isn’t it? Like all that education, and then you're just… scraping by.      My experience was a bit different. I left sixth form, couldn’t face uni, and just… started working. Best thing I ever did, honestly. I learned on the job, built something. But I do sometimes wonder what would've happened if I’d stuck it out. My brother did a law degree and he’s… miserable. Corporate lawyer, hates it.      It’s a weird one, isn’t it? The whole pressure to follow a certain path. My cousin, brilliant artist, always struggled with dyslexia.

Honestly, this week has been… a lot. Three essays to mark, a departmental meeting that achieved absolutely nothing, and now Mum’s decided she needs a full hip replacement.      Oh, Mum. Is she alright? I knew her knees were giving her trouble, but I didn’t realise it was  that  bad.      She’s putting on a brave face, of course. “Just a little wear and tear,” she said. But she admitted she’s struggling to get around the garden, which, as you know, is her life. And then she started talking about the waiting lists… it's terrifying. The NHS is just… strained beyond belief, isn’t it?      It is. It's a political hot potato, obviously, but it feels like nobody actually has a workable solution. Labour keeps talking about more funding, the Tories about efficiency… it’s all talk. It's horrifying to think what people are facing with healthcare. Especially with our generation starting to think about our  own  creaky bits.      Exactly! I'm starting to feel old just  listening  to her. And it makes you think about… well, everything. Private healthcare feels like a necessary evil, doesn’t it? But the cost! We’re relatively comfortable, thankfully, with both our jobs, but even so… it’s a huge chunk of change.      It is. We should probably revisit our policies, actually. I think we’re just on a basic one at the moment, covering the really catastrophic stuff. I meant to look into it last month, but then the university started that ridiculous restructure.      Oh, don’t even  start  me on the restructure. Another pointless exercise in bureaucracy, designed to make someone on the management board look busy. Honestly, they could have saved a fortune just asking the people who actually  do  the work what would make things better.      Precisely! It’s the same every time. They come up with these grand schemes, completely divorced from reality. And they wonder why morale is so low. Did you catch that documentary on Channel 4 about the decline of local news? It was depressing.      Briefly, I had it on in the background while marking. Something about shrinking budgets and reliance on agency reporters, wasn't it? It just feels like everything is crumbling around us. Quality journalism, the NHS, even just… reliable public services.      It's true. And it's not like Truss's mini-budget debacle didn't exacerbate things, did it?

...and honestly, the formatting on that manuscript was a disaster. Honestly, it looked like a toddler had been let loose with a text editor. I spent a good two hours just wrestling with the citations. It's amazing people with PhDs can't master Chicago style.      Oh, dear. Sounds frightfully stressful, love. Though, honestly, I always found the technicalities of academic writing a bit… dry. Give me a good Victorian novel any day. All that passion and drama! Though even  those  had their footnotes, didn’t they?      Speaking of dry, this chicken is lovely, ANON. Really lovely. You’ve outdone yourself. Reminds me of your mother's, actually. She always did a cracking roast.      It  is  good! You’ve always been a fantastic cook, ANON. And yes, PhDs don't automatically equal competence in everything! You'd be surprised. It's like they spend so long focusing on their specific niche they forget basic skills.      It's true, isn't it? Specialization. It has its merits, of course, but sometimes it seems to create people who are terribly blinkered. Do you remember old Mr. Hemmings from the English department? Brilliant Shakespearean scholar, utterly incapable of operating a video recorder.      Oh, Hemmings! Yes, I remember him. Tried to explain to him how to use the interactive whiteboard once. Nearly gave him a heart attack. Kept muttering about 'the devil's work'. It was quite a sight.      That’s hilarious! Things have changed so much, haven’t they? My little cousin, Leo, he’s seven, and he’s already building simple games on a tablet. It's astonishing. I remember being terrified of computers at his age! We had one at school, a massive beige thing, and we only used it for typing practice.      Typing practice! That’s all we did too. And learning LOGO. That little turtle… good heavens. Progress is relentless, isn’t it? Though, I confess, I still prefer a good book to scrolling through a screen. Something about the weight of it, the smell of the paper…      I'm with you there, Margaret. Give me a proper book any day. Although, I have to admit, I’ve been enjoying those nature documentaries on iPlayer. David Attenborough is a national treasure. Did you see the one about the Okavango Delta? Breathtaking.      Oh, the Okavango Delta one was incredible! The wildlife footage was stunning. They've got a new series on now, about fungi!

Right, dinner’s nearly ready. Liam, you’ve been awfully quiet over there. Still glued to that… whatever it is you’re playing on that device?      Uh-huh. It’s called ‘Aetherium Online’, Dad. It’s, like, a massively multiplayer online role-playing game. A MMORPG.      Oh, good grief, Finn! Carrots are for  eating , darling, not launching! Liam, honestly, how long have you been on that thing? You’ve been utterly absorbed since we got back from the park.      Aye, that’s what I was wonderin’. You barely said two words to Finn all afternoon, even when he was showin’ ye his amazing dinosaur roar.      It’s just…it’s a really important raid tonight, Dad. We’ve been planning it for ages. It's with my guild, The Crimson Hawks.      “The Crimson Hawks”? Sounds fierce. What are ye raidin’, a dragon or somethin’?      Sort of. It’s a corrupted AI construct, basically a super-powerful boss. We need a full team to take it down. It’s really strategic; you need to coordinate attacks, use different abilities…      Oh, you sound like your father explaining a server migration at work. “Strategic coordination, different abilities…” It’s just a game, love.      Now, now, Sarah. It’s good for him to have a hobby. Though a bit of fresh air never hurt anyone. Remember when  you  used to spend hours building miniature villages with your sister?      That’s different. That involved imagination and… glue. And didn’t require me to worry about eye strain. Though, honestly, Finn’s imagination is currently more destructive than constructive.      Hat!      I  did  go for a walk with you and Finn earlier, Mum. And I showed him the ducks.      That ye did, and he loved it. He kept pointin’ and yellin’ “Quack quack!” for a good ten minutes. But you were still checkin’ your phone every five minutes, weren’t ye?      Just checking guild chat. Important stuff.      Important stuff indeed. Look, Liam, it’s good you enjoy it, but it’s dinner time now. Phone down for a bit, alright? We want to hear about your week at school, not the intricate strategies of ‘Aetherium Online’.      Aye, and tell us what’s been happenin’ with yer mates. Any interestin’ news? Did ye finally convince old Mr. Henderson that your science project  wasn’t  a miniature nuclear reactor?      Okay, okay. You got me. And Mr. Henderson still thinks it  might  be.

...and honestly, the Year 9s are convinced that abstract art is just an excuse for not being able to  actually  draw anything. Little terrors, the lot of ‘em! Though, I did show them a Kandinsky, and one boy, bless him, said it looked like fireworks. Progress, I suppose.      Fireworks, eh? Right, that’s a good’un. Reminds me of old man Hemmings down the lane. Tried ‘is ‘and at painting once. Looked like a parrot ‘ad exploded in ‘is shed, it did. All colours and…well, not much else.      Oh, Arthur, you always have a story! It’s lovely to hear you laughing. Are we all set for Christmas dinner at Bethany’s, then? I’ve got the trifle ingredients, just need to assemble it tomorrow.      I’m really excited! Bethany’s new puppy is  so  cute. And she promised I could help with the decorations.      Yeah, me too! Though, the drive is a bit long, isn’t it? Especially with Dad driving. No offence, Mr. Thompson.      None taken, Lily. I’m aware I’m not exactly Lewis Hamilton. But I’ll take the scenic route, see if we can spot some horses. Always calms the nerves. Speaking of which, Bethany said something about her boyfriend, Ben, being there?      That's right, dear. Bethany's smitten. Apparently, he's very good with his hands – fixing things, building things. Good qualities for a young man. And he’s bringing a homemade gingerbread house!      Gingerbread, you say? Now  that’s  what I call a proper Christmas treat. Better than all this fancy French patisserie stuff. Though, I’ll eat anything, truth be told. Mind you, I need to get the old motor seen to. Sounds like a bag of spanners rattling around under the bonnet lately. Think I’ll book it in for a service after Christmas.      You really need a new car, Granddad. Honestly! It's older than  you  almost.      Cheeky girl! It’s perfectly serviceable, thank you very much. Been all over the country in that old girl. Seen things y’ wouldn't believe. Still gets me from A to B. That’s all that matters.      Bethany said Ben's dad owns a garage. Maybe he could take a look at it for you, Mr. Thompson?      That’s a thought, Lily. That would be very kind. Bethany’s a good girl to have such thoughtful friends. It’s been lovely getting to know Ben through her.

Honestly, Mark, this new agency is  exhausting . They want copy for everything - cat food, mortgages, funeral plans… you name it, I'm writing about it. It's a far cry from crafting catchy slogans for local garden centres, isn't it?      Sounds…varied, at least. Though I can see how it would be draining. Still, better than being stuck in endless meetings about performance indicators, eh? That’s my life these days. Honestly, sometimes I think I spend more time  talking  about work than actually  doing  it.      Tell me about it! My brain feels like overcooked spaghetti some days. Though, the pay is alright, which helps soften the blow. Speaking of softening blows… Mum, have you thought any more about what you want for your birthday? Dad keeps asking. He’s hovering like a particularly anxious hummingbird.      Oh, your father. He always worries so. Honestly, anything thoughtful will do. A nice scented candle, perhaps? Or… actually, you know what I’ve been craving? That little pottery painting place down by the harbour. We used to go when you were little, didn’t we, Mark?      We did. You were terrible at it, darling. Remember that monstrosity you tried to make that was supposed to be a cat? It looked more like a disgruntled badger.      I was six! And it was a perfectly respectable badger! It had… character. Anyway, it would be nice to revisit. Maybe just us three?      That sounds lovely, actually. A bit…therapeutic. I could definitely use some mindful pottery painting after churning out marketing copy all week. Though, I suspect my badger-esque talents haven’t improved much.      I'm in. We can make it a proper afternoon out. Fish and chips afterwards? There’s that new place near the harbour they say does a cracking portion.      Ooh, yes! Fish and chips  sound  perfect. Speaking of perfect, I bumped into Brenda at the shops yesterday. You remember Brenda, from the ward?      The one who married the baker? Vaguely. Lovely woman, wasn't she?      She is. She’s recently qualified as a therapeutic radiographer. Said it was a really challenging course, but incredibly rewarding. It reminded me why I stuck with nursing, you know? Even on the really difficult days, knowing you've made a difference… well, it's something.      That's amazing! Good for Brenda. It’s good to hear people finding their calling, especially after a bit of a career change.

Right pleasant this is, isn't it? Just a bit of quiet after all that fuss with young Mark and his… well, you know. Honestly, a man his age, carrying on like a schoolboy. Still, his mother always did spoil him rotten.      Spoiled is an understatement, Arthur. She bought him a motorbike at sixteen! A motorbike! I was lucky to get a new pair of shoes. And honestly, all this talk about ‘relationships’… he’s hardly had a proper one. Just flitting about with anyone who’ll look at him.      Now, now, Margaret. Let's not judge too harshly. Mark’s just… exploring. It’s a young man’s prerogative, isn't it? Though I agree, the details are rather tawdry. A mistress in Brighton? Really?      Brighton, you say? Sounds a bit ambitious, doesn’t it? Especially with the train fares these days. Speaking of which, I managed to snag some decent biscuits at Sainsbury’s. They were doing a three-for-two offer. Always good to stock up, you never know when we’ll be stuck indoors again. Remember that power cut last winter? Utter chaos.      Chaos is a mild word for it, David. I thought we were going back to the Stone Age! No heating, no telly… absolutely dreadful. I couldn’t even watch  Big Brother . Missed a whole week of drama.       Big Brother ! Honestly, Arthur, you're seventy-six! Shouldn’t you have more important things to occupy your mind? Like the church fete next month? I promised Reverend Thompson I’d bake a Victoria sponge.      The fete’s alright, I suppose. But it's not the same as a proper old-fashioned party. Remember the village hall dances, Margaret? Everyone dressed up, a live band… proper fun. Not like this modern music. All thumping and shouting.      Those village dances  were  good. I recall a particularly… spirited waltz with your sister, Arthur. Though I suspect her husband wasn’t entirely pleased.      Don’t you start, David. That was a lifetime ago. Still, she always had a good eye for a dancer. Unlike me, clumsy as an old bear.      Well, you’ve always been a man of discerning taste, Arthur. Perhaps that's why you prefer a quiet evening with your tea and  Big Brother ? Speaking of which, I’m thinking of having a small gathering next week, just to break the monotony. Nothing fancy, a few friends, some nibbles.

Right, this sauce needs a good whizzin’ – honestly, ANON’s kitchen is a right treasure trove of spices. Beats my student digs any day, that’s for sure. You wouldn’t believe what I was cookin’ on a hotplate last year.      Oh, don’t even  start  on student cooking. I remember the state of my flatmate’s kitchen after he tried to make… something involving lentils and a lot of questionable seasoning. It was a biohazard. Though, to be fair, my postgrad life isn’t  that  much better when it comes to culinary masterpieces. More instant noodles, less ambition.      Aye, ambition does tend to dwindle when you've got deadlines breathin’ down yer neck. So, what’ve you been up to since… well, since the last time we managed to actually coincide our free evenings? Feels like ages. Last I heard you were battling spreadsheets and a particularly stubborn production line.      You heard right. Spreadsheets are winning. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I’m herding cats, not controlling production. We’re launching a new line of… well, it’s complicated, but basically fancy dog collars. And everything is going wrong. One supplier's late, another sent the wrong buckles. It’s chaos. Need a glass of wine, definitely.      Fancy dog collars! That  is  a bit of a jump from… whatever it was you were working on before. Anyway, sounds stressful. Wine is a  very  good idea. I'm on it. How's your mum doin', by the way? I haven’t spoken to her since Christmas. She was talkin’ about gettin’ into ballroom dancing then - did that ever happen?      She did! And she’s  loving  it. Apparently, she’s got a real competitive streak, which I didn't know existed. She’s dragging my dad along too, of course. He's not thrilled, but he’s too polite to say no. She said she's bringing videos to the next family gathering, so prepare for a showcase. It's quite endearing to see them both trying something new.      That’s brilliant! Your mum's always been a bit of a whirlwind. Still, good on her. My nan keeps threatenin’ to take up skydiving. She says she wants to “live a little” before she turns eighty. It’s terrifying!      Oh my god. That  is  terrifying! Skydiving is a whole other level. You’d think she would stick to something slightly less… extreme.

…and honestly, I just don’t understand this constant push for another referendum. It feels like they're just…stirring things up for the sake of it, doesn't it? Especially after 2014.      Well, I dunno, Grandma. A lot's changed since then, hasn't it? Brexit, for one. Doesn’t that give them a reason to want to decide for themselves again? Mr. Davies was saying in Politics it’s about self-determination, that Scotland's been dragged out of the EU against its will.      Self-determination is a lovely phrase, lad, a  lovely  phrase. But it’s never as simple as it sounds, is it? You look at the mess Brexit’s made of things down south, and then imagine slicing another chunk off the United Kingdom. It'll be financial chaos, that’s what it’ll be. Remember when your Grandad and I used to go up to Scotland for holidays? Always felt like one country, one people, even with the accents and the bagpipes.      Yeah, but Scotland  is  different, isn’t it? They have their own Parliament, their own laws… it’s not like they're just a part of England. And people up there feel really strongly about it, apparently. Chloe’s dad’s Scottish, he's pretty passionate about independence. He was saying they feel like Westminster doesn’t understand them.      Passionate is one thing, sensible is another. And Westminster doesn't understand  anyone  these days, I’ll grant you that! But joining the EU as an independent nation… honestly, what guarantees do they have it’ll be any better? It’s not a magic bullet. And the border with England… imagine the hassle. All those checks, all that paperwork. It'd be like going back in time.      It wouldn't be  like  going back in time, Grandma. It'd be normal for European countries, wouldn't it? Like when we go to France on holiday. You show your passport… it’s not a big deal.      That’s a holiday, love. That's a temporary thing! This is about people living and working, businesses trading… it changes everything. I remember the miner’s strikes, you know. Before your time, of course. There was so much division then, communities pitted against each other. Another referendum feels a bit like reopening old wounds, stirring up that same kind of resentment.      But aren’t some wounds meant to be reopened, Grandma?

Oh, honestly. This woman’s story is… a lot. Like, a  lot  a lot. And honestly, the way she’s speaking… it’s hard to follow half of what she’s saying. It's not even just the subject matter, it's the elision! Everything's runnin' together.      You sayin’ that, lass? Coming from Doncaster, you? Don't tell me you've never dropped a ‘t’ or two in yer time. You lot practically invented it!      That’s different! We're  refined  in Yorkshire, alright? It’s a stylistic choice, a smoothness. It’s not… mumbled desperation. There’s a distinction. It's like, proper Yorkshire is melodic. This is just…noise.      Hold on, hold on. Both of you are being a bit harsh. Accents aren’t about being ‘refined’ or ‘desperate’. It’s just… how people speak, innit? Different areas, different influences. Plus, when people are stressed and upset, like these poor souls on Jeremy Kyle, they  are  going to talk faster and blur things together.      Aye, and don't forget, half of them are putting it on for the cameras! They know they need a strong storyline and a dramatic delivery. They think it makes for better telly. It's all a bit performative, isn't it?      Totally. I bet they practice their lines beforehand. "Oh, 'e cheated on me wiv me best mate, an' now I’m proper gutted!” It’s all a bit embarrassing, really. Though, I still watch it. Don't judge me.      No judgement here. It’s a guilty pleasure, alright? But you've got a point about the performance. I was listening to her – the woman on screen now with the bright pink hair – and she’s switching between sounding absolutely devastated and then practically shouting. It’s exhausting!      It's the vowels, too. All broad and stretched out. Makes it sound like it's takin’ ages to get through a sentence, doesn't it? I mean, I'm used to hearin' a good, solid Yorkshire vowel, not somethin’…drawn out like that.      So, you’re sayin' Derbyshire vowels aren’t good enough for you, eh? I thought we were friends!      No, no, love, Derbyshire’s lovely! It’s just… different. We’re a very particular bunch up north, you know? Very proud of our speech. Plus, growing up, everyone used to take the mickey out of our accents when we went down south.

Oof, that looked nasty. Honestly, the diving in this game is ridiculous. Feels more like ballet than football at times.      You say that every time, love. It  is  a bit overdone, I’ll grant you, but it’s part of the spectacle, innit? Adds to the drama. Besides, Sunderland weren’t exactly immune to a bit of tactical… embellishment back in the day.      That’s different! We were  passionate ! They’re just…flopping. And don’t bring up the old days, you know how sensitive I am about the Championship. Still recovering. Speaking of sensitive, did you finish that scarf you were knitting for your Mum? The Olympics are getting closer, she’ll want it for those chilly evenings watching the rowing.      Almost. Just the bobble edge to go. It's a proper labour of love, that one. She’s already started dropping hints about wanting Team GB pyjamas. Honestly, the woman has a wardrobe full of sportswear as it is! It’s amazing how the Olympics always get her into a patriotic frenzy. Do you think we’ll actually see a decent showing in the football this time?      Don’t hold your breath. They always seem to underperform. It’s the pressure, I reckon. Too much expectation. Though, I’d be happy just to see a bit of excitement. It’s been a bit of a dull season, hasn't it? Less drama on the pitch, more drama with managers getting sacked.      Definitely. And speaking of drama… have you given any more thought to baby names? We’re getting closer to needing to properly nail down a shortlist, aren’t we?      Ugh, don’t remind me. It’s paralyzing! I was scrolling through lists last night and just…felt overwhelmed. Everything either sounds stuffy and old-fashioned or aggressively trendy.      I know the feeling. I saw one the other day, "Zephyr." Seriously? Zephyr? Sounds like a wind chime.      Oh god, no! We need something…solid. Something that won’t get them relentlessly teased at school. I’ve been toying with the idea of something a bit more classic. Maybe something with a link to the North East?      Like what? Robson? No, that's a bit much, even for you.      I was joking! Though… maybe something like Alnwick? After the castle? It’s a bit different, but not  too  out there. Or maybe a girl's name – Rowan. It's nature-y, but not ridiculously ‘earth mother’.

...and honestly, the bit where Barry B. Benson sues the human race? It's surprisingly well-argued, isn't it? For a cartoon bee. It actually makes you think about our relationship with… well, with everything, really.      Bees are cool. They make honey. Can we have honey on our toast tomorrow?      But they  sting ! I got stung last summer. It  really  hurt.      Yes, they can sting, darling, but they only do it if they feel threatened. It’s a bit like… well, like King Arthur, really. He had to defend his kingdom, didn’t he? He only fought when he had to.      Who’s King Arthur? Is he a bee?      No, sweetheart, he wasn’t a bee. He was a very,  very  long time ago, a king. A bit like… the Royal Family, but even older. That reminds me, did you see what fruit they had on display at the farmers market? All those perfect peaches and plums, fit for a king – or a queen! It’s ridiculous how obsessed we are with “royal” things.      Why do you have to  pay  to see where the King and Queen live? That’s silly.      That  is  a good point, actually. It’s a bit strange, isn’t it? Paying to wander around Buckingham Palace. It makes you wonder if we shouldn't just be a republic. No kings or queens, everyone equal.      Does that mean no sparkly crowns?      Well, no sparkly crowns at state occasions, perhaps. Though, people would probably still  make  sparkly crowns, wouldn’t they? It's the spectacle, I think.      I'd be king! Then I could have all the Lego I wanted. And a robot.      You’d be a very generous king. Though, being king is a lot of work. Or being a politician, even. All that talking and trying to make everyone happy. No thank you! I'm quite happy marking essays. Although… sometimes I wonder if a politician’s life is less stressful!      Mummy, are you taking your vitamins? You said they make you less grumpy.      I did  not  say they make me less grumpy. I said they support my immune system. And yes, I took them this morning. It’s just… sometimes explaining fractions to seven-year-olds can be a bit draining.      We’re going to see diving at the Olympic Stadium! Will it be loud?      It might be a bit noisy, darling, with the cheering.

Oh, that’s much better. Honestly, I thought we’d be wrestling with cardboard boxes and rusty garden implements all day. My back is  killing  me.      It wasn’t so bad, dear. A bit of a kerfuffle with that old lawnmower, mind you. Nearly took my fingers off trying to get the cord started. Still, better out than in, as they say. The house felt…suffocated. Just  layers  of things.      Gran, you had a greenhouse  full  of gnomes. That’s a layer. A really creepy layer.      They were charming! And collectable! Your grandfather adored them. Though I suspect your mother secretly loathed them.      She did. She once tried to ‘re-home’ a particularly garish one during a school fete. Thankfully, I intercepted it. Still have Barnaby, you know. The one with the fishing rod.      Barnaby! Oh, goodness. That gnome has seen things. You’ve had Barnaby since before you and I even  met , David. It’s a family heirloom now, isn’t it?      A slightly chipped, resinous family heirloom. But yes, I suppose he is. Though honestly, the amount of stuff we've unearthed... It's amazing how much history accumulates in just one house. I found Mum's old Brownie camera, and a stack of letters from when she was a student. Proper handwritten letters!      Wow. Like, actual paper? What did people  do  before texting?      We talked, dear. Face to face. We wrote letters! It was a more thoughtful process. People actually considered what they were saying. Though, truthfully, Father was dreadful at letter writing. Always very brief. "Everything fine. Send money." That sort of thing.      Sounds familiar. My dad was the same. Conciseness was his strong suit. Though he did send a  very  long letter when I went to university… mostly instructions on how to do laundry!      Mum does that. Even though I'm at sixth form, she still sends me lists of things to pack for school trips. Like, seriously? I can handle a toothbrush, Mum!      It's a mother's job, I think. It’s ingrained. Speaking of ingrained habits, did you hear about old Mr. Henderson down the road? Apparently, he’s decided to take up competitive clog dancing.       What ? Mr. Henderson? The one who complains if the bins are one centimetre over the line? Competitive clog dancing?      Apparently so. His granddaughter told me. He’s entering a regional competition in Thirsk next month. Says it's "good for the circulation."      Thirsk!

Right, so, the Tate Liverpool’s doing that new pop art exhibition, yeah? Thought we could go Saturday, if you’re not swamped with… well, anything psychology-related. You always end up rescuing someone’s mental state on a weekend, don’t ya?      Very funny. It's usually paperwork, honestly. Ms. Davies had a bit of a wobble yesterday, needed some support processing a difficult family situation, but Saturday  should  be clear. The Tate sounds brilliant, actually. Bit of colour after this grey week. Though… parking is going to be a nightmare. Remember last time? Circling for half an hour?      Don't remind me. I aged ten years just looking for a space. We could get the ferry across, make a proper afternoon of it. Bit more expensive, mind you, but avoids the car park stress.      That's a good shout! The ferry’s nicer anyway, view of the docks and all. Speaking of money… I'm starting to seriously think about applying for that Masters in Clinical Psychology. But the fees… they’re scary.      Aye, they are. Properly frightening. Have you looked at funding options, scholarships, that sort of thing? You deserve to do it, though, you'd be brilliant. And think of the career boost.      I have, a bit. There’s a bursary, but it's competitive. And I need to start prepping for the interview. They want a case study analysis, apparently. I'm feeling a bit out of practice. How’s the teaching going? Any unruly scousers causing chaos?      You know it. Year 9 think ‘banter’ means being actively disruptive. But it’s alright, keeps me on my toes. Actually, I had a parent-teacher meeting today about young Liam O’Connell. Apparently, he's obsessed with weddings. Full-on mood boards and Pinterest boards. Asked me what my wife and I are planning!      Oh, bless him! That’s adorable. Honestly, teenagers are so strange. Remember when we were obsessed with…what was it? Collecting those miniature animal figures?      The Schleich ones! And arguing over who got the rarest horse. Good times. We should probably start thinking about Christmas presents, though. It's creeping up on us. Nan keeps asking if we've started lists. She's already got a stockpile of biscuits, apparently.      Oh, she will not be stopped when it comes to biscuits. I was thinking… maybe we finally get a dog? We’ve been talking about it for ages.

Honestly, I'm  drowning  in readings for History. Professor Davies is convinced we have infinite time. It’s just… endless 18th-century agricultural practices. Seriously?      Tell me about it! I'm battling with organic chemistry. It feels like learning another language. And Dr. Chen just breezes through things like it’s all obvious. Like, no, Doctor, I didn’t instinctively  know  the Krebs cycle!      Exactly! It’s the assumption that kills me. Like, we’re supposed to absorb information through osmosis or something. Anyway, enough complaining. How was your weekend? Did you manage to actually, you know,  live  a little?      It was alright, yeah. Went for brunch with my auntie and cousins down in Leicester. Proper good Filipino food – adobo, lumpia, the whole shebang. It was nice just catching up, proper family time. Your mum mentioned you were thinking of getting a tattoo?      Oh, yeah! I've been sketching designs for  ages . I’m thinking a tiny hummingbird on my wrist. It’s a bit cliché, I know, but they’re just… so delicate and bright. My nan's worried I’ll regret it, naturally. She thinks all tattoos are for sailors and ruffians.      Nan’s are the best at worrying. Mine was convinced I’d get a boyfriend just from going to university. Like, hello? I have exams to worry about! A hummingbird sounds lovely though, very you. Have you looked at many studios? I know a place in Nottingham that’s supposed to be really good, all custom designs and stuff.      I’ve been scrolling through Insta, honestly. It’s a rabbit hole! Everyone's got incredible work. Nottingham’s a bit of a trek, though. I was hoping to find something closer in London. What about you? Still obsessed with that Korean drama everyone was talking about?      Oh my god,  Crash Landing on You ? Still totally obsessed. It’s just…  chefs kiss . The storyline is ridiculous, I admit, but the male lead? Absolute snack. Have you seen any of the TikTok edits? They're wild.      Oh, please. Don’t get me started on TikTok. It’s a time vortex. I downloaded it for five minutes and ended up watching videos of cats falling off things for an hour. It’s a dangerous app. Though I did see one about recreating Disney film scenes with pets… that was actually quite good.      See! It’s not  all  bad. You just need to curate your ‘For You’ page properly.

Honestly, Mum, this new Pokémon raid is  brutal . I’ve used all my super potions and still can’t take down Regidrago. It keeps… oh, hello Auntie Sarah, and Oisin! Hi little man.      Hello, Leo. You and that Pokémon! Honestly, it’s a wonder you have time for homework. Oisin’s been trying to ‘catch’ the dust bunnies under the sofa all afternoon. It's a very similar dedication, actually. He’s got a little Tupperware box for them.      Bunnies! Got ‘em!  Mmm … biscuit?      He’s getting so good at asking for things, isn't he? Remember when it was just babbling? Though, I still think ‘biscuit’ is one of the first words  anyone  learns. Anyway, back to Regidrago… Have you seen that video online of the strategy? It involves timing your X-move perfectly.      Honestly, Leo, it all sounds like another language to me. Remember when playing outside was the ‘strategy’? We used to spend hours building dens in the garden. Though, I suppose you were a bit too young for that, weren't you?      I built a fort in my bedroom once, out of cushions and blankets. Dad wasn’t too pleased. Said I couldn’t see the floor. But it was epic! Speaking of which, are we still on for Ramen next week? I saw that new place opened in town.      Yes, absolutely. I promised Leo that for finishing his mocks, didn't I? Although… I’m a bit self-conscious about going out. I haven’t really… worn proper clothes in ages. Mainly just tracksuits and things.      What's wrong with tracksuits? They’re comfy! You look good, Mum.      It’s just… all the mums at the playgroup wear these lovely outfits, and I feel a bit… frumpy. And finding something that fits after having Oisin is… challenging. Honestly, everything feels too tight or too baggy. I even tried to squeeze into a pair of my old skinny jeans the other day… a disaster.      Ouch. Skinny jeans  are  evil. They’re just… restrictive. I wouldn't be caught dead in them. Actually, Mrs. Davies asked me today why I never wear anything other than jeans. I told her they're just practical.      That's a good answer. I think practicality  is  key. Oh, and I remembered – your Dad said he was going to try and tune his guitar tonight, maybe you could jam with him afterwards? He's been meaning to for ages.

Oh, goodness me. Look at this. Remember this little thing? It's… well, it  was  part of our gardening set, wasn’t it? A ridiculous little set, really. Everything was bright pink and orange.      Pink and orange, and utterly impractical! Honestly, you couldn't have grown a radish in those plastic plant pots. But we  tried , didn't we? Spent hours ‘gardening’ in the back garden, getting absolutely covered in mud. Your mum wasn't best pleased, I recall.      Best pleased is an understatement. She said we looked like a pair of chimney sweeps. And the ‘vegetables’… those plastic carrots and lettuce… I can almost smell the plastic now. It was the best though, wasn’t it? Especially when we convinced poor old Mr. Henderson next door that we were actually growing real vegetables to give to him.      Oh, that was brilliant! He was such a sweet man. He pretended to be so impressed. I remember him carefully examining those plastic tomatoes and saying something about the “lovely blush” on them. We were terrible little fibbers.      We were! It’s funny the things you remember, isn't it? I was dreading going through this cupboard, honestly. It's just…stuff. But then you pull out something like this, and it’s like a whole childhood comes flooding back. It makes it a bit harder to just chuck it all.      I know what you mean. I was rather hoping we'd find some of the Bako, though. Do you remember that? The little interlockable bricks? We built entire castles with that stuff. And spaceships. It was far more ambitious than the gardening.      Oh, Bako! Yes! We had the big box, the one with all the different shaped pieces. I was always trying to build something structurally sound, and you were all about aesthetics. Everything you built had flags and turrets and… well, it always looked fabulous, but it usually collapsed within five minutes.      It did  not  always collapse! Sometimes it lasted a good ten minutes! And it wasn't just about the aesthetics, I was an architect! A visionary! You were the engineer, obsessed with load-bearing walls. We made a good team.      We did, didn't we? It’s ridiculous how those little things bond you. Still, this cupboard… it's a bit overwhelming. I feel guilty just getting rid of things. It feels like throwing away pieces of ourselves.      It does, but we can’t keep everything.

Honestly, this is ridiculous. I’ve already got three bites, and we’ve barely been five minutes! Even in October, these mosquitoes are relentless. I thought they’d be gone by now.      You’d think, wouldn't you? It’s almost November. Maybe it's this weirdly warm weather we've been having. They’re loving it. Little bloodsuckers. Poor Leo, hopefully they aren’t bothering him in the buggy. I’ll check his legs when we get back.      I put repellent on him, but… well, you know how effective those things are. About as effective as trying to navigate the North Circular at rush hour. Speaking of which, did you see the article about the delays on the A3 this morning? Absolute chaos.      Oh, don’t even  start  me on the traffic. I deliberately left an hour early just in case, and  still  ended up being ten minutes late for that departmental meeting. Professor Davies was giving me the side-eye, naturally. He thinks punctuality is a moral failing.      He probably does. He also thinks post-structuralism is the answer to everything. Anyway, it's nice to escape it all for a bit, isn’t it? Even with the mosquito assault. This park is so peaceful, relatively.      It is. Though peaceful doesn't stop me thinking about that gig we wanted to go to next week. The one at the Lexington. It's a bit of a trek, though. I’m starting to worry about getting stuck in traffic again.      The Lexington! Oh, yes! I totally forgot. That band are supposed to be brilliant. It’s a shame it’s a Tuesday, though. Weekdays are always a nightmare for getting anywhere. We could get the train, I suppose? Though hauling a tired baby and all the paraphernalia onto a delayed train doesn't sound overly appealing.      No, you’re right. That sounds… ambitious. Maybe we should look into a taxi? Expensive, but potentially worth it for some sanity. We could book one for a specific time, hoping it's less affected by the gridlock.      That’s a thought. Or… maybe we could see if my sister’s free to babysit? She’s offered a few times now, and I feel terrible always making excuses. Plus, she actually  likes  looking after Leo.      That’s a really good idea, actually. We haven’t properly seen her in ages, and it would be nice to have a night out without constantly worrying about whether Leo’s okay or needs feeding.

Right, that’s me officially knackered. Another six hours on the course, dodging rain and trying to convince my swing it remembers what it's supposed to do. You had a better day, I hope? You've been glued to that laptop all afternoon.      Honestly? About as productive as watching paint dry. Another ten applications sent into the void. Recruitment processes are… draining. It's all 'tell us about a time you failed' and 'demonstrate your resilience'. Like, can’t I just  have  a job without needing a life story attached?      Tell me about it. It’s brutal out there. Remember when I was stressing about A-Levels? Seems a lifetime ago. At least  that  had a defined end point. This feels endless. What was this one for, anyway?      A marketing assistant role at a tech firm in Manchester. Apparently, they’re "disrupting the pet food industry." Seriously. Disrupting pet food. I spent an hour researching innovative dog biscuits. It was… humbling.      Manchester, eh? You reckon you’d actually move? Bit different to High Wycombe, innit?      I don’t know. It’s tempting, I guess. Anything’s tempting at this point. But leaving everything… the flat, Mum and Dad,  you … It's a big step. I just feel like I’m treading water here. I need to actually  do  something.      You are doing something! You’re smashing those applications. It's just a slow burn. And look, Manchester’s not the moon. We can visit. We could even go to some gigs – I hear the music scene is banging.      That’s true. Speaking of needing a distraction, have you seen what’s on at the Wycombe Swan this month? They’re doing a new production of  Macbeth .      Oh really? Fancy that. You and your theatre. I’m more of a telly man myself. Been trying to get into that new docuseries about Formula 1, but my phone keeps buzzing with silly golf updates. Honestly, it's a constant battle.      You need to turn notifications off! It's a digital detox waiting to happen. Though, I will admit, I doomscroll through TikTok for way too long. It’s a waste of time, but…      It’s addictive, yeah. I saw some mad Halloween decorations on there today. Massive inflatable ghouls and everything. Makes me think of when we were kids, trying to carve pumpkins. Yours always looked like a melted mess.      Hey! They were  atmospheric .

“…and the wheels on the bus go round and round, round and round, round and round…” Honestly, this song is stuck in my head  forever .      Ah, the joys of a four-year-old, Leo. It’s a beautiful torture, isn't it? You’ll miss it one day, even the endless repetition.      Easy for you to say, Liam. You’re not the one who’s heard it approximately seven hundred times  today . Honestly, I think little Rory’s trying to weaponize it. He knows it drives me bonkers.      “Round and round, round and round…”!      Now, now, Rory. Leave your Auntie Sarah alone with the vegetables. Tell you what, when dinner’s finished, maybe Leo can pick a film for us all to watch? Something… less musical?      Ooh, yeah! Can we watch that superhero one? The one with the really loud noises?      Maybe something a  little  quieter, Leo. My head’s already booming. Liam, is this stew nearly ready? I’m starving. And I'm worried about getting Rory to eat enough. He’s been picking at everything all day.      Just about. Another ten minutes. It’s a proper Irish stew, mind you. Lamb, potatoes, carrots… the works. Good and hearty. Should even tempt a picky eater like Master Rory. I used that new recipe I found online, the one with the Guinness in it.      Guinness? In stew? That sounds… weird.      Trust me, it adds a depth of flavour. It's brilliant. I was messing around with the cloud storage earlier, trying to back up all my old family recipes. Getting a bit worried about losing them, you know? Everything's digital now, feels a bit precarious.      You and your technology, Liam. Honestly. Back them up twice! Once on your hard drive, and then… well, I don’t know, print them out! Old fashioned, I know. But safe. Speaking of safe, do we have a plan for getting Rory to his swimming lesson tomorrow? I completely forgot to check if my mum can do it.      I can drop him off, no problem. I have that meeting in the city afterward. Though, trying to navigate Cork city traffic with a four-year-old on a swimming mission... that’s  the tricky part.      Can I come with you to the city? I want to see the big shops!      No, darling. You have homework. And I need you to occupy yourself quietly while I try to get Rory fitted for his new shoes.

Honestly, you look like you’re trying to smuggle a small melon down your trousers.      Very funny. It's called comfort, alright? And these are perfectly respectable pajama bottoms… when they fit. They shrink in the wash, I swear. It’s easier just to… you know, go commando with pants. Less constriction.      Ewww, Daddy! That's  disgusting !      Yeah, Daddy! Why would you do that? Pants are for wearing  over  things!      Right? It's a revolutionary concept, children. Underwear, then trousers. A cornerstone of civilization.      Look, it's a holiday. Rules are slightly more relaxed. Besides, these pants are soft. They’re practically a second skin. It’s like being…free.      Freezing! You’ll catch a cold!      I’ll be fine, Poppy. Honestly. Anyway, changing the subject before I’m subjected to a full interrogation... I was thinking about the house.      Oh? What about it? More ambitious garden plans? You’ve already conquered half of Suffolk with your vegetable patch.      It's bigger than the garden, actually. I was imagining extending the kitchen. Knocking through into the dining room. Proper island unit, the works.      Like on  Grand Designs ?      Exactly, Leo! Like on  Grand Designs . We could get one of those fancy taps that comes out sideways. And a wine fridge. Always a necessity.      A wine fridge? And where exactly are we going to put all this… luxury? Remember, we're in a slightly wonky, 17th-century cottage, not a minimalist box in the Cotswolds.      That's the challenge! I was thinking we could support it with a steel beam. Hidden, obviously. It'd be structurally sound, perfectly legal. I even found a bloke online who specialises in period property extensions...   Speaker_2  : You  found a bloke online ? Already? Before we’ve even had a proper conversation about it? This is always how it starts, isn’t it? You get fixated on an idea and then suddenly we’re living in a building site for six months.      I’m just…thinking aloud! Visualising! It would be amazing, though. Imagine the Christmas dinners we could have in a proper big kitchen. No more juggling pans and trying not to bump into each other.      We could have a bouncy castle  in  the kitchen!      And a slide!      Okay, okay, reign it in, you two. No bouncy castles. But a slightly bigger kitchen  does  sound nice. We could definitely use more counter space. Though I’m drawing the line at a sideways tap.

…and honestly, the magnolia was a mistake. A complete and utter mistake. It just…absorbs all the light, doesn’t it? Makes the whole room feel like a waiting room in a particularly grim doctor's surgery.      Magnolia. The colour of regret, they call it in my neck of the woods. A Tredegar saying, naturally. You’d think after living in Egypt for so long you’d be used to vibrant colours. I remember the souks, the sheer riot of it all.      Cairo  is  colourful, yes. But that’s a different kind of brightness. It’s the light, the dust, the… life. This is just…beige. My wife, bless her, insisted. Said it was ‘safe’. Safe is the enemy of all good interior design, I’m telling you. I’m thinking a deep teal, maybe? Something with a bit of character.      Teal’s a good shout. Bold. Though, knowing your wife, you'll end up with another shade of…inoffensive. Speaking of bold, have you heard anything more about the Rutherford funding application? I’m starting to feel a bit twitchy about it.      Ah, yes. I chased Professor Davies this morning. He said the panel is ‘deliberating’. That’s academic speak for ‘doesn't know its arse from its elbow and is likely to pass it to someone at Oxford’. I’m not optimistic, I’m afraid. They seem very keen on these 'impact' studies, and frankly, quantifying the societal benefit of understanding the Higgs boson feels…reductionist.      Reductionist is putting it mildly! It’s like asking a poet to justify their verses with a cost-benefit analysis. Still, we’ve got a strong case. The potential spin-offs with the Hadron Collider data – the medical imaging applications, the materials science… it's substantial.      Substantial and utterly lost on people who think research funding should be solely allocated to things they can  see  benefitting them directly. Like, I don’t know, slightly more efficient water companies. Honestly, the state of those privatised utilities…it’s a scandal.      Don't even get me started on the water companies. Back home, they're constantly digging up the roads. "Improving infrastructure", they say. More like lining shareholders' pockets. It’s infuriating. Reminds me of a trip I took to Italy a few years back. Stunning country, absolute chaos with the plumbing.      Italy! Now  there's  a place with good colour. Florence, particularly. I spent a semester there, back in the eighties.

Right, operation ‘Sort the Bricks’ is… not going well. Honestly, it looks like a Lego bomb went off in here. Elsie, darling, are you  sure  you weren't building a replica of the Millennium Falcon without telling me?      No! I was building a… a castle! For Hermione. She needs a really, really big castle. Bigger than Hogwarts.      And  I'm  building a lair! For Shredder! He needs a really sneaky lair, full of traps.      A sneaky lair, excellent. Okay, so castles and lairs. That explains… some of it. Elsie, if Hermione needs a bigger castle than Hogwarts, we need to at least try and keep the pieces a little organised, yeah? We’ve got colours, shapes… remember?      But what if the colours need to be  mixed  for the castle walls? Hermione likes sparkly walls.      Oh, sparkly walls are a very good point. Okay, sparkly walls are allowed. But everything else needs a home. How about we start with all the flat pieces? The plates and tiles?      Can Shredder have sparkly bits too? Like, laser beams?      Shredder  can  have laser beams. Lego laser beams are perfectly acceptable. You know, this is actually quite therapeutic. Better than watching The Simpsons, definitely. Although, I did enjoy the one last night with Bart trying to sell Lisa’s doll…      I don't like The Simpsons very much. It's not like Harry Potter. Harry Potter is much better. Did you know Hermione is really clever?      She  is  extraordinarily clever. You’re a clever girl too, Elsie. Maybe even cleverer than Hermione, you just haven’t had a chance to use spells yet. What do you think, Leo? Is Shredder clever?      Shredder's super clever! He tricked the Ninja Turtles loads of times. We are going to see the new Ninja Turtles film, aren’t we? Daddy said!      We are! We're going on Saturday. That's why we need to get this Lego sorted. A clear bedroom means a good cinema trip. Though, I am hoping it's not  too  loud. My ears are still ringing from Granny’s.      What about Granny? Is she okay?      She's fine, sweetheart. They've started the renovations at her house – new kitchen, new bathroom. It's a huge job, honestly. They found some really old wallpaper, with little flowers on it. Apparently, it was put up by  her  grandmother!      Wallpaper? That's boring. Lego is better. Can I build a crane to help Granny with her house?

Honestly, this risotto is  fighting  me. I swear, it either ends up gluey or still crunchy. It’s a culinary battle, I tell you. How was the flight home? You were gone for ages!      Oh, you and risotto. It always looks so easy on the Great British Menu, doesn't it? The flight was…fine. Long. Typical. Though I think I consumed my weight in miniature pretzels. It's good to be back though, really good. Smells… vaguely of garlic and desperation in here?      Desperation is the key ingredient, honestly. Pretzels sound good actually. I’ve been surviving on toast and existential dread since you left. Work's been mental. Mr. Henderson decided, mid-holiday for  both  of us, that the entire project timeline needs shifting. Like, drastically.      Ugh, Henderson. He’s the worst. Always needing everything yesterday. Is it  massively  different, or just one of his little panics? And what kind of project co-ordinator pulls a shift halfway through their own holiday?      A stressed one, apparently. It’s not massively different, it’s just… more. More meetings, more deliverables, and he keeps saying ‘synergy’ like it's a magical solution. I’m starting to hate that word. Anyway, enough about my woes, how was Gran’s? Did she manage to convince you to take up competitive knitting?      No knitting, thankfully. She tried to set me up with the vicar’s son though. Apparently, he’s “a good lad, firmly established.” Firmly established in the parish, maybe. He looked about seventy. Gran's good though, really good. A little quieter, but she loved having you call every day while I was there. Said it kept her spirits up.      Aw, that’s sweet. I felt bad leaving her with you for so long, but you needed the break. You’ve been working non-stop on the ward. Has anything particularly… harrowing happened since you’ve been back? Don't feel you have to tell me if not.      It's always something, isn't it? Just the usual barrage of underfunding and overwhelmed people. There was a young lad, Liam, come in last week. Seventeen, first psychotic episode. Terrifying for him, and hard to watch. Thankfully, we got him stabilised. It’s moments like those that make you question everything, you know? But then you see small improvements, and it reminds you why you do it.      Totally. It sounds exhausting. I sometimes forget how genuinely vital your job is, escaping into spreadsheets and Gantt charts all day.

Right, well, that’s the garden mostly sorted for today. Just need to give the roses a good feed tomorrow, but they’re looking promising. Honestly, I think the slugs had a right party while we were away last week though. Young lad, you wouldn’t believe the holes in the hostas!      Hmm? Oh, yeah. Saw a massive one yesterday. Nearly stepped on it. Disgusting.      Disgusting? In my day, we didn’t call ‘em disgusting. We just called ‘em a nuisance! And you’d get out there with a bit o’ salt and sort ‘em out. None of this fancy slug pellet stuff.      Aye, salt was the answer. Good for the garden, good for the constitution, building character! Though I remember your mother, bless her soul, used to pick ‘em up and fling ‘em over the fence into old Mr. Henderson’s garden. Said he liked ‘em for his ducks.      Oh, don’t you start on your mother and Mr. Henderson’s ducks, Arthur! That’s a story for another day. Honestly, the things she got up to… Anyway, I was thinking, Michael, about the loft insulation. I had a look yesterday. It’s looking a bit thin, especially around the edges.      Loft insulation? Ugh. Sounds boring.      It isn’t boring, it’s important! It’s costing us money, lad. Heat rising, all that. I was thinking perhaps we could get someone in to have a look, give us a quote?      You always were sensible about things, Margaret. Never one to let pennies slip through your fingers. Though Arthur here used to think a penny saved was a penny… well, he’d just spend it on sweets.      A man’s gotta have his pleasures! Though I haven't had a good humbug in… well, a good while now, truth be told. Dentist wouldn’t be pleased.      Speaking of dentists, I’ve got mine next week. Dread it. They always tell me to floss more. It's a conspiracy, I swear. They just  want  to see me more.      Now, now, don't be silly. You need to look after your teeth. It’s just like looking after the roses – a bit of preventative care saves a lot of trouble later on. Do you two want another brew? I’ve just made a fresh pot.      Oh, go on then, Margaret. Just a little one. And maybe a biscuit? You always have those nice ginger ones.

Right, who wants more beans with their toast? And honestly, honestly, did either of you  actually  pay attention to what I was saying about Great Ormond Street Hospital? It's all linked, you know.      Mmm-hmm. Sort of. I was drawing Tinkerbell. She needs glitter. Lots and lots of glitter.      I was building Neverland! See? That's Hook's ship, and that bit's the mermaids' lagoon.      Right. Of course. Neverland constructed from toast crusts. Logical. Look, J.M. Barrie, the man who  wrote  Peter Pan, he left all the copyright to the play and the book to Great Ormond Street. That's why they still get royalties from every single performance and film made of it. It's a massive amount of money that helps so many poorly children.      So… Peter Pan helps sick kids? Even now?      In a way, yes. His story does. It’s a lovely legacy, isn’t it? Now, we were talking about the different films… you both said you'd seen bits of  Pan ?      The one with the pirates, right? And the dust! Everything was covered in glowing dust. It was cool. But it wasn't like the cartoon.      No, it wasn’t. It was a sort of…origin story. Trying to explain  how  Peter Pan became Peter Pan. It got rather mixed reviews. Do you remember the Disney  Peter Pan  cartoon? That's the classic for a lot of people.      I love the Disney one! Tinkerbell is so pretty, but she's a bit bossy. She gets cross with Peter all the time.      She does, doesn't she? She’s got a strong personality! And that version captured the magic really well, I think. It’s funny, because the original story is…well, it’s a bit darker than the Disney version. Barrie wrote it as a way of coping with the loss of his brother. It’s quite sad when you know the background.      Darker? Like, scary? Does Captain Hook get, like,  really  scary?      He's menacing, definitely. He's a villain, after all. But it's not  jump-scare  scary. More… determined to get his revenge. He lost his hand to Peter, you see. Do you know the story of how that happened?      Peter tickled him and a crocodile ate his hand?      Well, there's a crocodile involved, yes! It ate a clock first, so it ticked, and that's how they knew it was coming.

Honestly, this is lovely. Just… quiet. And no marking. It’s a miracle, isn't it? Usually, a car journey with you two is a full-blown planning session for something.      Well, someone has to keep things ticking over, don't they? Though, admittedly, seeing as it’s dropping Sarah off at the airport, not much planning  can  be done right now. Just hoping her flight isn’t delayed. This M5 stretch can be brutal.      It’s a good job we left when we did, then. Even this early, it’s starting to build up. Remember that time we got stuck near Cullompton? Felt like we were living in the car.      Don't remind me! I nearly missed parents’ evening. Though, come to think of it, that was after we’d moved from Exmouth, wasn't it? Before Taunton?      That’s right. Exmouth was… nice. A bit  too  touristy for my liking, though. Always fighting for a parking space. Southend prepared me for crowds, admittedly, but this was different.      Taunton was a good patch. Closer to the Quantocks. I used to sneak off for walks whenever I could. Remember Mrs. Henderson next door? She was a whirlwind. Always lending us things, even before we’d asked for them!      Oh, Mrs. Henderson! She once gave us a whole box of marrows. Marrows! We didn't know what to do with them all. I ended up making chutney for everyone we knew.      I remember Sarah saying they were the best marrows she’d ever tasted, just to be polite. You were a marvel, dear, turning those things into something edible. Speaking of Sarah, how's she feeling about the move to Manchester? Still excited?      She seemed really positive on the phone last night. A bit nervous, naturally, but mostly excited. It’s a good opportunity for her career, isn’t it? And it’ll be nice for her to be closer to Emily.      Definitely. It's just… it feels like a big change. I always thought she'd settle somewhere closer to us.      People need to spread their wings, love. We’ve had our turn building a life here in Devon. Now it’s her turn. Though, naturally, Christmas will be tricky with her up north.      We could possibly go up to Manchester for a few days? It would be nice to see her settled in, and maybe a bit of Christmas shopping.

Oh, bless me. That track work is  exhausting  for an old girl, even with all the willing hands. Though, truth be told, willing hands don’t always equate to  knowing  hands, do they? Young Timmy nearly planted a rhododendron on top of Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning dahlias!      Aye, you get all sorts. Good intentions, mostly. I used to manage accommodation for the Nationwide, and you learn pretty quick that well-meaning folks can cause a right mess if left to their own devices. Needed constant supervision, they did. Are you with the working party then? On the station restoration?      That’s right. Trying to get Creech St. Michael looking a bit presentable again. It's a lovely little station, always has been, but it’s been…neglected. I'm Elsie, by the way. Elsie Penhaligon.      Arthur. Arthur Davies. Pleased to meet you, Elsie. Neglect is the word, isn't it? Everything's falling by the wayside. Reminds me a bit of how attitudes towards…well, towards everything have changed over the years. My wife, bless her, she always said things were simpler when she was a girl. Though I reckon she just missed having someone else doing all the work!      Oh, women and simplicity! A thorny subject, Arthur. It  seems  simpler, doesn’t it? But really, it was just a different set of constraints. I remember my mother, a clever woman, desperately wanting to train as a nursery teacher. But "a proper woman," they said, should be at home. It’s changed, thankfully. Though there’s still a ways to go, innit? Still a lot of terminology that makes my blood boil. "Man-hours," for instance!      Aye, that one gets me. As if a woman’s effort is somehow…less. She was a cracker, my wife, and could outwork most men I knew. Though she did enjoy a good Swedish massage now and then to ease the aches. Said it worked wonders. I never understood the appeal myself – too much poking and prodding for my liking.      Oh, I can see that! I've had a few myself, though. Lower back gets a bit troublesome, you know, with all the bending and lifting when I was running the gallery. And then there's the antique dealing - hoisting heavy bits of furniture about. It's surprisingly strenuous. It kept me fit, though. Not like now.      A gallery, you say? That sounds fascinating. We were discussing next year's ME event - the model engineering exhibition.

…and honestly, Mum, the thought of actually  booking  it feels… a bit terrifying. It's been so long since I've properly planned a holiday, anything beyond a weekend in Bristol.      Terrifying? Oh, don’t be daft, love. A little bit of planning is no bad thing. It’s exciting! Where are you dithering over now? Still Portugal?      Portugal  is  still the frontrunner, yeah. The Algarve, specifically. But I keep getting bogged down in the details. Flights are expensive, obviously, and then trying to find a villa that isn’t… well, a shoebox crammed next to a nightclub. And I want something near the coast, but not  right  on top of it, you know? Peaceful, but accessible.      Accessible is key. You don't want to be spending half your holiday driving up and down winding roads. That’s happened to us before, hasn’t it? Remember that disastrous trip to the Dordogne?      Oh god, don’t remind me. Dad swore he’d never look at another vineyard again. But that’s the thing, I feel responsible for making it good. Liam’s trusting me to sort it all, and Leo’s got his heart set on building sandcastles. The pressure!      You’re putting too much pressure on yourself. Liam and Leo will be happy just to be  away , honestly. It's a holiday, not an Olympic event. Have you tried using a travel agent? I used one last year for the cruise, and they took all the hassle away.      I thought about it, but I feel like they’re always more expensive? And I like the control of doing it myself, picking everything. Although, maybe I've lost that ability to be sensible about it all.      There are good and bad travel agents, that’s true. But even just talking to one can give you a benchmark, some ideas. And honestly, with your teaching schedule, you're stretched as it is. Don’t feel guilty about handing some of it over. Think of it as… delegation!      Delegation. I like that. It sounds very important and professional. So, you think I should at least get a quote?      Absolutely. No harm in it. And have you looked at Airbnb as well as villas? Sometimes you get absolute gems for a surprisingly reasonable price. We did that in Italy a few years back – little apartment overlooking Florence. Stunning.      I have, actually! There are some lovely apartments, but I’m worried about noise.

Right, okay. This is… baffling. Another twenty quid gone to ‘StreamLife Plus’? Seriously? I don’t even  use  StreamLife Plus anymore.      Twenty quid? Sounds like someone’s been a bit click-happy, eh? You and your subscriptions, Liam. It’s a wonder you have anything left for food, let alone going out.      I know, I know! It's just… automatic renewals, innit? I signed up for a free trial ages ago when I was knee-deep in dissertations and needed something to zone out to. Forgot all about it. It’s just annoying, especially as I’m trying to save for… well, you know.      The trip to see your mum? Good on you, son. She deserves a visit. Especially after that story she told me last week about Auntie Brenda trying to set her up with the village butcher.      Oh,  no . Brenda is relentless. Mum was practically in witness protection afterwards. I promised I’d try and get up there for a long weekend next month. It’s just… flights are a nightmare this time of year.      Tell me about it. Remember trying to get back to Barbados for Uncle Cecil’s 80th? Cost an arm and a leg. Still, family’s family. Speaking of which, how’s your sister doing? Still absolutely smashing it with the photography?      Yeah, she’s doing brilliantly. Got a commission for a fashion shoot in London next week. Proper excited, she is. Sent me a mood board, all dark and moody. Looked expensive.      That’s my girl! Always had an eye for something special, your sister. Reminds me a bit of Naomi Campbell, actually. That woman, she just  owns  a room, doesn't she? I saw an interview with her the other day, talking about her early days… incredible.      Yeah, she’s a legend. Though, honestly, I’m more into the football at the moment. Did you catch the City game yesterday? Absolute thriller.      Football? Oh, you know I can’t follow that. Too much running around. I prefer a bit of cricket, something a bit more… strategic. Though, I did hear City won. Your mate, Ben, was going on about it all day. He’s a proper fanatic, that one. Sent me about fifty voice notes.      Ben is… enthusiastic. He’s planning on going to every game next season, wants me to come with him. I think I’ll pass. My ears can’t take it.

Right, well, that’s the biscuit tin raided then. Not much left, is there, Doreen? You always were a bit of a biscuit fiend, weren't you? And David, you look… comfortable. Is that a new armchair?
