It’s about a guy who finds a box of old photographs and gets obsessed with uncovering the story behind them. It's got a bit of mystery, a bit of romance, a bit of… existential dread. You know, my usual.      Sounds right up your street. Berlin, though? You’ve never been, have you?      Nope. I’ve always wanted to go. Imagining it is half the fun, I think. Though I'm probably getting loads of details wrong. I was watching this documentary about it the other day, and the accents are something else.

…and honestly, Mrs. Davies’ feedback was just  brutal . Apparently, little Timmy thinks dinosaurs are purple now, because I told him a story about a lavender Stegosaurus. Lavender! Honestly, the imagination of a six-year-old…      Oh, Mum! You and Timmy, honestly. A lavender Stegosaurus sounds perfectly reasonable to me. It’s more interesting than the usual green, isn’t it? How are you finding it overall, though? Really? First few weeks settled now?      It's… a lot. More than I anticipated. I knew Year One would be energetic, but it's like herding cats sometimes. And the paperwork! Mountains of it. Still, the kids are sweet. And I think I'm finally remembering how to make glitter glue without getting it everywhere. Progress, right?      Definitely progress! You'll be a pro in no time. It’s a good school, isn’t it? I remember visiting with you when you were looking. Still, it sounds exhausting. You  need  a holiday.      Don’t even  mention  holidays. Your father keeps hinting at another caravan trip to Skegness. Honestly, I love him, but Skegness? Again? Last time, the seagull stole my sandwich, and the arcade gave me a headache.      Oh, Dad. He loves his Skegness. Though, I agree, maybe something a little…more sophisticated? We were talking at school, and Sarah mentioned a really lovely cottage in the Cotswolds she rents out. It's near Bourton-on-the-Water. It's beautiful there.      Bourton-on-the-Water…now  that  sounds lovely. Actual scenery, not just amusement arcades and chip shops. We could take Winston. He’d love a good walk in the countryside.      Exactly! And it wouldn’t be too far for us to come down and visit, maybe for a weekend? Or we could all go together for a longer stay. Speaking of which, have you finalised plans for Amelia’s christening? It’s just around the corner.      That’s the source of my current headache, actually. Aunt Susan is insisting on doing the cake. She keeps sending me pictures of increasingly elaborate Easter cakes she's made, and now she’s decided a christening cake  needs  marzipan sheep and a sugar glass fountain.      Oh, Aunt Susan. She does love a flourish, doesn’t she? I remember the Christmas cake with the edible reindeer. It was…ambitious.      Ambitious is an understatement! It looked like a reindeer exploded. I’ve tried to gently steer her towards something simpler, maybe just white icing with some fresh flowers, but she's convinced it won't be special enough.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of marking I had last week was ridiculous. Seventeen essays on the subjunctive mood! Seventeen! You wouldn’t believe the things they try to get away with. One student argued it was a conspiracy by older generations to make grammar difficult.      Oh, bless them. They always have an angle, don’t they? I’m getting that with Year 10 at the moment. They’re all convinced Shakespeare is irrelevant. I tried to explain the enduring themes of jealousy and ambition, but it just went over their heads. They were far more concerned with whether Hamlet had TikTok.      TikTok! Oh, that’s brilliant. Though, I suppose in a way, Shakespeare  was  the TikTok of his day – short, snappy, lots of drama to grab attention. I just feel like I'm constantly battling for their focus. It's exhausting. How’s school treating  you  these days? Still leading the history department?      Still here, still battling. Though, I’m now also on the governing body which…is a whole new level of paperwork and meetings. Honestly, I sometimes think I’d rather be chasing escaped goats. Speaking of which, how’s Barnaby doing? Last I heard he was terrorising the garden?      Terrorising is putting it mildly. He's decided the rose bushes are his personal climbing frame. I’ve got netting up, but he’s a determined little… bundle of fluff. He’s also developed a fondness for stealing my socks. It’s a full-time job just ensuring everything isn’t chewed. It’s the joys of a labrador, I suppose. You never have a dull moment.      Oh, I remember that stage well with Winston. Absolute chaos. Though, Winston preferred shoes to socks. And garden gnomes. He’d parade around with a gnome in his mouth like a prize. It was hilarious, until you realised how much they cost!      Oh, goodness! That's awful… and wonderfully silly. Speaking of things costing money, I was looking at that new skincare range you mentioned last month – the one with the sea buckthorn? It looks amazing, but it’s  so  expensive. Is it actually worth the hype?      It is, honestly. My skin's been awful since the menopause started, all dry and sensitive, and it’s genuinely made a difference. It’s an investment, definitely, but I’ve been using it for about six months now and I've noticed a real improvement.

...Honestly, the charoset was a nightmare to get right this year. I always feel like mine is either too chunky or too…paste-like. Auntie Sylvia’s is legendary, isn’t it? She’d probably scoff at my attempt.      Sylvia’s charoset  is  a masterpiece, darling. Years of perfecting it, I suspect. And she’s not shy about letting you know she’s perfected it. It's the apples, you know. She claims a specific variety, from Kent. Nonsense, probably, but she swears by it.      Kent? Blimey. I just chuck in whatever looks good at the market. Probably explains why mine ends up looking like something the cat dragged in. Though, to be fair, I only offered to do the matzah ball soup, which, thankfully, went down alright. Did anyone actually  like  it?      Mate, the soup was solid. Properly comforting. Though I did spend five minutes trying to figure out if you’d hidden a golf ball in one of the balls. They were massive.      That was the intention! Just kidding. I just…over-compensated, alright? Trying to impress the family.      You did impress, honestly. And it’s nice to see someone else attempt the cooking. It’s always me, slaving over a hot oven. Speaking of ovens, I’ve been thinking about a trip to Italy, specifically Naples. I want to learn proper pizza making.      Naples! Lovely. Though, be warned, their obsession with food rivals ours. And the noise! It's glorious, chaotic noise. Have you been to Paris recently, darling? They do a rather refined take on things there.      Paris is good, yeah. A bit…fussy though, isn’t it? Everything’s tiny portions and charges you £20 for a single olive. I need somewhere less pretentious. I was actually thinking of New York next, maybe over the summer. Do some engineering things, and eat a lot of bagels.      New York? Nice one! I’ve always wanted to go. Although, I'm slightly terrified of the portions. I’m a growing boy, but even  I  might struggle. Did you catch that documentary about food obsessions? The bit about people eating ortolan in France? Horrifying.      Oh god, the ortolan! Covering your head with a napkin and just…gobbling it down whole. Absolutely barbaric. Though, honestly, after a full day of baking, I can sympathise with wanting to shut out the world and just  eat .      It's a very ancient tradition, apparently, linked to ideas of guilt and atonement.

...Honestly, the pacing was just  awful . It felt like they were trying to cram three books worth of plot into a single film. And the casting! Don't even get me started on the casting. They didn’t even  look  like the characters as I pictured them.      Oh, you’re still on about “The Crimson Tide”? I thought you’d calmed down after last week! I quite enjoyed it, actually. Though, I’ll admit, Ms. Hawthorne was…a questionable choice. She lacked the gravitas. But the special effects were stunning.      I haven’t seen that one yet. Is it worth battling the crowds at the cinema for? I've been meaning to go, but work has been relentless. I’m still buried under year-end reports.      Crowds are the least of your worries, darling. It’s a visual spectacle, I’ll give it that. But if you loved the book, prepare to be…disappointed. It’s one of those adaptations that 'takes liberties', which is another way of saying ‘completely ignores the source material’. I'm finding I’m much happier sticking to the books these days.      See, I’m the opposite. I love a good film adaptation, even if it deviates. It’s a new interpretation, isn't it? Though I do understand your frustration when it’s a book you  really  love. Like with the “Bridgerton” series - the books are so much more nuanced, you know?      I’ve read the first “Bridgerton” but I’ve been mostly on an Agatha Christie kick lately. I downloaded a whole bunch to my Kindle. So convenient, isn’t it? I used to be so precious about physical books, but eBooks are a lifesaver when you commute.      Oh, don’t even mention Kindles! I tried, I really did. It just isn’t the same. The smell of the paper, the weight in your hands…you lose all that with an eBook. And the joy of a well-stocked bookshelf! It’s a statement, isn’t it? A personality portrait.      I’m with you on the bookshelves, definitely. Mine are a complete disaster zone, though. A mix of thrillers, biographies, a few gardening books… and a surprising amount of celebrity memoirs. Don’t judge! It’s a guilty pleasure.      No judgment here! I confess to enjoying a good celebrity tell-all. It's nice escapism. Speaking of escapism, are you still working on that blanket, Sarah?

Right, this is… optimistic of Nokia, innit? Making it this fiddly when you've already had three lagers. Honestly, feels like they  want  you to lose the little thing.      You’re such a drama queen, Klaus. It’s perfectly straightforward. See? Pop, click, done. Honestly, you’d think lecturing on the intricacies of the English language would equip you with the dexterity for a SIM card.      It’s a different kind of intricacy, Liv! Analyzing Keats doesn’t prepare you for microplastics! And Finnish pubs aren't exactly known for their bright lighting, are they? This is why I always preferred a good, solid Nokia brick back in the day. You knew where you were. You could practically build a house with one.      Oh, here we go. The Nokia nostalgia is kicking in. You and your 'back in the day' stories. These aren't bricks, Dad. They’re… sleek. And they do more than just make phone calls. Remember when you were moaning about needing a better camera for documenting all the…unique Finnish wildlife?      I wasn’t moaning. I was merely… observing a technological gap. And I eventually bought a separate camera, didn’t I? This one’s got a 64-megapixel lens. It’s obscene. All I need is to figure out how to actually  use  it.      I can help with that. I've been playing with the settings already. It's actually really intuitive. It has a "Pro" mode, if you want to get all fiddly like you love, but the auto-settings are genuinely good. Right, are you in? There we go. Now, let's get to the language settings. You wouldn't want it thinking you’re speaking Finnish, would you?      Good point. Though, honestly, trying to decipher Finnish menus is half the fun. Increases cognitive flexibility, or so I tell my students. Though, maybe not after three lagers. What about the roaming? Is it automatically set up, or…? I don’t want to come home to a bill the size of the national debt.      It should be. I set up international roaming with Vodafone before we left. But let’s double-check just to be sure. Hold on… Okay, it looks like it’s active. It's capped at £49 a day, so even  you  wouldn’t manage to rack up a national debt in a day.      I resent that. I’m perfectly capable of responsible phone usage.

Mum, do you think Leo would like a red panda for his birthday? Like a… stuffed one, obviously. Not a real one! Though, wouldn’t that be amazing?      A real red panda? Honey, as amazing as that  would  be, I think Leo’s mum might have a few things to say about a wild animal turning up on their doorstep! A stuffed one is a lovely idea, though. He did go on about them at the zoo, didn’t he? They’re a bit…faffy, aren’t they? Always hanging around in trees.      Yeah! He said they look like a mix between a bear and a fox. And they eat bamboo! It’s so cool. I still think a Malamute would be better, though. Remember that one we saw at the park? Huge and fluffy. Like a walking cloud.      Woof woof! Fluffy!      Someone agrees with you about the fluffy part! Yes, that Malamute  was  beautiful. But a Malamute needs so much exercise! And space. Leo’s garden isn’t exactly massive. Plus, you know,  we  barely have enough room for little Finn here and all his toys. Speaking of Finn, he's decided pots are instruments.      True. My cat, Winston, hardly needs any exercise. He just sleeps all day and judges me. It’s brilliant. Still, a dog would be good for playing football with. And maybe Leo feels a bit lonely since his Grandma moved to Spain.      That’s a good point, darling. Maybe a pet  is  something he’d really appreciate. Right, red panda versus… what else? Are we thinking specifically pet-themed for his present, or just generally? We still need to sort out the party, too. It’s only three weeks away.      I was thinking of doing a sort of animal theme for the party! We could have animal masks and… and a pin the tail on the… red panda! And maybe a cake with animal crackers around the edge?      Cake! More!      Always a fan of cake, aren’t you? Okay, animal theme sounds good. We'll need to book the community hall again, I think. It's easier than trying to fit everyone in here. And I need to ask Mrs. O’Malley if she'll make the sandwiches again - she makes the best ham and cheese triangles.      Okay, I can help with the decorations. And maybe I can ask Dad to help with the pin-the-tail game?

...and honestly, the sherry was flowing  free  that Christmas. Your Aunt Mildred, God rest her soul, believed a little tipple cured everything. A cold? Sherry. A bad argument? Sherry. The Queen on television? Definitely sherry.      Mildred was a character, alright. Though I always suspected she just liked an excuse. Remember when she tried to convince us eggnog was a health food? Something about the eggs being "full of goodness"?      Oh, I've heard the stories! Gran always said Mildred could sell ice to Eskimos. But Christmas at Bath was always… proper. Everything was so  organised . We didn’t have the chaotic fun we had up North, y'know? Everything had a place, a time… it was lovely, but a bit…stuffy.      Stuffy is a good word for it, yeah. My family Christmases were…loud. Manila is a whole different level of festive. It’s not just decorations, it’s just  everywhere . Music blasting, people visiting all day, the smell of lechon roasting… it’s relentless. And the karaoke. Oh, the karaoke.      Lechon? What’s that?      Roasted pig. Whole hog. Crispy skin, juicy meat… it’s a big deal. They put it on a spit and it’s the centrepiece of everything. Everyone fights for the crackling. It’s completely different to turkey, obviously.      Sounds…substantial. We always had a goose, mostly. A bit less fuss than a whole pig, eh? Though trying to carve a goose is a feat in itself.      Geese are notoriously difficult. I always maintained that turkey was the safest bet. Less bone, easier carving. And you can make fabulous stock with the carcass.      We’ve always done turkey. Though last year, me and my mates tried to deep-fry one at uni. That was…an experience. It nearly set the garden on fire. Landlord was  fuming .      Deep-fried turkey?! Seriously? That sounds… dangerous.      It was! We watched a YouTube tutorial, thought we were experts. Turns out, YouTube doesn’t account for a Lancashire gale!      Young people! Honestly. No common sense. Speaking of different places… I was thinking about when we went to Italy, Arthur. Remember Florence? The food was divine.      Florence was lovely. Though I did get a bit of grief trying to order a pint in a café. They looked at me like I’d asked for the moon. Everything’s espresso over there.      Yeah, you gotta adapt. I was in Barcelona last summer. Tried ordering a "large" drink, and they gave me… well, it was practically a thimbleful.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of audio I had to transcribe this week was  insane . It was all police interviews, thankfully not overly graphic, but just… endless. Three hours straight of someone describing the colour of a cardigan. A  cardigan , David!      Three hours? Good grief, Amelia. That does sound… tedious. You’d think they’d have a better grasp of cardigan colours by then. Though, I suppose details are details when you’re trying to build a case. How are you holding up? You looked a bit frazzled when you came in.      Speaking of frazzled, have either of you started that new Scandi-noir series, ‘The Frozen Shore’? It's utterly brilliant, but also deeply unsettling. The lead detective is  obsessed  with artisanal bread, which is a bizarre character trait, but somehow it works.      I haven’t, no. I’ve been lost in the world of cardigans, as you know. But I did download the first episode. It’s on the Kindle, isn’t it? I've been trying to get through my backlog on that thing. It’s a black hole of half-read books and free samples.      Oh, that’s the one Fiona was raving about. She said the plot twists are incredible, but warned me it’s seriously dark. I'm currently re-watching ‘Vera’. Brenda Blethyn is just… phenomenal. Solid, dependable detective work. No need for fancy bread or frozen shores. Just good, honest Northumberland grit.      ‘Vera’ is a classic! Though, I do enjoy a bit of complicated psychological turmoil with my crime fiction. Fiona has good taste. And yes, it’s on Amazon Prime, Amelia. You were right to download it. It’s far too good to miss. Are you thinking of ordering takeaway tonight? I’m completely lacking inspiration.      I’d be right up for that. I’m officially brain-fried from listening to people describe… things. Indian? Thai? Maybe even pizza? Anything that doesn't involve describing knitwear.      Indian sounds good to me. There's that new place, ‘Spice Haven’, opened near the High Street. Apparently, it's fantastic. Although, knowing our luck, we'll spend the entire evening trying to decipher the menu. Remember that Bangladeshi place last year where everything came with a warning about chili levels?      Oh god, yes! Poor Amelia nearly set her mouth on fire. I think she was muttering about needing a fire extinguisher with her naan bread.      It wasn’t  nearly  on fire!

Honestly, Marjorie, I don't know  what  to do with 'im. He's been moping about for a week now, ever since that letter came from the council.      Oh, Arthur, you mean David? Still on about the garden, is he? Honestly, a bit of overgrown rosemary isn’t the end of the world. He's worse than a child when he doesn’t get his own way.      Morning, you two. What’s all the grumbling about? Sounds like a storm brewing. Garden disputes again?      Not exactly a dispute, Charles. He's taken it as a personal attack. The council said the hedges were getting too high, blocking the pavement, and sent a notice. He's convinced they’re deliberately targeting  him . Says old Mrs. Higgins next door has been whispering to ‘em.      Oh, that man! Always imagining conspiracies. He’s got a wonderful imagination, David does, but it gets him into trouble sometimes. He insists Mrs. Higgins is jealous of his prize-winning dahlias.      Now, now. Let’s be reasonable. He’s always been a bit…sensitive, hasn’t he? And losing his gardening is a big thing for him, particularly after retiring. It’s what gave him structure.      Structure? He spent forty years pottering about! He's had plenty of structure. It's just the principle of it, I reckon. He hates being told what to do. Reminds me of his grandfather, stubborn as a mule, that one.      He  needs  a hobby, Arthur. Honestly, since he stopped volunteering at the library, he’s been lost. I suggested joining a walking group, but he said his knees couldn’t take it. And the book club? “Too many opinions,” he said. Honestly!      Walking group might have been ambitious, Marjorie. But the book club… that's a shame. Perhaps we need to frame this council notice differently. Not as an attack, but as a…a community responsibility.      Easy for  you  to say, Charles. You have your businesses and your meetings. He’s just… well, he’s not used to not  doing  something. He's always felt a bit useless, even though I tell him he's not. Never really found his footing career-wise, poor lad.      Don’t start on that again, Arthur. He tried a few things! Remember that short spell selling antiques? It lasted all of three weeks. And the attempt at learning to play the ukulele? That was… memorable.

Right, so, Horace is officially winding down. Twenty minutes left of his reign of spreadsheets, isn't it? Feels like a small victory for humanity, frankly.      Tell me about it. I swear, that man could find a way to make data entry  soul-crushing . Though, to be fair, the funding application deadlines  are  looming. At least we’re nearly through it. Anyone got plans for celebrating freedom?      I was thinking of just collapsing into a heap on my sofa with a large mug of something hot and a good book. Serious self-care is required after that project phase.      Sounds lovely, honestly. I might brave a trip to the pub. Need to re-socialise after staring at a screen for eight hours a day. Anyone fancy joining? The Eagle’s doing that two-for-one deal on craft beers.      Ooh, tempting! That does sound good, though I’m battling a slight urge to just…prep for next week. Old habits die hard, I guess, being American and all. We’re always gearing up for the ‘next thing’.      Prep can wait, Sarah! We deserve a bit of fun. Pub sounds brilliant. Though, before we get too carried away, I had a bit of a rescue mission on my way in.      Rescue mission? What, did Horace try to hold a data point hostage?      No, nothing so dramatic. A bee. It was trapped in the doorway of the printing house, buzzing frantically. I managed to coax it onto a piece of card and relocate it to the flowerbeds. Felt very David Attenborough for a moment.      Aw, that's sweet of you, Chloe. You’re a good egg. I’d probably just have panicked and run in the opposite direction. Bees and I have a…complicated relationship.      I admire your bravery! I'm usually the one screaming for someone else to deal with anything remotely creepy-crawly.      That’s really kind, Chloe. It’s those little acts that make a difference. Back home, we’re constantly hearing about declining bee populations. Every little helps, you know?      Absolutely. Though, you’ve now officially raised the bar. I’m going to have to save a kitten or something to compete with that. So, pub then? Around sixish?      Six sounds perfect. Gives us just enough time for Horace to completely disappear from our lives. And maybe a quick trip to the stationery cupboard to burn all remaining copies of his project reports….

...and then Mr. Davies actually  said  that my essay on Brontë was "lacking in…passion." Lacking in passion! Like, hello? It’s  Wuthering Heights ! It's literally built on obsessive passion, bordering on unhinged. What more does he want from me, a dramatic reading with interpretive dance?      Oh, Mr. Davies. He’s such a drama queen himself, it’s ironic he’d accuse anyone else of lacking passion. Seriously though, that  is  harsh. Your essays are always really well-written. Did you at least get a good mark?      A B+. A B+! I was aiming for an A . I put so much work into it, researching all the contextual stuff, the gothic influences, the social commentary… everything. It's just…frustrating. And Maya got an A . Maya, who spent the entire lesson doodling unicorns!      Ugh, Maya. She gets away with murder. Honestly, sometimes I think teachers just feel sorry for her because she’s… well, Maya. I got a B+ too, on the history assignment. The one on the Suffragettes.      No way! That's rubbish! You  love  history, and you’re brilliant at remembering dates and stuff. What did Mrs. Peterson say?      She said my analysis was “superficial.” Superficial! I wrote like, two pages on Emmeline Pankhurst’s tactics! What’s more analysis than that? It feels like they’re intentionally marking us down this term. Is it just me, or is everyone feeling it?      Definitely not just you. Everyone in English is moaning. Liam reckons Davies is having a bad divorce or something and is taking it out on us. Which, honestly, sounds plausible. It’s just… stressful. We’ve got mocks next month, and I need good grades for Sixth Form. My mum keeps going on about Cambridge, and I don't want to disappoint her.      Cambridge? Wow, big pressure. My parents are just happy if I pass. They’re like, “as long as you’re happy,” which is nice, but also kind of… unhelpful when it comes to figuring out what I actually  want  to do. I’m thinking maybe art school.      Really? That's cool! You're so talented. Remember that painting you did of the river last summer? It was amazing. Mr. Harrison in Art always raves about you.      Thanks. But it feels risky, you know? Not doing A-Levels, going down a different route. Everyone else seems to have it all planned out – medicine, law, engineering…

...and honestly, the client just kept going on about synergy.  Synergy ! Like I haven’t heard that buzzword a million times before. It was a fifteen-minute meeting that could’ve been an email, easily. How was your day, actually, Clara? You were pretty quiet on the drive over.      Oh, it was… a day. Mostly spreadsheets and fielding calls from people who’ve forgotten how to attach files to emails. Peak admin, really. It’s just… frustrating when you explain something five times and they  still  don’t get it. It feels so pointless sometimes.      Tell me about it, love. Sales is much the same, dealing with people who haven’t read the brochure. Or worse, read it and chosen to ignore it. Though at least with spreadsheets you’re battling inanimate objects. People are… more complicated. This lasagne is lovely, though. Really, really good. Did you make it from scratch, Clara?      Thanks, Mum. Yeah, I did. It’s a Jamie Oliver recipe, actually. Easier than it looks. I was trying to be productive, you know? Distract myself from the email abyss.      Jamie Oliver, eh? Fancy. I’m more of a beans-on-toast kind of guy, if I’m being honest. Though I can definitely appreciate a good lasagne. So, spreadsheets and email… still enjoying the admin life, then? You were talking about maybe looking at something different after your Masters?      I am enjoying  parts  of it. It's steady, I suppose, and the benefits are alright. It's just... not exactly  inspiring . I’ve been having a little browse on LinkedIn, seeing what’s out there, but nothing’s really jumped out at me yet. It’s hard, isn't it? Finding something that's both interesting  and  pays the bills.      It is, petal. Absolutely. Don't rush into anything. When your father retired, he jumped at the first thing that came along, a little consultancy job, thought it'd be grand. Turned out he hated it. Spent six months miserable before finally admitting it wasn’t for him. Sometimes no job is better than a bad job, you know?      She's right. You've got time, Clara. Don’t settle just to have something. What about using your German? You grew up over there, right? Could you maybe do something translation-related?      I did! Wegberg. I spent my early years there. It’s… funny, I don’t feel particularly German anymore, which is a bit weird.

Honestly, Sarah, it’s just been  one  of those weeks. The Henderson account is circling the drain, and then Leo gets a detention. A detention! For…talking back to Mr. Davies. Apparently.      Oh, Leo. That boy's got a mouth on him, hasn’t he? Mr. Davies is a bit of a stickler, though, I’ll give you that. My Darren got detention from him back in the day, for less, I reckon. What’d he say?      That’s the thing, he won’t  tell  me precisely. Just “disrespectful behaviour.” He's becoming so withdrawn lately, it's like pulling teeth to get a straight answer out of him. It’s probably just teenage angst, but it feels…different, you know? And then his auntie Carol called, saying she’s been having tests.      Carol? Oh, bless her. That's… that's not good. What kind of tests?      She wouldn’t say over the phone, just said the doctor wants to “rule things out.” Naturally, my mum’s already convinced it’s the worst-case scenario and has been ringing me every hour. I'm trying to stay positive, but… with everything else…      Right. Well, that's a lot to carry. It's amazing how one thing after another just piles up, isn't it? Look, don't get yourself worked up over Carol until you know for sure. Your mum, bless her heart, she’s always been a worrier. And Leo – teenagers, honestly. They're a mystery wrapped in an attitude.      You’re right. Easier said than done, of course. I’m supposed to be finalising the quarterly reports this weekend, but I just can’t focus. I was thinking of postponing that weekend trip to see Emily in Bristol. She just got her promotion, and I really wanted to celebrate with her.      Oh, Emily! That’s brilliant news for her! But maybe you  should  postpone. You sound absolutely exhausted. You need to be here, solid, for Carol, and for Leo. Bristol will still be there.      I suppose you’re right. Honestly, Sarah, I don’t know what I’d do without you being here. Not just for the cleaning - truly, thank you again for squeezing in extra hours this week, it’s been a lifesaver - but you just… keep things grounded.      It’s no bother at all, love. Honestly. And that's what friends are for. Plus, someone needs to tell you to stop running around like a headless chicken every now and then.

Honestly, I'm knackered. Proper knackered. That shift last night was a  mad  one. Bank Holiday weekend, you know how it is. Everyone decided Hull wasn't far enough to travel, and descended on our little pub like locusts.      Oh, no way! Bank Holiday shifts are the worst. I’m lucky, relatively speaking. My job at the bookshop is pretty chilled, even when it’s busy. Mostly just students needing last-minute textbooks or panicking about essays. What was so hectic?      Everything! Just sheer volume of people. And then the arguments. Honestly, you wouldn't believe the drama over a pint of lager. One bloke reckoned someone had deliberately spilled their drink, which turned into a full-blown shouting match. Had to break that up. Then another one tried to pay with Monopoly money!      Monopoly money?! You're joking! Some people are just…something else. I can't imagine dealing with that after a long day of studying. You did your Masters, right? Is bartending just… temporary then?      It was supposed to be temporary, yeah. After finishing my degree in Archaeology I thought I’d be, like, excavating Roman ruins or something. Instead, I'm pulling pints and dodging flying glasses. But honestly, the money’s good. And it's… surprisingly social. Plus, it pays the rent, which is a miracle in this city, never mind back home.      Salford  is  pricey. I'm still living with my parents in Nottingham during term time, which is a godsend, to be fair. I’m working to save up for a deposit for next year though. But a Masters in Archaeology? That's seriously cool! What were you hoping to do with that?      Always loved history, especially local history. Hull’s full of it, surprisingly. I wanted to specialise in maritime archaeology, bits of old ships and stuff. There just weren’t any jobs going and I needed something  now . It's a bit soul-crushing admitting I’m using a postgraduate degree to suggest people try the local ale.      Don’t beat yourself up about it! Loads of people end up doing stuff completely unrelated to their degrees. I’m doing A-Levels and I have absolutely no clue what I actually want to  do . I’m pretty sure I'll change my mind at least three times before uni applications are even due. My mum keeps saying I should train to be a solicitor, but honestly…      Solicitors are alright, I suppose.

...Honestly, the all-inclusive was a lifesaver. Not having to think about budgeting for every meal, or where to go… pure bliss. Though, Geoff did spend the entire week trying to convince the hotel chef to make him a proper Yorkshire pudding.      Oh, Geoff. That sounds… predictable. He's a stickler for his Yorkshire, isn’t he? My Sarah just wants sun, sea, and a good book. We’re thinking of Portugal next year, maybe the Algarve. It's a little more low-key than some of the places we’ve been.      Portugal’s lovely. I spent a few weeks in Lisbon years ago. The custard tarts are divine, absolutely divine! Though the hills… my legs were screaming at me by the end of it. You’d think after walking the Wicklow mountains, I’d be used to it, wouldn’t you?      Lisbon is fantastic. We did a team-building weekend there a couple of years back. Got absolutely lost in Alfama, but it was worth it. Speaking of hills, did anyone else follow the drama with that influencer who tried to climb Snowdon in flip-flops?      Oh,  that  one! Saw something about that on Facebook. Absolutely ridiculous! People have no sense. It’s a mountain, not a seaside stroll. Proper boots are essential. Though, I admit, I’m more of a beach person myself. Give me a deckchair and a good magazine, and I’m happy.      Flip-flops on Snowdon! Honestly! It’s a rescue waiting to happen. I quite like a bit of a hike, but I'm no base jumper or anything. More of a gentle ramble kind of chap. Sarah drags me on the more strenuous ones, says I need to ‘get out of my comfort zone’.      Comfort zones are overrated, love. Though I used to have a nephew who thought climbing a ladder was getting out of his comfort zone! He was a funny lad. We went to Majorca once, and he insisted on trying to order a pint of Guinness. The look on the barman's face… priceless.      Oh, brilliant! That  is  a good story. You get some real characters on holiday, don’t you? Last year in Greece, we had a gentleman who tried to barter with the souvenir shop owner using buttons.  Buttons !      Buttons?! Now that’s dedication to getting a bargain! I once tried to haggle over the price of a keyring in Spain, and the stallholder just looked at me like I'd lost my mind.

Oof, that looked nasty. Honestly, the diving in this game is ridiculous. Feels like every touch is an opportunity for a dramatic fall.      You’re telling me. It's worse than a soap opera, this. They’ve clearly been taking notes from the Premier League’s leading thespians. Still, gotta admire the commitment to the…art of deception, I suppose.      Art? It’s a disgrace! Proper football fans like my dad would be spinning in his grave. He’d say they need to bring back proper tackling, like in the old days. None of this tiptoeing around.      Your dad was a hard man, though, wasn't he? Remember him trying to explain offside to me at that Sunderland game? Took about an hour and a whiteboard. He was  passionate .      Passionate is an understatement. He lived and breathed Sunderland. It’s why I still follow them, even though they consistently break my heart. And you, supporting Villa… that's just asking for trouble.      Hey! Villa are coming up in the world. We’ve got Emery now, things are looking good. Besides, someone has to balance out your eternal pessimism. It’s a team effort. Speaking of effort, fancy ordering some food? This is proper viewing fuel territory.      Ooh, yes. I'm starving. What are you thinking? I’m craving something utterly unhealthy, like a proper chippy. A battered sausage, chips…the works. Proper northern comfort food.      A chippy? That’s a commitment. I was leaning more towards a burger, maybe a Deliveroo situation. We’ve got that new place, ‘Burger Bliss’, everyone’s raving about. Apparently, they do a double cheeseburger with bacon, onion rings  and  jalapenos…      Jalapenos? That sounds…intense. Look, I appreciate the burger suggestion, truly. But you haven't lived until you've had a proper Sunderland takeaway. It's a whole different league. They do this thing with mushy peas and curry sauce…it's a revelation.      Mushy peas and curry sauce? That  does  sound…interesting. A bit alien, frankly. I’m a ketchup man myself, simple and effective. See, this is exactly what I mean about our regional differences. It's built into our DNA! You lot up North have a different culinary code.      It's not a code, it's  superior taste , thank you very much! Seriously though, it's just…different. We appreciate a good, greasy, satisfying meal. It’s comforting. Makes you feel like everything will be alright, even if Sunderland are losing.

Right, this is proper nice, Mum. It feels…calm in here. Not like Manchester at all. Though I suspect the traffic’s still pretty fierce getting  to  Sale, eh?      Oh, Manchester's a whirlwind. Always has been. Loud and busy. Sale’s alright. A bit… slower, of course. But peaceful. And the buses are regular, which is the main thing when you don’t drive anymore. Though your grandfather, God rest him, he’d have a fit if he knew I relied on buses. He loved his cars. Remember that green Austin Healey? Beautiful thing.      Oh,  do  I. He polished that thing every Sunday without fail. Drove it like he stole it, your Granddad did. Nearly gave us all heart attacks a few times! You were just a little lad then, weren’t you, Liam? Barely big enough to see over the dashboard.      Just about. I remember the smell of leather and petrol mostly. And being told to  not  touch anything. Which, naturally, meant I wanted to touch everything. Speaking of which, I’m trying to get my head around this new project at work. Complete nightmare. They want me to streamline the entire logistics process, but nobody seems to agree on  how .      Streamline? Sounds like a fancy word for ‘make everyone do more with less’. They always want that, don’t they? Happened at the biscuit factory where your uncle worked. They streamlined him right out of a job!      Now, Mum! Don’t be so pessimistic. Liam’s a project manager, he’s good at this sort of thing. What’s the actual problem? Is it people being stubborn?      It's a bit of both, honestly. We’ve got a team in Germany who swear by one system, another one in Spain who think it’s utterly archaic, and then the folks here just want to stick with what they know. It’s like herding cats. I spent all morning on a video call just arguing about spreadsheets!      Spreadsheets! Good heavens. Back in my day, we used ledgers and pencils. And if something went wrong, you just…fixed it. No endless meetings and fancy computer programs. Though, I’ll admit, ledgers were messy. Your grandmother was always scolding me for my handwriting.      Your handwriting  was  terrible, Mum! I remember helping you with your letters to Auntie Mabel. It looked like a spider had walked across the page. Liam, maybe you need to get everyone in a room, all together?

Honestly, Leo, you’ve barely touched it. It’s Pancake Day! It’s practically a national requirement to devour at least three.      It’s…floppy. And there's lemon on it. I don’t  like  lemon.      Mine’s okay. I put loads of syrup on. But Miss Davies said in assembly today that too much sugar is bad for your teeth.      Well, Miss Davies is right, sweetheart. But it's Pancake Day! A little bit of a treat won’t hurt. She was talking about  all  the time though, wasn’t she? That whole assembly was a bit of a lecture on healthy eating. Though, seeing some of the packed lunches…it's a good job, really. I had one little boy today who genuinely hadn't had breakfast.      What did you  do ?      I snuck him a biscuit with his milk, Leo. Just a little one. It breaks your heart, doesn’t it? You think about children not having enough, and then you see it right there in your classroom. It makes you realise how lucky we are.      We had fish fingers and peas for tea last night. That’s lucky, isn’t it?      Very lucky indeed, darling. Very lucky. Leo, really? Not even a tiny bite? Think of all the children who would  love  to have even a floppy pancake with lemon.      But it’s…squishy.      Okay, okay. We’ll scrape off the lemon. Deal? Now, we were talking about weekend plans. I was thinking, if the weather holds, we could possibly go to the Science Museum? You two both loved it last time.      Ooh, yes! The space bit! Can we go to the bit with the rockets?      We can certainly try! Your Dad said he might be free to come with us, which would be lovely. Although… he mentioned something about a gig at the Festival Hall on Saturday evening.      Rockets are better than music.      That’s a strong opinion. Sometimes, music  is  pretty good. Remember when we went to that children’s concert last year? You enjoyed that, didn’t you?      Not  really . It was loud.      Fair enough. Now, finish your pancakes – even just a little bit – and then it’s teeth-brushing time. Honestly, it’s like a military operation getting you two to brush properly. You’d think you were being asked to climb Mount Everest.      I don’t like the minty toothpaste.      We talked about this, Leo.

Honestly, this Kung Pao chicken is  amazing . Best takeaway we’ve had in ages. Though, it’s probably just because I was starving after that…whole thing with Auntie Brenda’s funeral yesterday. Still feels a bit weird, doesn’t it? She was…a character.      It really does. And yes, massively weird. I keep expecting her to ring complaining about the cricket being on instead of Antiques Roadshow. Though, honestly, the service was lovely. Mum said she’d have been thrilled with the turnout. And the buffet afterwards was…substantial.      Substantial is an understatement! I think I ate my weight in sausage rolls. It was… a lot. But good, you know? It's nice to remember her like that, surrounded by family. It's just…weird not having her little jabs at my career choices anymore. She always said being an administrator was 'sensible, dear, but hardly exciting'.      She wasn’t wrong, was she? No offence, Amelia. Though, someone has to keep the world turning. I heard old Mr. Henderson from the village was there. Apparently, he’s convinced Brenda knew the secret to growing prize-winning marrows. Kept asking your Mum if she’d gotten the tip.      Seriously? Marrows? That’s Brenda’s legacy now? Giant vegetables? It’s… poetic, somehow. Speaking of weird legacies, remember when Ben tried to convince us he  was  Bob the Builder for like, a whole month after university?      Oh my god, yes! The hard hat, the little tool belt… he’d walk around saying “Can we fix it?” to absolutely everyone. Even the postman! It was mortifying when he tried it on Sarah’s mum.      I’d almost forgotten about that. He was a menace. It was peak Ben. Did anyone see that article about the new film coming out – the remake of that old disaster movie,  The Swarm ? It looks absolutely terrible. All CGI bees attacking Los Angeles.      I skimmed something about it. Predictable stuff, I expect. I’m more looking forward to that new documentary about the Amazon rainforest. Saw a trailer for it - looks genuinely important, and terrifying. It’s just… everything’s so doom and gloom in the news, isn't it?      Tell me about it. I was reading about that flooding in Pakistan. Awful. It's just relentless. No wonder everyone's glued to their phones, doomscrolling. You two seen Liam lately? We haven’t heard from him since… well, before the funeral.

…and honestly, Auntie Mabel always did have a knack for knowing  exactly  what everyone was up to. Even when she pretended she didn't! Remember when she ‘accidentally’ overheard us planning her surprise party? The look on her face was priceless, even though she immediately pretended to be indignant.      Indignant! That woman could weaponize indignation, she could. Though she had a good heart, Mabel. A good heart, despite being a bit of a… busybody. Reminds me a little of your grandmother, actually, Sarah. Always needing to know the details.      It’s definitely a family trait, isn't it? Mum’s the same. “Are you  sure  you’re warm enough, darling?” "Have you eaten properly?" Even now, she calls me at least twice a week just to check in. Though, to be fair, she was thrilled when I moved closer.      It’s comforting, isn’t it? Even when it’s a bit… smothering. I was thinking about old Mr. Henderson next door at the old house, though. He always used to sit on his porch, watching the world go by. I wonder what became of him?      Henderson…bless him. Proper gentleman. Used to offer me a biscuit whenever I was pottering about in the garden. Used to talk about his time in the RAF, he did. Said flying was the only thing that truly gave him a sense of freedom. Funny, considering how much everyone worries about flying these days.      It  is  odd, isn’t it? We’re statistically so much safer in planes now than ever before, yet everyone’s terrified. I had a bit of turbulence on the way back from that conference in Barcelona last month, and honestly, it was less the shaking that bothered me, and more the collective intake of breath from everyone on board!      Exactly! It's the  reaction  that's the scary part. It's all that collective anxiety. I saw something online about those driverless cars, and I feel the same way. People are so resistant to letting go of control, even if the technology is demonstrably safer.      Driverless cars! Honestly. I can barely trust young people to drive  with  a brain, let alone a computer! Though, I’ll admit, my eyesight isn’t what it used to be. I haven't driven since… well, since they took my license. Makes popping to the shops a bit of a mission, it does.      It's a good job you've got Sarah to run errands!

Right, almost ready! Just needs a little more soy sauce, I think. Honestly, this stir-fry is taking  ages . It's a bit ambitious for a Tuesday, especially after piano practice and...everything else.      Is it for the dragon, Miss Emily? A dragon needs  lots  of food, doesn't it?      It is sort of for the dragon, Lily. We're celebrating Chinese New Year, remember? Dragons are very important in Chinese New Year stories. They bring good luck!      I drew a dragon! Look! It's got, like, ten heads! And sparkly scales!      Wow, Thomas! Ten heads! That’s a  very  powerful dragon. You’ve used so many colours. It's amazing! It’s much better than mine, I just did a simple one.      Mine has wings! And it breathes fire,  whoosh ! Like a planet exploding!      Oh, so it’s a space dragon then? Exploding planets are good, very dramatic. You two are so creative. Speaking of planets, did you know that in Chinese astrology there's a zodiac, and each year is represented by an animal? This year is the Year of the Dragon. It's like a horoscope, but for the whole year.      Is it like when Mrs. Davies teaches us about the solar system? And Saturn has rings?      It's a bit like that, yes! Except instead of planets, it's animals. It’s a completely different way of thinking about time. Now, about this stir-fry... who's excited for noodles?      Me! Can we have prawn crackers too? And chopsticks?      Definitely prawn crackers. And yes, we can try chopsticks. Though, you know, forks are perfectly acceptable too! It’s tricky to master chopsticks. Remember last year, Thomas, when you tried to pick up a noodle and it landed on your head?      It was slippery! And mum laughed!      Your mum has a good sense of humour. So, Lily, how was aerial hoop today? Did you manage that new move Mr. Harrison showed you?      I  almost  got it! I did the pull-up part, but then I wiggled too much and nearly fell off! But it was fun! We talked about Barbie and the Great Adventure in between tries.      Barbie and the Great Adventure? That’s an oldie but a goodie! I remember watching that when I was little. You have a very busy schedule, you two. Drum lessons tomorrow, right, Thomas?      Yes! And I got a sticker from Mr. Nelson for playing the snare drum really loud.

...Honestly, the gelato here is just  different . I mean, I make a pretty decent pistachio gelato back home, but this… this is another level. It's lighter, somehow, and the pistachio actually  tastes  of pistachio, not just almond extract and green dye.      You’re telling me! I had a lemon one earlier, and it was like sunshine in a cone. Though, I’m still getting used to how quickly Italians knock back an espresso. Back in London, it’s a  ritual . A slow, considered thing. Here, it's down in three seconds flat and then back to business.      It’s a survival tactic, love. Gotta keep the energy up! Running a café teaches you that. Though Rome's a bit more laid-back than Birmingham, even. Everything feels… slower. Apart from the scooters, obviously. Those are terrifying.      Terrifying but efficient. Gotta respect the hustle. This is a good spot, though, yeah? Much quieter than some of the tourist traps we wandered through earlier. And the wine’s decent. Better than what I’m used to pouring at ‘The Bean Scene’ back in Melbourne, let me tell you.      It is lovely. I was worried our AirBnB would be miles out, but it’s actually a really good location. A little walk, but totally manageable. Did anyone else struggle with the check-in instructions though? It was all in Italian, and my Duolingo is  not  up to deciphering directions to a hidden key box.      Mate, don't even  start  on the AirBnB saga. I ended up just messaging the host a dozen times with increasingly frantic English. Thankfully, she spoke some. I’m fairly certain she thought I was completely incompetent. She kept replying with things like “Prossimo alla porta rossa” and I was just staring at my phone like a lemon.      Oh, that’s classic! I always try to learn a few basics before I go anywhere. “Buongiorno,” “Grazie,” “Dove il bagno?” – essentials, really. It at least shows you’re making an effort. Plus, it usually gets you a better price at the market. Italians appreciate politeness.      Fair enough. I'm useless with languages. Always have been. Tried learning Italian before, you know? Thought it'd be romantic, getting to order coffee like a local. Lasted about a week. Kept accidentally asking for a cat instead of a hat.      Oh no! That's brilliant! Okay, so, dinner plans. I was thinking Trastevere.

…and honestly, the Pinterest boards are just  stressing  me out. Like, do we  need  a bespoke macrame favour for every single guest? It feels…excessive, even for Jess.      Oh, absolutely excessive! Jess loves a bit of flair, but even she’d probably admit that’s taking the biscuit. Remember Sarah’s hen do? The personalised seed packets? Half of them ended up being accidentally composted.      Oh god, the seed packets! Disaster. Honestly, I’m leaning towards less ‘craft-a-thon’ and more ‘actually enjoy ourselves’. Jess isn’t massively into…well, all that. She's more of a cocktails and questionable dancing kind of girl.      Precisely! That’s why I was thinking we lean into the ‘glamour’ side of things. Maybe a cocktail-making class? Or a nice spa day? We could still  do  something, just…less glue and glitter. My brain hurts just thinking about it. Plus, I’ve sourced a couple of really cute venues – Rosie and Ali Bonds, remember? They do amazing afternoon tea.      Ooh, Rosie and Ali Bonds! That sounds perfect, actually. Jess  loves  a good afternoon tea. Much more her vibe. And a cocktail class…yes! That solves so many problems. We don’t have to be brilliant crafters, we just get to drink fancy things. It’s a win-win.      It is! I could potentially design some cute little cocktail recipe cards as favours, then? A little nod to the theme, but minimal effort on the day. And potentially reusable!      Brilliant idea, Chloe! See? You’re the Mac Artworker, you  solve  problems with visuals and clever design. I'm just good at supplying moral support and eating cake.      We all have our strengths! Okay, so afternoon tea at Rosie and Ali Bonds, then cocktail class…anyone allergic to anything? Or vehemently opposed to gin?      I'm fine with everything. Though, maybe a warning out to everyone about the prosecco. Last time Jess and I had a full bottle between us, we ended up trying to teach a pigeon to do tricks.      Oh my god, I completely forgot about that! The pigeon was  not  impressed.      Honestly, legendary. Okay, no pigeon-training allowed at the hen do. Strict rule. What about the guest list? Have we finalised everything? I keep getting messages asking if plus-ones are a thing.      I think we’re pretty much there. Just waiting on confirmation from a couple of Jess’s uni friends.

Right, so this is where I completely fail at risotto. It always ends up either gluey or still crunchy. You've made it a dozen times, haven't you? Seriously, how do you  do  it?      Loads of patience, mainly. And good stock. That's the key. You can’t skimp on the stock, you know? Though, to be fair, you were a bit under the weather last time you tried. Maybe the fine motor skills weren’t quite there.      Oh, don't remind me. I felt absolutely dreadful. That bug going around the school… knocked me sideways. I actually had to call in sick, which, let me tell you, is basically unheard of for me. I hate letting people down.      You needed to rest, though. You were looking peaky. Bright red face, all that. You pushed yourself too hard marking those art briefs, didn’t you? It's just paperwork, man.      Easy for you to say, Mr. ‘I spend my days discussing the nuances of the semi-colon’. They  matter ! It's students' grades. Besides, I was hoping to get a head start applying for that artist residency in Italy. They want a portfolio review, and... well, I'm still tweaking things.      Italy, eh? That sounds amazing. Whereabouts? Florence? Rome?      A little place near Bologna. It's a small, old farmhouse they've converted. All the artists stay on-site. I’ve been looking at hotels nearby, just in case it’s… not quite what I expect. Online photos can be deceiving, can't they? One looked lovely - ‘Rustic Charm!’ it said – but the reviews mentioned shared bathrooms and a rooster that starts crowing at 4am.      Rustic charm indeed. Sounds… authentic. Though a 4am rooster does sound a bit much. You're a light sleeper. Remember that hotel in Scarborough last year? You complained about the seagulls all night.      Okay, okay, point taken. I’m sensitive to noise. But seriously, I want to be able to  work . I need a reasonably peaceful environment. Which brings me back to the risotto failing. It’s a metaphor for my life - either a complete mess, or stubbornly refusing to yield.      Dramatic much? Just add the stock slowly, lad. One ladle at a time, and stir constantly. Think of it like… constructing a coherent argument. Small pieces building towards a larger point. Kind of like what  I  do all day, actually.      You and your analogies.

...Honestly, Doreen, I’m starting to feel like a right fool. I spent ages trying to find a card for young Thomas, and then realised I hadn’t a clue how old he was turning! Is he seven now? Or eight? Honestly, time just  vanishes .      Eight, dear, eight. And don’t beat yourself up about it. It happens to the best of us. Especially when they’re not  your  grandchildren, you haven’t got the constant updates, have you? I remember when little Emily started primary school – felt like yesterday. Though her mother was fiercely protective of the age on the cards, insisted on ‘Eight glorious years!’ sort of thing. A bit much, if you ask me.      Glorious years! Oh, Doreen. It's just a number, isn’t it? Though I suppose it’s nice for them. Makes them feel special. I was thinking of getting him one of those little calendar fobs, you know? With his name on it? They’re quite cheap, and he's always losing track of the date.      Oh, that's a good idea! Very practical. They do those with little pictures on too, don’t they? Maybe a football or something? Speaking of practical, I need to start on the shopping list for next week. I’m heading to Sainsbury’s on Tuesday morning. Anything you’re short on?      Yes, actually. Milk, definitely. And those digestive biscuits Thomas loves – the ones with the little chocolate chips. It wouldn't be a visit without them. Oh, and I'm running low on teabags. Yorkshire Tea, please. You always get the best.      Yorkshire Tea it is! Always. Makes all the difference, doesn’t it? It reminds me, when I was teaching, we used to do so much art and craft. Terrible mess, naturally, but they  loved  it. We had one little boy, Michael, who could build the most amazing things with just bits of cardboard and glue. He’d have been brilliant at engineering, I always thought.      Oh, the memories! I remember helping out with art days at the school when David was little. Glitter  everywhere . It took weeks to get rid of. They were doing papier-mâché, I think. It's funny the things you remember. Do you recall hockey boots? The smell of them was awful. David played for the school team, and his boots were always…ripe.      Oh, good heavens, yes! The hockey boot smell!

…Honestly, this is lovely. Really lovely, dear. So much brighter than that little flat in Southend. And a proper kitchen! Though, I’m still getting used to everything being so…rural. No chip shops on every corner, eh?      No chip shops, no, Dad. But honestly, after years of city living, it’s bliss. It's about a twenty-minute drive to the nearest one if you  really  need a fix, though. And honestly, the fresh air… it’s really done wonders for my allergies.      Speaking of bliss, have you both tried these biscuits? Mrs. Penhaligon next door made them. Elderflower and lemon – absolutely divine. She's been a godsend, honestly. Brought round a victoria sponge the day after we moved in.      Mrs. Penhaligon, you say? Sounds like a good sort. We haven't really met many people yet, just a quick hello to the postman. Still unpacking boxes, you see. Didn’t realise how much  stuff  one accumulates over the years. It’s a wonder the removal van didn’t sink.      He’s being modest. It was a mountain of boxes, Mum. Dad spent practically a week meticulously labeling everything. Honestly, he’s got a system for everything.      Organisation is key, my dear! It's what kept me sane during all those management meetings. Though, I suspect having everything neatly boxed up didn't translate to the same level of calm for  you  when trying to find the kettle.      Okay, fair point. But I’ve found most things now. And the garden! Mum, you wouldn't believe the garden. It's completely overgrown, but it has such potential. I'm thinking vegetable patch, maybe some roses...      You’ll need to watch out for the slugs, darling. They’re notorious here. Old Man Hemmings down the lane swears by beer traps. Says it’s the only way to keep them at bay.      Beer traps! That’s… resourcefulness. Speaking of resourcefulness, you mentioned the train line is running again? I was hoping to nip back to Southend for a visit before Christmas, just to see old friends.      Yes, it re-opened last week. It’s a bit…patchy, still. Apparently, they’re doing further repairs after the landslip. But it gets you to Exeter, and from there you can get pretty much anywhere. You’ll need to book well in advance though, it’s popular with commuters.      Have you managed to find a good bookshop in town yet, dear?

Honestly, this is pathetic. Another hour lost to… what  is  this even? Just endless scrolling through trainers I can’t afford.      You and your trainers, Liam. Seriously, you've been looking at shoes online for three days. What’s the attraction? You haven't worn a proper pair of shoes out the house in… well, a while.      It’s not the  shoes  exactly, it’s… the escape, yeah? Like, looking at stuff, building a little fantasy life where I’m not just… here. Stuck. It’s easier than facing the fact I sent off another ten applications this week and haven't heard a thing back.      I get that. But you’re letting it consume you. Remember when you used to build those amazing Warhammer models? You were  good  at that. Why don't you pick that back up? It's proper creative, and you’d actually  make  something, instead of just… wanting something.      Aye, well, that cost money too, didn’t it? And space. Mum would have a fit if I started covering the bedroom floor in plastic soldiers again. Besides, felt a bit… childish, I suppose. Proper geeky.      Childish? Liam, you have a history degree. You’re allowed a bit of fun! It’s not like you're applying to be Prime Minister. Honestly, sometimes I think you  want  to be miserable.      That's harsh, Jess! It's just… frustrating. Everyone else is moving on. You’re swotting for your A-Levels, going to uni next year, getting your life together. And I’m… what? A professional online shopper? A champion of sofa-based existence?      Don’t be daft. You're brighter than most people I know. But you're letting this unemployment thing define you. Have you even looked at those online courses your Gran was talking about? Digital marketing, that kind of thing?      I’ve glanced. All seems a bit… computer-y. I'm not brilliant with that stuff, you know. Remember when I tried to set up that smart speaker? Nearly set the house on fire.      You unplugged it from the wall  while  it was updating. That's not exactly a tech problem, that's a common sense problem. And they're not all like that! They have courses for complete beginners. It's worth a look, seriously. It's better than staring at trainers all day.      You sound like Mum.      Well, someone has to! Look, I’m just saying, you’re moping around, and it’s bringing you down.

...Honestly, the kitchen’s looking brilliant, John. You’ve really made this place your own already. That paint colour is  exactly  what it needed. Feels so much warmer in here now.      Well, thank you, Sarah. It was a bit…beige before, wasn’t it? Luckily, I remembered enough from all those dodgy DIY projects I ‘helped’ with as a lad with my dad. Though I’m still battling with the central heating. Keeps cutting out. Might need a professional, I fear. My pride’s taking a battering.      Professionals are worth their weight in gold when it comes to heating, John. Don't suffer in silence! Remember old Mrs. Higgins? Tried to fix her boiler herself… ended up flooding the whole house.      Oh, don’t remind me! I heard about that. A disaster. I just thought I’d give it a go, you know? Save a few quid. Speaking of which, what are we having for lunch? I’m famished after all that painting yesterday.      I was thinking soup and a sandwich? Quick and easy. I brought some lovely crusty bread from the village bakery.      Sounds perfect. And we can chat about the coastal walk while we eat. John, are you still aiming for Saturday?      Saturday’s good. Providing this weather holds, of course. I’ve been looking at the forecast. Apparently, there's a chance of showers, but nothing too drastic. I was thinking we could park at Clovelly and walk up to Hartland Quay? It's a good stretch, but not  too  taxing.      Hartland Quay sounds lovely. I’ve always meant to explore that stretch of coastline properly. And it has that fantastic pub, doesn’t it? The Wreckers Retreat?      Indeed! Perfect for a post-walk pint. Now, before I forget… I was browsing online last night. Trying to find a decent armchair for the living room. This old sofa… well, it's seen better days. It’s probably older than Sarah!      Hey! I resemble that remark! But you  are  right. It's…cosy, let's say. Have you looked at those furniture outlets down near Exeter? They sometimes have some good deals.      We could go next week? I have a free afternoon on Tuesday. We could make a proper day of it, lunch included. Though, knowing John, he’ll end up haggling over every last penny.      I do  not  haggle! I simply…appreciate value for money. It’s a skill!

Right, that was a  good  roast. Honestly, your mum really outdid herself. I think I needed that, a proper, comforting meal. Work’s been…a lot.      Glad you enjoyed it. She was fussing over the Yorkshire puddings for ages, convinced they wouldn’t rise. You know how she gets. And yes, you look like you’ve been run over by a bus, to be honest. Bad week?      Understatement of the century. It’s this new grant application. It's massive, potential to fund the whole research group for five years, but the scope… it's enormous. They want everything – longitudinal studies, intervention design, qualitative data, quantitative analysis… it's basically three PhDs worth of work crammed into one proposal.      Oh, goodness. That sounds hellish. You’re always so meticulous, though. You’ll get it done, even if you have to pull all-nighters fuelled by instant coffee. But, seriously, don’t. Remember last time? You were practically hallucinating.      I  thought  I was being productive! No, you’re right. I’m trying to be better about boundaries. But it's hard when everyone’s looking to you, you know? As the ‘expert’ in health behaviour change. Suddenly I’m expected to be brilliant at grant writing  and  complex statistical modelling  and  community engagement…      It’s the ‘expert’ thing, isn’t it? Everyone assumes because you’ve spent years studying something, you magically have all the answers and all the skills. It’s the same at work, to be fair. “Oh, you manage assessments, you must be a data wizard!” No, I’m an organised person who understands how exams work. There’s a difference.      Exactly! It feels like a moving goalpost. What's been happening with you, anyway? Besides rescuing Yorkshire puddings, I mean. How's the new curriculum rollout going?      It’s…challenging. It's the usual chaos, really. Teachers are stressed, resources are limited, and everyone's trying to figure out how to implement something that feels fundamentally flawed. The idea behind it’s good, genuinely, but the execution is just a mess. It feels like they’ve designed it all in a room with no actual teachers present.      That sounds so frustrating. You put so much effort into making sure everything runs smoothly for them. It must be disheartening when the system itself is working against you.      It is. And the endless meetings! Honestly, if I have to sit through one more powerpoint presentation on ‘synergistic learning outcomes,’ I might scream.

Honestly, this butternut squash is  divine . Reminds me of Mrs. Higgins’ garden, back in Kemsing. She always had the biggest, brightest orange squash you’ve ever seen. Used to win prizes at the village fete, she did.      Mrs. Higgins… now  there  was a woman. Always had a twinkle in her eye and a biscuit tin full of something delicious. You haven’t changed much yourself, love, still waxing lyrical about village life.      It’s charming, though, isn’t it? All that small-town gossip and prize-winning veg. I mean, my Instagram feed is all perfectly curated avocado toast and travel influencers, and it feels…empty, compared to stories about a giant squash.      Avocado toast? Sounds like rabbit food. Give me a good roast dinner any day. Proper food. Still, Mrs. Higgins, yeah, she was alright. Always offered me a cuppa when I was doing a job for her son, Derek. Reckon he still lives there? Bit of a loner, Derek was.      Speaking of Derek, and going slightly off-piste, did you all know he was left-handed? Old Mrs. Higgins used to get so cross, saying it was the devil’s work. She’d try to make him eat with his right hand.      Oh, bless her. That  was  a thing, wasn’t it? All that superstition. My nan was the same. Said left-handers were clumsy and awkward. I remember asking her if it meant I was clumsy because I write with my left hand, and she just patted my head and said “nonsense, dear, just a bit…different.”      It's funny the things we remember. I've been thinking about finances, actually. Given Sarah's considering moving out now she's got the copywriting job… we might need to look at re-mortgaging. Just to get a little cushion, you know?      Dad! We haven't even talked about that properly yet! I  might  be looking at places, but I'm definitely not committing to anything yet. And don't worry about a cushion, honestly. Moving back in if things go south is always an option.      Woah there, hold your horses. I'm just saying, it's sensible to plan ahead. Rent's ridiculous these days, even down here. Remember when I first started out, you could rent a whole house for… well, not much!      Things definitely were cheaper. It’s brutal for young people trying to get on the property ladder.

…and this one’s from that trip to the Lake District last summer, Grandad. Remember how much rain we had? Honestly, I think we spent more time in pubs than actually  in  the lakes.      Aye, I remember. Lakes, pubs… same thing when you’re northern, lass. A bit o’ damp never hurt anyone. Though I preferred it when we used to go to Blackpool. Proper seaside, that was. None of this… fancy hiking.      Blackpool's good fun, definitely. Bit…brash though, isn’t it? I went a couple of years ago with some mates. It was alright, but a bit too much arcade noise for my liking. I’m more of a countryside person myself. Though I wouldn’t say no to a decent fish and chips on the pier.      Oh, the fish and chips  were  good. They do a cracking one near the Pleasure Beach, even if the Pleasure Beach itself is terrifying. Grandad, you used to love a bit of excitement, though, didn't you? All those stories about working on the telephone exchange during the war...      Excitement? That weren’t excitement, pet. That was duty. Fixing lines, keeping communications open…vital work, that was. Though the stories I  could  tell you… there was this one time a pigeon got into the exchange… caused absolute chaos! Kept pecking at the relays.      A pigeon? Seriously? That sounds like something out of a film. I can't imagine having to troubleshoot a pigeon-induced telephone outage. My problems usually involve slightly temperamental servers and angry clients.      See, completely different worlds. You’re dealing with software, Grandad was dealing with… live wires and pigeons. I’m just dealing with words, trying to make sense of how people  use  language. It feels…a bit pointless sometimes, compared to all that.      Pointless? Don’t you say that, girl. Words are powerful things. They can start wars, build empires… and tell a good story. I’ve always loved a good story. Remember your grandmother? She could spin a yarn like nobody's business. Always had a tale about some neighbour or other.      My grandma was the same. Always had gossip. It was practically a competitive sport with her. Speaking of stories, have either of you ever been to Morocco? I spent a month there last year on a project, and the food was incredible. Tagines, couscous… everything served with mint tea.      Morocco? No, never! Sounds amazing, though.

...Honestly, the student feedback on the Baudrillard lecture was… mixed, to say the least. Half of them seemed genuinely intrigued, the other half looked like I was speaking Martian. I think I lost them at 'simulacra and simulation'.      Baudrillard to undergrads? You're a braver woman than I am, love. I stick to the concrete with my lot - mostly straightforward textual analysis. Easier to gauge comprehension when they're grappling with Dickens, not post-structuralism. What did the feedback  specifically  say? Was it the language, the concepts…?      A bit of both, I think. One said, and I quote, "Too much head, not enough heart." Another just wrote "Huh?" repeatedly. I tried to tie it into social media and reality TV, make it relatable, but… maybe it was a stretch. I’m thinking of reworking the opening for next year, maybe start with  The Matrix  instead.       The Matrix  is brilliant! That’s much more accessible. It visually  is  simulacra and simulation. See, you were on the right track, just needed a better entry point. It’s the same with the first-year intro to poetry. I always start with a Sheeran song. They groan, then suddenly Shakespeare doesn’t seem so alien.      Sheeran? Honestly! But you're right, it’s about bridging the gap. It's just frustrating when you believe in the importance of these ideas, you know? They're so relevant to understanding the world, but getting students to  care …      I completely get it. It’s the same with my Baudelaire module. Trying to explain  spleen  to a group of students who’ve never experienced existential angst is… challenging. Speaking of challenges, how’s the syllabus looking for your philosophy of mind course? We need to coordinate so we don't both bombard them with Descartes at the same time.      That’s a good point. It’s coming along. I've got the core texts sorted - Descartes, of course, then moving onto Dennett and Chalmers. I was thinking of adding a section on AI consciousness, given how rapidly that's developing. What do you think?      Ooh, that's smart. Very timely. Might even get some of the "Huh?" brigade engaged. I’m focusing more on the ethics of AI in my political philosophy course, so it could dovetail nicely. We could even suggest joint reading lists. It would show the students the interdisciplinary nature of things.      That’s a great idea!

Honestly, this coffee machine is driving me round the bend. It’s either lukewarm dishwater or scalding lava. There's no in-between. And I  need  a decent cup, you know? Especially with… all this going on.      You and that coffee machine. It’s been a running battle since Christmas. Maybe it’s time to admit defeat and go back to instant? Though, knowing you, that’d feel like surrendering.      Surrendering to convenience, eh? A slippery slope, that is. It’s the same with everything, isn’t it? Making things… easier. It takes the grit out of life. Speaking of grit, have you two had a chance to look at quotes for storage? This house clear-out is going to be  expensive .      Oh, don't even start on the storage, Arthur. I nearly had a fit when I saw the monthly rate for a container large enough for… well, half my life, it feels like. And removal companies are practically quoting ransom demands. It’s daylight robbery! I mean, we're not moving to Buckingham Palace, just downsizing.      I did a bit of digging online. Seems like prices have skyrocketed since… well, since everything. Demand's up, fuel costs, the usual. I found one place near Penrith that’s  slightly  less painful, but it's still a hit. We could try and do some of the smaller stuff ourselves, save a bit on man-hours.      That's what I was thinking. We’re not completely useless, are we? Although, shifting all those books of yours, Mary… that’ll be a project. You’ve a library, not a living room.      They're  important  books, Arthur! And I’ve catalogued them all, you know. Dewey Decimal System and everything. Habits die hard, I suppose, after forty years of teaching. Though, I'm starting to wonder if all that knowledge was… what was it all  for ? Seems the world's going to pot regardless of how many children I explained quadratic equations to.      Don’t go down that rabbit hole, Mary. You made a huge difference to so many kids. Mum always said you had a gift for explaining things. It’s just… the world's a mess right now, and it's easy to feel helpless.      Helpless, aye. It’s this Labour leadership business, I think. Starmer's… he’s trying to be something he’s not, isn’t he? All sensible shoes and measured tones.

...Honestly, the whole “pseudonym” thing has properly confused me. You’re telling me your nan’s been going by ‘Brenda the Boat’ for the last five years?      Yeah, well, it started as a joke, init? She got obsessed with canal boats after seeing one on the Regent’s Canal. Started calling herself that to wind up my uncle. It just…stuck. Now everyone at the boating club knows her as Brenda the Boat. It's proper weird.      That’s brilliant! I’ve got a regular who insists on being called ‘Captain’. Runs a little fishing tackle shop near the canal in Brum. Real character. Though 'Brenda the Boat' is next level.      Mate, that's fantastic. We don't really  do  canal boats back home. Too many crocs, probably. Though we've got plenty of rivers. Speaking of which, you called that little stream near your place the 'Lea'? Is that right? Sounds…subtle.      The Lea? Yeah, the River Lea. Pretty grim in bits, to be fair. Not like the Thames, all grand and important. Still, it’s got its own charm. And it feeds into the Thames, doesn't it? Always forgot the names of all these rivers when I was studying geography.      It’s funny how ingrained names are. My grandma, she’s super strict about kosher law, right? So, absolutely  no  mixing of dairy and meat. But she'll happily tell anyone the story of ‘Old Man Tiber’ and how the Romans built everything around the river. The dichotomy is wild.      Oh, kosher law's a whole thing. My sister tried going strictly kosher for a bit, for a boyfriend. Lasted about a week. Too much planning around condiments, apparently. It put her off Italian food for months.      Condiments are serious business. You Aussies take your Vegemite very seriously, just so you know. I’m craving a decent pasta though. This 'full English' action is great for a day, but sometimes you need some proper carbs.      You're preaching to the choir. The Italian place down the road does amazing carbonara. But you’d think they were giving away free gold the way they charge for it. Still, worth it. Honestly, I’m surprised they let us have the whole restaurant to ourselves on a Saturday.      They said they had a cancellation - some sort of corporate do fell through. Lucky us, I guess. Though it is a bit eerie being the only ones in here.

Right, honestly, this Tinder situation is a  mess . I swiped right on this lad, looked alright, decent profile… turns out he collects garden gnomes. Like, seriously? Garden gnomes.      No way! Garden gnomes? That's… a choice. You gotta admit, though, it's a good filter. If you can handle gnomes, you can handle anything, yeah? I’ve been having better luck, actually. Met a fella last week, seems alright. He actually  listened  when I talked about my dissertation. A rarity, that.      Listening is underrated, definitely. I've mostly just been getting requests from guys who say “Hey” and expect a full conversation to unfold. It’s exhausting. I’m starting to think the uni dating scene is just… bleak.      Bleak is an understatement, lass. It’s a desert. I keep matching with lads who went to private school and talk about their gap years in Australia. It’s giving major ‘out of touch’ vibes. Makes you wanna delete the app, doesn’t it? Speaking of deleting things, anyone else applying for house shares for next year already?      Oh God, yeah. It's stressing me out. It's either a shoebox for a fortune or a place that looks like it hasn’t been cleaned since the 90s. I saw one on Rightmove yesterday… avocado carpets. AVOCADO. Who  does  that?      Avocado carpets?! Oh, dear God. That’s a crime against interior design. I’m thinking of just staying in halls again, even though it’s a bit… chaotic. It's less risky than ending up with a housemate who insists on hosting interpretive dance evenings.      Halls  are  chaotic, but at least you've got built-in company. This guy I met, Liam, he's moving into a flat with some mates of his. Looks decent, actually. Proper kitchen, not just a hob and a microwave like some places.
