I'm thinking of going round for a 'casual look' maybe.      A casual look? You mean you’re scoping out his friends too? Fair enough, honestly. You need to assess the whole package. I'm thinking about finding someone who doesn’t spend their entire life in the library. I swear, some of these guys have never seen sunlight.      Sunlight is important! You need Vitamin D, you know. And a personality. Preferably one that doesn't involve photographing every single meal they eat. Honestly, the Instagram generation… it’s wild. And this gnome lad?

Honestly, Doris, this news is enough to give a man a proper headache. All this talk of tax cuts for the wealthy…doesn’t seem right, does it? Especially when folks are struggling just to put food on the table.      Tax cuts, eh? It’s always the same story, Arthur. They promise trickle-down economics, but all that trickles down is disappointment, if anything. Remember Thatcher? Promised prosperity. More like…well, you remember.      Here we go, you two. Try not to get yourselves all worked up before elevenses. A nice cuppa usually helps. And honestly, haven't we learned to just expect disappointment from politicians? It's practically a national pastime now.      Easier said than done, Margaret. It’s just…seeing the benefits squeezed tighter and tighter. I know we’re alright, relatively speaking, but what about young families? Having to choose between heating and eating...it's grim. I was reading about this new energy cap, it’s hardly a solution, is it?      Grim is an understatement. I remember when a pension could actually  mean  something. Now, it's just…keeping your head above water, and even that's getting harder. They tell you to downsize, sell the house. Sell the house?! Where are we supposed to go? Back to living in a shed?      Now, now, George, don’t get yourself all agitated. You’ve got your garden, your memories…that’s worth more than any fancy flat. But he’s right, Arthur. The benefits system is broken. I used to help out with a few families when I was childminding, and the hoops they had to jump through to get even a little help…it was scandalous.      Scandalous is a good word. And it’s all presented as if people are just…scroungers. Lazy and wanting a handout. It's a convenient narrative, isn't it? Keeps the blame away from the real culprits.      Exactly! My nephew, bless him, he's workin' his socks off down at the docks, doin' a proper physical job. And he still struggles. He was tellin’ me they're cuttin’ back on overtime, so he's earnin’ less, and then the price of everything goes up. It's a vicious circle.      Speaking of vicious circles...did anyone see that program last night about the state of the NHS? Appalling. Waiting lists longer than my arm. I was speaking to old Mrs. Higgins from next door, and she's been waiting six months for a hip replacement.

Right, that should do for the pasta bake. Honestly, it feels like I haven’t sat down all day. How was your day battling the charity world, then? Anything exciting happen with the fundraising?      Exciting? That's a strong word. It was… persistent. Mrs. Higgins, bless her, decided today was the day to renegotiate her pledge  again . Apparently, her grandson needs braces and suddenly a substantial donation to the wildlife sanctuary is less pressing. It's always something. Did you manage to get to the library today? You were talking about needing a new book.      Oh, don't even  start  me on library opening times. Apparently, Tuesday afternoons are now strictly “community engagement hours” which translates to a toddler group having a very loud singalong right where the new fiction is. I gave up. Ended up scrolling through endless rubbish on the television instead. Honestly, everything is reality TV these days, isn’t it?      It is, isn't it? I caught a bit of that “Bake Off: The Professionals” earlier. Bit stressful to watch, all that pressure over a croquembouche. Makes a pasta bake seem rather sensible. Speaking of sensible, how’s your mum doing? She hasn't called this week, which is unlike her.      She's alright, I think. Spoke to her yesterday. Still obsessed with the weather forecast, naturally. Apparently, a chance of frost in October is a national crisis. She’s been trying to get Derek to put up his Christmas lights already. Honestly, it's September! I told her she was being ridiculous. She said it "brightens things up".      That sounds like your mum. Always needing a bit of sparkle. Derek’s a good egg, though. Always willing to indulge her little eccentricities. It’s nice to see. Though, Christmas lights in September… a bit much, even for Derek. Did Sarah ring about the children? Are they still coming down next weekend?      Yes, she did. They’re both  so  excited. Apparently, Leo's been building a fort in his bedroom out of every cushion and blanket he could find. He’s declared it “Headquarters”, and refuses to let his sister anywhere near it. Classic Leo. Poppy, predictably, is trying to infiltrate it with a team of stuffed animals.      Sounds like chaos. Wonderful chaos. I'm looking forward to it. It’s just… not the same when they're not here. The house feels a bit too quiet, you know?

Honestly, this grey is relentless. It's been like this for days. Reminds me a bit of Cambridge, actually, but without the…well, without everything else. You get used to a certain quality of grey, you know? The Cambridge grey feels…intellectual. This is just…damp.      Tell me about it. I'm starting to forget what sunshine even  feels  like. It’s just blah. Though, I suppose it’s better than the ice we had last week. Still recovering from that cold I picked up then, actually. My throat feels like sandpaper.      Oh, darling, that sounds awful. Still? You'd think a week would be enough. It's funny, isn't it? I never used to get properly ill when I was younger. Now it feels like a constant battle. I put it down to the stress of… everything.      Yeah, I think you’re right. Stress does a number on you. Speaking of stress, I’m still agonizing over going back for Great-Auntie Maureen's funeral. It feels…a long way to go for a funeral, even though she  was  family. And honestly, the thought of my mum’s side of the family all crammed into one room…      Oh, bless you. That  does  sound challenging. It's good of you to go, though. Family is…well, it’s complicated, isn’t it? But important. I’ve been thinking a lot about ‘home’ lately. It's a silly thing, really. I haven't  felt  at home anywhere in years. Not even Cambridge, anymore.      I know what you mean. I used to think Bury was 'home', completely and utterly. But after uni, and travelling, and now living out here…it feels more like a place I  from . Different, you know? It’s weird. What was your favourite job, if you don't mind me asking? When you were…working, I mean.      That’s a tricky one. Probably…the library. It wasn’t glamorous, but it felt…right. Quiet. Surrounded by stories. I quite liked the order of it all. And people were mostly polite. The TEFL is okay, if a little draining. It’s just…it’s not  fulfilling . It doesn’t feel like I’m  doing  anything. What about you? Loving the TEFL life?      I do, actually! It’s surprisingly rewarding. Watching someone finally ‘get’ something, seeing their confidence grow… it’s brilliant. It’s exhausting, managing a class full of teenagers, but I wouldn't trade it.

…and honestly, the brief was  wild . "Evoke nostalgia for a washing machine." Like, how do you even  do  that? It felt less like copywriting and more like abstract performance art.      Oh, my god, that's brilliant. That's awful, but brilliant. Honestly, sounds like something my dad would get given at work – some bizarre marketing challenge. Are you seriously paid to find the emotional core of a household appliance?      Pretty much. Apparently, they're targeting… grandparents? Trying to link the washing machine to happy family memories. I suggested a campaign featuring old photos, maybe a little jingle about the smell of clean laundry. They wanted something "edgier”.      ‘Edgier’ washing machines. Right. Well, at least it's a story for the pub, yeah? My week's been relentlessly… beige. Survey programming is not exactly a hotbed of creative inspiration. Mostly just making sure people don't accidentally select multiple answers about their biscuit preferences.      Biscuit preferences are vital research, don’t downplay that! It’s the backbone of the nation! Though, yeah, sounds a bit… repetitive. Is the dissertation coming along okay at least? Still wrestling with the semiotics of garden gnomes, was it?      Don't remind me. It's… a slog. I've narrowed it down to the gnome as a symbol of repressed suburban anxieties. Which sounds amazing when I say it quickly, but really just means I'm reading a lot of academic papers about picket fences and societal expectations.      Oof. Sounds intense. I’m glad I’m just writing about suds and spin cycles for a living. Speaking of necessities, I need to actually  get  some food. I’ve been surviving on Pret sandwiches all week. It’s extortionate, but convenient.      Tell me about it. I keep meaning to try and cook more, but after a day of staring at code, the idea of staring at a chopping board… it’s just too much. Although, there's that little market on Brick Lane, remember? The one with the amazing fruit and veg? We should go sometime this weekend.      Oh, I love that one! Proper bargains. And you can get those amazing samosas. Yes! That’s a brilliant idea. We could actually attempt a vaguely healthy meal. Have you heard from Chloe recently? I haven't seen her since her birthday.      No, not really. She’s been super busy with that internship, apparently. Last I heard, she was practically living at the gallery.

Ugh, honestly. What time  is  it? Feels like I only just closed my eyes.      It's eight o'clock, Mummy! And Leo woke me up ages ago, he was doing…um…circus things!      I was  not  doing circus things! I was perfecting my ninja stealth! It requires rope - which is… these tea towels.      Ninja stealth with tea towels, right. And what woke  me  up was definitely not a tiny ninja practicing. It was more a small person announcing a highly important strategic mission.      It  was  important! We needed to know if the toast would be ready before the timer beeped!      A vital question, indeed. Alright, alright. Toast is happening. What are we thinking for today? It's Saturday, which means... freedom! Though, I did promise Mrs. Davies I'd look over some of the Year 4 science projects.      Can we go to the park? Pleeeease? With the swings?      The park is definitely on the cards. Maybe after I've done a little bit of work. And before that, breakfast. Speaking of which, anyone fancy pancakes?      Ooooh, pancakes! With sprinkles?!      Of course with sprinkles. It’s Saturday! Everything is better with sprinkles. Right, I’ll get those going. You two, are you having a ‘before pancake’ discussion about ninja tactics and circus skills?      I’m thinking of learning to juggle. Leo said he saw someone do it at the Neon Moon event last week.      Neon Moon? Oh dear, that sounds chaotic! Did you both have fun?      It was AMAZING! There were lights everywhere and music and…and someone was trying to teach everyone how to say things in Australian!      Australian? What things?      Like… “G’day!” and “No worries!” and this one that sounded like “Arvo.” Apparently, it means afternoon!      “Arvo” is a good one. Aussies do love their shortened words. Honestly, it's a whole different language sometimes. It's funny you say that, actually. My cousin Sarah moved to Perth last year. She’s started sending me texts full of slang. I have to google half of it.      Can we learn Australian too? We could pretend to be explorers!      We absolutely can. We’ll have an Australian lesson after pancakes, okay? Maybe we can even try making some Anzac biscuits.      What are Anzac biscuits?      They’re a bit like oat cookies... really sweet. They were sent to soldiers during the wars, apparently. A bit of history with your sprinkles.      Cool! Can we play explorers  and  be ninjas after the park?

Honestly, this is lovely. Just getting out of London, breathing proper air. Though I do wish Gareth hadn’t insisted on taking the ‘scenic route’ via every single B-road in Cornwall. My spine is starting to resemble a washboard.      Now, now, Bronwyn. It’s not  every  B-road. Just the most…characterful ones. And it’s beautiful, isn't it? Besides, we’re almost into Wales now. Think of the proper tea and Welsh cakes awaiting us at my sister’s.      It  is  pretty. Although, the signal’s been dreadful. Trying to finish this reading for uni – it’s on the impact of post-Brexit agricultural policy on Welsh hill farms, ironically.      Oh, don't even  start  on Brexit, Rhys. I can barely stomach the thought. It feels like the country’s been…well, fraying at the edges ever since.      It’s a complex issue, Bronwyn. You can’t lay all the blame at its door. There were issues long before 2016. Deindustrialisation, the north-south divide… it’s been brewing for decades. My grandfather, old Dai, used to say the same about the decline of the coal industry back in the valleys. Different catalyst, same fundamental problems.      Your grandfather was a wise man. But surely, deliberately isolating ourselves wasn’t the answer? Look at the mess with the fishing industry, the red tape for businesses… And the feeling of division it’s created. Truly awful.      It’s definitely hit the farmers hard. The subsidies, or lack thereof now, are a huge issue. Apparently, there's a lot of talk about ‘public money for public goods’, but figuring out what that actually  means  in practice is… a nightmare. It’s all so vague.      That’s the Whitehall way, isn’t it? Wonderful theory, disastrous execution. It’s the same with so many policies. They design them in London, with no real understanding of how they’ll affect people on the ground. Bronwyn, you’ve edited enough manuscripts to know that a story only works when it’s grounded in reality. It's the same with governance.      Exactly! It’s about nuance, about understanding the complexities. That’s what's been lost. It's all become soundbites and simplistic solutions. It makes me furious, honestly. My aunt Elsie – remember her, Gareth? Lived down in Pembrokeshire? – she’s absolutely  incandescent  about the changes to rural bus routes. Says she can’t get to the doctor anymore.

...and then the badger, right, he wasn’t  actually  trying to steal the jam, he was trying to… to distract Mrs. Higgins so Old Man Fitzwilliam could sneak in and replace her prize-winning marrow with a pumpkin! It's much more dramatic, don’t you think?      A pumpkin? But pumpkins are orange! Marrows are… marrow-coloured. It’s silly!      Fitzwilliam  hates  Mrs. Higgins because she won last year. He said her marrow was ‘unfairly plump.’      Exactly! You’ve got it, Leo. He’s terribly competitive, Old Man Fitzwilliam. And that’s the key to a good story, isn’t it? Real motivation. Honestly, you two are brilliant co-authors. We've barely started and it's a masterpiece.      Can the badger drive a little car? A tiny, red car?      Oh, Elsie, you always add the best details. Yes, absolutely. He drives a tiny, red car, and it has a little spoiler. He has to weave between the vegetable patches.      And the pumpkin has googly eyes!      Googly eyes! Perfect! It’s a sentient pumpkin, plotting revenge on all the marrows. This is getting wonderfully bonkers. Speaking of stories, I was looking at the Linton Book Festival programme. It's next weekend.      What’s that?      It's a big festival with lots of authors coming to talk about their books. I was thinking we could go on Saturday. They've got Helen Moss doing a talk.      Helen Moss? The one who wrote the  Adventure Island  books?      The very same! You both loved those, didn’t you? Remember how we read them all before our trip to the Isle of Wight?      I liked the bit where Jack found the secret cave! And the parrot talked!      I liked the map. It was really complicated and had lots of skull and crossbones.      See? Helen Moss is brilliant at adventure. It might be inspiring for our badger and his pumpkin escapade. Plus, they do other fun stuff at the festival – storytelling tents, craft stalls… maybe even face painting.      Can I get a pirate face?      Absolutely. If you're good. Actually, even if you're a little bit naughty. It's the school holidays after all. What do you think, Elsie? Worth a day trip?      Can we take the badger and the pumpkin?      They're coming with us in spirit, darling. We can definitely write some more of their adventures on the journey there. Maybe they sneak into the festival too?

…Honestly, the texture is what gets me. Even with all the clever science, that’s the bit I can't get past with the lab-grown stuff. It just  feels  wrong, you know? Like… eating something that never lived, even though, technically, it  is  meat.      That’s a weird paradox to get your head around, isn’t it? Never lived, but still… meat. I get it. But think about the alternative, Liv. The actual living things. The conditions they’re kept in. I read this report… honestly, it's horrifying what they do to maximise yield. I’m starting to think ‘shmeat’ is the lesser evil.      Lesser evil is a strong phrase, isn’t it? Feels a bit… dystopian. But I see your point. I was watching a documentary about hunting the other day, and weirdly, it felt  less  cruel than an abattoir. At least with hunting, there’s a chance, a tiny one, of escape. It’s quick. Abattoirs… that’s just systematic.      See, I’ve always thought that was a really uncomfortable argument. Hunting feels…sporty. Like a power dynamic. A bloke and his gun. It’s inherently about dominance over an animal. Whereas an abattoir tries to hide it all away, pretends it’s just… processed food. Both are awful, obviously, but the hunting feels  actively  celebratory of the killing.      But that’s a human construct, isn’t it, Liv? The ‘sport’ aspect. Historically, humans hunted for survival. It’s ingrained. Abattoirs? That’s pure, industrialised greed. And look at the environmental impact! The land cleared for grazing, the methane emissions… it’s a disaster. That’s why I’m trying to cut down, even though I do love a good Sunday roast.      Methane is a big one. Mum was going on about it last time I visited. She’s gone almost entirely plant-based, says it’s the only way forward. She's taking every vitamin supplement under the sun though, convinced she’s going to be deficient if she doesn't. Honestly, it’s like watching a health anxiety spiral.      Oh God, don't even mention vitamins. Mrs. Henderson came in today convinced she needed triple the recommended dose of B12 because she’d been “feeling a bit tired.” Had to explain to her, very gently, that a good night’s sleep and a balanced diet might be more effective. People just self-diagnose now, don't they?

Honestly, this internet’s been dreadful all afternoon. Keeps dropping out mid-recipe. I was trying to find a new way to do Brussels sprouts, you know, make them slightly less…offensive.      Brussels sprouts? You’re attempting Brussels sprouts again, are you, love? After last year’s…incident?      It wasn’t  that  bad! Brenda just said they were a bit…firm. She’s always polite, Brenda. Even when something tastes like rubber.      I think ‘firm’ is Brenda-speak for ‘inedible’. She once told Auntie Maureen her fruitcake was “remarkably sturdy”.      Oh, that’s brilliant! Maureen was fuming for weeks. Still brings it up, actually, whenever Brenda’s around. Speaking of throwing things away, have you seen my good screwdriver? I need to fix that wobbly leg on the kitchen table.      Didn’t you leave it in the garage last week when you were fiddling with the washing machine? Honestly, that machine is on its last legs. I swear it sounds like a jet engine taking off every time I put a wash on.      I did? Blast. Probably buried under all your…craft supplies. You've got bits of wool and glitter in every conceivable corner of that garage, you know.      They’re  not  bits of wool and glitter, they are  potential . Potential winter decorations, potential gifts…      You were saying last week you were thinking of making knitted tea cosies for everyone for Christmas.      Well, I was! But then I saw a really lovely set online, much quicker, less…finger-pricking. Though, honestly, the online shopping experience is getting worse and worse. Constant pop-ups, asking for data… it's exhausting.      It is. Remember when the internet was just…the internet? No targeted ads, no algorithms trying to predict your next purchase. Simpler times. Speaking of simpler times, you remember New Year's Eve at the pub in Southport? Old Man Hemmings always trying to get everyone to sing Auld Lang Syne before midnight.      I've heard stories! Apparently he'd start on the first verse at eleven-thirty and just keep going.      Those were good times. We should do something special this year, don’t you think? We haven’t really celebrated properly since…well, you know.      We could have a little party, invite a few friends. Maybe try your…improved Brussels sprouts?      Don’t push it. How about just a nice quiet evening? Good food, a film. What are you watching at the moment, darling?

Honestly, you two. Butterfly forks for spaghetti? Really? It's just…not how it’s done. It’s Bolognese, not a garden party.      But Mum, they  look  nicer! And it helps twirl the spaghetti, doesn’t it? Leo said they do it in Italy.      Yeah! Leo’s been to Italy, remember? He said everyone uses fancy forks. Makes it more… sophisticated.      Leo also once told me pigeons were government drones. Sophistication is perhaps not his strong suit. Look, the point of a fork is to get the food  into  your mouth. These just make it harder. Now, eat up. We need to be quiet soon, don’t forget.      Oh yeah! The two minutes silence. For, um… what exactly are we being silent for again?      Remembrance Day, darling. To remember everyone who’s fought in wars and kept us safe. It’s this Sunday, but we’re doing it now as O and I won’t be around on Sunday. It’s important.      So, just…no talking for two whole minutes? That feels  really  long.      It is a little bit, but it’s a sign of respect. You can think about things, remember people… It’s not about the silence itself, but what it represents.      Okay. I guess. It’s just… hard. Especially after a big plate of spaghetti.      I understand. Speaking of hard things, has anyone thought about what they want for their birthdays? They’re both coming up quickly, aren’t they?      I want a new gaming headset! Mine’s crackling. It’s really annoying when you’re trying to communicate with your team.      A gaming headset, noted. And you, Leo? Anything specific?      I’m not sure. Maybe… some new art supplies? Or… um… actually, I was reading about Russia today in history. It's kind of scary, everything that’s going on.      It is. It's a very complicated situation, isn't it? Lots of history there, and a lot of suffering.      Is it going to be a war? Like in the olden days?      It’s…difficult to say. There's conflict happening, certainly. And a lot of people are hoping it doesn’t escalate further. It’s important to remember that war isn’t glorious, it’s awful, and it affects real people. That’s partly why we have Remembrance Day. To remember that cost.      My grandad fought in a war. He never really talked about it.      Your grandad was a very brave man.

Right, so, Adventure Island. Series three is  wild . Honestly, the cliffhanger? I nearly threw the remote at the television.      Ooh, ooh! Was it Captain Blackheart? Did he get the ruby?      No, it was the spooky ghost pirate! He had glow-in-the-dark hands!      Well, you two are both partially right. It’s… complicated. But it’s given me a bit of thinking time, actually. About the summer holidays. I really need to finalise something.      Cornwall! Can we  please  go to Cornwall again? The beach was the bestest! And we built a huge sandcastle!      And I found a crab! A real one! It pinched my bucket!      I know, I know, Cornwall was lovely. But it’s a  long  drive, and honestly, I'm a bit burnt out on driving after all this exam marking. Mountains of papers, honestly. It feels like I’ve aged ten years in the last month.      But the sea! And the ice cream!      The sea and the ice cream  are  very good points. But… I was thinking maybe something a little different this year? I saw an advert for a V&A exhibition on childhood toys. It looks amazing. We could do a couple of days in London.      London? Is it like a castle?      Not exactly a castle, darling. It's a huge museum with loads of old things, including toys! And we could go to a park, and maybe even see a show? It’d be less driving and we could get the train.      But Cornwall has proper waves for bodyboarding…      We could look at doing a weekend somewhere with waves another time, perhaps. But I'm also trying to be sensible. I’ve been feeling a bit… off lately. Remember me saying I felt a bit bloated after Mrs. Higgins’ birthday party?      She had a big cake with pink flowers!      She did. Turns out, I think I might be slightly intolerant to… well, something. Dairy, possibly. The doctor’s suggesting I eliminate things to see. So Cornwall, with all the clotted cream and Cornish ice cream… might not be the best idea this year.      No clotted cream? That’s  terrible !      I know, sweetheart. It is a bit rubbish. But we can have dairy-free ice cream! They do really good ones now. And the museum will be fun, honestly. Plus, we can plan something really exciting for next year. Maybe even a proper adventure  to  an island!

...Honestly, Mr. Davies is  obsessed  with the French Revolution. It's all he talks about. Like, I get it, it's important, but five lessons a week? Five! And he keeps asking us hypothetical questions like, "If  you  were Robespierre, what would you do?" Who  wants  to be Robespierre?!      Tell me about it. It's the same with Mrs. Peterson and Shakespeare. Every single sentence has to be dissected for hidden meaning. It’s exhausting. I swear she sees symbolism in the colour of my socks.      No way! Seriously? That’s mental. At least Davies is… passionate. Peterson just feels… judgmental. Remember when Ben sneezed in class and she gave him the side-eye like  he’d  started the Gunpowder Plot?      Oh god, yes! Poor Ben. He’s allergic to dust, for crying out loud. It’s not his fault the school hasn’t been properly cleaned since… well, ever. Speaking of allergies, are you still going to Liam’s party on Saturday? I know his mum makes a killer chocolate cake, but she also uses nuts in  everything .      Yeah, I’m going. Told my mum about the nut thing, she's packing me a backup sandwich, just in case. It’s Liam’s 16th, can't really miss it, can we? Though knowing Liam, it'll be mostly just him trying to impress Chloe and a lot of awkward silences.      Ha! You know him too well. Remember last year when he tried to do a magic trick and accidentally set his hair on fire? Chloe nearly died laughing. Good times.      Legendary. Although, seriously, the school prefects were  fuming . They were all, "Health and Safety breach!" and "Irresponsible behaviour!". Like it was some grand conspiracy, not just a kid messing around with a lighter.      Oh, the prefects. Don’t even get me started. Especially Emily Carter. She patrols the corridors like she owns the place. She gave me a warning today for… wait for it… walking  too quickly . Apparently, I was disrupting the ‘learning environment’.      Seriously? That’s ridiculous! She just craves power, doesn’t she? Honestly, I wouldn’t mind being a prefect just so I could, like, subtly undermine all their ridiculous rules.      Tempting, but the scrutiny… not for me. I'd rather spend my free periods perfecting my bike jumps at the park. Have you been down there lately? They rebuilt that ramp after the storm. It’s insane.

...Honestly, the roundabout at the A19 and the A1018 is just  criminal . Every time I drive that stretch, I brace myself. People just don't seem to understand the concept of yielding. It’s a free-for-all.      You say that like it's unique to Sunderland. Roundabouts are the bane of every driver’s existence, aren't they? Down south, they're obsessed with building these massive, multi-lane ones and expecting everyone to intuitively know where to be. It’s terrifying.      Aye, but ours just feels… particularly aggressive. And the lorries! They just barrel through. It’s a miracle there aren't more accidents. You wouldn’t believe the near misses I’ve had. I swear, some drivers think indicator signals are optional accessories.      Totally. It’s like they’re actively trying to confuse everyone. Though, to be fair, I get distracted sometimes too. Been thinking about getting back into cycling, actually. Might be a safer option than battling with Sunderland traffic.      Cycling? Really? You, the formula one driver of the motorway? Thought you'd be all about speed and horsepower.      No, seriously. I’m getting a bit… restless. Desk job, you know? Need to move more. And honestly, the traffic's getting worse. A bike would be quicker for some of my site visits in town. Plus, good for the environment, that sort of thing. It wouldn't be a road bike, mind. Something a bit more robust for the lanes around Harpenden.      That’s… unexpectedly sensible. Though, knowing you, you’ll probably end up modifying it with something ridiculous, like a mini-turbocharger.      Don't underestimate my engineering tendencies. Maybe just a really powerful headlight. Speaking of sensible, how's the corpus work going? Still battling with tagging inconsistencies?      Oh, don't even  start  me. Someone decided that "football" and "soccer" are completely different concepts and needs separate tags. As if anyone actually cares! It's… it’s exhausting. Sometimes I dream in metadata. Honestly, I'd rather be watching the cricket.      Oh, the Ashes are on, aren’t they? I was meaning to ask. Any good?      It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster, to be honest. England got absolutely hammered in the first test, but then they pulled it back in the second. Root’s batting has been incredible, though. Proper class.      Heard he was on form. I haven't had much chance to watch, been swamped with a project.

Honestly, this is a disaster. They're saying minimum order is £25! For  what ? A couple of spring rolls and some noodles?      Twenty-five quid? Blimey. Which place are you trying, again? Golden Dragon? They used to be good.      Golden Dragon  are  awful now. Seriously, last time I ordered from them, the sweet and sour sauce tasted like watered-down ketchup. Remember that, Liam? You were practically wearing it.      I do, actually! It was a… sticky situation. But they were quick, weren’t they? That’s why I kept going back. Still, £25 is a rip-off.      It is! And I’m craving properly good Kung Pao chicken. I had it in Manchester last month and it was… transformative. This is the let-down of living back in Peterborough, isn’t it? The good Chinese food is just… absent.      Okay, dramatic much, Clara? We've got Happy House. It's not Manchester-level, obviously, but it's decent. A little greasy, maybe, but decent.      Happy House? Isn’t that the one where the delivery driver always looks profoundly disappointed to see me?      He just looks tired, love. He's probably driving all over Peterborough all night. It’s a big place, you know. Relatively.      Fair point. But their noodles are always a bit… soggy, don't you think? I need  chew . I need noodles with structural integrity!      You’re such a noodle snob. Seriously. Okay, how about we try Lucky House? I haven't ordered from them in ages, but I remember they did a really nice salt and chilli chicken.      Lucky House? Isn’t that a bit further out? It’ll take ages to get here. And they don’t do contactless delivery anymore, do they?      Oh god, you're right. I really don't want to have to fumble for cash at the door. It's so 2019.      Okay, new proposition. Let's look on Just Eat and filter by rating. Maybe there’s a hidden gem we haven’t discovered. We could even try that new place, ‘Eastern Delight’? It's got five stars, but only three reviews. Risky, I know.      Five stars and three reviews screams ‘friends and family only’ to me. Too dangerous. Let's stick to a place we  sort of  know. How about we just… compromise? Happy House, and you, Clara, can order separately next week when you fancy really good noodles?

...Honestly, the waiting list for Mrs. Davies down the street is getting ridiculous. She needs a hip replacement, you know? Been in pain for months. And they keep pushing it back. It's just… demoralising, seeing good people stuck like that.      Aye, it is. That’s the state of it, isn’t it? The NHS is… well, it’s brilliant when it's brilliant, but it’s buckling under the strain. I was speaking to a colleague, Dr. Anya Sharma, just last week. She’s doing research on the impact of funding cuts on primary care. The statistics are… sobering.      Sobering is putting it mildly. I’m on the front line, seeing it every day. We’re constantly triage-ing, prioritizing, trying to do more with less. It's exhausting. And the guilt, you know? Knowing you  could  be doing more for someone if you just had the resources.      I can imagine. It’s a horrifying ethical burden to carry. It’s just… you look at countries like Finland, and they seem to have cracked it. Universal healthcare, decent funding, happy staff… though I suppose every system has its issues. I was in Helsinki a few years back for a conference, absolutely lovely place. Clean, efficient, and everyone seemed genuinely content.      Finland, eh? Always sounds a bit idyllic. I’ve never been, though my sister Carol went on a skiing trip last winter. Said it was expensive, even for that, but the healthcare was amazing. She had a minor ankle twist and was seen by a doctor within the hour, no fuss.      See? It's possible. It's not magic. It’s about priorities, isn’t it? About valuing people. Back in Germany, things are different, of course. A lot more private involvement. It’s… complicated. Always a trade-off, I suppose. But the sheer scale of the shortages here feels particularly acute at the moment.      It is. And it doesn't help having neighbours like old Mr. Henderson. He's constantly calling ambulances for things that could easily be handled by a walk-in centre. Says it’s his right! He's a nightmare. Honestly, drains the system for everyone else.      Oh, bless him. You get all sorts, don’t you? We’ve got Mrs. O’Malley next door, convinced she’s allergic to the Wi-Fi. Complains to everyone, including the postman. Says it’s giving her headaches.      Oh my god!

...Honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork they expect you to fill out for even a small research grant is unbelievable. You’d think they  want  you to give up before you even start. It’s a right headache, it is.      Aye, paperwork. Always has been, lad. Back in my day, it was National Service forms, then claiming dole money when there was nowt about. Still a mountain o’ paper, just different reasons for it. At least you’re  doing  something with yours, though. Not like some, just… existing.      You know, I was chatting to a colleague about that, actually. About the welfare system. And it's complicated, isn't it? He was saying how it’s become so focused on getting people ‘back to work’ without actually  creating  the work. It feels… almost punitive at times.      Punitive? That’s a fancy word for ‘mean’, isn’t it? They always have been mean, the lot of ‘em. Remember old Mrs. Higgins down the street? Her husband, bless him, worked down the docks 'til his lungs gave out. They barely gave her a penny when he died. Said he hadn’t paid enough National Insurance. She was heartbroken.      That’s awful. And it's happening now, different circumstances, maybe, but the same feeling of… abandonment. I had a student the other day, a refugee from Syria. Bright lad, desperate to learn, working two part-time jobs just to survive. He was explaining the hoops he had to jump through just to get a basic maintenance grant. It's demoralising. And then there's the whispers about these raids, you know. The police turning up, checking immigration status...      Aye, I saw vans on Harrington Street last week. Big, unmarked vans. Looked like something out of a film. Used to be, you’d see a Bobby on the beat, you’d nod hello, maybe have a chat about the football. Now… feels like they’re looking for something, someone. And it's always the vulnerable that get caught in the net.      It's unsettling. It feels like the atmosphere’s changed. There's more suspicion. It's not the Liverpool I remember, even growing up here – and I've only been back properly for fifteen years. It used to be a city built on welcoming people, on offering a hand.      That’s progress for you. Or what  they  call progress. More people, more problems, more rules.

...Honestly, the sheer volume of data we're wading through for the pronunciation project is  mental . It’s fascinating, of course, but also a bit terrifying. Like, how do you meaningfully categorise every single variation?      Tell me about it! I spent all morning trying to refine the tagging criteria for intonation patterns. It feels like every time I think I've nailed it, another recording throws a spanner in the works. Especially with regional accents – it’s not a neat, tidy system, is it?      Aye, you’re telling me. I'm knee-deep in transcriptions, and the amount of variation even  within  Sunderland is wild. You think you know what to expect, then someone throws a completely different vowel sound at ye. It's not what you learn in school, that's for sure.      Absolutely. And that's the beauty of it, isn’t it? The messiness. From a research perspective, that variation is gold. We're trying to move away from these prescriptive ‘correct’ pronunciations and really capture how people  actually  speak. It's just… a huge undertaking. Publishing needs something concrete, though. They want deliverables!      Deliverables, always deliverables. It’s the same in publishing. Everyone wants a neat little package, nicely labelled, easy to market. They don't want to hear about the ambiguities and the nuances. Though, actually, we're trying to push for more authentic voice in our materials. It's slow going.      It is. It's tempting to fall back on Received Pronunciation, just to make things easier, but that’s so... exclusionary. And increasingly irrelevant, let's be honest. I was chatting to Professor Davies about it earlier, and she was saying they’re getting pushback from students who feel it doesn’t represent them.      Good! It shouldn't. I mean, I’ve had folk down south take the mickey out of my accent since I was a bairn. It's not something you forget. You become very aware of how language marks you out.      That's a really good point, actually. It’s easy to get caught up in the analytical side of things – the phonetic details, the statistical significance – and forget the social implications. Our work impacts how people perceive each other.      It does. And that’s why incorporating a wider range of accents is so crucial. I remember doing some work in the States where people genuinely struggled to understand broad regional accents from different parts of the country.

…and honestly, the bandwidth in that village was appalling. I mean,  appalling . Trying to upload a single, relatively small dataset for my thesis felt like sending messages by carrier pigeon. It just kept timing out.      Carrier pigeon! You're not wrong, though. Rural broadband’s a joke, isn't it? My aunt lives near Scunthorpe, and she’s constantly moaning about it. She says she spends more time waiting for a page to load than actually  on  the page. It’s a different world, Yorkshire versus… well, Bath, really.      It is. Completely different. Bath's alright, tech-wise, but that little stint doing fieldwork in Devon really opened my eyes. You take things for granted. You assume everyone has access to… well, everything. And then you try to explain the complexities of Bayesian inference to someone who’s barely seen a proper internet connection.      That’s… a challenging situation. Speaking of explaining things, I've been doing some mentoring with a couple of undergrads, and it's reminded me how much we just  assume  prior knowledge. They didn’t even know what a control group was in an experiment! It’s frightening.      Oh, goodness. Teaching, is it? I’ve always admired people who can do that properly. I’m dreadful. All those undergraduates staring at me… expecting wisdom. I just feel like a fraud, really. I'm still struggling with the wisdom part myself.      Don't be so hard on yourself. It's not about being all-knowing; it’s about guiding them to figure things out. One of mine was convinced AI was inherently biased because of all the negative news cycles. It took a good hour to unpack  why  that might be, but not necessarily a given, and the role of training data. It was a good conversation though, actually. Got me thinking.      That  is  a good point. The biases baked into algorithms are genuinely terrifying. I was reading an article the other day about facial recognition software misidentifying people of colour at a significantly higher rate. It’s a real ethical minefield.      Absolutely. And it’s not just race, it’s gender too. It all stems from who’s building the tech and what data they’re using. Honestly, it makes you wonder if we're just reinforcing existing societal prejudices through technology.      Exactly! It’s… disheartening. It makes you think about cultural differences as well. I spent a bit of time in Japan a few years ago, doing some preliminary research.

Right, well, that’s the garden mostly sorted for today. Just need to give the roses a good feed tomorrow, but they’re looking promising. Honestly, I think the slugs had a right party while we were away last week though. Young lad, you wouldn’t believe the holes in the hostas!      Hmm? Oh, yeah. Saw a massive one yesterday. Nearly stepped on it. Disgusting.      Disgusting? In my day, we didn’t call ‘em disgusting. We just called ‘em a nuisance! And you’d get out there with a bit o’ salt and sort ‘em out. None of this fancy slug pellet stuff.      Aye, salt was the answer. Good for the garden, good for the constitution, building character! Though I remember your mother, bless her soul, used to pick ‘em up and fling ‘em over the fence into old Mr. Henderson’s garden. Said he liked ‘em for his ducks.      Oh, don’t you start on your mother and Mr. Henderson’s ducks, Arthur! That’s a story for another day. Honestly, the things she got up to… Anyway, I was thinking, Michael, about the loft insulation. I had a look yesterday. It’s looking a bit thin, especially around the edges.      Loft insulation? Ugh. Sounds boring.      It isn’t boring, it’s important! It’s costing us money, lad. Heat rising, all that. I was thinking perhaps we could get someone in to have a look, give us a quote?      You always were sensible about things, Margaret. Never one to let pennies slip through your fingers. Though Arthur here used to think a penny saved was a penny… well, he’d just spend it on sweets.      A man’s gotta have his pleasures! Though I haven't had a good humbug in… well, a good while now, truth be told. Dentist wouldn’t be pleased.      Speaking of dentists, I’ve got mine next week. Dread it. They always tell me to floss more. It's a conspiracy, I swear. They just  want  to see me more.      Now, now, don't be silly. You need to look after your teeth. It’s just like looking after the roses – a bit of preventative care saves a lot of trouble later on. Do you two want another brew? I’ve just made a fresh pot.      Oh, go on then, Margaret. Just a little one. And maybe a biscuit? You always have those nice ginger ones.

Honestly, this air is just… different. Even after three years, I still notice it every time we walk. Not  better  necessarily, just… different than Norwich. It feels thicker, somehow.      You’re right. And the smells! It’s a mix of everything – cooking, exhaust fumes, blossoms… Norwich smells mostly of the Yare and damp stone, doesn't it? Very… specific.      Very. And slightly melancholy, if I’m honest. Speaking of specific smells, did you get the photos back from developing? The ones from that little tea house in Hangzhou?      I did! They’re lovely. I scanned a few onto the laptop. Want to look later? There’s one of old Mrs. Li, the owner, beaming at us. She insisted on refilling our cups about twenty times.      Oh, yes, please! She was adorable. And the tea was incredible. It’s just… I miss having proper coffee sometimes. Chinese tea is wonderful, but a flat white is a craving that’s hard to shake.      I feel you. I’ve been experimenting with making it at home, but it's never quite right. The milk just isn’t the same. Remember Sarah and Ben’s wedding? We had a practically religious experience with the coffee van they hired.      Oh god, yes! Ben was over the moon about the latte art. He kept trying to get the barista to do a tiny version of their dog, Winston. Did you hear back from Sarah, by the way? I sent her a message about our trip to Guilin.      I did. She’s absolutely gutted she couldn’t make it over. Work’s been manic. She sent photos of Winston, looking very regal on a new dog bed. Apparently, he’s developing a fondness for socks again.      Oh, Winston. Some things never change. It's funny how life carries on, isn’t it? Even when you're thousands of miles away. It almost feels like we’re living parallel lives sometimes.      That’s a good way to put it. Separate, but connected. Makes you appreciate the video calls even more. You know, I was thinking... we should definitely try and visit the Lake District next summer. It’s been ages.      Oh, yes! I'd love that. Proper walking weather, hopefully. Maybe we could drag James and Emily along? They haven't been back to the UK in far too long either.      Good idea. James is always talking about a proper hike.

...Honestly, my feet are  killing  me. I swear, those platforms weren't made for dancing, they were made for torture.      Tell me about it! I thought I was going to lose a heel in that mosh pit during ‘Mr. Brightside’. Honestly, people go  wild  to that song, don't they? It's almost primal.      Primal is the word. I saw Chloe nearly take someone out with her handbag. It was chaos. And then Ben kept trying to get me to do shots. Shots! Like I need to add to the mess that was already happening.      Ben, eh? Still pushing the drinks, is he? You'd think someone would tell him “no” eventually. My cousin Jessa's boyfriend is like that, always trying to get everyone to join in. It’s exhausting. I just want a quiet night in with a face mask and, honestly, my cat.      Oh, Leo! How’s the fluffy tyrant doing? He’s getting so big! Last time I saw him he was still kittenish, all paws and mischief.      He’s enormous! He basically rules the house now. Mum jokes he’s paying rent in emotional support. And he’s so picky. He turns his nose up at anything that isn’t salmon pate. Honestly, he’s got better taste in food than half the boys I’ve dated.      That’s a low blow! But a fair one, probably. Speaking of which, did you see Liam last night? He was trying to impress Zara with his… football knowledge. It was pathetic. He kept saying “offside” at completely random moments.      Oh,  please . Liam trying to be smooth is always a disaster waiting to happen. Zara deserves better than someone who thinks knowing the name of Ronaldo makes him an expert. I mean, I know nothing about football, absolutely nothing, but even  I  could tell he was just making it up as he went along.      Exactly! It was embarrassing for everyone involved. I think even Zara was cringing. Did she even respond to your Insta story from last night? I tagged you in that dodgy picture of Daniel attempting to breakdance.      Oh god, I completely forgot to look! Let me… Oh. Oh dear. She’s liked it, but hasn’t commented. Which is probably for the best. Daniel's breakdancing is…an experience. More like collapsing in a vaguely rhythmic fashion.      An experience is putting it mildly. He nearly took down a table trying to spin on his head.

...Honestly, the amount of detail you can pick up in these esports recordings is  insane . Like, they’re dissecting frame-by-frame what a player’s mouse movement says about their strategy. It's a bit much, really, but it pays the bills. So, about Gran… are we still on for picking her up on Friday?      Friday’s grand, love. Though, I'm still not convinced she understands why we moved all the way up here to Hunsonby. She keeps asking if there’s a proper chip shop nearby. Says this one’s “too… minimalist.” Minimalist! Honestly.      She's a woman of simple pleasures, your mother. She believes a good chip shop is a fundamental human right. And Hunsonby  is  a bit quiet, even for me. Still, the scenery's alright. Better than Walsall, at least. Though, I do miss a proper curry house.      It’s a lovely area, though, isn't it? Peaceful. Gran will appreciate that… eventually. I’ve got the spare room ready for her, fresh bedding, everything. Did you remember to tell her about the steep hill up to the house? She’ll be furious if she can’t manage it.      I tried, I really did. She just waved her hand and said, “I climbed Croagh Patrick, girl, a little hill won't kill me.” Croagh Patrick was thirty years ago, Mother! And involved a donkey for part of the way, I seem to recall.      She’s always been a bit… dramatic. Remember that time she swore young Timmy next door deliberately kicked a football into her prize-winning begonias? Turned out it was the wind. She nearly called the police.      Oh, God, I've heard that story! It’s legendary. Speaking of football, anyone watched the FIFA final last night? Absolutely brutal. Argentina deserved it, but honestly, the refereeing…      Football. Honestly. All that shouting and leaping about. Give me a nice quadratic equation any day. Though, I did try watching a bit with your father last year. He was explaining offside. For twenty minutes. Twenty minutes! I zoned out after the first five. It's just… running, isn’t it?      It’s a bit more to it than running, Deirdre. It’s strategy, discipline, teamwork… Although, you’re right, the referee last night was a disaster. So many questionable calls. I think Mbappé was genuinely robbed. It felt…  unfair , you know?      Totally unfair. And the amount of diving!

...Honestly, the whole bin strike thing is just ridiculous. It’s been weeks, hasn’t it? The smell is getting… potent. I saw Old Man Hemmings from next door trying to navigate a mountain of recycling bags with his walker this morning. It was a disaster.      You’re not wrong. It’s a disaster. I tried to explain to Mum and Dad why the streets are looking like a landfill site when they arrived. Dad just went on about “health and safety gone mad” and how he never saw anything like it in his day.      That's always the way, innit? Everything's 'gone to the dogs' these days, according to your father. Remember when he complained about self-service checkouts? Said they were taking away honest work.      He’s a character, your Dad is. Though, I  do  sympathise with the neighbours trying to manage. It’s bad enough at work, dealing with… everything, without having overflowing bins on top of it. I had Mrs. Peterson practically in tears yesterday because she couldn’t get her wheelchair past the rubbish outside her block.      See? It’s affecting everyone! And don’t even get me started on the fact we're paying council tax and getting...this. Anyway. Enough complaining. Mum, do you want another scone? I made a fresh batch this morning.      Oh, go on then, don't mind if I do. They  are  lovely, love. Light as a feather. You've always been a good baker, just like your Gran. I used to love her Victoria sponge.      Speaking of things that are a bit broken… I think my laptop’s finally giving up the ghost. The brake's gone completely. It just randomly shuts down if I move it slightly. I’ve been trying to back everything up, but it's so slow.      Oh, that’s a nightmare! Have you tried one of those little compressed air canisters? Sometimes dust build-up causes overheating. It might just buy you some time.      I’ve had a go, yeah. Didn't seem to make much difference. Think I might need to bite the bullet and get a new one. It's just...money.      You deserve a new one, honestly. You’re always on it for work. Have you looked at those refurbished ones? They can be a good deal. Plus, you're such a whizz with tech, you could probably fix anything yourself if it did pack up.

Honestly, this coffee is  much  better than that place we tried near the market yesterday. It's actually…comforting. Which is what I need, I think.      Definitely. Tram does a proper flat white. And you look like you could use comforting. You’ve been a bit quiet since we sat down. How are you holding up? It’s getting darker earlier now, isn’t it? Proper SAD weather back home.      It is. It’s hitting me harder this year, I think. Being away… it amplifies everything. Did you see the football results? Man City lost! Absolutely pathetic. I was hoping for a little bit of cheer.      No way! Really? I haven’t checked yet. I’ve been swamped with exam preps. It’s infuriating, honestly. They have their mock speaking tests next week, and one of my students, Kamil, is just…frozen. He knows the grammar, he understands the vocabulary, but the second I ask him to  speak , he just clams up.      Oh, bless him. It's awful when you feel responsible for these kids. Wanting them to do well. Is he a quiet boy generally?      Generally, yes. And he’s so worried about making mistakes. I keep telling him mistakes are  how  you learn, but it doesn’t seem to sink in. It's like he thinks a single error will invalidate everything. It makes me wonder if I’m doing enough.      You are. You’re a fantastic teacher, you know that. It's just some people take longer to build confidence. Remember old Mr. Henderson on the farm? He wouldn’t speak to anyone unless spoken to first, and then he’d answer in grunts. Took years for him to warm up.      Oh god, Mr. Henderson! He always smelled of hay and damp wool. That farm was a world away from all this. Tarnow… it's nice, but sometimes I just crave…familiarity. I got a message from Sarah last night – she’s got a new puppy, a little spaniel. It just made me ache for home.      I know that feeling. A little piece of England. Have you seen many dogs here? I’ve spotted a few being walked, but nothing like back home. It feels odd.      Not loads, no. More small yappy ones than proper working dogs. Actually, talking of home… have you seen what’s in the British media about the cost of living? It’s terrifying.

Right, who wants more gravy wi’ their roasties? Honestly, I’m startin’ to feel a bit stuffed, but this is proper good, even if I do say so myself. Beats conference centre catering, that's for sure.      Aye, gimme a bit more. Proper lush, this is. You’re a dab hand in the kitchen, Liv. Beats anything me mum makes, an’ she’s a good cook, mind. Conference catering, eh? Sounds… grim. What’s the worst thing you’ve had to eat?      Oh, don't even  ask  about conference catering, Liv. I've had to manage logistics for events where the "chef" thought quiche Lorraine was just…egg in pastry. Deadly. But yeah, more gravy for me too, please. So, how's the new job going, actually? Still wrangling chaotic attendees?      Chaotic is an understatement, Chloe. It’s like herding cats, honestly. Last week, we had a speaker who insisted his water had to be exactly 4 degrees Celsius.  Four  degrees! And then he complained it wasn't sparkling enough. Honestly. It’s exhausting. And the people! Loads of 'important' people think the rules don’t apply to them.      Four degrees? Blimey. Some people are just… extra. Makes you appreciate a simple life, like diggin’ holes, yeah? No one askin’ for ice-cold water, just askin’ you to get on with it. Though Mrs. Henderson last week  did  complain my boots were too muddy near her begonias.      Oh, Liam! You and Mrs. Henderson. That’s a classic Cambridge clash of cultures. Begonias are sacred around here. Speaking of sacred... I saw Ben last night.      Ooh, Ben? The one with the… questionable fashion sense? Did he finally ditch those luminous orange trainers?      Sadly, no. They were there, in all their glory. He's still convinced they're "ironic." He was going on about a dating app called 'Spark'. Apparently, it matches you based on your Spotify playlists.      Spotify playlists? That’s… something. Can’t say I’d trust a bloke who doesn’t like The Smiths, though. That's a dealbreaker, that is.      You're such a romantic, Liam. I tried online dating once, it was a disaster. One fella turned up wearin' a full suit of armour. Said it was his 'aesthetic'. I made me excuses and left pretty sharpish. I'm stickin' to meetin’ people the old-fashioned way, even if that means bein’ single forever.      A suit of armour?!

…and honestly, it’s a bit of an improvement, isn’t it? They’ve really let the lime trees mature. Remember when this place was just… bare patches and little saplings? Smelled strongly of dog mess too, if I recall.      Oh, absolutely. Used to avoid walking through here after dark, frankly. Though I’ve always liked lime trees. That sort of… hazy, summery scent. Speaking of smells, did you hear about Old Man Hemmings? Apparently, he almost had a run-in with a chugger today, offering him a direct debit to ‘save the badgers’.      Hemmings and chuggers. A classic pairing. He'd probably offer  them  a cup of tea and a biscuit, then lecture them on the proper conservation of the Somerset Levels. Speaking of which, I’m starting to think I need a proper break. Devon, maybe? Just drive around, get lost in the lanes.      Devon’s good. Slow. Though driving in rural areas is always a bit… an adventure, isn't it? Narrow roads, tractors, tourists in campervans who’ve never driven on the left before. You’d think after all these years they’d work it out. It reminds me of trying to get to the Isle of Wight. A logistical nightmare.      Don't even  mention  getting to the Isle of Wight. Pure chaos. Anyway, Devon… it’s a long way from China, though. Which is where my brain keeps wandering back to. I was talking to Li yesterday, about birthdays, and it’s so different, isn’t it? No big cake tradition like we have.      Really? I’d assumed, with how much they’re embracing Western culture these days, that cake would be massive. I always associate China with pandas, bizarrely. And bears, actually. I remember reading something about bear bile farming… grim stuff.      It is. And pandas are… well, they’re  everywhere  in the tourism industry. But Li was explaining her grandmother’s birthday – lots of red envelopes with money, a long-life noodle dish, but no coconut cake and coffee! That’s my entire PhD supervisor’s obsession, by the way. Coconut cake. Drives me mad.      Sounds… intense. So, how’s the PhD going, actually? Still wrestling with the linguistic nuances of TEFL in a Chinese context? You were sounding a bit frayed last time we spoke.      Still wrestling. My supervisor keeps pushing me towards focusing more on the political implications, but honestly, the practical issues are fascinating.

Honestly, this signal is shocking out here. You’d think with all the money they spend on roadworks, they'd sort the radio reception too.      You and your radio. Everything's got to be  just so , doesn’t it, Liv? It's a wonder you haven’t built your own transmitter.      Don't even joke. I  have  considered it. It's a matter of principle, you know? Being stuck in traffic without decent music… it’s barbaric. So, how was the presentation with Henderson and Co? Did old man Henderson actually manage to say something without rambling about his prize-winning begonias?      Surprisingly, no begonias. Though he  did  attempt to steer the conversation toward the upcoming horticultural show. I managed to politely but firmly redirect. The presentation went well, actually. They're leaning towards the sustainable drainage system. It’s a fairly big deal for the development, apparently.      Good, good. That sounds… complicated. Remind me again why sustainable drainage is important? Not in engineer-speak, please. Just, basic Liv-understanding levels.      Right. Okay. Basically, it’s about managing rainwater better than just chucking it all into the sewers. Think of it like this: instead of a big rush of water potentially flooding things, we slow it down, filter it through natural materials, and even reuse some of it. It’s better for the environment and reduces the strain on the existing infrastructure.      Right, okay, that makes sense. So, less chance of Auntie Mabel’s basement flooding when it pours down?      Precisely. Less chance of Auntie Mabel’s basement flooding. Though, to be fair, Auntie Mabel's basement probably has underlying structural issues regardless.      Probably. She’s convinced it’s haunted, though. Says she hears tapping. It's just the plumbing, Mabel. Anyway, glad it went well. You were up late working on it, weren't you? You looked knackered this morning.      I was. It’s a lot of modelling and simulations. I’m starting to dream in hydrological charts, honestly. Which is not a good sign. I need a proper weekend. Remember we were talking about going up to the coast? Maybe Bamburgh?      Oh, aye! Bamburgh sounds amazing. Proper bracing walks. And fish and chips. We haven’t done a proper coastal trip in ages. Is next weekend good for you? I can check if I'm on rota at work, but I think I should be fairly clear.      Next weekend would be perfect.

This is proper good, ANON, seriously. You’ve outdone yourself. Reminds me a bit of my nan’s, though she always puts a bit too much garlic in for my liking.      Yeah, it is alright. Not what me mum makes, mind. She does a good lasagne, proper layers and everything. Though, to be fair, anything tastes good when you’re starving after a day on a building site.      You two are relentless with the food comparisons. It’s nice to hear you both appreciate it though. Honestly, it’s a bit of stress relief cooking. Work's been… something else this week.      Oh, aye? What's up then? Still battling with that new supplier? You were saying last time they were being right pain in the backside.      Worse, actually. Old Mr. Henderson – the one who’s been with the company for thirty years - had a bit of a scare. Collapsed at his desk. Thankfully, someone found him quickly, but they’re saying it’s his heart.      Blimey. That's rough. Is he… is he alright now?      He’s stable, in Addenbrooke’s. They’re running tests. His wife, Margaret, is absolutely devastated. I volunteered to help with some of the workload, obviously, but it’s chaos. And it’s just… made me think, you know? About how quickly things can change.      It does, doesn’t it? Makes you realise life's a bit fragile. My Auntie Brenda was fit as a fiddle one minute, then boom – stroke. Changed everything.      My grandad was the same. Always out in the garden, building stuff… then just, gone. Quick as you like. Always seems unfair, especially when it's someone who's always worked hard.      Exactly! And it’s distracted me so much I’ve been a complete mess with… well, with Liam.      Oh, Liam. How's  that  going? Still doing the… distant brooding thing?      It’s complicated. He’s been even more withdrawn since Mr. Henderson collapsed. He said it reminded him of his own dad, who had a heart attack when Liam was younger. But he’s not  talking  about it, y’know? Just getting all… silent and prickly.      Sounds about right. Men are rubbish at talking about feelings, aren’t they? My brother's the same. Bottles everything up until it explodes.      They really are! It’s like pulling teeth getting anything out of them. Have you tried just… sitting with him? Not pushing, just being there?

Honestly, Chloe, I'm  dreading  Monday. It’s not even the work, particularly. It’s… Mark.      Mark from the project team? The one who keeps talking about his crypto investments? Ugh, what’s he done now? Last time I heard anything, he was convinced Dogecoin was going to make him a millionaire.      Worse, actually. He’s been… well, he's been relentlessly pursuing Sarah since her breakup with Ben. It's just awful to watch. She's clearly not interested, she’s barely spoken two words to him all week, but he just  won’t  take a hint. He brings her coffee every morning, offers to walk her home... it’s borderline harassment.      Oh,  no . Poor Sarah. Ben really did a number on her, didn’t he? She was absolutely gutted. She doesn't need that on top of everything. And Mark… he’s always been a bit… oblivious, hasn’t he? Not malicious, just… lacking self-awareness.      Oblivious is putting it mildly. He cornered her by the photocopier yesterday and started going on about how he's always been a "shoulder to cry on" and that she should "give him a chance". I had to pretend I needed to make a copy just to interrupt. It was so awkward.      That’s terrible. You did the right thing, though, stepping in. She’s probably completely frozen, not knowing how to shut him down without causing a scene. It's hard enough navigating a breakup without adding unwanted attention. How is she  actually  doing, though? Beyond the initial shock, is she… coping?      It's up and down, I think. She’s trying to be brave, putting on a front at work. But I saw her in the ladies’ the other day and she was… well, she was properly crying. She keeps saying she thought Ben was 'the one'. You know how she is, she really throws herself into things.      I do. She's a wonderful person, and she deserves so much better than Ben treating her like that, and definitely better than Mark’s misguided attempts at chivalry. Honestly, it makes my blood boil. Honestly, sometimes I wish I could just march over there and tell Mark to back off. But I guess that would make things worse.      Exactly. It's a workplace thing, you can't just… intervene directly. I’ve subtly mentioned to our manager that Sarah seems a bit stressed and needs space, hoping they might keep an eye on things.

Right, so we've got meddling Merlin, sneaky goblins, and… what was that character again, Leo? The one with the glowing eyes?      Old Man Tiber. He wasn’t  evil , exactly. Just… misunderstood. He guarded the bridge, and asked riddles. If you couldn’t answer, he kept you!      That's not fair! Keeping people isn't fair. Even if they’re rude.      It wasn’t very nice, was it? Old Man Tiber. And that’s a really good point, Elsie. Fairness is important. Do you think Old Man Tiber was trying to be  bad , or just… lonely?      Lonely! He probably didn't have any friends. Maybe he just wanted someone to  talk  to, but he didn't know how.      He had a raven. A really big one. It told him everything.      Well, a raven is good company, I suppose. But still, holding people hostage for not knowing a riddle...that feels a bit much. It gets us thinking about what makes someone truly ‘evil’, doesn’t it? Is it just  doing  bad things, or is it  wanting  to do bad things?      If you  want  to be mean, that's worse! Wanting is inside. Doing is just… what you do.      Elsie, that’s incredibly insightful. You’ve hit on something really clever there. Wanting to be mean… that’s about your character, about what's  in  you. What do you think about Merlin? He did some pretty questionable things, even though he was supposed to be good. Remember how he tricked Uther Pendragon?      He made him look like someone else! So he could pretend to be the king! That’s… a cheat!      It is a bit of a cheat, isn’t it? He had good intentions, apparently. He wanted a strong king for Britain. But was it okay to lie and deceive to get there?      No! Lying is  always  wrong, Miss Davies said so at school. Even little white lies.      Miss Davies is right to emphasize that. It’s tricky, isn’t it? Sometimes people think they’re doing the right thing, even when it means doing something… not very nice. It’s like… sometimes we get cross with each other, even though we love each other. Are we being 'evil' then?      No! Just… frustrated. Like when Elsie borrows all my dinosaurs!      They're  better  dinosaurs! And you have plenty of others!      See? Frustration, not evil. But even frustration can lead to doing something unkind, if we're not careful.

...and honestly, the whole filming thing felt a bit… chaotic. Apparently, little Leo nearly wandered onto the A14 while they were filming the traffic sequence! Mrs. Davies was  not  impressed.      Blimey! Leo? That doesn’t surprise me. He’s a wanderer, that one. Is ANON alright though? She seemed really excited about it all. Did she get a good part?      I was a tree! A really, really important tree.      I was a policeman! I had a hat and everything! But I tripped over a cable.      You both were brilliant. ANON, you were a very stately oak, and Thomas, well… you were a very enthusiastic, momentarily grounded policeman. They got it on film, thankfully. It’s for the school’s road safety video.      Right, sensible. Though, risking life and limb for a school film feels a bit… much. Speaking of risking things, it’s getting colder at night, isn’t it? I woke up shivering last night.      It is. I put the heating on for a bit, but I’m trying to hold off as long as possible. The bills are… already looking alarming. Is your leg still playing up, Thomas? You were limping about earlier.      It hurts when I run. Like,  really  hurts.      He took a tumble in the garden yesterday, trying to be Spider-Man. Honestly, the drama. I’ve put some ice on it, and he seems a bit better now. But he’s requested I build him a Spider-Man web.      Good luck with that. Maybe distract him with the promise of doughnuts? That usually works. Right, I’m thinking about going to the gym after school. Need to blow off some steam after dealing with thirty seven seven-year-olds and a potential A14 escapee.      Go for it. I was considering it myself, but… motivation is low. I signed up for that new running machine programme they have, you know, the one with the virtual coaching.      Oh, how is that? Are you enjoying pretending to run through Tuscany?      It's... something. It's definitely impressive. But honestly? It’s just a running machine. And the virtual coach is relentlessly cheerful. “Push harder, Mark! You’ve got this!” I just want to tell him to mind his own business while I'm trying to avoid a cardiac arrest.      I want a doughnut! A pink one!      We  might  be able to arrange a pink doughnut later. After gym, I was thinking of making a proper dinner.

…and honestly, the rheumatologist just shrugged. Said it’s ‘age-related wear and tear’. Wear and tear! As if I've been a pair of wellies left out in the garden. It’s becoming quite debilitating, you know? Getting up from the chair is a whole  operation  now. Oh, Arthur, that's rough, that really is. I’ve been getting twinges myself, mostly in the knees. Old football injuries catching up with me, I reckon. Nothing a bit of liniment and stubbornness can’t fix, though. You should try some arnica. My Doreen swears by it. Doreen’s remedies are… comprehensive, to say the least. I think she believes in crystals too, doesn’t she? No offence, of course. She's a lovely woman. It's just, I’d rather a solid diagnosis, rather than a poultice of lavender and good intentions. None taken! She’s a woman of faith, that one. Keeps me grounded, she does. Speaking of grounded, did you hear about old Mr. Henderson down at the boot sale? Apparently, he’s decided to run for the Green Party in the local elections. Henderson! The man who used to sell us petrol in those massive metal cans, completely illegally, back in the day. You’re pulling my leg. Henderson? The Green Party? That's…unexpected. I remember him complaining about the cost of unleaded just last month. Hypocrisy, thy name is Henderson. Though, I suppose everyone’s entitled to a change of heart. I still can't bring myself to vote for them, though. It's a bizarre turnaround. Apparently, his granddaughter got him all fired up about climate change. These young people, they’re a force of nature, aren’t they? Makes you think. But I agree, a bit rich coming from a man who basically ran a black market fuel operation. It’s all a bit performative, if you ask me. Still, it'll liven up the usual council elections. Liven it up is one word for it. It’s just… I worry about the jobs. All this talk about phasing out petrol cars, switching to renewables. What happens to the blokes down at the garage? Or the ones at the power station? They’ve got mortgages to pay, families to feed. That’s a fair point, Arthur. That’s  always  the rub, isn’t it? These sweeping changes, they impact real people. I had a young lad working for me, did a cracking job with the website.

…and honestly, the audacity of that woman at the garden centre. Telling  me  how to prune a clematis! As if! I’ve been nurturing those things since I was a bairn, helping Grandad in his greenhouse.      Oh, the garden centre know-it-alls. They’re a breed apart, aren’t they? Always got an opinion, usually wrong. Clematis are tricky, though, you have to get the timing just right. You were well within your rights to ignore her.      Ignore? I nearly launched into a full explanation of the different pruning groups! Luckily, I remembered I was trying to have a relaxing Saturday, not give a masterclass. Speaking of relaxing, this is a good pub. Much nicer than the one near your department, isn’t it? All students and… well, you know. Loud.      Definitely. That one's permanently packed with people debating post-structuralism or something equally intense. This is…civilised. And the ale’s better. You've got good taste. Though, I'm not convinced anyone should be allowed to talk about pruning techniques whilst consuming alcohol. It's a dangerous combination.      Oh, hush. It's a perfectly sensible combination. It’s practically horticultural therapy. Though, it does remind me, I need to repot the succulents. I’ve been meaning to for weeks, but research deadlines are… brutal, you know?      Tell me about it. I’m swimming in data at the moment. Trying to make sense of years of financial modelling is starting to feel like a personal attack. Honestly, the sheer complexity. It makes dissecting Trump’s latest pronouncements seem straightforward.      Ugh, don’t even start on Trump. I saw a clip of him the other day... the man is a walking, talking contradiction. It’s utterly exhausting. I end up just switching off, it’s too draining. It’s all just noise, isn’t it?      Pretty much. It’s scary how easily people get caught up in the manufactured outrage. I’ve started limiting my news intake. It’s better for my blood pressure. And my PhD. Actually, speaking of manufactured…did you see what Bethany was wearing to the Faculty dinner?      Oh. Oh dear. That dress?      The  dress . It looked like something Liberace rejected. Sequins, feathers… it was a statement alright. A very loud one.      She’s always been… bold. I respect that, honestly. She does what she wants. Though, I would never be caught dead in something like that.

Honestly, it’s just… lovely to be away from marking for a bit. Even Mum’s endless questioning about when we’re having kids is a pleasant distraction, comparatively.      You say that now, but give it another hour and you’ll be strategizing escape routes involving strategic biscuit offerings. Still, you’re right. Grading essays on the socio-political impact of early Renaissance art is wearing, even for a well-adjusted art historian. How’s the new intake looking? Any budding Michelangelos or just a lot of students misunderstanding chiaroscuro?      A bit of both, truthfully. There's one chap, Daniel, incredibly bright, really  sees  things. But another… well, he argued that Botticelli was a proto-surrealist. I almost choked on my tea. It's the confidence, you know? The sheer audacity.      Oh, the confidence of youth. Reminds me of my first year. I genuinely believed I could revolutionize Victorian literature with a post-structuralist reading of  Oliver Twist . My tutor was…patient. How are  you  coping with the impact of all the streaming services on student engagement? Seems less and less about reading and more about expecting everything to be a visual feast.      It’s dreadful. They’ve all been raised on hyper-stimulation, ironically. I was having a debate with Sarah yesterday about the impact of violent imagery on television – a direct link to their shorter attention spans and decreasing analytical skills, I argued. She thinks it's a rather simplistic view.      Sarah always plays devil’s advocate. It’s endearing, but frustrating. I do think it’s complex, though. My cousin’s kids watch… well, a lot of stuff. But they’re also obsessed with documentaries about killer whales. Seriously, they can tell you the pod structures and hunting techniques of orcas off the coast of British Columbia. It’s amazing.      That  is  fascinating. Perhaps there's hope then. It’s just…the constant barrage of quick cuts and sensationalism. It’s diluting everything. It makes me nostalgic for… I don’t know,  Blue Peter ? Remember how genuinely inventive and wholesome that was?      Vaguely. I was more of a  Noel’s House Party  guy, if I’m honest. Though I did covet a Blue Peter badge. They felt truly prestigious. Remember Mr. Blobby?      Don't remind me! That was terrifying as a child. Although… you know, speaking of slightly unsettling things, I was reading an article about the rise in squatting amongst young people.

Cor, look at this one, Doris. That’s young Michael, bless ‘im, trying to build a den in the garden. Nearly took the washing line down with it, he did. Reckon he always had a knack for…well, for  something  mechanical, that boy. Always fiddling with bits and bobs.      Oh, my goodness, is that the one with the garden shed demolition attempt? He was a little terror, wasn’t he? Such a clever lad though. Different from David, our David was always a bookworm. Though I do recall him trying to dismantle a clock once… didn’t go well.      Sounds like a typical childhood, really. A bit of destruction is good for the soul, keeps you thinking. You two reminiscing again? Found the photo archives, have you?      Just a wander through the past, Martin. Got me thinking about what Michael's up to with that hostel of his. Managing a place like that… it's a fair undertaking, innit? All sorts of people coming and going. Seems a world away from building dens.      It’s ambitious, that’s for sure. He’s always been ambitious. Said it reminded him a bit of when he was volunteering at the youth centre, trying to keep everything running smoothly on a shoestring. Though a hostel is… commercially different. He’s got a good head for figures, though. Inherited that from someone, I suspect.      Speaking of needing a good head, poor old Elsie’s in hospital again. Her hip. She’s getting so frail. I went to visit yesterday, and she could barely lift her cup. It breaks your heart, doesn’t it?      Terrible news about Elsie. A dear woman.
