Remember when she ran that little sweet shop down the High Street? Always a kind word, and a handful of sweets for us cheeky youngsters. Her husband, bless him, worked so hard in the abattoir. Gruesome work, that, but they made an honest living.      Hardworking people, both of them. It's a different world now. Elsie told me she worries about the food they sell these days. All those additives and things. Says nothing tastes like it used to.      Oh, she’s right, you know. Everything’s so processed. I used to help my mother in her bakery. Proper ingredients, everything made from scratch. You could  taste  the difference. Now it’s all about speed and cost cutting.      It's the same with cars, isn’t it?

...Honestly, the essays I’m marking at the moment are… a mixed bag, to put it mildly. You wouldn’t believe the referencing errors. It's like they haven’t  seen  a Harvard guide.      Tell me about it. It’s a perennial problem, isn't it? I’m finding similar things with my undergraduates. Though, to be fair, some of them are first-generation university students. It’s a steep learning curve for them, this whole academic writing thing.      That’s true, you have to factor that in. But even some who  should  know better… it's baffling. It makes me wonder about the preparation they received in their A-levels – or equivalent. It feels like academic literacy isn't being stressed enough earlier on.      Precisely! It’s a skill that needs nurturing throughout their education, not just bolted on when they reach university. Though, thinking about preparation… it’s funny, isn’t it, hearing you say that? Considering you used to be in recruitment. Didn’t you spend half your time assessing communication skills?      You’ve dug that up, have you? Yes, quite a contrast, really. From sifting through CVs and conducting interviews to deciphering undergraduate essays. It was a different kind of assessment, though. Recruitment was much more about  potential  and personality, spotting someone who could learn and fit a role.      So, a lot less focus on the intricacies of argumentative structure and properly formatted citations?      Vastly less! Though, I did have to assess written communication, obviously. Cover letters were a nightmare sometimes. Basic grammar and spelling errors were rife. But even then, it was assessing if they could  communicate  effectively for the role, not if they could write a nuanced dissertation on post-structuralism.      A fair point. And I suppose weeding out the truly hopeless was a fairly quick process then. A badly written cover letter is pretty telling.      It was. Though you’d be surprised how many people thought they could get away with generic templates. "Dear Sir/Madam…" when the recruitment ad specifically named the hiring manager. It showed a real lack of attention to detail. Which, ironically, is  exactly  what I’m seeing in these essays.      So, you’re finding the lack of detail, the slapdash approach, echoes what you saw in the job market?      Absolutely. It’s almost like a cultural thing now, this expectation of instant gratification and minimal effort. They think they can get away with cutting corners.

Right, I officially need a biscuit break. And possibly a new brain. This econometrics is  killing  me.      Tell me about it. I spent all morning trying to convince someone that a slightly chipped mug is  still  a perfectly good mug. Retail, eh? It’s…character building.      Character building and soul-destroying, if we’re being honest. I'd take econometrics any day. At least there's a logical answer somewhere, even if I can’t find it. I’m Chloe, by the way. I think we’ve seen each other around, library regulars?      Hey Chloe! I’m Anya. And you're so right about the soul-destroying part. Though chipped mugs  are  a tragedy. This is…Liam, isn’t it? We’re in the same history seminar.      The one where the lecturer talks for two hours straight about the nuances of Victorian wallpaper? Yeah, that's me. Liam. Nice to properly meet you both. And believe me, arguing about wallpaper patterns is a skill I’ve unknowingly honed.      Hi. I’m Priya. Sorry, I didn't mean to eavesdrop, just…needed the quiet. And the Wi-Fi is good here.      No worries at all, Priya! We’re basically announcing our life stories to anyone within a five-metre radius. What are you working on? Looks rather intense.      It is, a bit. I’m doing my Masters in Computer Science. Trying to debug this algorithm…it’s refusing to cooperate. It’s supposed to predict customer behaviour, but currently, it’s predicting everyone will buy eighteen inflatable flamingos.      Eighteen inflatable flamingos?! That’s…remarkably specific. And potentially a very lucrative business idea. Forget the econometrics,  that’s  the market research I need!      See? Algorithms are just having a bit of fun. Probably fuelled by a rogue dataset. I once tried to sell a customer a garden gnome in December. My sales manager wasn’t impressed. Said it was “seasonal inappropriateness.”      Oh, I’ve had worse. Tried to explain to someone why a garden statue of a badger playing the bagpipes was a perfectly reasonable purchase. They didn’t see my vision.      Badgers  should  play the bagpipes. It makes perfect sense. It’s a surprisingly overlooked cultural phenomenon.      Clearly! We need to start a campaign. "Badgers with Bagpipes: A Movement." I’m in. So, Priya, computer science, then? That’s a world away from history and…whatever Liam does with chipped mugs.      Hey! I'm a vital link in the consumer chain!

Right, honestly, this lasagne is  divine . You really outdid yourself, ANON. Better than anything I could whip up back in Donny, that’s for sure. Speaking of which, Mum keeps sending me recipes… all Yorkshire puddings and parkin. Like I don’t get enough carbs already!      Glad you like it! I found this little Italian deli near work, they make everything fresh. And your Mum sounds… traditional. Parkin’s lovely, though. Bit rich for every day, mind. So, how was the conference last week? Did everything run smoothly? You sounded stressed on the phone.      Oh, it was… an experience. Mostly smooth, yeah. But we had this delegate, right, retired Colonel, absolute stickler for everything being  just so . Kept complaining about the room temperature being “unbecoming of a man who served Queen and country.” Honestly! It was 21 degrees! And then he wanted a detailed seating plan based on military rank, even though half the attendees were… marketing executives.      Seriously? A seating plan based on rank? That’s… dedicated. Or possibly bonkers. You handled that, didn’t you? You’re good under pressure.      I  think  I handled it. I subtly redirected him to the coffee station a lot. And pointed out the merits of networking. He still mumbled about protocol, but eventually cracked. It got me thinking though… my grandad served in the Royal Engineers. Never really talked about it much. Just said it was “a job.”      It's funny how different generations are about that. My uncle did a tour in Northern Ireland. He’s only started really opening up about it in the last few years. It’s… a lot to process, I think. It's not something people readily discuss. Changed him though, definitely. Speaking of things changing people, have you seen that new sci-fi flick, 'Nexus Point'? It’s all about AI and the military.      'Nexus Point'? No, haven’t had a chance. Been drowning in spreadsheets and event logistics lately. Is it any good? I’m a bit picky with sci-fi. I want action, no overly philosophical navel-gazing, you know? And good special effects, obviously.      Oh, it’s  brilliant . The effects are amazing, and it’s genuinely thought-provoking, but in a fast-paced way. It's got this whole ethical debate about autonomous weapons systems. Made me think about that Colonel again, actually. What happens when the ‘protocol’ is programmed into a machine?

Honestly, the game was…intense. My legs are screaming. Though, it was a good distraction. From  everything .      Tell me about it. I think I pulled something reaching for that rebound. Distraction is a good word, though. Needed one. This week’s been a complete write-off for creativity. Just staring at footage, feeling…stuck. Speaking of distractions, how was having your cousin down from London? The one who thinks everything north of the M25 is basically the Wild West?      Oh,  God , don’t even get me started. Barnaby is…a lot. He kept asking if we had reliable internet, like we were living in a yurt. And the passive-aggressive comments about the ‘pace of life’ were relentless. He nearly had a heart attack when he saw a tractor on the road.      Classic Barnaby. He genuinely thinks anyone not commuting on the Tube at rush hour is somehow failing at adulthood. Did he at least appreciate the pub? I thought the Black Swan might redeem things.      He did like the Black Swan. Mostly because they had a craft ale he hadn’t seen on Instagram. Took about twenty photos of the pump clips, naturally. But then he started going on about property prices and how ‘undervalued’ everything is up here, which is just… tone-deaf.      It’s always about property with him. He asked me if I thought Winchester was ‘up and coming’. I just stared at him. Winchester is  Winchester . It's been ‘up and coming’ for centuries!      You handled that brilliantly. Honestly, he makes me tired just thinking about him. It’s not even about the London-North divide, it’s just…the attitude. It's always subtly looking down on everything. Reminds me a bit of that guy I was seeing, actually.      Oh? The architect one? What happened there? I thought you two seemed pretty keen.      Turns out ‘keen’ was code for ‘only interested in talking about his own work’. And his opinions on…well, everything. He actually started  correcting  my designs during a casual dinner conversation. Said my use of concrete was ‘pedestrian’. Pedestrian!      Oh, the audacity!      Seriously? That’s just…insulting. I had a date last week who spent the entire time trying to convince me documentary filmmaking was ‘not a real art form’. Said it was just ‘glorified journalism’. I walked out.      Good for you! You shouldn’t have to sit through that. It’s exhausting, isn’t it?

Lovely little flat you’ve got here. Really cosy. Though a bit…modern for my liking, if I’m honest. All these gadgets! Back in my day, you had a kettle, a hob, and you were lucky.      Oh, don’t be like that, Arthur. It’s practical! And much cleaner. Look at all the storage, darling. Though, I do think a nice patterned tea towel would brighten things up a bit. This plain cream is a little…clinical.      It's a work in progress, honestly. We’re still finding our feet, making it feel like home. And Mum, you’re right, a tea towel is on the list. It’s just…priorities, you know? Like getting the window cleaner booked. They're extortionate these days.      They  are ! I nearly choked when I saw the quote. But honestly, after that wind we had last week, they’re desperately needed. I tried to tackle them myself and… well, let's just say it wasn't my finest moment.      Window cleaning. Always a chore. Reminds me of old Mr. Hemmings down the road. Used to do all the windows on our street. Steady as a rock, he was. Lived to be ninety-eight, he did. Ninety-eight! Amazing. Probably all that climbing kept him fit.      Ninety-eight! Goodness. My Auntie Maggie made it to ninety-five, but the last few years…well, it wasn't living, was it? Just existing. Had diverticulitis something awful. Doc said it was her diet. Too much rich food, apparently.      That’s rough. We were talking about that actually, cholesterol and all that. I’ve started trying to be a bit better – less bacon sandwiches, more…well, more vegetables. Though a full English is a national treasure, isn't it?      Absolutely. It's a  requirement  when you’re back visiting family. Speaking of requirements… Dad, you haven't mentioned your bike yet! Are you missing it? You were practically pining for it before we left London.      Missing it? Terribly! This Sussex countryside is lovely, but it’s  hills , love! My old Raleigh’s not built for hills. Plus, I haven't had the energy to get out on it. Getting old isn't for the faint of heart, you know. Feels like everything is starting to… creak.      You’re not old, Arthur! You’re…mature! And don’t talk like that. You’ll be cycling around Brighton before you know it.

...Honestly, the sheer  audacity  of some of the comments on that article about the council tax increase. You’d think people hadn’t looked at a newspaper in five years, the way they're moaning about everything going up. It's just… the world, innit?      Yeah, it's always the way. Easier to blame someone else than to actually consider the complexities, isn't it? I was scrolling through Twitter earlier, and it was a total echo chamber of outrage. Makes you wonder if anyone actually  reads  anything beyond the headline.      Exactly! I spend my days wading through text data for my job, and people’s ability to construct a coherent argument online is… diminishing. It's all knee-jerk reactions. Speaking of work, I’m drowning in annotation requests at the moment. This new project is a nightmare. Trying to tag sentiment in tweets about… well, everything, really.      Sentiment analysis, eh? Sounds… draining. I'm proper busy too, just not with words. I’m on site most days now, out by Addenbrooke's. They’re building a new access road, and it’s proving… challenging. Ground conditions are awful. Pure clay.      Oh, sounds lovely. Mud and paperwork. Is it at least interesting engineering?      It's  okay . It's not designing a suspension bridge, put it that way. Though it’s good practical experience, I suppose. Gets me away from the desk. It's just everything is taking twice as long as it should, and the budget… don't even get me started. You wouldn't believe the price of aggregate these days.      Tell me about it! Even basic food shopping is a shock now. I tried to make a proper shepherd's pie last weekend, you know, from scratch? The lamb alone was… embarrassing. I swear, house prices aren’t the only thing going through the roof.      A proper shepherd’s pie. That’s ambitious. I usually just go for a pasta bake. Less effort, less expense. I've been looking at properties in the city, just out of curiosity, and it's utterly ridiculous. Even a tiny terrace house costs a fortune. My mate just bought a place in Tunbridge Wells... apparently it’s slightly more reasonable there.      Tunbridge Wells? That’s posh! I think I’d have to win the lottery to even  consider  buying anything around here. Sunderland’s cheaper, obviously, but… I don't know if I could go back.

Honestly, the state of the ward is getting me down. Old Mr. Henderson’s daughter phoned  again  yesterday, complaining about his dinner. Honestly, he’s a fussy eater at the best of times, but it's relentless. You’d think she doesn’t realise we’re trying to look after twenty other people as well!      Oh, bless him. But parents  are  like that aren't they? Especially when it comes to their dads. Still, that sounds exhausting. It must be non-stop pressure. How are the new agency nurses settling in? Are they any good?      They’re… variable. One’s a lovely girl, very eager, but a bit green. The other… well, let’s just say I spent a good twenty minutes showing her how to properly apply a pressure dressing. It's worrying, really. You rely on them to be competent. It's not like you can stand over them every minute.      Tell me about it. At the residential home, we've got a new lad, fresh out of school, thinks he knows everything. Tried to tell Mrs. Davies she couldn't have a cup of tea before lunch. Nearly had a revolt on my hands! She’s 92, she's earned a cuppa when she wants one.      Oh, Mrs. Davies! She’s a character. She told me off for wearing bright pink shoes last week. Said they were "far too flamboyant for a Tuesday."      That's amazing! You two must have some stories. It’s funny, working with words all day, you’d think I’d be a silver-tongued diplomat, but I’d be absolutely useless in either of your jobs. The thought of dealing with demanding relatives and 92-year-old fashion critics… no thank you!      It's not all bad, honestly. There are good days. When you actually make a difference, or just get a genuine ‘thank you’. But the paperwork… oh, the paperwork! It’s multiplied tenfold since I started. I swear half my shift is spent filling out forms.      Don’t even  start  me on the paperwork. They want a full life story for every paracetamol. It's ridiculous. Though, I did have a lovely moment with Mr. Peterson this morning. He remembered my name! He usually just stares blankly. Small victories, eh?      That  is  a victory! It's the little things. My Nan's been a bit poorly lately, just a chest infection, but it’s making me worry.
